Let $O\colon [0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ be a commutative and associative binary operation with neutral element $1$ (so $O(x,1)=x$ for all $x\in[0,1]$). For a finite subset $A=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subseteq[0,1]$, define
$$\beta_O(A)=O(x_1,O(x_2,\ldots,O(x_{n-1},x_n)\ldots)),$$
with $\beta_O(\emptyset)=1$ and $\beta_O(\{x\})=x$ (commutativity and associativity make this independent of ordering).

The map $\beta_O$ is called a witness map if, in addition, for every finite set $A\subseteq[0,1]$ and every subset $X\subseteq A$,
$$\sum_{X\subseteq Z\subseteq A}(-1)^{|X|+|Z|}\,\beta_O(Z)\;\ge\;0.$$

Characterize all such operations $O$ for which $\beta_O$ is a witness map.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $B(H)$ denote the C*-algebra of all bounded linear operators on $H$, equipped with the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $N(H) \subseteq B(H)$ be the class of all normal operators (those $S \in B(H)$ satisfying $S^*S = SS^*$).

Given a binary relation $R(S,X)$ on $B(H)\times B(H)$, say that the proposition
$$ \forall S \in D(H),\ \forall X \in B(H),\ R(S,X) $$
is closed in $B(H)\times B(H)$ when
$$ D(H) = \{ S \in B(H) : \forall X \in B(H),\ R(S,X) \}, $$
i.e. $D(H)$ is exactly the set of all operators $S \in B(H)$ for which $R(S,X)$ holds for every $X \in B(H)$.

It is known that the inequality
$$ \|S^{2}X\| + \|X S^{2}\| \;\geq\; 2\,\|SXS\| $$
holds for every $S \in N(H)$ and every $X \in B(H)$.

Determine the closure, in $B(H)\times B(H)$, of this operator inequality. Explicitly, characterize the set
$$ D(H) \;=\; \bigl\{\, S \in B(H) \,:\, \|S^{2}X\| + \|X S^{2}\| \geq 2\,\|SXS\| \text{ for every } X \in B(H) \,\bigr\}. $$

The problem of characterizing the closure of the inequality $\|S^2 X\| + \|X S^2\| \geq 2\|SXS\|$ on $B(H)\times B(H)$ is posed as an open problem in Seddik's 2011 paper "Closed operator inequalities and open problems" (Math. Inequal. Appl., vol. 14). Subsequent works by Seddik and others (e.g. "Operator inequalities and characterizations", arXiv:2005.08299, and related papers on the Corach–Porta–Recht inequality) treat closely related inequalities and provide partial characterizations, but none of the sources located gives the full closure of this specific inequality. The status appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
An (abstract) polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ with a least face $F_{-1}$ and a greatest face $F_n$, in which every maximal chain (called a flag) has exactly $n+2$ elements, which is strongly flag-connected, and which satisfies the diamond condition: whenever $F < G$ with $\operatorname{rank}(G)-\operatorname{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$. Two flags are $i$-adjacent ($0\le i\le n-1$) if they differ exactly in their face of rank $i$; the unique flag $i$-adjacent to a flag $\Phi$ is denoted $\Phi^i$.

The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits.

The Petrie scheme through a base flag $\Phi_0$ is the sequence of flags
$$\Phi_0,\ \Phi_1,\ \Phi_2,\ \dots$$
defined recursively by
$$\Phi_{k+1} = \Phi_k^{\,i_k}, \qquad \text{where } i_k \equiv k \pmod{n},$$
that is, one applies the adjacencies $0,1,2,\dots,n-1,0,1,\dots$ cyclically until the sequence closes up to $\Phi_0$. The Petrie scheme is called acoptic if every proper face of $\mathcal{P}$ is contained in at most one flag of the scheme (so the scheme does not "self-intersect" through any proper face).

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a chiral abstract polytope $\mathcal{P}$ under which its Petrie scheme is acoptic.

A function $T:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ is called a triangular norm (t-norm) if it is commutative, associative, non-decreasing in each argument, and satisfies $T(x,1)=x$ for all $x\in[0,1]$. For two t-norms $T_1$ and $T_2$, write $T_1\le T_2$ if $T_1(x,y)\le T_2(x,y)$ for all $(x,y)\in[0,1]^2$.

Given two distinct t-norms $T_1$ and $T_2$ with $T_1\le T_2$ pointwise, define their opposite diagonal splice $[T_1,T_2]:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ by
$$[T_1,T_2](x,y)=\begin{cases} T_2(x,y), & \text{if } x+y-1>0,\\ T_1(x,y), & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Characterize, as completely as possible, all pairs $(T_1,T_2)$ of distinct t-norms with $T_1\le T_2$ for which the opposite diagonal splice $[T_1,T_2]$ is again a t-norm on $[0,1]$.

representations.normalized:
An abstract polytope is a partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) are ranked, satisfying the standard axioms generalising the face lattice of a convex polytope: it has a least face and a greatest face, every maximal chain (flag) has the same length, it satisfies the diamond condition (between any face of rank i−1 and any face of rank i+1 incident with it there are exactly two faces of rank i), and it is strongly flag-connected. The automorphism group of an abstract polytope P acts freely on the set of flags. P is called regular if this action is transitive, and chiral if it has exactly two flag-orbits under the automorphism group such that adjacent flags always lie in different orbits.

For a chiral polytope P of rank n, fix a base flag Φ and let σ_1, …, σ_{n−1} be the distinguished generators of Aut(P) that map Φ to its i-adjacent flag's orbit representative (so σ_i changes only the face of rank i). The left Petrie motion is the automorphism σ_1 σ_2 ⋯ σ_{n−1}, and the right Petrie motion is σ_1 σ_2^{−1} σ_3 σ_4^{−1} ⋯ (alternating). The orbits of the edges of P under the cyclic group generated by the left (respectively right) Petrie motion, traversed by following the action on edges, are called the left Petrie paths (respectively right Petrie paths) of P. Such a path is said to be a polygon when it closes up into a finite cycle without self-intersection in the appropriate combinatorial sense (i.e. it is a genuine finite polygonal closed path rather than an unbounded or improperly-closing walk).

Question: Does there exist a chiral polytope P such that every left Petrie path of P is a polygon while at least one right Petrie path of P is not a polygon?

representations.normalized:
A triangular norm is a binary operation $T:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ that is commutative, associative, monotone non-decreasing in each argument, and satisfies $T(x,1)=x$ for all $x\in[0,1]$. A triangular conorm is a binary operation $S:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ that is commutative, associative, monotone non-decreasing in each argument, and satisfies $S(x,0)=x$ for all $x\in[0,1]$.

The classical Frank functional equation seeks all pairs $(T,S)$ consisting of a triangular norm $T$ and a triangular conorm $S$ such that
$$T(x,y)+S(x,y)=x+y\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in[0,1],$$
which corresponds to the case where $T_0=T_{\mathbf{M}}$ (the minimum), $T_0=T_{\mathbf{P}}$ (the product), or $T_0=T_{\mathbf{L}}$ (the Łukasiewicz t-norm $\max(x+y-1,0)$), and $S_0$ is its dual conorm $S_0(x,y)=1-T_0(1-x,1-y)$.

Generalized problem. Fix an arbitrary triangular norm $T_0$ and an arbitrary triangular conorm $S_0$. Characterize all pairs $(T,S)$, where $T$ is a triangular norm and $S$ is a triangular conorm, satisfying
$$T(x,y)+S(x,y)=T_0(x,y)+S_0(x,y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in[0,1].$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Several follow-up works in the fuzzy-logic/copula literature address generalizations of the Frank functional equation, including a "note on a generalized Frank functional equation" and works on convex-linear T–S functions and the Frank inequality. These provide partial characterizations (e.g., associative copulas satisfying the Frank inequality must be Frank copulas or certain ordinal sums, and broader associative aggregation versions yield only two extra solutions, the projections), but no complete characterization for arbitrary fixed $(T_0,S_0)$ appears to be established.

Let $G$ be an infinite group. For a subset $A \subseteq G$, define the covering number
$$\operatorname{cov}(A) = \min\{|S| : S \subseteq G \text{ and } G = SA\},$$
where $SA = \{sa : s \in S, a \in A\}$. Define the covering spectrum
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G) = \{\operatorname{cov}(A) : A \subseteq G\}.$$
Let $[1, |G|]$ denote the set of all cardinals $\kappa$ with $1 \le \kappa \le |G|$.

Determine whether for every infinite group $G$ one has $\operatorname{Cov}(G) = [1, |G|]$; that is, whether every cardinal $\kappa$ with $1 \le \kappa \le |G|$ is realized as $\operatorname{cov}(A)$ for some subset $A \subseteq G$.

representations.normalized:
An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ (with elements called faces, ranked from $-1$ to $n$) satisfying the standard axioms: it has a unique minimum face $F_{-1}$ and unique maximum face $F_n$; every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly $n+2$ faces; $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected; and it satisfies the diamond condition (whenever $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces strictly between $F$ and $G$).

The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts freely on the set of flags. The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called chiral if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly two orbits on the flags, and adjacent flags (differing in exactly one face) lie in distinct orbits. For a chiral polytope, fix a base flag $\Phi=\{F_{-1},F_0,\dots,F_n\}$; then there exist generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ of $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$, where $\sigma_i$ fixes all faces of $\Phi$ except $F_{i-1}$ and $F_i$ and cyclically permutes consecutive $i$-faces in the section $F_{i+1}/F_{i-2}$.

For a chiral $4$-polytope, define the right Petrie element $\rho_R = \sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3$ and the left Petrie element $\rho_L = \sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_3$. The orbits of edges (or equivalently, the closed zig-zag paths through the $1$-skeleton that turn alternately right/left at successive faces) under $\langle\rho_R\rangle$ and $\langle\rho_L\rangle$ are called the right Petrie paths and left Petrie paths, and their common lengths are the orders of $\rho_R$ and $\rho_L$ respectively.

Determine all pairs $(m,n)$ of positive integers for which there exists a chiral $4$-polytope whose right Petrie paths have length $m$ and whose left Petrie paths have length $n$.

representations.normalized:
Let $G$ be an infinite group with identity element $e$. For a subset $A \subseteq G$:

- $A$ is called $2$-thin if $|gA \cap A| \le 2$ for every $g \in G$ with $g \ne e$.
- $A$ is called self-linked if $gA \cap A \ne \emptyset$ for every $g \in G$; equivalently, $G = AA^{-1}$.

Question: Does every infinite group $G$ contain a subset $A \subseteq G$ that is simultaneously $2$-thin and self-linked?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is recorded as an open question in the literature on combinatorial size and packing/covering of subsets of groups. Partial results are known: every countable group admits a thin subset $A$ with $G = AA^{-1}$, and the statement is true under additional hypotheses such as $G$ being abelian. No proof or counterexample for arbitrary infinite groups appears to be available.

representations.normalized:
A spherical space-form is a quotient manifold of the form $S^n/\Gamma$, where $S^n$ is the unit $n$-sphere (with $n \geq 2$) equipped with its standard round metric and $\Gamma$ is a finite group of isometries of $S^n$ acting freely on $S^n$.

An abstract polytope of rank $n+1$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ with a strictly monotone rank function whose elements (called faces) have ranks in $\{-1, 0, 1, \dots, n+1\}$, satisfying: (i) there is a unique least face (rank $-1$) and a unique greatest face (rank $n+1$); (ii) every maximal chain (flag) has exactly $n+3$ elements; (iii) $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected; and (iv) the diamond condition holds, namely for any two faces $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$ there are exactly two faces strictly between $F$ and $G$. A tessellation of a spherical space-form $S^n/\Gamma$ is a face-to-face decomposition of $S^n/\Gamma$ into closed convex spherical cells that realises geometrically an abstract polytope of rank $n+1$.

Two flags of $\mathcal{P}$ are $i$-adjacent if they differ exactly in their rank-$i$ face. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ of an abstract polytope acts freely on flags. A polytope (or tessellation) is called regular if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts transitively on the flags, and chiral if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly two orbits on the flags such that adjacent flags lie in distinct orbits. Equivalently, a chiral tessellation has maximal rotational symmetry but no symmetry that reverses orientation/flag-orbit.

Question: Does there exist an integer $n \geq 2$, a finite fixed-point-free group $\Gamma$ of isometries of $S^n$, and a chiral tessellation of the spherical space-form $S^n/\Gamma$?

Web search found extensive literature on chiral abstract polytopes and on symmetric (regular/chiral) tessellations of Euclidean space-forms (where it is known that only the n-torus admits chiral tessellations, and only for n=2), but no source confirming a resolution of the analogous question for spherical space-forms. representations.normalized:
Background. An effect algebra is a structure $(E, \oplus, 0, 1)$ where $\oplus$ is a partial binary operation on $E$ satisfying: (E1) commutativity — if $a\oplus b$ is defined then $b\oplus a$ is defined and $a\oplus b = b\oplus a$; (E2) associativity — if $a\oplus b$ and $(a\oplus b)\oplus c$ are defined then $b\oplus c$ and $a\oplus(b\oplus c)$ are defined and equal; (E3) for every $a\in E$ there is a unique $a'\in E$ with $a\oplus a' = 1$; (E4) if $a\oplus 1$ is defined, then $a = 0$. A partial order is defined by $a\le b$ iff there exists $c\in E$ with $a\oplus c = b$.

An element $a\in E$ is an atom if $0<a$ and $0<x\le a$ implies $x=a$. The effect algebra $E$ is atomic if for every nonzero $b\in E$ there is an atom $a\le b$, and is Archimedean if for every atom $a$ the iterated sum $na = a\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a$ ($n$ times) fails to exist for some finite $n$.

An element $z\in E$ is central if $E$ decomposes as $E\cong [0,z]\times [0,z']$ via the natural map. The set $C(E)$ of central elements is a sub-effect-algebra of $E$, called the center.

For an arbitrary indexed family $\{a_i\}_{i\in I}\subseteq E$, the effect-algebraic sum $\bigoplus_{i\in I} a_i$, when it exists, is the supremum of the finite partial sums (formed by $\oplus$).

Problem. Let $E$ be an Archimedean atomic effect algebra and let $C(E)$ be its center, which is itself atomic.

(a) Find necessary and sufficient conditions on $E$ for the effect-algebraic sum $\bigoplus\{c : c\text{ is an atom of }C(E)\}$, computed in $E$, to exist and to equal $1$.

(b) Find necessary and sufficient conditions on $E$ for the following property to hold: for every subset $D\subseteq C(E)$ such that at least one of the sums $\bigoplus_{d\in D} d$ computed in $E$ or $\bigoplus_{d\in D} d$ computed in $C(E)$ exists, both sums exist and are equal.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The problem concerns characterizations related to atomic centers of Archimedean atomic effect algebras. Related works (Paseka–Riečanová and others, around 2010) give sufficient conditions, e.g., when the supremum of all central atoms equals 1 the effect algebra decomposes as a direct product of irreducibles; it was also shown that C(E) need not be a bifull sublattice. However, no source directly stating that the full equivalent-conditions characterization asked here has been completely settled was located, so the status is taken as unknown.

Let $H$ be a separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and let $L(H)$ denote the C*-algebra of all bounded linear operators on $H$. For a linear functional $f$ on $L(H)$, define
$$\alpha(f) = \{(A,B) \in L(H)\times L(H) : f(AX) = f(XB) \text{ for every } X \in L(H)\}.$$
Equip $L(H)\times L(H)$ with coordinatewise addition and multiplication, the natural scalar multiplication, the involution $(A,B)^* = (A^*, B^*)$, and the norm $\|(A,B)\| = \max(\|A\|,\|B\|)$ (so $L(H)\times L(H)$ becomes a C*-algebra).

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the linear functional $f$ under which $\alpha(f)$ is a C*-subalgebra of $L(H)\times L(H)$.

(b) Equivalently, characterize those pairs $(A,B) \in L(H)\times L(H)$ that can belong to $\alpha(f)$ for some linear functional $f$ in a way that ensures $\alpha(f)$ has the structure of a C*-algebra.

representations.normalized:
An abstract d-polytope is a ranked partially ordered set (with rank function taking values −1, 0, 1, …, d) satisfying the standard combinatorial axioms of abstract polytopes: it has a unique minimum face and a unique maximum face, every maximal chain (flag) has exactly d+2 elements, it is strongly flag-connected, and it satisfies the diamond condition (for any two faces F < G with rank(G) − rank(F) = 2 there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G). The facets of a d-polytope are its faces of rank d−1, and the vertex-figure at a vertex v is the section consisting of all faces strictly between v and the maximum face; both are themselves abstract (d−1)-polytopes.

An automorphism of an abstract polytope is an order-preserving bijection of its face lattice. A d-polytope P is called regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on the flags, and chiral if the automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits (so P admits all "rotational" symmetry but no reflections).

A (d−1)-polytope is called spherical if it is isomorphic to the face lattice of a convex (d−1)-polytope (equivalently, its order complex is a (d−2)-sphere), and toroidal if its underlying topological space is a (d−2)-torus (the standard locally toroidal case studied for d = 4, 5, 6).

Problem. Determine all pairs (K₁, K₂) of spherical or toroidal (d−1)-polytopes, with at least one of K₁ or K₂ being chiral, such that there exists a chiral abstract d-polytope whose facets are all isomorphic to K₁ and whose vertex-figures are all isomorphic to K₂.

representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a complex locally convex topological vector space, let $A$ be a complex algebra, and let $T\colon A \to L(X)$ be a representation of $A$ on $X$, where $L(X)$ denotes the algebra of continuous linear operators on $X$. Write $T_a$ for the operator representing $a\in A$.

Call $T$:
- irreducible if there is no proper closed subspace $Y\subsetneq X$ with $T_a(Y)\subseteq Y$ for all $a\in A$;
- $n$-fold irreducible if for every $n$-tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of linearly independent vectors in $X$, the orbit $\{(T_a x_1,\dots,T_a x_n) : a\in A\}$ is dense in $X^n$ (in the product topology);
- totally irreducible if $T$ is $n$-fold irreducible for every positive integer $n$.

The commutant of $T$ is $\{S\in L(X) : ST_a = T_a S \text{ for all } a\in A\}$.

Question: If $T$ is irreducible and its commutant consists only of scalar multiples of the identity operator on $X$, must $T$ be totally irreducible?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question, posed by Fell and Doran, is known to be open in full generality for representations on arbitrary complex locally convex spaces. Partial affirmative results are known: for instance, Żelazko (Studia Mathematica, 1998) proved that on the F-space (s) and more generally on infinite topological products of the scalar field, every irreducible representation with trivial (scalar) commutant is totally irreducible. No general resolution for arbitrary locally convex X appears in the literature.

representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $B(X)$ denote the algebra of all bounded linear operators on $X$, equipped with the strong operator topology. For a positive integer $n$, a closed subspace $M \subseteq X^n$ is said to be in general position if its projection onto each coordinate factor is dense (and $M$ is not reducible to a subspace of $X^k$ with $k<n$ in any coordinate-permutation sense). To each such $M$ associate the subalgebra
$$A(M) = \{\, T \in B(X) : (x_1,\dots,x_n) \in M \ \Rightarrow \ (Tx_1,\dots,Tx_n) \in M \,\}.$$
Each $A(M)$ is a strongly closed unital subalgebra of $B(X)$. A proper strongly closed subalgebra $A \subseteq B(X)$ is said to be of order $n$ if $A \subseteq A(M)$ for some closed subspace $M \subseteq X^n$ in general position, but $A$ is not contained in any $A(N)$ with $N \subseteq X^k$ in general position for any $k<n$. A maximal strongly closed algebra (m.s.c.a.) is a proper strongly closed subalgebra of $B(X)$ that is maximal among such subalgebras with respect to inclusion.

Prove or disprove: every proper strongly closed subalgebra $A$ of $B(X)$ is contained in some m.s.c.a.; moreover, $A$ is contained in some m.s.c.a. of the same order as $A$.

representations.normalized:
A map on a surface is an embedding of a connected graph (or multigraph) into a closed surface such that each connected component of the complement of the embedded graph (a face) is homeomorphic to an open disk. An automorphism of the map is a permutation of its flags (incident vertex–edge–face triples) induced by a self-homeomorphism of the surface preserving the embedded graph. The automorphism group of a map on an orientable surface acts semi-regularly on the set of flags; the map is called orientably regular if its orientation-preserving automorphism group acts transitively (hence regularly) on the set of arcs (directed edges). Such a map is called reflexible if it additionally admits an orientation-reversing automorphism, and chiral if it does not (so the map and its mirror image are distinct but isomorphic as abstract structures, with two orbits of flags under the full automorphism group). Equivalently, a chiral polyhedron in this combinatorial sense is a chiral orientably regular map.

Determine the set of all positive integers g such that there exists a chiral map on the closed orientable surface of genus g.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The complete characterization of genera supporting chiral maps remains open. Partial results are known: Garbe (1969) showed there are no chiral maps for genus 2–6; Conder and Dobcsányi (2001) enumerated chiral maps for genus 7–15; and Conder has extended computational classifications up to genus 301. Infinitely many gaps in the genus spectrum of chiral maps are known to exist, but a full description of which positive integers g arise is not available.

A map is a 2-cell embedding of a connected graph into a surface (without boundary). A map is of Schläfli type {p,q} (with p,q ∈ {3,4,5,...} ∪ {∞}) if every face is a p-gon (a ∞-gon being an infinite-sided face) and every vertex has valency q. The automorphism group of a map acts freely on its flags (incident vertex–edge–face triples). A map is called regular if its automorphism group is transitive on flags, and chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags always lie in different orbits (equivalently, the map admits all rotational symmetries about faces and vertices but no reflective symmetries). Such maps are equivalently described as abstract polyhedra (rank-3 abstract polytopes) that are chiral.

Determine the set of all pairs {p,q} with p,q ∈ {3,4,5,...} ∪ {∞} for which there exists an infinite chiral map (equivalently, an infinite chiral abstract polyhedron) of Schläfli type {p,q}.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a closed, densely defined, self-adjoint operator on $H$ with domain $\mathrm{Dom}(A)$ and spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}(A) \subset \mathbb{R}$. Let $(L_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of finite-dimensional closed subspaces with $L_k \subset \mathrm{Dom}(A)$, and let $P_k : H \to L_k$ be the orthogonal projection onto $L_k$. Assume that $P_k \to I$ strongly as $k \to \infty$. Define the finite-dimensional compression $A_k := P_k A\big|_{L_k} : L_k \to L_k$, and let $\mathrm{Spec}(A, L_k) := \mathrm{Spec}(A_k) \subset \mathbb{R}$.

Question: Does one always have, for every such $A$ and every such sequence $(L_k)$,
$$ \lim_{k \to \infty} \mathrm{Spec}(A, L_k) = \mathrm{Spec}(A) $$
in the sense that the set-theoretic limit (e.g., Hausdorff limit on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}$) of $\mathrm{Spec}(A, L_k)$ equals $\mathrm{Spec}(A)$?

$$ \lim_{k \to \infty} \mathrm{Spec}(A, L_k) = \mathrm{Spec}(A) $$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The answer is known to be negative in general: the Galerkin (projection) method applied to a self-adjoint operator can produce so-called "spectral pollution" — limit points of $\mathrm{Spec}(A, L_k)$ that lie in gaps of the essential spectrum of $A$ but do not belong to $\mathrm{Spec}(A)$. This is well documented in the literature on spectral pollution and motivates a variety of pollution-free schemes.

An abstract polytope is a ranked partially ordered set satisfying the standard incidence axioms generalizing the face lattice of a convex polytope. Its automorphism group acts on flags (maximal chains). The polytope is called regular if this action is transitive on all flags; it is called chiral if the automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits (so the polytope has maximal rotational symmetry but admits no reflection-type automorphism). A regular honeycomb in hyperbolic n-space is a regular tessellation of hyperbolic n-space H^n by congruent regular polytopes filling space face-to-face; the regular honeycombs of H^3, H^4, and H^5 are the classical ones given by their Schläfli symbols (e.g., {3,5,3}, {4,3,5}, {5,3,4}, {5,3,5} in H^3; {3,3,3,5}, {5,3,3,3}, {5,3,3,4}, {4,3,3,5}, {5,3,3,5}, {3,4,3,4} in H^4; {3,3,3,4,3}, {3,4,3,3,3}, {3,4,3,3,4}, {4,3,3,4,3} in H^5).

A chiral quotient of a regular honeycomb H is a finite abstract polytope obtained as a quotient of H (equivalently, of its automorphism group acting on flags) that is itself chiral as an abstract polytope.

For each regular honeycomb H in hyperbolic 3-space, hyperbolic 4-space, and hyperbolic 5-space, determine whether there exists an infinite family of finite chiral abstract polytopes that arise as chiral quotients of H.

The polytope is called regular if this action is transitive on all flags; it is called chiral if the automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits (so the polytope has maximal rotational symmetry but admits no reflection-type automorphism). A regular honeycomb in hyperbolic n-space is a regular tessellation of hyperbolic n-space H^n by congruent regular polytopes filling space face-to-face; the regular honeycombs of H^3, H^4, and H^5 are the classical ones given by their Schläfli symbols (e.g., {3,5,3}, {4,3,5}, {5,3,4}, {5,3,5} in H^3; {3,3,3,5}, {5,3,3,3}, {5,3,3,4}, {4,3,3,5}, {5,3,3,5}, {3,4,3,4} in H^4; {3,3,3,4,3}, {3,4,3,3,3}, {3,4,3,3,4}, {4,3,3,4,3} in H^5).

A chiral quotient of a regular honeycomb H is a finite abstract polytope obtained as a quotient of H (equivalently, of its automorphism group acting on flags) that is itself chiral as an abstract polytope.

For each regular honeycomb H in hyperbolic 3-space, hyperbolic 4-space, and hyperbolic 5-space, determine whether there exists an infinite family of finite chiral abstract polytopes that arise as chiral quotients of H.

An abstract polytope is a ranked partially ordered set satisfying the standard axioms generalizing the face lattices of convex polytopes (existence of greatest and least elements, the diamond condition on intervals of length 2, and strong flag-connectedness). For an abstract n-polytope P, its automorphism group Γ(P) acts on the flags of P. The polytope P is called regular if Γ(P) is transitive on flags. If P is regular, its rotation subgroup (the subgroup generated by the products of consecutive standard generating reflections) has index 1 or 2 in Γ(P); when the index equals 2, P is called orientably regular. The polytope P is called chiral if Γ(P) has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits.

Given an abstract n-polytope K, a chiral extension of K is a chiral (n+1)-polytope all of whose facets are isomorphic to K.

Question: Does every orientably regular abstract polytope K admit a chiral extension that has infinitely many faces (i.e., an infinite chiral extension)?

An abstract d-polytope is a ranked partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) have ranks from -1 to d, with a unique minimum face of rank -1 and a unique maximum face of rank d, such that every maximal chain has length d+2, and which satisfies the diamond condition and strong flag-connectedness. The faces of rank 0 are called vertices and the faces of rank d-1 are called facets. An abstract d-polytope is said to be flat if every facet is incident with every vertex. An abstract d-polytope is regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on the set of maximal chains (flags), and is chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

Question: For every integer d ≥ 3, does there exist a flat abstract d-polytope that is either regular or chiral?

An abstract d-polytope is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ with a least element $F_{-1}$ and a greatest element $F_d$, satisfying the following: every maximal chain (called a flag) has exactly $d+2$ elements, so each element has a well-defined rank in $\{-1,0,1,\dots,d\}$; $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected; and $\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the diamond condition (for every pair $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two elements $H$ with $F<H<G$). Two flags are called $i$-adjacent if they differ in exactly the rank-$i$ element. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts freely on the set of flags.

The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called regular if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts transitively on flags. It is called chiral if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly two orbits on flags, with the property that adjacent flags always lie in different orbits.

For each integer $d\ge 3$, define
$$m^{\mathrm{ch}}_d \;=\; \min igl\{\,|\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{P})|\,:\, \mathcal{P}	ext{ is a chiral abstract }d	ext{-polytope} igr\},$$
where $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{P})$ denotes the set of flags of $\mathcal{P}$, and the minimum is taken over all finite chiral $d$-polytopes (set $m^{\mathrm{ch}}_d=\infty$ if no chiral $d$-polytope exists in rank $d$).

Determine the function $d\mapsto m^{\mathrm{ch}}_d$ for all $d\ge 3$.

The problem of determining the minimum number of flags of a chiral d-polytope as a function of d appears to remain open in general. The classification problem is only partially resolved. It is known that chiral polyhedra (rank 3) in ordinary 3-space have been completely enumerated by Schulte, that no finite chiral polyhedron exists in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and that chiral polytopes of full rank can occur only in ranks 4 and 5 (with concrete examples constructed, e.g. a finite chiral 4-polytope in $\mathbb{R}^4$ and an infinite chiral 4-polytope in $\mathbb{R}^3$). Let $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \geq 2$) be a real-analytic, nonsingular hypersurface. The modified Schwarz potential of $\Gamma$ is defined as a function $u_\Gamma$, defined in a neighborhood of $\Gamma$, satisfying
$$\Delta u_\Gamma = 1, \qquad u_\Gamma\big|_{\Gamma} = 0, \qquad \nabla u_\Gamma\big|_{\Gamma} = 0.$$
By the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem, such a $u_\Gamma$ exists and is unique in some neighborhood of $\Gamma$, and it admits a (possibly multi-valued) analytic continuation to $\mathbb{R}^n$ outside its singular set.

Suppose that the only singularities of (the analytic continuation of) $u_\Gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are isolated polar singularities, i.e., there exist finitely many points $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that, near each such $x_0$,
$$u_\Gamma(x) = O\!\left(|x - x_0|^{-m}\right)$$

Let $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \geq 2$) be a real-analytic, nonsingular hypersurface. The modified Schwarz potential of $\Gamma$ is defined as a function $u_\Gamma$, defined in a neighborhood of $\Gamma$, satisfying
$$\Delta u_\Gamma = 1, \qquad u_\Gamma\big|_{\Gamma} = 0, \qquad \nabla u_\Gamma\big|_{\Gamma} = 0.$$
By the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem, such a $u_\Gamma$ exists and is unique in some neighborhood of $\Gamma$, and it admits a (possibly multi-valued) analytic continuation to $\mathbb{R}^n$ outside its singular set.

Suppose that the only singularities of (the analytic continuation of) $u_\Gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are isolated polar singularities, i.e., there exist finitely many points $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that, near each such $x_0$,
$$u_\Gamma(x) = O\!\left(|x - x_0|^{-m}\right)$$
for some $m > 0$, and $u_\Gamma$ extends real-analytically to $\mathbb{R}^n$ minus this finite set of points.

Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, $\Gamma$ must be a sphere.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is part of a circle of conjectures around the Khavinson–Shapiro program on singularities of the Schwarz potential and characterizations of spheres/ellipsoids. Surveys and recent literature (e.g., Lundberg's work on Laplacian/elliptic growth, the AMS Surveys volume 232 by Ebenfelt–Khavinson–Shapiro, and the Notices article "A Tale of Ellipsoids in Potential Theory") discuss this and related conjectures as outstanding problems. No published proof or counterexample establishing that isolated polar singularities of the modified Schwarz potential force $\Gamma$ to be a sphere has been located, so the problem appears to remain open.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $B(H)$ denote the C*-algebra of all bounded linear operators on $H$, with operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ and adjoint $X \mapsto X^*$. Let $I(H)$ be the set of invertible elements of $B(H)$. Define the following two subclasses of $I(H)$:
- $C^*S_0(H)$: the class of all invertible normal operators $S \in B(H)$ whose spectrum is contained in a union of straight lines passing through the origin of $\mathbb{C}$;
- $R^*U(H)$: the class of all $S \in I(H)$ such that $\|SXS^{-1}\| + \|S^{-1}XS\| = 2\|X\|$ for every $X \in B(H)$.

For a binary relation $R(S,X)$ on $B(H) \times B(H)$, say that the proposition "for every $X \in B(H)$, $R(S,X)$ holds" is closed in $B(H)$ if the set $\{S \in B(H) : R(S,X) \text{ holds for every } X \in B(H)\}$ equals exactly the class of operators on which this proposition is asserted to hold. The closure of an inequality "for every $S$ in a class $\mathcal{C}$ and every $X \in B(H)$, $R(S,X)$ holds" is the largest such class $\widehat{\mathcal{C}} \supseteq \mathcal{C}$ for which the statement remains true; i.e. $\widehat{\mathcal{C}} = \{S \in B(H) : R(S,X) \text{ holds for every } X \in B(H)\}$.

Determine the closures (in this sense) of each of the following two operator inequalities:

(1) For every $S \in R^*U(H)$ and every $X \in B(H)$,
$$\|SXS^{-1} + S^{-1}XS\| \le 2\|X\|.$$

(2) For every $S \in C^*S_0(H) \cup R^*U(H)$ and every $X \in B(H)$,
$$\|SXS^{-1} + S^{-1}XS\| \le \|S^*XS^{-1} + S^{-1}XS^*\|.$$

$$\int_{\partial\Omega} g(z)\, ds(z) = 0 \quad \text{for every } g \in E^1(\Omega).$$

Let $T(z)$ denote the unit tangent vector to $\partial\Omega$ (defined a.e. on the rectifiable boundary), viewed as a complex-valued function on $\partial\Omega$.

Question: Does the ALNQD condition above force $T$ to extend from $\partial\Omega$ to an analytic function on all of $\Omega$? That is, does there exist a function $h$ holomorphic in $\Omega$ whose nontangential boundary values agree a.e. on $\partial\Omega$ with the unit tangent vector $T$?

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk and $\mathbb{T}=\partial\mathbb{D}$ the unit circle. Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, and let $\varphi:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a univalent (conformal) map with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi'(0)>0$. Consider the family of univalent maps $f(\cdot,t):\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}\setminus K(t)$ (with $f(\cdot,0)=\varphi$) governed by the nonlinear Loewner-type evolution
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(z,t)\;=\;z\,f'(z,t)\int_{\mathbb{T}}\frac{z+\zeta}{z-\zeta}\,\frac{|d\zeta|}{|f'(\zeta,t)|^{\alpha}},\qquad z\in\mathbb{D},$$
where $f'$ denotes the derivative in $z$ and the boundary values $f'(\zeta,t)$ are understood in a suitable (e.g., nontangential) sense. The increasing family of compact "hulls" is $K(t)=\mathbb{C}\setminus f(\mathbb{D},t)$.

In any regime in which this evolution is well posed (existence and uniqueness of $f(\cdot,t)$ on some time interval $[0,T)$), establish geometric properties of the hulls $K(t)$. Specifically:

(a) Prove or disprove that for $t\in(0,T)$ the boundary $\partial K(t)$ enjoys some degree of regularity (for example, that it is a Jordan curve, locally connected, Hölder, or smoother), and identify the optimal regularity as a function of $\alpha$ and of the regularity of $\varphi$.

(b) Prove or disprove stability of the evolution with respect to the initial datum: if $\varphi_n\to\varphi$ in a suitable topology of conformal maps on $\mathbb{D}$, do the corresponding solutions $f_n(\cdot,t)$ converge to $f(\cdot,t)$ (equivalently, do the hulls $K_n(t)$ converge to $K(t)$, e.g., in the Carathéodory or Hausdorff sense) on the common interval of existence?

Consider the modal logic S4u, defined as the propositional modal logic S4 (with modal operators □ and ◇) augmented with a universal modality ∀ (and its dual ∃), interpreted on topological spaces in the standard topological semantics: □ is interpreted as the topological interior operator, and ∀φ holds at a point of a space X iff φ holds at every point of X.

Now extend the language of S4u by adding, for each positive rational number a, two binary "metric distance" operators:
- ∃^{≤a}: for a formula φ, the formula ∃^{≤a}φ holds at a point x of a metric space (X,d) iff there exists y ∈ X with d(x,y) ≤ a such that φ holds at y;
- ∃^{>a}: similarly, ∃^{>a}φ holds at x iff there exists y ∈ X with d(x,y) > a such that φ holds at y.

Models are metric spaces (X,d) with a valuation of propositional variables, and the topological connectives of S4u are interpreted via the metric topology induced by d.

Determine the logical behaviour of this extension of S4u by the operators ∃^{≤a} and ∃^{>a}: in particular, provide a complete and sound axiomatization of the set of formulas valid in all metric spaces, and determine the decidability and computational complexity of its satisfiability/validity problem.

representations.normalized:
Consider the following family of nonlinear Loewner-type planar growth processes. Let $K_0 = \overline{\mathbb{D}}^c \cup \{\infty\}$ be the exterior of the closed unit disk, and consider a growing family of compact hulls $K_t \supset K_0$, $t \ge 0$, in the Riemann sphere whose complements are simply connected. For each $t$, let $g_t : \mathbb{C} \setminus K_t \to \{|z|>1\}$ be the unique conformal map fixing $\infty$ with $g_t'(\infty)>0$. Given a parameter $\alpha > 0$ and a probability measure $\mu_t$ on the unit circle, the family $(g_t)$ is required to satisfy the weighted Loewner-Kufarev equation
$$\partial_t g_t(z) = g_t(z) \int_{|\zeta|=1} \frac{g_t(z)+\zeta}{g_t(z)-\zeta} \, |g_t'(z)|^{-\alpha}\bigg|_{\text{boundary push-forward}} \, d\mu_t(\zeta),$$
so that, heuristically, the inward normal velocity of the boundary $\partial K_t$ at a point $w \in \partial K_t$ is proportional to $|g_t'(w)|^{\alpha-1}$ times a local driving density. The case $\alpha = 2$ corresponds to Hele–Shaw / Laplacian growth and has been studied extensively (Carleson–Makarov and others), where one obtains existence, scaling limits, and information on the limit shapes.

Investigate the case $\alpha = 1$, in which the normal velocity of the boundary is (formally) a constant independent of conformal distortion, so that the evolution is heuristically an Eden-type isotropic growth and is conjecturally related to the $\alpha = 1$ Hastings–Levitov regime $\mathrm{HL}(1)$. Specifically: establish existence and uniqueness of solutions $K_t$ for natural classes of driving measures $\mu_t$; describe the scaling limit and the regularity (e.g. smoothness or roughness) of $\partial K_t$; and determine whether the limit shapes coincide with, or qualitatively differ from, those produced by random $\mathrm{HL}(1)$ / Eden aggregation in an appropriate scaling limit.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The α = 1 case of nonlinear Loewner-driven planar aggregation (and the related Hastings–Levitov HL(1) model) is widely identified as a critical and subtle regime. While the α = 2 (Hele–Shaw/Laplacian) case is well developed via Carleson–Makarov and successors, no complete description of existence, scaling limits, and limit shapes for the α = 1 deterministic Loewner growth or rigorous matching with HL(1) appears in the literature as of 2026; partial results exist for anisotropic/regularized Hastings–Levitov families and related stationary HL(0) models, but the α = 1 case remains open.

representations.normalized:
Consider the modal logic MT with two unary modal operators interpreted on metric spaces as follows. For a metric space (X,d), an MT-model is a valuation V assigning to each propositional variable a subset of X. The language extends propositional logic with:
- a "distance" operator ◇^a, for each positive rational a, with semantics: x ⊨ ◇^a φ iff there exists y ∈ X with d(x,y) < a and y ⊨ φ;
- a topological "closure/interior" modality based on the metric topology.
(More generally MT may be taken as the natural combined modal language for metric and topology in which formulas are built from propositional variables using Boolean connectives, the parameterised distance modalities ◇^a (a ∈ ℚ_{>0}), and the topological closure modality, interpreted in metric spaces in the standard way.)

A formula is MT-valid over the real line if it is true at every point of every MT-model based on (ℝ, |·|) with the usual Euclidean metric. It is known that the satisfiability problem for MT over (ℝ, |·|) is decidable.

(a) Provide a transparent (e.g., finite or otherwise perspicuous recursive) axiomatisation of the set of MT-formulas valid in every MT-model based on the one-dimensional Euclidean space (ℝ, |·|).

(b) Determine the exact computational complexity of the satisfiability problem for MT over (ℝ, |·|).

The problem is posed as an open problem in the literature on modal logics of metric spaces. While decidability of MT-satisfiability over ℝ is known, no transparent axiomatisation and no tight complexity bound for MT over the real line appear in the available sources; related results axiomatise only the pure topological fragment (which coincides over ℝ with S4 and is PSpace-complete) or treat distance fragments without topology. No subsequent work resolving both axiomatisation and exact complexity of full MT over ℝ was located.

Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $H^2 = H^2(\mathbb{D})$ be the Hardy space consisting of all holomorphic functions $g(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ on $\mathbb{D}$ such that
$$\|g\|_{H^2}^2 := \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |a_n|^2 < \infty.$$
A function $g \in H^2$ is called inner if its non-tangential boundary values satisfy $|g(e^{i\theta})| = 1$ for almost every $\theta \in [0, 2\pi)$.

Consider the function
$$f(z) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{1+z}{1-z}\right), \qquad z \in \mathbb{D}.$$
It is classical that $f$ is an inner function (in fact, a singular inner function with point mass at $z=1$), and the standard proof relies on inspecting the boundary values $|f(e^{i\theta})|$ on the unit circle.

Provide a proof that $f$ is inner using only $H^2$-information encoded in its Taylor series at the origin. More precisely, write $f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ and establish the inner property of $f$ by working solely with the Taylor coefficients $\{a_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ and intrinsic Hilbert-space properties of $H^2$, without invoking any boundary-value characterization of inner functions on the unit circle.

Let $H$ be a separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $L(H)$ denote the algebra of all bounded linear operators on $H$, equipped with the operator norm. For $A, B \in L(H)$, define the generalized derivation $\delta_{A,B}: L(H) \to L(H)$ by $\delta_{A,B}(X) = AX - XB$, and write $R(\delta_{A,B})$ for its range. The pair $(A,B)$ is called generalized finite if $\|I - (AX - XB)\| \geq 1$ for every $X \in L(H)$, where $I$ is the identity operator. A bounded linear functional $f$ on $L(H)$ is called normal if it is weak-* continuous (equivalently, given by trace duality with a trace-class operator), and self-adjoint if $f(X^*) = \overline{f(X)}$ for all $X \in L(H)$.

Question: Suppose there exists a nonzero normal, self-adjoint linear functional $f$ on $L(H)$ such that $f(Y) = 0$ for every $Y \in R(\delta_{A,B})$. Must the pair $(A,B)$ be generalized finite?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

An axiomatisation of CSL over minspaces (distance spaces in which the relevant infima are attained) has been given by Alenda, Olivetti and Schwind, with accompanying tableaux calculi extended to arbitrary distance spaces and to triangular/metric models. However, complete finite axiomatisations of CSL over the full classes of metric spaces and of Euclidean spaces appear not to have been established, and undecidability/complexity results (via tree automata and Diophantine equations) suggest substantial obstacles. The general problem therefore appears only partially solved.

Let $n \geq 2$ and let $\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be an infinite discrete set of points (with no finite accumulation point), and let $\{a_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers ("masses") satisfying the convergence condition
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{a_k}{|x_k|^{n-1}} < \infty.$$
Define the associated gravitational force field on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{x_k : k \geq 0\}$ by
$$F(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \, \frac{x_k - x}{|x - x_k|^n}.$$
Equivalently, $F = -\nabla U$, where $U$ is the corresponding logarithmic ($n=2$) or Newtonian ($n \geq 3$) potential generated by the masses $a_k$ at the points $x_k$.

Question: Must there always exist a point $x^* \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{x_k\}$ with $F(x^*) = 0$? Equivalently, must $U$ always possess at least one critical point?

Let CSL (the logic of comparative concept similarity) be the propositional modal-style language built from a countable set of propositional atoms by Boolean connectives together with a binary similarity connective ⇔, where a formula A ⇔ B is intended to express "the points satisfying A are at least as similar (close) to the current point as the points satisfying B are". Interpret CSL over R^n equipped with a fixed distance (e.g. the Euclidean metric, or more generally any metric or minspace structure on R^n), so that a valuation assigns to each atom p a subset V(p) ⊆ R^n, and the truth of x ⊨ A ⇔ B is defined in the standard way using infima of distances from x to V(A) and to V(B).

Now restrict the class of admissible valuations as follows: a valuation V is admissible iff for every atom p, the set V(p) is a convex subset of R^n (and more generally consider analogous geometric restrictions on V(p) suggested by conceptual-space semantics, such as being a convex polytope, a Voronoi cell, or a closed connected set).

Problem: Determine the computational properties — in particular, decidability and computational complexity of the satisfiability and validity problems — of CSL, and of natural extensions of CSL (for example with distance operators or with additional similarity comparators), interpreted over R^n under such convexity-type restrictions on the admissible valuations of atomic predicates.

representations.normalized:
Consider the manna-division problem: a fixed bundle of perfectly divisible, unproduced goods (a "cake") is to be divided among a finite set of agents. Each agent has an arbitrary preference relation over their share that is convex and monotonic (more of every good is weakly better, and preferences have convex upper-contour sets). A mechanism associates to every population (finite set of agents) and every profile of such preferences an allocation of the entire cake among the agents.

Define the following properties of a mechanism:

1. Pareto Optimality: at every profile, the allocation chosen is not Pareto-dominated by any other feasible allocation of the cake.

2. Population Monotonicity: if a new agent joins the population sharing the same cake (so the cake is now split among more agents), then no pre-existing agent strictly prefers the new allocation to the old one — equivalently, every pre-existing agent weakly loses.

3. No Domination: at every profile, the chosen allocation never assigns to any agent a bundle that is strictly larger in every coordinate (every good) than the bundle assigned to some other agent.

4. Equal Split Guarantee: at every profile, every agent weakly prefers their assigned bundle to receiving the equal-split bundle (the per-capita share 1/n of the cake, where n is the number of agents).

Question (b): If such a mechanism exists, can one in addition require it to satisfy Equal Split Guarantee?

Consider the manna-division problem: a fixed bundle of perfectly divisible, unproduced goods (a "cake") is to be divided among a finite set of agents. Each agent has an arbitrary preference relation over their share that is convex and monotonic (more of every good is weakly better, and preferences have convex upper-contour sets). A mechanism associates to every population (finite set of agents) and every profile of such preferences an allocation of the entire cake among the agents.

Define the following properties of a mechanism:

1. Pareto Optimality: at every profile, the allocation chosen is not Pareto-dominated by any other feasible allocation of the cake.

2. Population Monotonicity: if a new agent joins the population sharing the same cake (so the cake is now split among more agents), then no pre-existing agent strictly prefers the new allocation to the old one — equivalently, every pre-existing agent weakly loses.

3. No Domination: at every profile, the chosen allocation never assigns to any agent a bundle that is strictly larger in every coordinate (every good) than the bundle assigned to some other agent.

4. Equal Split Guarantee: at every profile, every agent weakly prefers their assigned bundle to receiving the equal-split bundle (the per-capita share 1/n of the cake, where n is the number of agents).

Question (a): Does there exist a mechanism on this domain (arbitrary convex monotonic preferences over a divisible heterogeneous manna) that simultaneously satisfies Pareto Optimality, Population Monotonicity, and No Domination?

Question (b): If such a mechanism exists, can one in addition require it to satisfy Equal Split Guarantee?

A web search did not surface a published resolution of this combined axiomatic question for manna division with arbitrary convex monotonic preferences. Related literature (e.g., the competitive/Nash rule for mixed manna by Bogomolnaia–Moulin–Sandomirskiy–Yanovskaya, and work on population/resource monotonicity in cake-cutting) establishes monotonicity properties of specific Pareto-optimal rules in restricted domains, but does not appear to settle the existence of a Pareto-optimal mechanism satisfying both Population Monotonicity and No Domination (and additionally Equal Split Guarantee) on the general convex monotonic domain. Status appears to remain open.

Standard "similarity" or "distance" modal/first-order languages for metric spaces are crisp: their formulas are evaluated in a metric space (X, d) and refer to exact numerical thresholds, e.g. via operators such as ∃^{≤a}φ ("there exists a point at distance at most a satisfying φ") or comparative-similarity predicates of the form "y is at least as close to x as z is", with truth values in {0,1}.

Design a logical formalism for reasoning about metric (or, more generally, distance) spaces in which distances themselves, or the truth values of distance assertions, may be approximate or uncertain. Concretely, propose a syntax and a semantics — over a class of distance structures (X, d) possibly enriched with a probability measure, a fuzzy similarity relation, or a vagueness/tolerance structure — satisfying the following requirements:

1. The language should contain analogues of the crisp distance/similarity operators (such as ∃^{≤a}, ∀^{≤a}, or comparative-closeness predicates), but with truth values taken in a suitable algebra (e.g. the real interval [0,1] under a t-norm, a probability algebra, or a many-valued algebra modelling vagueness) so that formulas can express graded, fuzzy, or probabilistic distance statements (for instance, "φ holds with high probability at some nearby point" or "x is approximately as close to y as to z").

2. Give a precise model-theoretic semantics interpreting the language in the chosen class of uncertain distance structures.

3. Investigate the resulting logic: in particular, axiomatize it (sound and complete deductive calculus) and determine the decidability and computational complexity of its satisfiability/validity problem.

The task is to develop such a formalism, or to prove that any reasonable formalism meeting these criteria must fail one of the desired meta-properties (e.g. recursive axiomatizability or decidability).

The problem is a programmatic open problem asking for the development of logics for metric/distance reasoning with uncertainty. While various related formalisms exist — fuzzy modal logics for similarity reasoning, probabilistic metric spaces, behavioural (pseudo)metrics with characteristic quantitative modal logics, and similarity-based fuzzy metric spaces — no single accepted formalism has been developed that subsumes the crisp similarity/distance modal logics for metric spaces and extends them to vague, fuzzy, or probabilistic distances with a full axiomatization and decidability analysis. The general challenge therefore remains open, although there has been substantial partial progress along each of the suggested directions.

Work in the finite projective space $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ over the field $\mathbb{F}_q$, where $n\geq 1$ and $q$ is a prime power. A pseudo-oval (also called a generalized oval, or $[n-1]$-oval) is a set
$$\mathcal{O} = \{\pi_0, \pi_1, \ldots, \pi_{q^n}\}$$
of $q^n+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ satisfying the tangent-space condition: every three distinct elements of $\mathcal{O}$ span a $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace (equivalently, they are in general position), and for each $\pi_i\in\mathcal{O}$ there exists a $(2n-1)$-dimensional subspace $T_i$ (the tangent space at $\pi_i$) containing $\pi_i$ and meeting every $\pi_j$, $j\neq i$, trivially.

The standard field-extension construction produces a so-called regular pseudo-oval as follows. Let $\mathcal{O}'$ be an oval (a set of $q^n+1$ points, no three collinear) in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$. Viewing $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$ as $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ by restriction of scalars from $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ to $\mathbb{F}_q$, each point of $\mathcal{O}'$ becomes an $(n-1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspace, and the resulting collection is a pseudo-oval in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$. A pseudo-oval is called regular if it is projectively equivalent to one obtained in this way.

Question: Is every pseudo-oval in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ regular?

Let $q$ be an odd prime power and let $n$ be a positive integer. A pseudo-oval (or generalized oval) $O = O(n,n,q)$ in the projective space $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1, q)$ is a set of $q^n + 1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots, \pi_{q^n}$ with the property that any three of them span a $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace (equivalently, they span the whole space). For each element $\pi_i \in O$ there is a unique $(2n-1)$-dimensional subspace $\tau_i$ of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$, called the tangent space of $O$ at $\pi_i$, that contains $\pi_i$ and is disjoint from every other element of $O$. In the dual projective space $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)^*$, the $q^n + 1$ tangent spaces $\tau_0, \tau_1, \dots, \tau_{q^n}$ (viewed as points of the appropriate Grassmannian via duality) themselves form a pseudo-oval, denoted $O^* = O^*(n,n,q)$, and called the translation dual of $O$.

Question: For every odd prime power $q$ and every positive integer $n$, is every pseudo-oval $O(n,n,q)$ projectively isomorphic to its translation dual $O^*(n,n,q)$?

representations.normalized:
Let $A$ be a self-adjoint (in general unbounded) operator on a complex Hilbert space $H$ with domain $\mathrm{Dom}(A)$, and let $\mathrm{Spec}(A) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ denote its spectrum. For any finite-dimensional subspace $L \subseteq \mathrm{Dom}(A)$, define the second-order relative spectrum of $A$ with respect to $L$ by
$$\mathrm{Spec}_2(A,L) := \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \exists\, u \in L \setminus \{0\} \text{ with } \langle (A-zI)u, (A-zI)v\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } v \in L \}.$$
Equivalently, $z \in \mathrm{Spec}_2(A,L)$ iff the compression of $(A-zI)^2$ to $L$ is singular. Let $(L_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ be an increasing sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces of $\mathrm{Dom}(A)$ whose union is dense in $H$ (in the graph norm of $A$). Define the limit set
$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathrm{Spec}_2(A,L_k) := \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \exists\, z_k \in \mathrm{Spec}_2(A,L_k) \text{ with } z_k \to z \}.$$
It is known that this limit set contains every isolated eigenvalue of $A$ of finite multiplicity. Determine whether, for every such sequence $(L_k)$, one has
$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathrm{Spec}_2(A,L_k) \supseteq \mathrm{Spec}(A).$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been resolved in the negative: Shargorodsky (2012/2013) showed that second-order relative spectra do not in general approximate the whole essential spectrum of a bounded self-adjoint operator, so the inclusion of the full spectrum in the limit set fails in general. Earlier work by Boulton established the positive direction only for isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity.

Let q be a prime power and n a positive integer. A pseudo-oval of PG(3n−1, q) is a set
  O(n, n, q) = {π_0, π_1, …, π_{q^n}}
of q^n + 1 mutually disjoint (n−1)-dimensional subspaces of PG(3n−1, q) such that any three of them span PG(3n−1, q). For each i there is a unique (3n−1−n)=(2n−1)-dimensional subspace τ_i, called the tangent space at π_i, that contains π_i and meets every other π_j (j ≠ i) trivially in the sense required by the pseudo-oval (equivalently, the unique (2n−1)-space through π_i skew to all π_j for j ≠ i in the appropriate dual sense). When q is even, the tangent spaces τ_0, …, τ_{q^n} all share a common (n−1)-dimensional subspace η, called the nucleus of O(n, n, q).

Fix a (2n−1)-dimensional subspace PG(2n−1, q) of PG(3n−1, q) that is skew to π_i (resp. skew to η). Define
  S_i = {ξ_i, ξ_0, ξ_1, …, ξ_{q^n}} \ {ξ_i-duplicate},
where ξ_i = τ_i ∩ PG(2n−1, q) and ξ_j = ⟨π_i, π_j⟩ ∩ PG(2n−1, q) for j ≠ i; this is an (n−1)-spread of PG(2n−1, q).
When q is even, define analogously
  S = {ζ_0, ζ_1, …, ζ_{q^n}}, where ζ_j = PG(2n−1, q) ∩ ⟨η, π_j⟩;
this is also an (n−1)-spread of PG(2n−1, q).

Recall that an (n−1)-spread of PG(2n−1, q) is called regular (Desarguesian) if for any three of its elements the unique regulus they determine is contained in the spread; equivalently, the spread arises from the field-reduction of a 1-spread of PG(1, q^n).

Problem. Assume q is even. Determine the structural consequences for the pseudo-oval O(n, n, q) (and for the associated translation generalized quadrangle T(O)) under each of the following hypotheses:
 (a) the (n−1)-spread S defined via the nucleus η is regular;
 (b) for some (equivalently, every) i, the (n−1)-spread S_i defined via the tangent space τ_i is regular.
In particular, does regularity of S (resp. S_i) force O(n, n, q) to be a pseudo-conic (i.e., to arise from field reduction of a conic in PG(2, q^n)), and consequently force T(O) to be isomorphic to the classical generalized quadrangle Q(4, q^n)?

Let $q$ be an even prime power and let $n\ge 1$ be an integer. A pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ is a set of $q^n+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ such that any three of them span the whole space. The pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}$ is called classical (or elementary, arising from a conic) if there exists a conic $C$ in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$ such that, after applying field reduction from $\mathrm{GF}(q^n)$ to $\mathrm{GF}(q)$, the points of $C$ become precisely the elements of $\mathcal{O}$.

The collineation stabiliser $G\le \mathrm{P}\Gamma\mathrm{L}(3n,q)$ of $\mathcal{O}$ is said to act $2$-transitively on $\mathcal{O}$ if for any two ordered pairs of distinct elements of $\mathcal{O}$ there is an element of $G$ sending the first pair to the second; it acts transitively on $\mathcal{O}$ if any single element of $\mathcal{O}$ can be mapped to any other.

It is known that, for $q$ even, $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ is classical if and only if it admits a $2$-transitive collineation group.

Question: Can the hypothesis of $2$-transitivity be weakened to mere transitivity? That is, is every pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ with $q$ even that admits a transitive collineation group necessarily classical?

Significant partial progress has been made. Bamberg–Penttila ("Transitive eggs", 2006) and subsequent work by Bamberg, Glasby, Popiel and Praeger (2016) showed that a pseudo-oval (not an oval) admitting an insoluble transitive collineation group is elementary, arising via field reduction from a conic, an elliptic quadric, or a Suzuki–Tits ovoid. Rottey and Van de Voorde (arXiv:1701.09126) classified regular pseudo-ovals in even characteristic for prime $n$. However, the full question—whether transitivity alone (without insolubility or regularity hypotheses) forces classicality of $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ in even characteristic—does not appear to have been settled in full generality.

Let $q$ be a prime power and let $n\ge 1$ be an integer. In the finite projective space $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$, an egg (also called a pseudo-ovoid, generalized ovoid, or $[n-1]$-ovoid), denoted $O(n,2n,q)$, is a family $\mathcal{E}$ of $q^{2n}+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces such that:

(i) any three distinct elements of $\mathcal{E}$ span a $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace; and
(ii) at every element $E\in\mathcal{E}$ there exists a unique $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace $T_E$ (the tangent space at $E$) which contains $E$ and is disjoint from every other element of $\mathcal{E}$.

Such an egg is called regular (a regular pseudo-ovoid) if the $q^{2n}+1$ tangent spaces $\{T_E : E\in\mathcal{E}\}$ form the dual of an egg in $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$; equivalently, every hyperplane of $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$ either contains exactly one tangent space or contains exactly $q^n+1$ tangent spaces.

Question: Suppose $q$ is even. Is every egg $O(n,2n,q)$ in $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$ necessarily regular?

Let q be a power of 2 and let n be a positive integer. Work in the projective space PG(4n-1, q). An egg O(n, 2n, q) is a set of q^{2n}+1 mutually disjoint (n-1)-dimensional subspaces (called egg elements) of PG(4n-1, q) such that:
(i) any three distinct egg elements span a (3n-1)-dimensional subspace, and
(ii) for every egg element E there exists a unique (3n-1)-dimensional subspace T_E (the tangent space at E) containing E and disjoint from all other egg elements.

The tangent spaces {T_E : E ∈ O} of an egg O = O(n, 2n, q) themselves form an egg in the dual projective space of PG(4n-1, q); this egg is called the translation dual of O and is denoted O^*(n, 2n, q). Two eggs are isomorphic if there is a collineation of the ambient projective space (in the appropriate sense) mapping one onto the other.

Question: For every egg O(n, 2n, q) with q even, is O necessarily isomorphic to its translation dual O^*(n, 2n, q)?

Consider the delay difference equation
\[ x_{n+1} = \frac{A}{x_n^2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x_{n-1}}}, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, \]
where $A > 0$ is a real parameter and the initial conditions $x_{-1}, x_0$ are arbitrary positive real numbers (so that all iterates $x_n$ remain positive).

A period-two cycle is a nonconstant positive solution $(x_n)$ satisfying $x_{n+2} = x_n$ for all $n$, i.e. alternating between two distinct positive values $\phi$ and $\psi$ with
\[ \phi = \frac{A}{\psi^2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\phi}}, \qquad \psi = \frac{A}{\phi^2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\psi}}. \]
Such a cycle is called asymptotically stable if, for every sufficiently small perturbation of the initial conditions, the resulting solution converges to the cycle.

Prove or disprove: for every $A > 15/4$, this recurrence admits an asymptotically stable period-two cycle.

A sub pseudo-conic of an egg O(n, 2n, q) is a subset of q^n + 1 of its elements that all lie in a common (3n−1)-dimensional subspace and form a pseudo-conic there.

Question: Must every egg O(n, 2n, q) that contains a sub pseudo-conic be good?

Such an egg E is said to be good at an element π ∈ E if for every two distinct elements π′, π″ of E ∖ {π}, the (3n−1)-dimensional space ⟨π, π′, π″⟩ contains exactly q^n + 1 elements of E; the egg E is called good if it is good at some element.

A pseudo-oval in PG(3n−1, q) is a set of q^n + 1 mutually disjoint (n−1)-dimensional subspaces, every three of which span PG(3n−1, q). A pseudo-oval is called regular if it arises by field reduction from an oval O₁ in PG(2, q^n); when O₁ can be taken to be a (nondegenerate) conic, the regular pseudo-oval is called a pseudo-conic.

A sub pseudo-conic of an egg O(n, 2n, q) is a subset of q^n + 1 of its elements that all lie in a common (3n−1)-dimensional subspace and form a pseudo-conic there.

Question: Must every egg O(n, 2n, q) that contains a sub pseudo-conic be good?

For q even, results of Brown and Lavrauw show that an egg O(n,2n,q) containing a pseudo-conic is classical (arising from an elliptic quadric), and classical eggs are good at every element; thus the answer is affirmative in even characteristic. For q odd, no general resolution of the question appears in the literature found, so the problem appears to remain open in the odd case.

Consider a Fizeau-type optical interferometric imaging system consisting of two circular apertures of diameter D separated by a baseline of length B, mounted on a common alt-azimuth platform so that the baseline orientation with respect to the sky can take prescribed angles θ_1,…,θ_p. For each baseline orientation θ_k the instrument records, on a two-dimensional detector of N×N pixels, a noisy image

   g_k(x) = (H_k * f)(x) + n_k(x),    x ∈ Ω ⊂ ℝ^2,  k = 1,…,p,

of the same astronomical target with intensity distribution f(x) ≥ 0. The blurring is assumed to be linear, but the point-spread function (PSF) H_k(x, y) depends not only on the baseline orientation θ_k and on the residual adaptive-optics correction in the field, but also on the position x in the field of view, so that

   (H_k * f)(x) = ∫ H_k(x, y) f(y) dy,

i.e. H_k is space-variant. The system can produce simultaneous images of a finite set of natural reference stars located at positions {x_j} inside the field of view, from which samples H_k(x_j, ·) of the PSF are available.

Devise a multiple-image deconvolution procedure for estimating f from the data {g_k}_{k=1}^p which:

(i) from the star images {H_k(x_j, ·)}, builds a model of the spatial variation of each H_k(x, ·) across the field;

(ii) partitions the field of view Ω into a collection of overlapping subdomains Ω_1,…,Ω_M on each of which H_k can be approximated, with prescribed accuracy, by a space-invariant PSF H_k^{(m)};

(iii) on each subdomain Ω_m performs a multiple-image deconvolution of the restricted data, using a method (for instance a maximum-likelihood iteration for Poisson noise such as the Ooe–Richardson–Lucy or Scaled Gradient Projection scheme) that correctly handles the boundary effects produced by the truncation of the convolution to Ω_m;

(iv) recombines the local reconstructions {f̂_m}_{m=1}^M into a single mosaic estimate f̂ of f over Ω in a way that ensures continuity and consistency in the overlap regions.

Provide a fully specified algorithm together with the convergence and accuracy guarantees required for it to constitute a practical solution of the space-variant multiple-image reconstruction problem for such a Fizeau interferometer.

Consider a modal language MS interpreted over metric models. A metric model is a pair $(M,\nu)$ where $M=(W,d)$ is a metric space — that is, $W$ is a nonempty set and $d:W\times W\to\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}$ satisfies (i) $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$, (ii) $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and (iii) $d(x,z)\leq d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ — and $\nu$ assigns to each predicate letter a subset of $W$ and to each nominal a singleton subset of $W$. Formulas (terms) of MS are built from predicate letters and nominals using Boolean negation, set difference, and distance modalities. In the fragment under consideration, only the following two distance modalities are allowed, with parameter $a\in\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}$:
\[\exists^{\leq a}\tau, \qquad \exists^{> a}\tau.\]
Semantics: $x\models \exists^{\leq a}\tau$ iff there exists $y\in W$ with $d(x,y)\leq a$ and $y\models\tau$; $x\models \exists^{> a}\tau$ iff there exists $y\in W$ with $d(x,y)>a$ and $y\models\tau$. A formula $\varphi$ is satisfiable in this class if there is a metric model and a point $x$ such that $x\models\varphi$.

Determine the exact computational complexity of the satisfiability problem for formulas of this fragment over metric models, under the convention that all rational numerical parameters $a$ occurring in the input formula are encoded in binary.

Consider a Fizeau interferometric imaging system that produces multiple long-exposure images $g_j$, $j=1,\dots,p$, of the same astronomical scene at different parallactic angles, each modeled as

$$g_j = K_j f + b_j + n_j,$$

where $f \ge 0$ is the unknown sky brightness distribution defined on a discrete pixel grid, $K_j$ is a known linear shift-invariant imaging operator (convolution with the corresponding point spread function of the interferometric baseline at orientation $j$), $b_j$ is a known background, and $n_j$ is Poisson photon noise. Assume the target $f$ has the form

$$f = c\,\delta_{x_0} + h,$$

i.e.\ the superposition of one (or several) bright point sources of unknown intensity $c>0$ located at known positions $x_0$ and a non-negative diffuse component $h \ge 0$ representing extended faint structure, such that the integrated flux ratio between the point source and the diffuse component is very large (high dynamic range) and the angular support of $h$ contains $x_0$ (the bright source overlaps spatially with the diffuse emission rather than being well separated from it).

Design a reconstruction algorithm — for instance a regularized maximum-likelihood method of the form

$$\min_{c \ge 0,\, h \ge 0}\; \sum_{j=1}^p D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(g_j \,\|\, K_j(c\,\delta_{x_0}+h)+b_j\big) + \mu\, R(h),$$

with $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ the Kullback–Leibler (Csiszár) divergence appropriate for Poisson data and $R$ a smoothness-promoting regularizer acting on the diffuse component — that, in the overlapping high-dynamic-range regime, simultaneously recovers (i) the intensity $c$ of the bright point source and (ii) the diffuse structure $h$ underneath it, without the point source's reconstruction artifacts contaminating the recovered diffuse emission. Establish convergence and stability properties of the resulting iterative scheme, and prove (or characterize) the conditions on the dynamic range, on the point spread functions $\{K_j\}$, and on the regularization functional $R$ under which the diffuse component beneath the bright source can be faithfully recovered.

Consider a multi-frame imaging model in which p observed images g_j : Z^2 -> R_{>=0} (j = 1, ..., p) of a common astronomical object f : Z^2 -> R_{>=0} are produced by convolution with unknown point-spread functions (PSFs) K_j : Z^2 -> R_{>=0}, possibly corrupted by Poisson noise:

   g_j ≈ Poisson(K_j * f),   j = 1, ..., p.

The object f and each PSF K_j are required to satisfy the following physical constraints:
  (i) Nonnegativity: f >= 0, K_j >= 0.
  (ii) Normalization / flux conservation: sum_x K_j(x) = 1.
  (iii) Band-limiting: the Fourier transforms of the K_j are supported in a prescribed bounded region Ω ⊂ R^2 (the optical transfer function support of a Fizeau interferometric aperture).
  (iv) Strehl-ratio information: a known lower bound s_j ∈ (0,1] on the Strehl ratio of K_j, defined as the ratio of the peak of the in-focus PSF to that of the corresponding diffraction-limited PSF.

The joint blind (or myopic, when partial knowledge of K_j is available) deconvolution problem is to recover (f, K_1, ..., K_p) from the data {g_j} by minimizing a data-fidelity functional (e.g. the Kullback–Leibler divergence)

   J(f, K_1, ..., K_p) = sum_{j=1}^p D_{KL}(g_j || K_j * f)

subject to constraints (i)–(iv).

Tasks:

(a) Reformulate this constrained joint estimation problem as a nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) problem, identifying the matrices whose nonnegative factorization corresponds to (f, K_1, ..., K_p) and showing how the constraints (i)–(iv) translate into constraints on the factors.

(b) Using this reformulation, design a computationally efficient iterative algorithm (for example, of multiplicative-update or alternating-projection type) that enforces all constraints (i)–(iv) at every iteration.

(c) Provide a rigorous convergence analysis: prove that the iterates produce a monotonically nonincreasing sequence of objective values and that limit points are stationary points of J on the constraint set.

(d) Establish identifiability/uniqueness conditions (up to natural ambiguities) under which the joint reconstruction of f and the K_j is well-posed given the constraints (i)–(iv).

For a subset $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and a real parameter $\alpha\ge -1$, define the upper $\alpha$-density of $A$ by
$$\overline{d}_\alpha(A)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{k\in A,\,k\le n}k^\alpha}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^\alpha}.$$
It is known that the map $\alpha\mapsto \overline{d}_\alpha(A)$ is non-decreasing on $[-1,\infty)$, so the limit
$$\overline{d}_\infty(A)=\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\overline{d}_\alpha(A)$$
exists. Recall also the upper uniform (Banach) density
$$u(A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{k\ge 0}\frac{|A\cap[k+1,k+n]|}{n},$$
and the asymptotic (natural) density $d$ on subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ where it is defined. Let
$$\mathcal{S}(A)=\{B\subseteq\mathbb{N}:d(A\triangle B)=0\},$$
where $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference.

It is straightforward that $\overline{d}_\infty(A)\le u(A)$ and that every $B\in\mathcal{S}(A)$ shares all $\alpha$-densities with $A$, hence
$$\overline{d}_\infty(A)\le \inf\{u(B):B\in\mathcal{S}(A)\}.$$

Problem: Characterize $\overline{d}_\infty(A)$ in terms of intrinsic combinatorial or structural properties of the set $A$. In particular, determine the precise relationship between $\overline{d}_\infty(A)$, the upper Banach density $u(A)$, and the quantity $\inf\{u(B):B\in\mathcal{S}(A)\}$; decide whether either of the inequalities above can be equalities in general, and if not, give examples and a complete description of the gap.

representations.normalized:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. The modal language $\mathcal{MT}$ for metric spaces has, for every positive rational $a>0$, two unary modal operators $\exists^{\le a}$ and $\exists^{<a}$ (often written $\langle\le a\rangle$ and $\langle <a\rangle$), interpreted in a model $(X,d,\nu)$, where $\nu$ assigns a subset of $X$ to each propositional variable, by
$$x\models \exists^{\le a}\varphi \iff \exists y\in X\,(d(x,y)\le a\wedge y\models\varphi),$$
$$x\models \exists^{<a}\varphi \iff \exists y\in X\,(d(x,y)< a\wedge y\models\varphi),$$
with the usual Boolean connectives. Extend the language $\mathcal{MT}$ to a hybrid language $\mathcal{MT}(\mathsf{nom})$ by adding a countable set $\mathsf{Nom}$ of nominals (location constants) $i,j,\dots$, where each nominal is required to be interpreted by a singleton subset $\{x_i\}\subseteq X$, and where nominals appear as atomic formulas (so the satisfaction clause is $x\models i\iff x=x_i$).

Determine the logical and computational properties of $\mathcal{MT}(\mathsf{nom})$ interpreted over the class of all metric spaces. In particular:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Axiomatize the set of $\mathcal{MT}(\mathsf{nom})$-formulas valid in every metric space, and decide whether this logic is finitely axiomatizable.
\item Determine the decidability and, if decidable, the computational complexity of the satisfiability problem for $\mathcal{MT}(\mathsf{nom})$ over arbitrary metric spaces, and over natural subclasses such as the real line $\mathbb{R}$, Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$, and finite metric spaces.
\item Analyze whether adding nominals to $\mathcal{MT}$ changes the expressive power, the finite model property, and the complexity in comparison with plain $\mathcal{MT}$.
\end{enumerate}

Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ be a set of positive integers with positive asymptotic density $d$, meaning $\lim_{n\to\infty} n/a_n = d \in (0,1]$.

(a) Does there always exist a subset $B=\{b_1<b_2<\cdots\}\subseteq A$ having positive asymptotic density $d_0$ with $0<d_0\le d$, such that the convergence $n/b_n\to d_0$ is faster than the convergence $n/a_n\to d$? Equivalently, do there exist such a $B$ and a function $f:\mathbb{N}\to(0,\infty)$ with $f(n)\to 0$ for which
$$b_n=\frac{n}{d_0}\bigl(1+o(f(n))\bigr)\qquad(n\to\infty)?$$

(b) In particular, can this be achieved with the explicit rate $f(n)=1/\log n$, i.e. can one always find $B\subseteq A$ of positive asymptotic density $d_0\in(0,d]$ with
$$b_n=\frac{n}{d_0}\Bigl(1+o\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\log n}\right)\Bigr)?$$

Either prove that such a subset $B$ always exists, or exhibit a set $A$ of positive asymptotic density for which no such $B$ exists.

representations.normalized:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. The modal-style distance language $\mathrm{MT}$ is built from a countable set of propositional variables using Boolean connectives together with, for every positive rational $a>0$, two unary "distance" operators
$$\exists^{<a}\varphi, \qquad \exists^{\le a}\varphi.$$
A model is a pair $(X,d,\nu)$ where $\nu$ assigns to each propositional variable a subset of $X$. The semantics is defined inductively in the usual Boolean way, with
$$x\models \exists^{<a}\varphi \iff \exists y\in X\ (d(x,y)<a \text{ and } y\models\varphi),$$
$$x\models \exists^{\le a}\varphi \iff \exists y\in X\ (d(x,y)\le a \text{ and } y\models\varphi).$$
A formula $\varphi$ is satisfiable in a metric space $(X,d)$ if there exist a valuation $\nu$ and a point $x\in X$ such that $x\models\varphi$.

Let $\mathrm{Sat}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ denote the set of $\mathrm{MT}$-formulas satisfiable in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with its standard metric, and more generally let $\mathrm{Sat}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ denote the set of $\mathrm{MT}$-formulas satisfiable in some subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the inherited metric.

Question: Is $\mathrm{Sat}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ recursively enumerable? Is $\mathrm{Sat}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ recursively enumerable? Furthermore, do the answers change if the non-strict distance operators $\exists^{\le a}$ are removed from the language (leaving only $\exists^{<a}$)?
