Let $n \geq 2$ and let $L : \mathbb{C}^n \to (0,\infty)$ be a positive continuous function. For an entire function $F : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ and a nonzero direction $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$, the function $F$ is said to have bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{b}$ if there exists a nonnegative integer $m_0$ such that, for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$,
$$\frac{|\partial^k_{\mathbf{b}} F(z)|}{k!\, L(z)^k} \leq \max_{0 \leq j \leq m_0} \frac{|\partial^j_{\mathbf{b}} F(z)|}{j!\, L(z)^j} \qquad \text{for all } k \in \mathbb{N}_0,$$
where $\partial_{\mathbf{b}} F(z) = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i \frac{\partial F}{\partial z_i}(z)$ is the directional derivative and $\partial^k_{\mathbf{b}}$ denotes its $k$-th iterate. The least such $m_0$ is called the $L$-index of $F$ in the direction $\mathbf{b}$.

Determine the smallest (in the sense of inclusion, or of minimal cardinality) subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$ with the following property: for every entire function $F : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$, if $F$ has bounded $L$-index in every direction $\mathbf{b} \in A$, then $F$ has bounded $L$-index in every nonzero direction $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$.

A partial word over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is a sequence whose entries are either letters of $\Sigma$ or a special "hole" symbol $\diamond$ that is considered to match every letter (and itself). A pattern is a nonempty word $p$ over an alphabet of variables. An infinite partial word $w$ over $\Sigma$ is said to meet the pattern $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h$ from the variable alphabet to nonempty partial words over $\Sigma$ such that $h(p)$ occurs as a factor of $w$ in the sense that every defined position matches the corresponding position of $w$ (with $\diamond$ matching anything). Otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. The partial word avoidability index of $p$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that there exists an infinite partial word over a $k$-letter alphabet (with infinitely many holes) that avoids $p$, or $\infty$ if no such $k$ exists.

An entire function $F : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to have bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{b}$ if there exists a nonnegative integer $m$ such that for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$,

Let $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ be a fixed direction, let $F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ be an entire function, and let $L:\mathbb{C}^n\to(0,\infty)$ be a continuous positive function. For each $z_0\in\mathbb{C}^n$ define the one-variable slice $g_{z_0}:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ and slice weight $l_{z_0}:\mathbb{C}\to(0,\infty)$ by
$$g_{z_0}(t)=F(z_0+t\mathbf{b}),\qquad l_{z_0}(t)=L(z_0+t\mathbf{b}).$$
Recall that for a (nonconstant) entire function $g$ of one variable and a positive continuous weight $l$, the $l$-index $N(g,l)$ is the least nonnegative integer $m$ (if any) such that for every $t\in\mathbb{C}$,
$$\frac{|g^{(k)}(t)|}{k!\,l(t)^k}\le \max_{0\le j\le m}\frac{|g^{(j)}(t)|}{j!\,l(t)^j}\qquad\text{for all }k\ge 0,$$
and the directional $L$-index $N_{\mathbf{b}}(F,L)$ is the least nonnegative integer $m$ such that for every $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$,
$$\frac{1}{k!\,L(z)^k}\Big|\frac{\partial^k F}{\partial \mathbf{b}^k}(z)\Big|\le \max_{0\le j\le m}\frac{1}{j!\,L(z)^j}\Big|\frac{\partial^j F}{\partial \mathbf{b}^j}(z)\Big|\qquad\text{for all }k\ge 0,$$
where $\partial F/\partial\mathbf{b}$ denotes the directional derivative along $\mathbf{b}$.

Determine the minimal conditions on a subset $A\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ of base points that guarantee
$$N_{\mathbf{b}}(F,L)=\sup\{\,N(g_{z_0},l_{z_0}):z_0\in A\,\}.$$
In other words, find the weakest geometric/measure-theoretic requirement on $A$ ensuring that the global directional $L$-index of $F$ can be recovered as the supremum of the one-variable $l_{z_0}$-indices of its slices along $\mathbf{b}$ over base points in $A$.

Let an alphabet be a finite set of letters and let ⋄ denote a special symbol called a hole. A partial word over an alphabet Σ is a (finite or infinite) sequence with entries in Σ ∪ {⋄}; positions containing ⋄ are called holes and are considered compatible with every letter of Σ. A factor of a partial word is any contiguous block of its entries. For a positive integer λ, a partial word is said to be λ-sparse if every factor of length λ contains at least one hole.

A pattern is a nonempty word p over a pattern alphabet of variables. An occurrence of p in a partial word w is a morphism h sending each variable to a nonempty partial word such that the image h(p) is compatible with some factor of w (i.e., matches it in every non-hole position); the occurrence is called trivial if h sends some variable to a partial word consisting of a single hole, and non-trivial otherwise. The partial word w avoids p if no occurrence of p appears in w; it avoids p non-trivially if no non-trivial occurrence appears.

For a binary pattern p (a pattern over an alphabet of two variables) and an integer k ≥ 1, define
- ms(p,k) = the smallest positive integer λ such that there exists an infinite λ-sparse partial word over a k-letter alphabet that avoids p, and ms(p,k) = ∞ if no such infinite λ-sparse partial word exists for any λ;
- ms*(p,k) = the analogous quantity where avoidance is required only non-trivially.

Problem: For every binary pattern p and every alphabet size k ≥ 1, determine the values of ms(p,k) and ms*(p,k) (including determining when they are infinite).

A partial word over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is a sequence $w \in (\Sigma \cup \{\diamond\})^*$ or $w \in (\Sigma \cup \{\diamond\})^\omega$, where the symbol $\diamond$ denotes a "hole" (a do-not-care position). Two full words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$ of the same length are abelian equivalent if every letter of $\Sigma$ occurs the same number of times in $u$ as in $v$. A partial word $w$ is said to contain an abelian $n$-th power if there exist factors $w[i_0..i_1-1], w[i_1..i_2-1], \dots, w[i_{n-1}..i_n-1]$ of $w$, all of the same length, such that for some choice of full words $u_1, \dots, u_n \in \Sigma^*$ that are pairwise abelian equivalent, each factor is compatible with the corresponding $u_j$ (i.e., agrees with $u_j$ at every non-hole position). Otherwise $w$ is called abelian $n$-free.

It is known that there exist infinite abelian $n$-free partial words containing infinitely many holes, but that no such partial word can have the gaps between consecutive holes bounded by a constant.

Question: For each integer $n \ge 2$, determine the smallest possible asymptotic growth rate of the gaps between consecutive holes in an infinite abelian $n$-free partial word over some finite alphabet that contains infinitely many holes. In particular, can such a partial word be constructed in which the distance between consecutive holes is bounded above by a polynomial in their index (rather than only by an exponential function)?

Let $n\geq 2$ and let $l:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{R}_+$ be a continuous positive function. For each $j=1,\dots,n$, define $l_j:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+$ by $l_j(z)=l(z_j)$, where $z=(z_1,\dots,z_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n$. Let $e_j$ denote the $j$-th standard coordinate direction in $\mathbb{C}^n$.

Recall that an entire function $F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ is said to be of bounded $l_j$-index in the direction $e_j$ if there exists $N\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ such that for all $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$ and all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_+$,
$$\frac{1}{k!}\,\frac{\left|\partial^k F(z)/\partial z_j^k\right|}{l_j(z)^k} \leq \max_{0\le m\le N}\frac{1}{m!}\,\frac{\left|\partial^m F(z)/\partial z_j^m\right|}{l_j(z)^m}.$$
The smallest such $N$ is the $l_j$-index of $F$ in direction $e_j$.

For a fixed point $(z_1^0,\dots,z_{n-1}^0)\in\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$, the entire function $g(w)=F(z_1^0,\dots,z_{n-1}^0,w)$ of one variable is said to be of bounded $l$-index if there exists $N\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ (possibly depending on $(z_1^0,\dots,z_{n-1}^0)$) such that for all $w\in\mathbb{C}$ and all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_+$,
$$\frac{|g^{(k)}(w)|}{k!\,l(w)^k}\leq \max_{0\le m\le N}\frac{|g^{(m)}(w)|}{m!\,l(w)^m}.$$

Suppose an entire function $F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For each $j=1,\dots,n-1$, $F$ has bounded $l_j$-index in the direction $e_j$.
\item For every fixed $(z_1^0,\dots,z_{n-1}^0)\in\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$, the entire function $w\mapsto F(z_1^0,\dots,z_{n-1}^0,w)$ has bounded $l$-index in $\mathbb{C}$.
\end{enumerate}
Determine whether $F$ must have bounded $l_n$-index in the direction $e_n$ (in the uniform sense, i.e., with a single bound $N$ valid at all points of $\mathbb{C}^n$).

Let $n \geq 3$. For an entire function $F : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$, a nonzero direction vector $\mathbf{b} = (b_1, \dots, b_n) \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$, and a positive continuous function $L : \mathbb{C}^n \to (0, \infty)$, recall the following.

(a) The function $F$ is said to have bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{b}$ if there exists a nonnegative integer $m$ such that for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$,
$$\frac{|\partial_{\mathbf{b}}^k F(z)|}{k!\, L(z)^k} \le \max_{0 \le j \le m} \frac{|\partial_{\mathbf{b}}^j F(z)|}{j!\, L(z)^j} \quad \text{for all } k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},$$
where $\partial_{\mathbf{b}} F(z) = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i \frac{\partial F}{\partial z_i}(z)$ is the directional derivative. The smallest such $m$ is the $L$-index of $F$ in the direction $\mathbf{b}$.

(b) For each fixed $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}^n$, the slice function $g_{z_0}(t) = F(z_0 + t\mathbf{b})$ is an entire function of one complex variable $t \in \mathbb{C}$. Set $\ell_{z_0}(t) = L(z_0 + t\mathbf{b})$. The slice $g_{z_0}$ is said to have bounded $\ell_{z_0}$-index if there exists a nonnegative integer $m_{z_0}$ such that
$$\frac{|g_{z_0}^{(k)}(t)|}{k!\, \ell_{z_0}(t)^k} \le \max_{0 \le j \le m_{z_0}} \frac{|g_{z_0}^{(j)}(t)|}{j!\, \ell_{z_0}(t)^j} \quad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{C},\ k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}.$$

Construct an explicit triple $(F, \mathbf{b}, L)$ with $n \geq 3$ such that every slice $g_{z_0}$ has bounded $\ell_{z_0}$-index (the bound $m_{z_0}$ being allowed to depend on $z_0$), while $F$ does not have bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{b}$.

Define a magic matrix of order $n$ to be an $n\times n$ matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ with real entries such that:
(i) every entry $a_{ij}$ belongs to $\{1,2,\ldots,n^{2}\}$;
(ii) all entries are distinct, i.e. $a_{ij}\neq a_{kl}$ whenever $(i,j)\neq(k,l)$;
(iii) the sum of the entries in each row, in each column, on the main diagonal, and on the antidiagonal are all equal (necessarily to $n(n^{2}+1)/2$).

Decide whether the following statement holds:

For every magic matrix $A$ of order $n$, if $n$ is odd then $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$, and if $n$ is even then $\operatorname{rank}(A)<n$.

Either prove the statement, or exhibit a counterexample.

Let $k\ge 2$ be an integer, and let $G$ be a finite simple graph with $m$ edges and vertex set $V(G)$. Define
$$h(m)=\sqrt{2m+\tfrac14}-\tfrac12.$$
For a partition $(V_1,V_2,\dots,V_k)$ of $V(G)$ into $k$ (possibly empty) parts, let $e(V_i)$ denote the number of edges of $G$ with both endpoints in $V_i$, and let
$$e(V_1,V_2,\dots,V_k)=m-\sum_{i=1}^{k} e(V_i)$$
denote the number of edges of $G$ with endpoints in distinct parts. Does there always exist a partition $(V_1,V_2,\dots,V_k)$ of $V(G)$ such that both of the following hold simultaneously:
$$e(V_1,V_2,\dots,V_k)\ \ge\ \frac{k-1}{k}\,m+\frac{k-1}{2k}\,h(m)-\frac{k-2}{8k},$$
$$\max_{1\le i\le k} e(V_i)\ \le\ \frac{m}{k^2}+\frac{k-1}{2k^2}\,h(m)\,?$$

Each of the two bounds is known individually (proved by Bollobás and Scott). The question of whether a single partition can achieve both bounds simultaneously was raised by Bollobás and Scott as an open problem (Problem 1 in their judicious-partitions problem list). Recent surveys and work on judicious k-partitions (e.g., Ma and collaborators) discuss progress on related judicious partition problems but the simultaneous version for all k≥2 does not appear to have been fully resolved.

$$-\Delta u = |u|^4 u + \lambda u \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial \Omega,$$
where solutions $u : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ are sought in the classical (smooth) sense. Note that the nonlinearity has the critical Sobolev exponent $5 = (n+2)/(n-2)$ for $n=3$, and it is known that for $\lambda$ in this range any nontrivial solution must be non-radial and sign-changing. Determine whether there exists a solution $u \not\equiv 0$ to this problem for every $\lambda \in (0, \lambda_1/4]$.

Let G = (V, E, w) be an edge-weighted planar graph with nonnegative edge weights w : E → ℝ≥0. A bisection of G is a partition of V into two disjoint sets V1, V2 with V = V1 ∪ V2 satisfying ||V1| − |V2|| ≤ 1. The weight (or cost) of a bisection is the sum of w(e) over all edges e ∈ E with one endpoint in V1 and the other in V2. The minimum bisection problem on weighted planar graphs asks, given such a G, to compute a bisection of minimum cost.

Determine the computational complexity of this problem: is it solvable in polynomial time, or is it NP-hard?

The complexity of minimum bisection on (weighted) planar graphs appears to remain open: it is not known whether the problem is in P or NP-hard. Work by Lee–Loh–Sudakov and subsequent papers (including a note in the Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society and the article "On judicious bisections of graphs") provide upper bounds of the form $c(k)\le 1/4 - \Omega(1/k)$ that are asymptotically tight as $k\to\infty$, but the exact value of $c(k)$ for each fixed $k\ge 1$ is not determined. The problem is generally cited as still open.

It is known that every graph $G$ with $m$ edges and minimum degree at least $2k$ or $2k+1$ admits a bisection $(S,T)$ satisfying
$$\max\{e(S),e(T)\}\le\left(\frac{k+1}{2(2k+1)}+o(1)\right)m,$$

Determine whether the $o(1)$ error term can be removed. That is, decide whether every graph with $m$ edges and minimum degree at least $2k$ (respectively at least $2k+1$) admits a bisection $(S,T)$ with
$$\max\{e(S),e(T)\}\le\frac{k+1}{2(2k+1)}\,m.$$

$$\Delta u_i = u_i\, |\nabla u|^2, \qquad i = 1, 2, 3, \qquad |u| = 1 \text{ in } \Omega,$$
with prescribed boundary data
$$u(x,y) = g(x,y) \text{ on } \partial\Omega.$$
Fix a constant $R \in (0,1)$ and choose the boundary datum

$$\lambda = \frac{1}{R} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{R^2} - 1}, \qquad \mu = \frac{1}{R} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{R^2} - 1},$$

A graph G is k-connected if it has more than k vertices and remains connected after the deletion of any fewer than k vertices. An induced path in G is a path P such that the subgraph of G induced by V(P) is exactly P (i.e., no chords). For a subgraph H of G, let G - V(H) denote the graph obtained from G by deleting the vertices of H together with all incident edges.

Prove or disprove: for every integer l ≥ 3, there exists an integer f(l) such that for every f(l)-connected graph G and every pair of distinct vertices x, y of G, there exists an induced x–y path P in G for which G - V(P) is l-connected.

(It is known that such an f exists with f(1) = 3 and f(2) = 5; the question concerns all l ≥ 3.)

The induced-path removal conjecture of Lovász/Kriesell is verified for l = 1 (Tutte's wheel theorem) and l = 2 (Kriesell; Chen et al.). For l ≥ 3 the existence of f(l) remains open. Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple undirected graph. A (proper) coloring of G is an assignment of colors to the vertices of G such that no two adjacent vertices receive the same color. For an integer k ≥ 1, the Coloring problem takes as input a graph G and an integer k, and asks whether G admits a proper coloring using at most k colors.

An induced cycle in G is a cycle whose vertex set induces, in G, exactly the edges of that cycle (a chordless cycle). Call a graph even-cycle-free if it contains no induced cycle of even length, and even-anticycle-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to the complement of an even-length cycle.

Determine the computational complexity (e.g., polynomial-time solvable, NP-complete, or otherwise) of the Coloring problem in each of the following two cases:
(a) the input graph G is restricted to be even-cycle-free;
(b) the input graph G is restricted to be even-anticycle-free.

A graph G=(V,E) is called chordal bipartite if it is bipartite and every induced cycle in G has exactly four vertices (equivalently, G is bipartite and contains no induced cycle of length at least 6).

Consider the following two decision problems on chordal bipartite graphs:

(a) LIST 3-COLORING. Given a chordal bipartite graph G=(V,E) together with a list assignment L: V → 2^{{1,2,3}}, decide whether there exists a proper coloring c: V → {1,2,3} such that c(v) ∈ L(v) for every v ∈ V and c(u) ≠ c(v) whenever uv ∈ E.

(b) 3-PRECOLORING EXTENSION. Given a chordal bipartite graph G=(V,E), a subset W ⊆ V, and a proper coloring c_W : W → {1,2,3}, decide whether c_W can be extended to a proper 3-coloring c: V → {1,2,3} of G.

Determine the computational complexity of each of these two problems on the class of chordal bipartite graphs: is each of them solvable in polynomial time, or is it NP-complete?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The complexity of List 3-Coloring and 3-Precoloring Extension restricted to chordal bipartite graphs is reported as open in the literature. Related results show that 4-List Coloring is NP-complete on P8-free chordal bipartite graphs, 4-Precoloring Extension is NP-complete on P10-free chordal bipartite graphs, and 3-Precoloring Extension is NP-complete on bipartite (and planar bipartite) graphs in general, but no resolution of the 3-coloring variants on chordal bipartite graphs has been found.

In particular, decide whether this restricted problem is solvable in polynomial time or is NP-complete.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is widely cited as open. It is known that k-Coloring is NP-complete for graphs of maximum degree at most k + ⌈√k⌉ − 1, and combined with Brooks' theorem the smallest unresolved case is exactly 5-Coloring on graphs of maximum degree 6. Recent surveys on graph coloring complexity continue to list this as an open problem.

For a nonnegative integer $p$, call a graph $G$ a "complete $+pv$" graph if there exists a set $S\subseteq V(G)$ with $|S|\le p$ such that $G-S$ is a complete graph. Consider the following two problems on complete $+pv$ graphs:

(1) List Coloring: each vertex $v$ is given a list $L(v)$ of admissible colors; decide whether there is a proper coloring $c$ of $G$ with $c(v)\in L(v)$ for every vertex $v$.

(2) Precoloring Extension: given an integer $k$ and a partial proper $k$-coloring of a subset of vertices of $G$, decide whether it extends to a proper $k$-coloring of all of $G$.

Determine the parameterized complexity of List Coloring and of Precoloring Extension on complete $+pv$ graphs when parameterized by $p$. In particular, decide for each problem whether it is fixed-parameter tractable, admits a polynomial kernel, or is $\mathrm{W}[1]$-hard with respect to $p$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem was resolved by Hermelin, Kratsch, and others (STACS 2020): with respect to the size $k$ of a clique modulator (equivalently the parameter $p$ for complete $+pv$ graphs), List Coloring admits an $O^*(2^k)$ randomized FPT algorithm, and Precoloring Extension admits a kernel with at most $3k$ vertices. This directly answers the open question.

In the online graph coloring model, the vertices of a graph G are revealed one at a time together with all edges connecting the newly revealed vertex to previously revealed vertices; upon revelation, each vertex must be assigned a color (a positive integer), different from the colors of its already-revealed neighbors, and this assignment is irrevocable. An online coloring algorithm is a (deterministic) rule that produces such a coloring for any input order. For a graph G, let chi_OL(G) denote the minimum, over all online coloring algorithms A, of the maximum number of colors used by A over all possible vertex orderings of G. A class C of graphs is said to be online chi_OL-bounded if there exists a function h: N -> N and an online coloring algorithm A such that for every G in C and every ordering of V(G), the algorithm A uses at most h(chi_OL(G)) colors on G. For a positive integer k, let P_k denote the path on k vertices, and call a graph "P_k-free" if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to P_k.

Question: For every integer k >= 1, is the class of P_k-free bipartite graphs online chi_OL-bounded?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question is known to hold for small values of k: P_k-free bipartite graphs are online chi_OL-bounded for k up to 9 (results by Micek and others, e.g., the P_8- and P_9-free bipartite cases were established with explicit competitive algorithms). However, the general question "for every k" remains open; no positive result is known for all k, and the broader problem of whether bipartite graphs themselves admit an online competitive algorithm is also still open.

Let $H_1, H_2, H_3$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $C \subseteq H_1$ and $Q \subseteq H_2$ be nonempty closed convex sets, and let $A: H_1 \to H_3$ and $B: H_2 \to H_3$ be bounded linear operators. The split equality feasibility problem (SEFP) is to find $x \in C$ and $y \in Q$ such that
$$A x = B y.$$
An alternating algorithm is an iterative scheme that, given current iterates $(x_n, y_n)$, updates $x_{n+1}$ using the current $y_n$ and then updates $y_{n+1}$ using $x_{n+1}$ (rather than updating both coordinates simultaneously). The question is whether there exists an alternating iterative algorithm producing sequences $\{x_n\} \subset C$ and $\{y_n\} \subset Q$ that converge strongly (in norm) to a solution $(x^*, y^*)$ of the SEFP, under reasonable assumptions on $C, Q, A, B$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Moudafi's original alternating CQ algorithm yielded only weak convergence, and he posed the strong-convergence variant as an open question. Subsequent works have given affirmative answers: improved/relaxed alternating CQ algorithms and simultaneous iterative algorithms have been shown to converge strongly to a solution of the split equality (feasibility) problem in real Hilbert spaces.

Setup. A partial word over a finite alphabet A is a sequence whose entries are either letters of A or a distinguished "hole" symbol ⋄ (which is compatible with every letter). A pattern p is a (full) word over a pattern alphabet E = {α, β, γ, …} of variables. A pattern p is said to be k-avoidable in partial words if there exists an infinite partial word w over some alphabet of size k such that no factor of w is a "partial-word instance" of p, where a partial-word instance is obtained by applying a non-erasing morphism h: E* → A* (assigning to each variable a nonempty full word) and then allowing some positions of the resulting word to be replaced by ⋄ provided each occurrence pattern is preserved up to compatibility. The partial-word avoidability index μ_p(p) is the least integer k ≥ 1 such that p is k-avoidable in partial words (and ∞ if no such k exists, in which case p is called unavoidable in partial words).

Restrict attention to ternary patterns, i.e., patterns over exactly three variables {α, β, γ}.

Problems.
(a) For every ternary pattern p, determine the partial-word avoidability index μ_p(p), or, failing that, give nontrivial upper and lower bounds for μ_p(p).
(b) Determine an explicit bound L such that every ternary pattern of length greater than L is avoidable in partial words (equivalently, bound the length of the longest unavoidable ternary patterns).

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $\diamond \notin A$ denote a "hole" symbol that matches every letter of $A$. A partial word over $A$ is an infinite sequence $w \in (A \cup \{\diamond\})^{\mathbb{N}}$; a filling of $w$ is any word in $A^{\mathbb{N}}$ obtained from $w$ by replacing each occurrence of $\diamond$ with some letter of $A$.

Two finite words $u, v \in A^*$ are called abelian-equivalent if they have the same length and the same multiset (Parikh vector) of letters. For an integer $n \geq 2$, an abelian $n$-th power is a finite word of the form $u_1 u_2 \cdots u_n$ where $u_1, \dots, u_n$ are pairwise abelian-equivalent nonempty words. A partial word $w$ is said to avoid abelian $n$-th powers if there exists a filling of $w$ whose infinite word contains no factor that is an abelian $n$-th power.

For each $n \in \{3, 4, 5\}$, determine the minimum size $|A|$ of an alphabet $A$ for which there exists an infinite partial word over $A$ containing infinitely many holes that avoids abelian $n$-th powers.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of the minimum alphabet size needed for an infinite partial word with infinitely many holes avoiding abelian n-th powers (for n = 3, 4, 5) appears in the literature on abelian pattern avoidance in partial words as an explicit open problem. While related results have been obtained (e.g., constructions over binary alphabets avoiding abelian 6th powers, and resolved bounds for abelian squares), the exact thresholds for n = 3, 4, 5 with infinitely many holes do not appear to have been determined in subsequent work.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a smooth compact two-dimensional surface of revolution embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with induced metric, surface area $|\Omega|$, Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta_{\mathcal{S}}$, and Gaussian curvature $K(x)$ that varies along $\mathcal{S}$. Assume that the source-neutral Green's function $G(x;x_0)$ on $\mathcal{S}$, defined by
$$\Delta_{\mathcal{S}} G(x;x_0) = \tfrac{1}{|\Omega|} - \delta(x-x_0), \qquad \int_{\mathcal{S}} G(x;x_0)\,dS = 0,$$
is available in closed analytic form (e.g. by separation of variables in geodesic polar coordinates adapted to the rotational symmetry).

Consider a singularly perturbed activator–inhibitor reaction–diffusion system on $\mathcal{S}$ (for instance, a Schnakenberg- or Gierer–Meinhardt-type model with small activator diffusivity $\varepsilon^2 \ll 1$) admitting quasi-equilibrium localized spot solutions concentrated at points $x_1(t),\ldots,x_N(t) \in \mathcal{S}$ with slowly varying source strengths $S_1(t),\ldots,S_N(t)$.

(a) Derive, by matched asymptotic expansions in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$, an explicit differential-algebraic system of equations (DAE) governing the slow evolution of the spot locations $\{x_j(t)\}$ and source strengths $\{S_j(t)\}$ on $\mathcal{S}$, in which $G$ and its regular part $R(x_0) := \lim_{x\to x_0}(G(x;x_0)+\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\log d(x,x_0))$ enter as the only geometric data.

(b) Using the explicit form of $G$ on the surface of revolution, analyze the resulting DAE: characterize equilibrium spot configurations, their linear stability under slow translational perturbations, and determine whether the spatial variation of the Gaussian curvature $K$ can pin one or more spots at specific locations of $\mathcal{S}$ (i.e. produce isolated stable equilibria of the DAE that depend on $K$ rather than only on inter-spot interactions).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as an open direction: deriving and analyzing explicit DAE spot dynamics on general surfaces of revolution with varying curvature, and establishing curvature-induced pinning, has been treated rigorously only on the sphere (constant curvature). Subsequent works on curved-surface reaction-diffusion (e.g. weakly nonlinear analyses, curvature-dependent diffusion of Turing patterns, Turing pattern dynamics on curved surfaces in 2024–2025) study related phenomena but do not provide the explicit DAE reduction and pinning analysis requested here. No definitive resolution was located.

Background and definitions. A partial word over a finite alphabet A is a sequence whose letters belong to A together with a special symbol ⋄ (called a hole) that is regarded as "undefined" and is compatible with every letter of A. Two full words u, v over A of the same length are abelian equivalent (written u ~_ab v) if v is a permutation of the letters of u, equivalently if for every a ∈ A the number of occurrences of a in u equals the number of occurrences of a in v. A pattern is a nonempty word p over a pattern alphabet E = {x_1, x_2, …} of variables. A partial word w over A is said to meet the pattern p in the abelian sense if there exists a non-erasing morphism-like assignment that replaces each occurrence of a variable x_i in p by a factor of w in such a way that the resulting consecutive factors of w are pairwise abelian-equivalent whenever the corresponding variables are equal (and the holes ⋄ in w are treated as wildcards compatible with this equivalence). Otherwise, w avoids p in the abelian sense. A pattern p is called binary if it uses exactly two distinct variables.

Known bound. It is known that for every binary pattern p of length at least 360, there exists an infinite binary partial word containing infinitely many holes that avoids p in the abelian sense.

Problem. Determine the smallest integer N (or improve the value 360 as much as possible) such that the following statement still holds: for every binary pattern p of length at least N, there exists an infinite binary partial word with infinitely many holes that avoids p in the abelian sense.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Search located the original result establishing the length-360 sufficient bound for abelian avoidance of binary patterns by binary partial words with infinitely many holes (Blanchet-Sadri et al., RAIRO ITA 2014). Subsequent improvements for full words (e.g., every binary pattern of length > 14 is abelian-2-avoidable, MFCS 2016) do not address the partial-word setting with infinitely many holes. No source was found that explicitly improves the 360 bound in the partial-word setting, so the status is unclear.

Let $f:[0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be a continuous, decreasing function with $f(0)=b>1$ such that the map $x\mapsto xf(x)$ is increasing and bounded on $[0,\infty)$. For a parameter $h>0$, consider the second-order difference equation with delayed constant-yield harvesting
$$x_{n+1}=x_n f(x_{n-1})-h,\qquad n=0,1,2,\dots,$$
with initial conditions $(x_{-1},x_0)\in[0,\infty)^2$. Say that a solution persists if $x_n\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 0$ and the sequence does not become negative or extinct in finite time. Let
$$D_h=\{(x_{-1},x_0)\in[0,\infty)^2 : \text{the solution with these initial conditions persists}\}$$
be the largest persisting set for harvesting level $h$.

Prove or disprove: $D_h$ is monotone decreasing in $h$; that is, for all $0<h_1\le h_2$ one has $D_{h_2}\subseteq D_{h_1}$.

Consider the unit ball $B=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:|x|\le 1\}$ with boundary $S^2=\partial B$. On $S^2$, let $u(\xi,t)$ and $v(\xi,t)$ denote the activator and inhibitor concentrations of a Brusselator reaction-diffusion system, and inside $B$ let $U(x,t)$ denote a passively diffusing bulk concentration. The coupled bulk-surface system is

$$U_t = D_b\,\Delta_x U, \quad x\in B,\qquad U(x,0)\text{ given},$$
$$u_t = \varepsilon^2 \Delta_{S^2} u + E(\xi,t) - u + f\,u^2 v,\qquad \xi\in S^2,$$
$$\tau\, v_t = D\,\Delta_{S^2} v + \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\bigl(u - u^2 v\bigr),\qquad \xi\in S^2,$$
with coupling boundary conditions on $S^2$ of Robin/flux type
$$D_b\,\partial_\nu U + \kappa\bigl(U|_{S^2} - u\bigr)=0,\qquad E(\xi,t)= \beta\,U|_{S^2}(\xi,t),$$
so that the fuel supply $E$ on the surface represents an exchange flux between the surface activator and the bulk concentration. Here $0<\varepsilon\ll 1$, $D>0$ is large, $\tau,f,\beta,\kappa,D_b>0$ are parameters, $\Delta_{S^2}$ is the Laplace–Beltrami operator, and $\partial_\nu$ is the outward normal derivative.

In the singular limit $\varepsilon\to 0$, $D\to\infty$, construct strongly localized $N$-spot quasi-equilibrium solutions on $S^2$, with spot centers $\xi_1(t),\dots,\xi_N(t)\in S^2$ and source strengths $S_1(t),\dots,S_N(t)$. Derive the differential-algebraic system (DAE) governing the slow dynamics of the spot locations $\xi_j(t)$ and source strengths $S_j(t)$, together with the algebraic constraints coupling them to the boundary trace of $U$. Analyze the resulting localized spot-pattern dynamics: in particular, determine
(i) how bulk-surface coupling alters the existence thresholds, equilibrium configurations, and slow-time motion of the spots as compared to the uncoupled Brusselator on $S^2$;
(ii) the linear stability of the quasi-equilibrium spots with respect to amplitude (competition and self-replication) and shape (peanut-splitting) instabilities;
(iii) whether equilibrium spot configurations correspond to elliptic Fekete point sets on $S^2$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work has derived and analyzed the DAE for spot dynamics in a bulk-membrane-coupled Brusselator on the sphere/ball, establishing existence of quasi-equilibrium spot solutions, linear stability thresholds, and showing that bulk-membrane coupling can restrict spot existence via a recirculation mechanism (e.g., Gomez–Ward–Wei and related works, 2019–2021). Connections of equilibria to elliptic Fekete points have been verified numerically for small N. Thus the problem is partially resolved, with full classification of stability and global dynamics still being investigated.

Consider the normalized delayed Pielou harvesting difference equation
  x_{n+1} = b x_n / (1 + x_{n-1}) − h,  n = 0, 1, 2, …,
with real parameters b > 1 and 0 < h < 1, and positive initial values x_{-1}, x_0. The positive equilibria are the positive roots of x = bx/(1+x) − h, i.e. solutions of x^2 + (1 − b + h)x + h = 0. When these roots are real and positive, denote them by 0 < x̄_{1,h} < x̄_{2,h} (the lower and upper positive equilibria).

A solution {x_n} is called persistent if it remains positive for all n ≥ -1 and stays bounded away from 0 and from ∞.

Question: For every choice of parameters (b, h) with b > 1 and 0 < h < 1 for which both positive equilibria exist, is it true that every persistent solution {x_n} whose terms eventually satisfy x_n > x̄_{1,h} converges to the upper equilibrium x̄_{2,h} as n → ∞?

The question is posed as a conjecture about the delayed Pielou harvesting equation. Literature on related discrete delay logistic and Pielou-type harvesting models discusses stability and persistence but does not establish the conjectured global attractivity of the upper equilibrium for all persistent solutions exceeding the lower equilibrium. Consider the scalar discrete-time population model with no delay and periodic stocking
\[ x_{n+1} = x_n f(x_n) + h_n, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, \]
where:
- $f:[0,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ is a continuous, positive function such that $x \mapsto x f(x)$ is a (smooth) "contest competition" map: $x f(x)$ is bounded, has a unique positive fixed point, and is such that the unstocked equation $x_{n+1} = x_n f(x_n)$ has a globally attracting positive equilibrium on $(0,\infty)$;
- $\{h_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is a $p$-periodic sequence of nonnegative real numbers (stocking quotas) with $\sum_{n=0}^{p-1} h_n > 0$.

Under these hypotheses, for every choice (i.e. every cyclic ordering) of the quotas $h_0, h_1, \dots, h_{p-1}$, the equation admits a globally attracting positive $p$-periodic solution $\{x_n^*\}$. Define the temporal average over one period
\[ \bar{x}_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{1}{p}\sum_{n=0}^{p-1} x_n^*. \]

Now let $\sigma$ be any permutation of $\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$, and let $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{av}}$ denote the analogous average of the globally attracting $p$-periodic solution corresponding to the permuted stocking sequence $h_{\sigma(0)}, h_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, h_{\sigma(p-1)}$.

Determine the relationship between $\bar{x}_{\mathrm{av}}$ and $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{av}}$. In particular, decide whether $\bar{x}_{\mathrm{av}} = \hat{x}_{\mathrm{av}}$ holds for every permutation $\sigma$, every period $p$, and every admissible map $f$; and if not, characterize the orderings of the quotas that maximize and minimize the average $\bar{x}_{\mathrm{av}}$.

Fix constants $K>0$ and $\mu>1$, and let $p\ge 2$ be an integer. Consider the periodically harvested Beverton–Holt difference equation
$$x_{n+1} \;=\; \frac{K\mu\, x_n}{K+(\mu-1)x_n} \;-\; h_n, \qquad n=0,1,2,\dots,$$
where $\{h_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is a $p$-periodic sequence of nonnegative harvesting quotas. Assume the quotas $(h_0,h_1,\dots,h_{p-1})$ are chosen so that the equation admits a nonempty persistent set (i.e., there exist initial conditions for which $x_n>0$ for all $n$) and a globally attracting $p$-periodic cycle $(\bar x_0,\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_{p-1})$ on this set. Define the attractor average
$$\bar x_{\mathrm{av}} \;=\; \frac{1}{p}\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}\bar x_n.$$
Let $\sigma$ be any permutation of $\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$, and set $\hat h_n = h_{\sigma(n)}$ extended $p$-periodically. Assume the permuted equation
$$y_{n+1}=\frac{K\mu\, y_n}{K+(\mu-1)y_n}-\hat h_n$$
also has a nonempty persistent set with globally attracting cycle $(\hat x_0,\dots,\hat x_{p-1})$, and let $\hat x_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}\hat x_n$. Determine the precise relationship between $\bar x_{\mathrm{av}}$ and $\hat x_{\mathrm{av}}$: characterize those permutations $\sigma$ for which $\hat x_{\mathrm{av}}=\bar x_{\mathrm{av}}$, and for the remaining permutations decide whether $\hat x_{\mathrm{av}}\le \bar x_{\mathrm{av}}$ or $\hat x_{\mathrm{av}}\ge \bar x_{\mathrm{av}}$, or otherwise describe how the attractor average changes under permutation of the harvesting quotas.

Subsequent work (AlSharawi et al., "The effect of maps permutation on the global attractor of a periodic Beverton–Holt model," Applied Mathematics and Computation, 2020) addresses this problem. The authors show that the total harvesting yield is invariant under permutation, that all permutations within the dihedral group (rotations and reflections of the cyclic ordering) yield the same attractor average, and obtain a characterization based on block reflections of the harvesting quotas describing when other permutations change the attractor average. The problem is therefore partially resolved, though a complete comparison for arbitrary permutations is not fully closed.

Consider the second-order difference equation (a normalized delayed Pielou-type model with harvesting)

    x_{n+1} = (b x_n)/(1 + x_{n-1}) - h_n,    n = 0, 1, 2, ...,

where b > 0 is a parameter, the initial data x_{-1}, x_0 are positive, and h_n is a real sequence ("harvesting") chosen so that the iterates remain positive.

In the constant-harvesting case h_n ≡ 1, the function

    I_b(u, v) = ((1 + b)/(1 + u)) · ((1 + b)/(1 + v)) · (1 + u + v)

is an invariant of the dynamics, in the sense that I_b(x_n, x_{n-1}) is constant along every orbit (x_n) of the recurrence with h_n ≡ 1.

Now perturb the harvesting term to

    h_n = 1 ± ε_n,

where (ε_n) is either a periodic sequence of small real numbers or a more general nonautonomous bounded sequence with ε_n → 0 (or |ε_n| small).

Problem. Determine what happens to the invariant I_b under such perturbations. Specifically:
  (a) Does there exist a modified invariant (a function J_b(n, u, v), possibly depending on n through the perturbation, or an adiabatic/approximate invariant) which is exactly or approximately conserved by the perturbed dynamics?
  (b) Describe the behavior of the quantity I_b(x_n, x_{n-1}) along orbits of the perturbed equation: is it bounded, does it drift, and at what rate (in terms of ε_n) does it evolve?
  (c) In the periodic case ε_{n+p} = ε_n, analyze the long-term dynamics (existence, stability, and structure of periodic orbits) using these (possibly modified) invariants.

A graph is triangle-free if it contains no three mutually adjacent vertices. A graph is bipartite if its vertex set can be partitioned into two parts so that every edge has its endpoints in different parts. For a graph G, let b(G) denote the minimum number of edges whose deletion from G yields a bipartite graph.

Determine whether the following holds: for every real number ε > 0, there exists an integer n(ε) such that every triangle-free graph G on n > n(ε) vertices satisfies
   b(G) ≤ (1/25 + ε) n².

The statement is a conjecture of Bollobás and Scott on connected k-partitions. Surveys and follow-up works on judicious/max k-cut partitions (e.g., the Bollobás–Scott program, the Ma–Yen paper "On several partition problems of Bollobás and Scott", and "Better Bounds for k-Partitions of Graphs") list this connectivity-strengthened lower bound as a still-standing conjecture, with related partial results proved in special cases (e.g., k = 2 corresponds to known Edwards-type bounds for connected graphs), but no general resolution for arbitrary k ≥ 3 has been located.

Let $k \ge 2$ be an integer. For a (finite, simple) graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, a $k$-partition of $G$ is an ordered partition $(V_1, V_2, \dots, V_k)$ of its vertex set $V(G)$. For $S \subseteq V(G)$, let $e(S)$ denote the number of edges of $G$ with both endpoints in $S$.

(a) Prove or disprove: there exists a function $f_k(n) = O(n)$ (depending only on $k$) such that every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges admits a $k$-partition $(V_1, \dots, V_k)$ satisfying
$$\max_{1 \le i < j \le k} e(V_i \cup V_j) \;\le\; \frac{6m}{\binom{k+2}{2}} + f_k(n).$$

(b) Show, moreover, that there exists a constant $c(k) > 0$ such that if the minimum degree $\delta(G) \ge c(k)\, n$, then the additive $O(n)$ term in (a) can be removed; that is, $G$ admits a $k$-partition with
$$\max_{1 \le i < j \le k} e(V_i \cup V_j) \;\le\; \frac{6m}{\binom{k+2}{2}}.$$

The conjecture was described as "wildly open" in the surveyed literature. Subsequent work by Fan and Hou (Random Structures & Algorithms, 2017, "Bounds for pairs in judicious partitioning of graphs") and by Xu and Yu ("Better bounds for k-partitions of graphs", Combinatorics, Probability and Computing) establishes improved bounds approaching the conjectured value and resolves related problems of Bollobás and Scott in the affirmative, providing partial/asymptotic progress, but the exact bound 6m/binom(k+2,2) + O(n) for all k ≥ 2 (and the dense-graph statement without O(n)) does not appear to be fully settled.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph and let $M\subseteq E$ be a maximum matching of $G$. Denote by $V(M)$ the set of vertices incident with some edge of $M$. For an edge $xy\in M$ and a vertex $u\in V\setminus V(M)$, say that $x$ is a free neighbor of $u$ (with respect to $M$) if $xu\in E$ but $yu\notin E$. For each $u\in V\setminus V(M)$, let $F_M(u)$ denote the set of free neighbors of $u$. Two unmatched vertices $u,v\in V\setminus V(M)$ are said to have different free-neighbor sets if $F_M(u)\neq F_M(v)$.

Define $r(M)$ to be the maximum number of (vertex-disjoint) pairs $\{u_i,v_i\}$ of unmatched vertices such that $F_M(u_i)\neq F_M(v_i)$ for each pair, and define
$$r(G)=\max\{r(M): M\text{ is a maximum matching of }G\}.$$

It is known that for any fixed maximum matching $M$, $r(M)$ can be computed in polynomial time. Question: can $r(G)$ be determined in polynomial time (in $|V|+|E|$)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The statement is a folklore conjecture in graph partitioning. It has been verified for restricted subclasses of planar graphs (e.g., plane triangulations, where a minimum balanced bipartition with at most n cut edges has been shown to exist, with both parts inducing connected near-triangulations) and analogous O(n) or improved bounds are known for planar graphs without separating triangles, but no proof for all planar graphs has been published as of 2025.

Let $(A,\rightharpoonup,\rightsquigarrow,1)$ be a pseudo-BCK algebra, where $\rightharpoonup$ and $\rightsquigarrow$ are binary operations and $1$ is the top element with respect to the induced order $x\le y\iff x\rightharpoonup y=1\iff x\rightsquigarrow y=1$. Call $A$ an implicative pseudo-BCK algebra if, for all $x,y\in A$,
$$(x\rightsquigarrow y)\rightharpoonup x=x\quad\text{and}\quad(x\rightharpoonup y)\rightsquigarrow x=x.$$
A nonempty subset $F\subseteq A$ is a pseudo-filter if it is upward closed (with respect to $\le$) and, for all $x,y\in A$, $x\in F$ together with $x\rightharpoonup y\in F$ or $x\rightsquigarrow y\in F$ implies $y\in F$. A pseudo-filter $F$ is called:
- a Boolean filter if for all $x,y\in A$, $(x\rightharpoonup y)\rightsquigarrow x\in F\Rightarrow x\in F$ and $(x\rightsquigarrow y)\rightharpoonup x\in F\Rightarrow x\in F$;
- an implicative pseudo-filter if for all $x,y\in A$, $(x\rightharpoonup y)\rightharpoonup x\in F\Rightarrow x\in F$ and $(x\rightsquigarrow y)\rightsquigarrow x\in F\Rightarrow x\in F$.

Prove or disprove: $A$ is an implicative pseudo-BCK algebra if and only if every pseudo-filter of $A$ is a Boolean filter, and equivalently if and only if every pseudo-filter of $A$ is an implicative pseudo-filter.

Let k ≥ 3 and t ≥ 1 be fixed integers. Let P_t denote the path on t vertices. A graph G is P_t-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to P_t. A graph is bipartite if its vertex set admits a partition into two independent sets. A proper k-coloring of G is a function c : V(G) → {1,…,k} with c(u) ≠ c(v) whenever uv ∈ E(G).

Consider the following decision problems restricted to bipartite P_t-free graphs:

(A) k-Precoloring Extension. Input: a bipartite P_t-free graph G and a partial map c₀ : W → {1,…,k} defined on some subset W ⊆ V(G) such that c₀ is a proper coloring of G[W]. Question: can c₀ be extended to a proper k-coloring of G?

(B) List k-Coloring. Input: a bipartite P_t-free graph G together with a list assignment L : V(G) → 2^{{1,…,k}}. Question: does there exist a proper coloring c of G with c(v) ∈ L(v) for every v ∈ V(G)?

Determine the computational complexity (polynomial-time solvable vs. NP-complete) of:

  • k-Precoloring Extension on bipartite P_t-free graphs for each of the cases t ∈ {7, 8, 9} with k ∈ {3, 4, 5} or any fixed k ≥ 6, and for t ≥ 10 with k = 3.

  • List k-Coloring on bipartite P_t-free graphs for t = 7 with k ∈ {3, 4, 5} or any fixed k ≥ 6, and for each of t = 8, t = 9, and t ≥ 10 with k = 3.

Let $\mathbb{C}^m$ denote complex Euclidean $m$-space equipped with its standard Hermitian structure, with almost complex structure $J$ and standard flat Kähler metric. For an isometric immersion $f:M\to\mathbb{C}^m$ of a Riemannian manifold $M$, and for a point $p\in M$ and a nonzero tangent vector $X\in T_pM$, the Wirtinger angle $\theta(X)\in[0,\pi/2]$ is defined as the angle between $JX$ (viewed via $df$) and the tangent space $df(T_pM)\subset T_{f(p)}\mathbb{C}^m$. The immersion $f$ is called a slant immersion if $\theta(X)$ is constant, i.e.\ independent of both $p\in M$ and of the nonzero vector $X\in T_pM$. (Holomorphic immersions correspond to $\theta\equiv 0$ and totally real (in particular Lagrangian) immersions to $\theta\equiv\pi/2$; proper slant means $0<\theta<\pi/2$.)

A grid graph is a finite induced subgraph of the infinite graph whose vertex set is $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ and in which two vertices $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ are adjacent if and only if $|x_1-x_2|+|y_1-y_2|=1$. (Equivalently, a grid graph is the Cartesian product $P_m \square P_n$ of two paths, or an induced subgraph thereof.)

For a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, a proper $k$-coloring of $G$ is a map $c:V(G)\to\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $c(u)\neq c(v)$ whenever $uv\in E(G)$. A partial $k$-coloring of $G$ is a map $c_0:W\to\{1,\dots,k\}$ defined on some subset $W\subseteq V(G)$ such that $c_0(u)\neq c_0(v)$ whenever $u,v\in W$ are adjacent.

The Precoloring Extension problem takes as input a triple $(G,k,c_0)$, where $G$ is a graph, $k$ is a positive integer, and $c_0$ is a partial $k$-coloring of $G$, and asks whether there exists a proper $k$-coloring $c$ of $G$ such that $c(v)=c_0(v)$ for every vertex $v$ on which $c_0$ is defined.

Determine the computational complexity of Precoloring Extension when the input graph $G$ is restricted to be a grid graph.

Let $(\tilde M, J, \tilde g)$ be a Kähler manifold, with complex structure $J$ and compatible Riemannian metric $\tilde g$. A Riemannian submanifold $M \subset \tilde M$ is called a CR-submanifold if there exist two orthogonal smooth distributions $\mathcal D$ and $\mathcal D^\perp$ on $M$ with $TM = \mathcal D \oplus \mathcal D^\perp$ such that $\mathcal D$ is holomorphic (i.e. $J\mathcal D_p = \mathcal D_p$ for every $p \in M$) and $\mathcal D^\perp$ is totally real (i.e. $J\mathcal D^\perp_p \subset T_p^\perp M$ for every $p \in M$). An isometric immersion of a Riemannian manifold $M$ into a Kähler manifold realizing $M$ as a CR-submanifold is called a CR-immersion.

Recall that an (abstract) CR structure on a smooth manifold $M$ is a complex subbundle $H \subset T_{\mathbb C}M = TM \otimes \mathbb C$ such that $H \cap \overline H = 0$ and $H$ is involutive (i.e. $[H,H] \subset H$). Set $\mathrm{Re}(H \oplus \overline H) := \{X + \overline X : X \in H\} \subset TM$, a real distribution on $M$.

Three known necessary conditions for a Riemannian manifold $M$ to admit a CR-immersion into some Kähler manifold are:
(i) $M$ carries a CR structure $H$;
(ii) the orthogonal complementary distribution $(\mathrm{Re}(H \oplus \overline H))^\perp$ in $TM$ is integrable;
(iii) the distribution $\mathrm{Re}(H \oplus \overline H)$ is a minimal distribution (its leaves, where defined, are minimal).

Problem: Determine whether there exist additional obstructions, beyond conditions (i)–(iii), that prevent a Riemannian manifold $M$ from admitting a CR-immersion into a Kähler manifold; and if so, exhibit and characterize such obstructions.

(ii) the orthogonal complementary distribution $(\mathrm{Re}(H \oplus \overline H))^\perp$ in $TM$ is integrable;
(iii) the distribution $\mathrm{Re}(H \oplus \overline H)$ is a minimal distribution (its leaves, where defined, are minimal).

Problem: Determine whether there exist additional obstructions, beyond conditions (i)–(iii), that prevent a Riemannian manifold $M$ from admitting a CR-immersion into a Kähler manifold; and if so, exhibit and characterize such obstructions.

Chen's program list only the three classical obstructions. The problem appears to remain open.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold with Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$ acting on smooth functions. A smooth map $\phi : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ into a Euclidean $m$-space is said to be of finite type if it admits a decomposition
$$\phi = \phi_0 + \phi_{t_1} + \phi_{t_2} + \cdots + \phi_{t_k},$$
where $\phi_0$ is a constant map, $k$ is a positive integer, and for each $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$ the $\mathbb{E}^m$-valued component $\phi_{t_i}$ is a nonconstant eigenmap of $\Delta$, i.e. $\Delta \phi_{t_i} = \lambda_{t_i}\, \phi_{t_i}$ for some real number $\lambda_{t_i}$, with the $\lambda_{t_i}$ pairwise distinct. An isometric immersion $\phi: M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ is of finite type if it is of finite type as a map. An isometric immersion of $M$ into a real space form $N^m(c)$ of constant sectional curvature $c$ is said to be of finite type if its composition with the standard isometric embedding of $N^m(c)$ into a Euclidean space is of finite type in the above sense.

Determine intrinsic and/or extrinsic obstructions (geometric, topological, or analytic conditions on $M$) that prevent $M$ from admitting:

(a) a finite-type isometric immersion into some Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^m$;

(b) a finite-type isometric immersion into some real space form $N^m(c)$ (where $N^m(c)$ is given its standard isometric embedding into a Euclidean space).

In particular, characterize necessary conditions a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ must satisfy in order to admit such finite-type isometric immersions.

Let $G = (V,E)$ be a finite simple graph. Three pairwise distinct vertices $u, v, w \in V$ form an asteroidal triple if between any two of them there is a path in $G$ that avoids the closed neighborhood of the third. An asteroidal set in $G$ is an independent set $S \subseteq V$ such that every three vertices of $S$ form an asteroidal triple. The asteroidal number of $G$, denoted $\mathrm{an}(G)$, is the maximum size of an asteroidal set in $G$.

For an integer $k \ge 1$, consider the following decision problems on an input graph $G$:
- $k$-Coloring: does there exist a proper coloring $c: V \to \{1, \dots, k\}$?
- $k$-Precoloring Extension: given a subset $W \subseteq V$ and a proper coloring $c_W: W \to \{1, \dots, k\}$, does $c_W$ extend to a proper coloring $c: V \to \{1, \dots, k\}$?
- List $k$-Coloring: given lists $L(v) \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$ for each $v \in V$, does there exist a proper coloring $c$ with $c(v) \in L(v)$ for all $v$?

Problem: For every pair of fixed integers $k \ge 3$ and $p \ge 3$, determine the computational complexity (polynomial-time solvable vs. NP-complete) of each of $k$-Coloring, $k$-Precoloring Extension, and List $k$-Coloring when restricted to the class of graphs $G$ with $\mathrm{an}(G) \le p$.

An undirected simple graph G is called a comparability graph if each of its edges can be assigned a direction so that whenever (u,v) and (v,w) are directed edges of the resulting orientation, (u,w) is also a directed edge (i.e., the orientation is transitive). For a class of graphs F and a non-negative integer p, define:
- F − pe = { G : there exists a set E' of at most p edges of G such that G − E' ∈ F }, i.e., graphs obtainable from a member of F by adding at most p edges; equivalently, graphs that become a member of F after deleting at most p edges.
- F + pv = { G : there exists a set S of at most p vertices of G such that G − S ∈ F }, i.e., graphs from which one can delete at most p vertices to obtain a graph in F.

The Coloring problem asks, given a graph H and an integer k, whether H admits a proper k-coloring (an assignment of colors 1,…,k to vertices such that adjacent vertices receive distinct colors), where the chromatic number is to be determined.

Let F be the class of comparability graphs. Determine the parameterized complexity, with parameter p, of the Coloring problem on the graph classes F − pe and F + pv. In particular, decide whether Coloring on each of these classes is fixed-parameter tractable, in XP, W[1]-hard, or para-NP-hard when parameterized by p.

Let $\lambda$ be an infinite cardinal and let $I$ be a set with $|I|=\lambda$. An ultrafilter $D$ on $I$ is called regular if there exists a family $\{X_i : i\in I\}\subseteq D$ such that every $i_0\in I$ belongs to only finitely many of the $X_i$. Form the ultrapower $(\omega,<)^I/D$ of the standard linear order on the natural numbers.

For infinite regular cardinals $\kappa_1,\kappa_2$ with $\kappa_1+\kappa_2\le |I|$, say that $(\omega,<)^I/D$ has a $(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)$-cut if there exist sequences $\langle a_\alpha : \alpha<\kappa_1\rangle$ and $\langle b_\beta : \beta<\kappa_2\rangle$ in the ultrapower such that:
- $\alpha<\alpha'<\kappa_1 \Rightarrow a_\alpha < a_{\alpha'}$ in $(\omega,<)^I/D$,
- $\beta<\beta'<\kappa_2 \Rightarrow b_\beta > b_{\beta'}$ in $(\omega,<)^I/D$,
- $a_\alpha < b_\beta$ for all $\alpha<\kappa_1$, $\beta<\kappa_2$,
- there is no element $c$ of $(\omega,<)^I/D$ with $a_\alpha<c<b_\beta$ for all $\alpha<\kappa_1$, $\beta<\kappa_2$.

Define the cut spectrum
$$C(D)=\{(\kappa_1,\kappa_2): \kappa_1,\kappa_2 \text{ infinite regular cardinals with } \kappa_1+\kappa_2\le|I|, \text{ and } (\omega,<)^I/D \text{ has a }(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)\text{-cut}\}.$$

Determine, as $\lambda$ varies over infinite cardinals and $D$ varies over regular ultrafilters on sets of size $\lambda$, exactly which subsets of $\{(\kappa_1,\kappa_2):\kappa_1,\kappa_2\text{ infinite regular},\ \kappa_1+\kappa_2\le\lambda\}$ arise as $C(D)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of fully characterizing the possible cut spectra $C(D)$ of regular ultrafilters is a longstanding open question studied extensively by Malliaris and Shelah. Major partial results are known: regular ultrafilters cannot omit $(\kappa,\kappa)$-cuts under suitable treetops hypotheses, and the celebrated $p=t$ theorem of Malliaris–Shelah arose from related symmetric-cut analysis. However, the full classification of which sets can occur as $C(D)$ remains open, with the question continuing to drive current work on ultrafilter construction and Keisler's order.

For regular infinite cardinals $\kappa_1, \kappa_2$, a $(\kappa_1, \kappa_2)$-pre-cut in $(\omega, <)^I/D$ is a pair of sequences $\langle a_\alpha : \alpha < \kappa_1\rangle$, $\langle b_\beta : \beta < \kappa_2\rangle$ with $a_\alpha < a_{\alpha'} < b_{\beta'} < b_\beta$ for $\alpha < \alpha' < \kappa_1$, $\beta' < \beta < \kappa_2$; such a pre-cut is unfilled (a cut) if there is no element $c$ of the ultrapower with $a_\alpha < c < b_\beta$ for all $\alpha < \kappa_1, \beta < \kappa_2$. $$C(D) = \{(\kappa_1, \kappa_2) : \kappa_1, \kappa_2 \text{ regular infinite, and } (\omega,<)^I/D \text{ has an unfilled } (\kappa_1,\kappa_2)\text{-cut}\}.$$

In the online graph coloring model, the vertices of a graph are revealed one at a time in some adversarial order. When a vertex v is revealed, all edges between v and previously revealed vertices are also revealed, and the online algorithm must irrevocably assign v a proper color (different from the colors already given to its revealed neighbors), based only on the induced subgraph seen so far. For a graph G, let χ_OL(G) denote the online chromatic number of G, that is, the minimum over all online coloring algorithms A of the maximum, over all presentation orders of V(G), of the number of colors used by A on G.

A class C of graphs is said to be online χ_OL-bounded if there exists a function f: ℕ → ℕ and an online coloring algorithm A such that for every graph G ∈ C and every presentation order of V(G), the algorithm A uses at most f(χ_OL(G)) colors.

For an integer n ≥ 1, let P_n denote the path on n vertices and C_n the cycle on n vertices. A graph G is called (C_3, P_6)-free if it contains neither C_3 nor P_6 as an induced subgraph (equivalently, G is triangle-free and induced-P_6-free).

Question: Is the class of (C_3, P_6)-free graphs online χ_OL-bounded?

Let $I$ be an infinite set of cardinality $\lambda$, and let $D$ be a regular ultrafilter on $I$ (i.e., $D$ contains a family $\{X_i : i \in I\}$ such that every $\alpha \in I$ belongs to only finitely many $X_i$). Consider the linear order $(\mathbb{N}, <)^I / D$. A pair $(\kappa, \theta)$ of regular cardinals is said to belong to the cut spectrum $\mathcal{C}(D)$ if there exist sequences $(a_\alpha)_{\alpha < \kappa}$ and $(b_\beta)_{\beta < \theta}$ in $(\mathbb{N}, <)^I / D$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
\item $a_\alpha < a_{\alpha'}$ for $\alpha < \alpha' < \kappa$,
\item $b_\beta > b_{\beta'}$ for $\beta < \beta' < \theta$,
\item $a_\alpha < b_\beta$ for all $\alpha < \kappa$ and $\beta < \theta$,
\item there is no $c$ with $a_\alpha < c < b_\beta$ for all $\alpha, \beta$ (i.e., the pre-cut is unfilled).
\end{itemize}
Say that $D$ has uniqueness for the regular cardinal $\kappa$ if whenever $(\kappa, \theta)$ and $(\kappa, \theta')$ both belong to $\mathcal{C}(D)$, then $\theta = \theta'$.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a regular ultrafilter $D$ on $I$ for $D$ to have uniqueness for every regular cardinal $\kappa \le \lambda$.

Let $\mathfrak{p}$ denote the pseudo-intersection number, that is, the least cardinal $\kappa$ for which Martin's axiom $\mathrm{MA}_\kappa$ restricted to $\sigma$-centered partial orders fails. (Equivalently, the least cardinality of a family $\mathcal{F}$ of infinite subsets of $\omega$ that is closed under finite intersections, has the strong finite intersection property, and admits no single infinite subset of $\omega$ almost contained in every member of $\mathcal{F}$.)

The invariant $\mathfrak{p}$ may be viewed model-theoretically as a saturation cardinal associated with a particular complete first-order theory. Consider the following two combinatorially natural complete first-order theories:

(a) $T_{\mathrm{feq}}$: the model companion of the theory of a parametrized family of independent equivalence relations. The language has a binary predicate $E(x,y;z)$ such that for each parameter $z$, $E(\cdot,\cdot;z)$ is an equivalence relation, and the family of these equivalence relations is generic/independent; $T_{\mathrm{feq}}$ is the theory of its existentially closed models.

(b) $T_{3,2}$: the theory of the Fraïssé limit (generic structure) of the class of finite $3$-uniform hypergraphs that omit the complete $3$-hypergraph on $4$ vertices (the "tetrahedron-free generic $3$-hypergraph").

For each such theory $T$, one may associate a cardinal invariant $\mathfrak{p}(T)$ measuring the least $\kappa$ for which a natural saturation/realization property at level $\kappa$ fails (analogous to how $\mathfrak{p}$ arises from the saturation of a specific theory), with $\mathfrak{p}(T) \ge \mathfrak{p}$ since these theories are properly weaker (in Keisler's order, or in associated combinatorial complexity) than the theory giving rise to $\mathfrak{p}$.

Problem: Do the weaker saturation notions corresponding to $T_{\mathrm{feq}}$ and $T_{3,2}$ give rise to natural and interesting cardinal invariants of the continuum? In particular, identify such invariants $\mathfrak{p}(T_{\mathrm{feq}})$ and $\mathfrak{p}(T_{3,2})$, determine their ZFC-provable relationships with the standard invariants $\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{t}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{d}, \dots$, and decide whether any of them can be proved strictly greater than $\mathfrak{p}$ in ZFC.

Let $\mathbb{S}^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the unit sphere. Fix an integer $N\ge 2$ and a small parameter $0<\epsilon\ll 1$, and set $\nu=-1/\log\epsilon$. Consider $N$ "spots" with locations $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb{S}^2$ (pairwise distinct) and source strengths $S=(S_1,\dots,S_N)^T\in\mathbb{R}^N$ governed by the slow differential–algebraic system

$$\frac{dx_j}{d\sigma}=\frac{2}{A_j(S_j)}\bigl(I-x_jx_j^T\bigr)\sum_{i\ne j}\frac{S_i\,x_i}{|x_i-x_j|^2},\qquad j=1,\dots,N,$$

on the slow time scale $\sigma=\epsilon^2 t$, coupled to the nonlinear constraint

$$[\,I-\nu(I-E_0)\mathcal G\,]\,S+\nu(I-E_0)\,\chi(S)-\frac{2E}{N}\,e=0,$$

where: $\mathcal G$ is the symmetric $N\times N$ matrix with entries $\mathcal G_{ij}=\log|x_i-x_j|$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mathcal G_{ii}=0$; $e=(1,\dots,1)^T\in\mathbb{R}^N$; $E_0=\frac{1}{N}ee^T$; $\chi:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^N$ acts componentwise with a fixed scalar nonlinearity $\chi$; and $A_j(S_j)$ and the constant $E$ are the prescribed positive scalar quantities arising from the inner core problem of the singularly perturbed Brusselator reaction–diffusion model on $\mathbb{S}^2$.

Using only analytical tools (e.g. equivariant ODE/group-theoretic methods, and stability arguments analogous to those used for Eulerian point vortices on a circle), rigorously prove the following equilibrium and orbital-stability statements for the above DAE system at small $N$:

1. For $N=3$, the symmetric three-spot ring (three equally spaced spots on a great circle) is an equilibrium and is orbitally stable.
2. For $N=4$, the regular tetrahedral configuration is an orbitally stable equilibrium.
3. For each $N\in\{5,6,7\}$, the $(N-2)+2$ configuration consisting of two antipodal polar spots together with $N-2$ equally spaced spots on the equator is an orbitally stable equilibrium.
4. For every $N\ge 4$, any single-ring (coplanar equally spaced) equilibrium pattern is unstable.
5. For $N=8$, the $(N-2)+2$ configuration is unstable, and perturbations of it evolve under the DAE flow to a "twisted cuboidal" equilibrium configuration.

Let I be an infinite index set and let D be a regular ultrafilter on I (regular: there exists a family {X_i : i ∈ I} ⊆ D such that every index of I lies in only finitely many X_i).

For a cardinal λ, D is called λ-good if every monotonic function f: [λ]^{<ω} → D (i.e., u ⊆ v implies f(u) ⊇ f(v)) has a multiplicative refinement, that is, a function g: [λ]^{<ω} → D with g(u) ⊆ f(u) for all u and g(u ∪ v) = g(u) ∩ g(v) for all finite u, v. Say D is good if D is |I|^+-good.

Say D is good for equality if for every set X with |X| ≤ |I| and every function h: I → X, there exists a "distribution" producing internal representatives realizing equality types: more precisely, for every such h there is a refinement assigning to each pair (i, j) the truth value of h(i) = h(j) in a way that is multiplicative on D, capturing the existence of internal maps between small sets up to D-equality.

Let C(D) denote the set of cuts (a, b) in the linear order (ω, <)^I/D of cofinalities (κ_1, κ_2) with κ_1, κ_2 regular uncountable cardinals ≤ |I| that are not realized in this ultrapower (equivalently, the "symmetric cut spectrum" of D as customarily defined for regular ultrafilters).

Question: If D is good for equality, must C(D) = ∅? Equivalently, must every regular ultrafilter that is good for equality be good (i.e., |I|^+-good)?

representations.normalized:
Consider the Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion system on the unit sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb{R}^3$:
$$v_t = \varepsilon^2 \Delta_S v - v + B\, u v^2, \qquad \tau u_t = D\, \Delta_S u + (1-u) - u v^2,$$
where $\Delta_S$ is the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $S^2$, $D>0$ and $\tau>0$ are fixed, and the feed parameter scales as $B = O(\varepsilon/\nu)$ with $\nu = -1/\log\varepsilon$, in the singular limit $\varepsilon\to 0^+$. In this limit the activator $v$ concentrates near $N$ localized spots at points $x_1(t),\dots,x_N(t)\in S^2$ with strengths $S_1(t),\dots,S_N(t)$. Standard matched-asymptotic analysis yields a differential-algebraic system (DAE) coupling the spot locations $x_j$ and strengths $S_j$ via the reduced-wave Green function $G(x;\xi)$ on $S^2$, defined as the unique solution of
$$\Delta_S G(x;\xi) - D^{-1} G(x;\xi) = -\delta_{S^2}(x-\xi), \qquad x\in S^2,$$
with local behavior $G(x;\xi) = -\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\log|x-\xi| + R(\xi) + o(1)$ as $x\to\xi$, where $R(\xi)$ is the regular part and $|x-\xi|$ denotes the chordal (Euclidean) distance in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Develop a tractable theoretical and computational framework to analyze the slow dynamics, equilibrium configurations (ring patterns, polyhedral configurations, etc.), and linear stability of $N$-spot quasi-equilibrium patterns governed by this DAE in the case where $G(x;\xi)$ and its regular part $R(\xi)$ are not available in simple closed form. Specifically: characterize the equilibrium spot configurations $\{x_j^\ast\}$ and equal-strength equilibria, classify their stability with respect to translational, amplitude, and shape (peanut-splitting) modes, and identify possible bifurcations as $D$, $N$, and the feed strength vary.

representations.normalized:
Let $\lambda$ be an infinite cardinal and let $D$ be a regular ultrafilter on $\lambda$ (that is, $D$ contains a family $\{X_\alpha : \alpha < \lambda\} \subseteq D$ such that every $i \in \lambda$ lies in only finitely many $X_\alpha$). For a sufficiently large cardinal $\mu$, let $H(\mu)$ denote the set of all sets hereditarily of cardinality less than $\mu$, and form the ultrapower
$$N = (H(\mu), \in)^\lambda / D.$$
An element $g \in N$ is called an internal function (of $N$) if $N \models$ "$g$ is a function"; equivalently, $g = [\langle g_i : i < \lambda\rangle]_D$ where each $g_i$ is a function in $H(\mu)$.

Say that $N$ is $\lambda^+$-saturated for functions if, whenever $f$ is a partial function from $N$ to $N$ with $|\mathrm{dom}(f)| \le \lambda$, there exists an internal function $g \in N$ such that $g(x) = f(x)$ for every $x \in \mathrm{dom}(f)$.

Recall that $D$ is called good (i.e., $\lambda^+$-good) if every monotonic function $h : [\lambda]^{<\aleph_0} \to D$ admits a multiplicative refinement, i.e., a function $h' : [\lambda]^{<\aleph_0} \to D$ with $h'(u) \subseteq h(u)$ for all $u$ and $h'(u \cup v) = h'(u) \cap h'(v)$ for all $u, v \in [\lambda]^{<\aleph_0}$.

Question: Must every regular ultrafilter $D$ on $\lambda$ for which $N = (H(\mu), \in)^\lambda/D$ is $\lambda^+$-saturated for functions (for sufficiently large $\mu$) be good?

Let ABC be a triangle in the Euclidean plane, and for any point P in the plane let P* denote the triangle whose vertices are the orthogonal projections of P onto the three (extended) sides BC, CA, AB of ABC (the pedal triangle of P with respect to ABC).

Consider the following two known concurrence criteria, each of which gives a characterization of a special point of the triangle in terms of pedal-triangle constructions of the type P → P*:

(i) (Gergonne-point criterion) A characterization of the Gergonne point of ABC — the point at which the three cevians joining each vertex of ABC to the point where the incircle touches the opposite side concur — expressed via the operation P ↦ P*.

(ii) (Nagel-point criterion) A characterization of the Nagel point of ABC — the point at which the three cevians joining each vertex of ABC to the point where the opposite side is touched by the corresponding excircle concur — expressed via the same operation P ↦ P*.

Provide proofs of these two concurrence criteria that are purely synthetic / geometric in nature, avoiding any reliance on computer algebra systems or extensive symbolic computation. The goal is to obtain proofs whose steps consist of classical Euclidean-geometric arguments (for example using Ceva's theorem, isogonal/isotomic conjugacy, projective duality, properties of pedal triangles, Desargues' or Brianchon's theorem, trigonometric identities, etc.) rather than coordinate or algebraic verification.

Let ABC be a triangle in the Euclidean plane and let P be an interior point. Define the cevian traces
- P_A = AP ∩ BC,
- P_B = BP ∩ CA,
- P_C = CP ∩ AB.

At each trace erect the line perpendicular to the corresponding side of the triangle: let ℓ_A be the line through P_A perpendicular to BC, ℓ_B the line through P_B perpendicular to CA, and ℓ_C the line through P_C perpendicular to AB. When the three perpendiculars ℓ_A, ℓ_B, ℓ_C are concurrent, denote their common point by P^*; in this case call P "dual-perpendicular admissible" and call P^* the dual-perpendicular companion of P.

Investigate the following for each of the classical triangle centers P ∈ {centroid G, circumcenter O, incenter I, orthocenter H, Gergonne point Ge, Nagel point Na}:

(a) Determine whether P is dual-perpendicular admissible for every triangle ABC (i.e., whether ℓ_A, ℓ_B, ℓ_C are always concurrent for that choice of P). If admissibility holds only on a proper subfamily of triangles, characterize that subfamily.

(b) When P^* exists, identify the point P^* as a named triangle center (or give explicit barycentric/trilinear coordinates for P^* in terms of the side lengths a, b, c of ABC).

(c) Describe the locus of points P in the interior of ABC for which the three perpendiculars ℓ_A, ℓ_B, ℓ_C are concurrent, and describe the map P ↦ P^* on this locus.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$. An isometric immersion $\varphi:M\to\mathbb{E}^m$ into Euclidean $m$-space is called minimal if its mean-curvature vector field $H$ vanishes identically, equivalently if Beltrami's identity
$$\Delta\varphi=-nH$$
yields $\Delta\varphi=0$, where $\Delta$ is the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $(M,g)$ acting componentwise on the position vector $\varphi$.

Determine intrinsic conditions on $(M,g)$ — of topological nature (e.g., on the homotopy or (co)homology of $M$), of Riemannian-geometric nature (e.g., on curvature invariants such as the Ricci tensor, sectional curvature, scalar curvature, or Chen-type $\delta$-invariants), or of any other intrinsic geometric nature — that obstruct the existence of an isometric minimal immersion $\varphi:M\to\mathbb{E}^m$ for some $m$. In other words, find necessary conditions on $(M,g)$ for the existence of such a minimal isometric immersion into some Euclidean space.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem of identifying all obstructions to minimal isometric immersions of a Riemannian manifold into Euclidean space is a long-standing fundamental question. Several partial necessary conditions are known: a classical one is that the Ricci tensor must be nonpositive somewhere (more precisely, for a minimal submanifold in Euclidean space, Ric is not positive-definite everywhere; in fact for compact minimal submanifolds of Euclidean space they cannot exist, so Ric ≥ 0 is incompatible with compactness). Chen's δ-invariants and subsequent work provide further obstructions (in real and complex space forms), and recent results give obstructions for warped-product immersions. However, no complete characterization is known, so the problem remains generally open with substantial partial progress.

representations.normalized: Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian $n$-manifold, and let $\mathbb{C}^n$ denote complex Euclidean $n$-space endowed with its standard flat Kähler structure (Euclidean metric, standard complex structure $J$, and Kähler form $\omega$). An isometric immersion $f:M\to \mathbb{C}^n$ is called Lagrangian if $f^*\omega=0$; equivalently, $J(df(T_pM))$ is the normal space of $f(M)$ at each $p\in M$, so $f(M)$ is a totally real submanifold whose real dimension equals the complex dimension of the ambient Kähler manifold (the smallest possible codimension for a totally real submanifold). The question was answered negatively by J. van Mill, who constructed a Polish (hence metric) CDH space containing a dense connected open subset that is rigid (its only self-homeomorphism is the identity), and so in particular is not CDH. Thus open subspaces of metric CDH spaces need not be CDH.

Let $(\tilde M^{2n}, J, g, \omega)$ be a flat Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n$ (in particular, the complex Euclidean space $\mathbb{C}^n$ with its standard Kähler structure). An isometric immersion $f: M^n \to \tilde M^{2n}$ of a Riemannian $n$-manifold is called Lagrangian if $f^*\omega = 0$, i.e. $J(f_*T_pM) = (f_*T_pM)^\perp$ for every $p \in M$. More generally, for a constant angle $\theta \in [0, \pi/2]$, an isometric immersion $f: M^k \to \tilde M^{2n}$ of a Riemannian $k$-manifold is called $\theta$-slant if for every $p \in M$ and every nonzero $X \in T_pM$, the angle between $J f_*X$ and $f_*(T_pM)$ equals $\theta$ (Lagrangian immersions correspond to $\theta = \pi/2$).

Known obstructions (of Riemannian, topological, or curvature-theoretic type, e.g. Chen-type $\delta$-invariant inequalities, Maslov-class restrictions, and constraints from the mean curvature) rule out many Riemannian manifolds from admitting such immersions into $\mathbb{C}^n$ or into a flat Kähler ambient space.

Problem. Find further topological and geometric obstructions (beyond the currently known ones) that prevent a Riemannian manifold $M$ from admitting:
(a) a Lagrangian isometric immersion into $\mathbb{C}^n$ (or, more generally, into a flat Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n$), and
(b) a $\theta$-slant isometric immersion into $\mathbb{C}^n$ (or into a flat Kähler manifold) for some constant slant angle $\theta \in (0, \pi/2]$.

Let $M$ be a Riemannian $n$-manifold and let $(n_1,\ldots,n_k)$ be a $k$-tuple of integers with $2\le n_i\le n-1$ and $n_1+\cdots+n_k\le n$. For each point $p\in M$, B.-Y. Chen's $\delta$-invariant is defined by
$$\delta(n_1,\ldots,n_k)(p)=\tau(p)-\inf\{\tau(L_1)+\cdots+\tau(L_k)\},$$
where $\tau$ denotes the scalar curvature, the infimum is taken over all $k$-tuples $(L_1,\ldots,L_k)$ of mutually orthogonal subspaces $L_i\subset T_pM$ with $\dim L_i=n_i$, and $\tau(L_i)$ denotes the scalar curvature of the section $L_i$. For an isometric immersion $\varphi:M\to\mathbb{E}^m$ into Euclidean $m$-space with squared mean curvature $\|H\|^2$, Chen's general inequality states
$$\delta(n_1,\ldots,n_k)\le c(n_1,\ldots,n_k)\,\|H\|^2,$$
where
$$c(n_1,\ldots,n_k)=\frac{n^2\bigl(n+k-1-\sum_i n_i\bigr)}{2\bigl(n+k-\sum_i n_i\bigr)}.$$
The immersion $\varphi$ is called $\delta(n_1,\ldots,n_k)$-ideal if equality holds identically on $M$ (interpreted geometrically as $M$ receiving the least possible tension from the ambient Euclidean space at every point).

Problem: Determine topological and geometric conditions on $M$ that obstruct the existence of a $\delta(n_1,\ldots,n_k)$-ideal isometric immersion $\varphi:M\to\mathbb{E}^m$ for some $m$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is resolved. L. B. Lawrence proved that the ω-power of every subset of the Cantor set is homogeneous, and Dow and Pearl extended this by showing that every zero-dimensional first-countable T_0 space has a homogeneous ω-power. Since every subset of R is first-countable, X^ω is homogeneous for every zero-dimensional X ⊆ R.

Let $\mathbb{C}^n$ denote complex $n$-space with the Hermitian inner product $\langle z, w\rangle = \sum_{j=1}^n z_j \overline{w_j}$ and norm $|w|^2 = \langle w,w\rangle$. For a fixed direction $b \in \mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ and a continuous positive function $L : \mathbb{C}^n \to (0,\infty)$, an entire function $F : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to have bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if there exists a non-negative integer $N$ such that for every $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$,
$$\frac{|\partial_b^m F(z)|}{m!\, L(z)^m} \le \max_{0\le k\le N} \frac{|\partial_b^k F(z)|}{k!\, L(z)^k}\qquad \text{for all } m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},$$
where $\partial_b F(z) = \sum_{j=1}^n b_j \tfrac{\partial F}{\partial z_j}(z)$ and $\partial_b^m$ denotes its $m$-fold iterate. The least such $N$ is called the $L$-index in the direction $b$; if no such $N$ exists, $F$ is said to have unbounded $L$-index in the direction $b$.

For $a\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ and a non-negative integer $p$, let
$$g(\zeta, p) = (1-\zeta)\exp\!\left(\zeta + \frac{\zeta^2}{2} + \cdots + \frac{\zeta^p}{p}\right)$$
be the Weierstrass primary factor, and consider entire functions $F$ built from products of the form
$$F(z) = \prod_{k} g\!\left(\frac{\langle z, a_k\rangle}{|a_k|^2},\,p\right),$$
whose zero set is the union of the complex hyperplanes $\{z : \langle z, a_k\rangle = |a_k|^2\}$ (such zeros are called planar zeros).

Problem. Given two nonparallel directions $b_1, b_2 \in \mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ (i.e., $b_1$ and $b_2$ are not scalar multiples of each other), and a positive continuous function $L$, construct an entire function $F$ of the above product form with planar zeros such that $F$ has bounded $L$-index in the direction $b_1$ but unbounded $L$-index in the direction $b_2$.
