Call a topological group $G$ S-separable if for every topological group $H$ in which every closed subgroup is separable, every closed subgroup of the product $G \times H$ is separable.

Determine the frontiers of the class of S-separable topological groups. In particular, resolve the following:

1. Is every separable locally compact topological group S-separable?
2. Is the additive group $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ of real numbers with its usual Euclidean topology S-separable?
3. Does there exist a separable metrizable topological group that fails to be S-separable?
4. Is the free topological group $F([0,1])$ on the closed unit interval $[0,1]$ S-separable?

(Recall that a topological space is separable if it contains a countable dense subset, and that the free topological group $F(X)$ on a Tychonoff space $X$ is the unique topological group containing $X$ as a topological subspace, algebraically free on $X$, with the universal property that every continuous map from $X$ into a topological group extends uniquely to a continuous homomorphism from $F(X)$.)

A topological group is a group $G$ equipped with a topology making the group operations (multiplication and inversion) continuous. A topological space is called separable if it contains a countable dense subset. A topological group $G$ is totally disconnected if the connected component of the identity (equivalently, of every point) is trivial. A quotient group of a topological group $G$ is a group of the form $G/N$ where $N$ is a closed normal subgroup of $G$, endowed with the quotient topology.

Question: Does every non-totally disconnected topological group $G$ admit a closed normal subgroup $N$ such that the quotient topological group $G/N$ is both infinite and separable?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered in the negative. A 2017 work (published in the Israel Journal of Mathematics, 2019) shows that not every non-totally disconnected topological group has a separable quotient that is (i) non-trivial, (ii) infinite, (iii) metrizable, or (iv) infinite metrizable; all four versions, including the "infinite" version posed here, are resolved negatively. Positive answers are established for special classes such as compact groups, locally compact abelian groups, σ-compact locally compact groups, abelian pro-Lie groups, σ-compact pro-Lie groups, and pseudocompact groups.

For a Tychonoff space $Z$, let $A(Z)$ denote the free abelian topological group over $Z$ in the sense of Markov; that is, $A(Z)$ is an abelian topological group containing $Z$ as a closed subspace such that $Z$ algebraically generates $A(Z)$ and every continuous map of $Z$ into an arbitrary abelian topological group $H$ extends to a unique continuous homomorphism $A(Z) \to H$. Recall that a family $\mathcal{N}$ of subsets of a space is a network if for every point $x$ and every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ there exists $N \in \mathcal{N}$ with $x \in N \subseteq U$; a space has a countable network if it admits such a family that is countable. A space is Lindelöf if every open cover has a countable subcover.

Question: Does it hold that for every Lindelöf (Tychonoff) space $X$ and every infinite (Tychonoff) space $Y$ with a countable network, there exists an open continuous surjective homomorphism $A(X) \to A(Y)$?

Let $L_1 = L_1[0,1]$ denote the Banach space of (equivalence classes of) Lebesgue-integrable real-valued functions on $[0,1]$ with the norm $\|f\|_1 = \int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt$, and let $\ell_1$ denote the Banach space of absolutely summable real sequences with the norm $\|(a_n)\|_1 = \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|$. A closed subspace $X \subseteq L_1$ is called complemented if there exists a bounded linear projection $P: L_1 \to L_1$ with range $X$. Two Banach spaces are said to be isomorphic if there exists a bounded linear bijection between them whose inverse is also bounded.

Question: Is it true that every infinite-dimensional complemented closed subspace of $L_1$ is isomorphic (as a Banach space) either to $L_1$ or to $\ell_1$?

Work in the real (or complex) Banach space $L_1 = L_1[0,1]$. Recall the following definitions.

• A bounded linear operator $T$ between Banach spaces is called Dunford–Pettis (or completely continuous) if it maps weakly null sequences to norm null sequences.
• A Banach space $X$ has the Schur property if every weakly null sequence in $X$ is norm null; equivalently, the identity operator on $X$ is Dunford–Pettis.
• A closed subspace $Y \subseteq L_1$ is called complemented if there exists a bounded linear projection $P: L_1 \to L_1$ with range $Y$.
• A bounded operator $T \in \mathcal{L}(L_1, Y)$ is said to fix a copy of $L_1$ if there is a closed subspace $Z \subseteq L_1$ isomorphic to $L_1$ such that $T$ restricted to $Z$ is an isomorphism onto its image. Such an operator is called an Enflo operator.

Note that a projection $P \in \mathcal{L}(L_1)$ is non-Dunford–Pettis if and only if its range $P(L_1)$ fails the Schur property.

Question: Must every non-Dunford–Pettis bounded projection $P \in \mathcal{L}(L_1)$ be an Enflo operator? Equivalently, is every complemented subspace of $L_1$ that fails the Schur property isomorphic to $L_1$?

A closed subspace $X\subseteq L_p$ is called complemented if there exists a continuous linear projection $P:L_p\to L_p$ with range $X$. Two quasi-Banach spaces are isomorphic if there exists a bijective continuous linear map between them whose inverse is also continuous.

Question: Is every infinite-dimensional complemented subspace of $L_p$ isomorphic to $L_p$ itself?

Let $\omega_1$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Consider the compact abelian group $\{-1,1\}^{\omega_1}$ (with coordinatewise multiplication) equipped with its normalized Haar measure $\mu$, which coincides with the product probability measure assigning mass $1/2$ to each of $-1$ and $1$ in every coordinate. For a real number $p$ with $1 \le p < \infty$ and $p \neq 2$, let $L_p(\{-1,1\}^{\omega_1}, \mu)$ denote the (nonseparable) Banach space of equivalence classes of $p$-integrable real-valued functions on $\{-1,1\}^{\omega_1}$, with the usual norm $\|f\|_p = (\int |f|^p\, d\mu)^{1/p}$.

Recall that a family $(e_\gamma)_{\gamma \in \Gamma}$ in a Banach space $X$ is an unconditional (Schauder) basis if every $x \in X$ admits a unique representation $x = \sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma} a_\gamma e_\gamma$ that converges unconditionally in norm.

Question: For every $p$ with $1 \le p < \infty$ and $p \neq 2$, does the Banach space $L_p(\{-1,1\}^{\omega_1}, \mu)$ admit an unconditional basis?

Fix $1 \le p < \infty$ with $p \ne 2$. Let $E_p = L_p([0,1]^2)$ (with Lebesgue measure), and let $F_p \subset E_p$ denote the closed subspace of functions depending only on the first coordinate (so $F_p$ is isometric to $L_p[0,1]$).

Consider the following two questions:

(A) Separable model problem: Does $E_p$ admit an unconditional Schauder basis of the form $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \cup (g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is an unconditional basis of $F_p$ whose unconditional constant equals that of the full basis $(f_n)\cup(g_n)$ of $E_p$?

(B) Nonseparable problem: Does $L_p(\{-1,1\}^{\omega_1})$ (with the product of uniform probability measures on $\{-1,1\}$, indexed by the first uncountable ordinal $\omega_1$) admit an unconditional basis (in the appropriate uncountable Schauder sense, i.e., a transfinite unconditional basis indexed by a set of cardinality $\aleph_1$)?

Question: Does an affirmative answer to (A) formally imply an affirmative answer to (B)?

A band is a semigroup $(B,\cdot)$ in which every element is idempotent, i.e. $x\cdot x = x$ for all $x\in B$. A band $B$ is called a left regular band if it satisfies the identity $x\cdot y\cdot x = x\cdot y$ for all $x,y\in B$; it is called a right regular band if it satisfies $x\cdot y\cdot x = y\cdot x$ for all $x,y\in B$. For a fixed integer $n\ge 1$, let $B$ denote the free left regular band (respectively, the free right regular band) on the generators $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$.

Consider the integral semigroup ring $\mathbb{Z}(B) = \mathbb{Z}[B]$, whose elements are finite $\mathbb{Z}$-linear combinations of elements of $B$ and whose multiplication extends that of $B$ by linearity. Define on $\mathbb{Z}(B)$ the operation
$$ a\wedge b := a\cdot b,\qquad a\vee b := a + b - a\cdot b\quad\text{(or its right-handed analogue)}, $$
and let $\mathbf{S}(B)$ be the smallest subset of $\mathbb{Z}(B)$ that contains $B$ and is closed under both $\wedge$ and $\vee$. A skew lattice is an algebra $(S,\wedge,\vee)$ such that $\wedge$ and $\vee$ are each associative and idempotent and satisfy the absorption identities
$$ x\wedge(x\vee y)=x=x\vee(x\wedge y),\qquad (x\wedge y)\vee y = y = (x\vee y)\wedge y. $$
The set $\mathbf{S}(B)$ forms a skew lattice under $(\wedge,\vee)$, called the skew lattice generated by $B$ inside $\mathbb{Z}(B)$.

Problem: Describe explicitly and in detail the structure of the skew lattice $\mathbf{S}(B)$. In particular, give a presentation or canonical form for its elements; determine its $\mathcal{D}$-class decomposition and the structure of each $\mathcal{D}$-class; describe its maximal lattice image; describe the natural partial order; and give its cardinality (or growth in $n$) when finite, or a description of its elements when infinite.

A skew lattice is an algebra $(S; \wedge, \vee)$ where $\wedge$ and $\vee$ are associative, idempotent binary operations satisfying the absorption identities $x \wedge (x \vee y) = x = x \vee (x \wedge y)$ and $(x \wedge y) \vee y = y = (x \vee y) \wedge y$. A skew lattice is called normal if it satisfies the identity
$$x \wedge y \wedge z \wedge w = x \wedge z \wedge y \wedge w,$$
and conormal if it satisfies the dual identity
$$x \vee y \vee z \vee w = x \vee z \vee y \vee w.$$
The normal skew lattices form a variety $\mathbf{N}$ and the conormal skew lattices form a variety $\mathbf{C}$, each being a subvariety of the variety $\mathbf{SL}$ of all skew lattices. Let $\mathbf{N} \vee \mathbf{C}$ denote the join of $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ in the lattice of subvarieties of $\mathbf{SL}$, i.e., the smallest subvariety of $\mathbf{SL}$ containing both $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

Describe the variety $\mathbf{N} \vee \mathbf{C}$: find a set of identities axiomatizing it (relative to $\mathbf{SL}$), and characterize its members structurally.

representations.normalized:
Consider a semiclassical model of gravitational collapse and black-hole evaporation in which a massive body collapses to form a black hole bounded by an event horizon, and quantum fields propagating on the resulting curved spacetime produce Hawking radiation at infinity. An asymptotic exterior observer has access only to the radiation degrees of freedom; the interior degrees of freedom (those causally disconnected behind the horizon) are traced out, yielding a reduced density matrix on the exterior that, in the standard Hawking calculation, is thermal (mixed) and depends only on a few macroscopic parameters (mass, charge, angular momentum) of the initial collapsing matter. Quantum mechanics, on the other hand, demands that the global evolution of an initially pure state remain unitary, so that the final state after complete evaporation should also be pure and should encode all information about the initial matter configuration and any subsequent perturbations.

Problem: Provide a mathematically consistent description of the entire formation-and-evaporation process — including a precise specification of the global Hilbert space, the in/out state spaces, and the evolution map between them — such that:
(i) the total evolution from the initial collapsing-matter state to the final post-evaporation state is unitary;
(ii) any pure initial state evolves to a pure final state supported on the exterior radiation Hilbert space after the black hole has fully evaporated; and
(iii) the information characterizing the initial matter (and any infalling perturbations) is recoverable, in principle, from the final exterior quantum state via some explicit decoding map.

Equivalently, determine whether such a unitary, information-preserving description exists, and if so exhibit it; otherwise prove that no such description is compatible with the standard semiclassical assumptions (locality of effective quantum field theory outside the horizon, validity of general relativity in low-curvature regions, and the equivalence principle near a smooth horizon).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The black hole information problem remains a central open question in theoretical physics. Significant progress since 2019–2020 via the "island formula" and replica wormhole computations has reproduced a unitary Page curve for the radiation entropy in certain semiclassical gravitational path-integral calculations, providing strong evidence consistent with unitarity. However, a complete, mechanism-level resolution—an explicit unitary map and information-recovery protocol within a fully consistent semiclassical (or quantum-gravitational) framework—is not established, and the problem is widely regarded as still open.

Setup. Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a variety of algebras of a fixed signature containing a distinguished constant symbol $0$. A ternary term $d(x,y,z)$ of $\mathcal{V}$ is called a dual binary discriminator (with discriminating constant $0$) on an algebra $A \in \mathcal{V}$ if, for all $a,b,c \in A$,
$$d^A(a,b,c) = \begin{cases} c & \text{if } a = b, \\ 0 & \text{if } a \neq b. \end{cases}$$
The variety $\mathcal{V}$ is called a dual binary discriminator variety if there is a single ternary term that realises the dual binary discriminator on every member of a generating class of $\mathcal{V}$ (equivalently, on a class of algebras whose generated variety is $\mathcal{V}$).

For an algebra $A$ with a constant $0$ and a congruence $\Theta \in \mathrm{Con}\,A$, write $[0]\Theta = \{a \in A : a\,\Theta\,0\}$ for the $0$-class of $\Theta$. The algebra $A$ is said to be dually congruence distributive at $0$ (equivalently, dually congruence $0$-distributive) if, for all $\Theta,\Psi,\Phi \in \mathrm{Con}\,A$,
$$[0]\bigl((\Theta \wedge \Psi) \vee \Phi\bigr) = [0]\bigl((\Theta \vee \Phi) \wedge (\Psi \vee \Phi)\bigr).$$
A variety is dually congruence distributive at its discriminating constant if every algebra in it has this property.

Problem.
(a) Give an intrinsic (e.g. equational or ideal-theoretic) characterisation of those dual binary discriminator varieties that are dually congruence distributive at their discriminating constant $0$.
(b) More generally, for each natural subclass of pointed discriminator varieties sitting inside the class of dual binary discriminator varieties, provide a characterisation of its members in terms of ideal-theoretic properties (e.g. properties of the lattice of ideals, ideal generation, or commutator-type operations on ideals) of the algebras involved.

Consider a four-dimensional Schwarzschild black hole of mass M and horizon radius r_s = 2GM/c^2, treated semiclassically: the metric g_{\\mu\\nu} satisfies the classical Einstein equations while a quantum matter field on this background possesses a renormalized stress-energy expectation value <T_{\\mu\\nu}> together with fluctuations \\delta T_{\\mu\\nu} = T_{\\mu\\nu} - <T_{\\mu\\nu}>. Allow the background to be perturbed by a metric correction h_{\\mu\\nu} sourced through the linearized Einstein equations by these stress-tensor fluctuations near the horizon, and let h_{\\mu\\nu} accumulate either over a light-crossing time of order r_s/c or over the full evaporation lifetime of order G^2 M^3/(\\hbar c^4). Such corrections are called \"soft\" if they remain small in local curvature invariants (so that an infalling observer crossing the horizon experiences no large tidal forces, in accordance with the equivalence principle) yet are coherent enough to imprint nontrivial correlations on the outgoing Hawking radiation.

Determine whether soft horizon corrections of this type can:
(a) modify the Hawking spectrum and induce nonlocal correlations between early and late Hawking quanta sufficient to render the full evaporation process described by a unitary S-matrix from infalling matter to outgoing radiation, while
(b) preserving the equivalence principle in the sense that no observer-detectable high-energy structure (firewall) appears at or near the horizon for a freely falling observer, and
(c) yielding quantitative, in-principle testable predictions distinguishing this scenario from strict semiclassical evolution.

Provide either a derivation establishing such corrections with quantitative estimates of their magnitude and information-carrying capacity, or an obstruction showing that no soft corrections satisfying (a) and (b) simultaneously can exist.

Background. (a) Recall the duality for sheaf representations of distributive-lattice-ordered algebras: given a distributive lattice D, soft sheaf representations of D over a stably compact base space correspond bijectively to certain continuous decompositions of the Priestley dual space of D satisfying an interpolation property; this lifts to a duality-theoretic description of sheaf representations of algebras whose congruence lattice contains a distinguished distributive sublattice of commuting congruences (distributive-lattice-ordered algebras), expressing them as global sections of sheaves of simpler quotient algebras over Priestley-type base spaces.

(b) Recall the duality for strongly distributive skew lattices: a skew lattice (S; ∧, ∨) is a non-commutative generalization of a lattice in which ∧ and ∨ are each associative and idempotent and satisfy the absorption identities x∧(x∨y)=x=(y∨x)∧x and x∨(x∧y)=x=(y∧x)∨x; it is strongly distributive when it is symmetric, normal (i.e., x∧y∧z∧w = x∧z∧y∧w), and the commutative image S/D is a distributive lattice. The category of strongly distributive skew lattices with top is dually equivalent to a category of étale-like sheaves of nonempty sets over Priestley spaces (globally-supported Priestley sheaves), with the skew operations recovered from the local structure of the sheaf.

Problem. Determine whether there is a mathematical relationship between the two dualities described in (a) and (b). If such a relationship exists, describe explicitly how the sheaves appearing in (a) — sheaves of quotient algebras representing a distributive-lattice-ordered algebra — are related to the sheaves appearing in (b) — globally-supported Priestley sheaves dual to strongly distributive skew lattices — for example by exhibiting a functor between the two sheaf-theoretic frameworks, a common generalization, or a translation showing how one duality may be derived from or interpreted within the other.

Multiple theoretical studies have established partial distinguishing criteria: naked singularities without photon spheres produce qualitatively different shadow/photon-ring structures, brighter and harder accretion-disk spectra, modified ISCO and frame-dragging, and altered particle-collision and GW signatures compared with Kerr/Schwarzschild black holes. However, naked-singularity models possessing a photon sphere can closely mimic black-hole images, and no observation to date has provided a decisive discrimination. The problem of a complete and observationally conclusive distinction therefore remains open in general, while partial signatures are known.

A double band is an algebra $(X,\vee,\wedge)$ of type $(2,2)$ such that both $(X,\vee)$ and $(X,\wedge)$ are bands, i.e. each of $\vee$ and $\wedge$ is associative and idempotent. On any band $(X,\cdot)$ define the natural preorder by $x \preceq y \iff x = x\cdot y\cdot x$ (equivalently $y\cdot x\cdot y = y$) and the natural partial order by $x \le y \iff x\cdot y = y\cdot x = x$. A double band $(X,\vee,\wedge)$ is called:
- a quasilattice if the natural preorders of $(X,\vee)$ and $(X,\wedge)$ dualize each other, i.e. $x \preceq_\wedge y \iff y \preceq_\vee x$;
- a paralattice if the natural partial orders of $(X,\vee)$ and $(X,\wedge)$ dualize each other, i.e. $x \le_\wedge y \iff y \le_\vee x$.
Both the class $\mathbf{Q}$ of all quasilattices and the class $\mathbf{P}$ of all paralattices are varieties (equationally definable classes) of algebras of type $(2,2)$.

Problem: Give an explicit description (for example, by a finite or otherwise transparent axiomatization, or by a structural characterization of its members) of the join $\mathbf{P} \vee \mathbf{Q}$ in the lattice of subvarieties of double bands, that is, the smallest variety containing both $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$.

Let $(L,\wedge,\vee,\odot,\to,0,1)$ be a residuated lattice; that is, $(L,\wedge,\vee,0,1)$ is a bounded lattice, $(L,\odot,1)$ is a commutative monoid, and $\odot,\to$ form an adjoint pair: $x\odot y \le z$ iff $x\le y\to z$. A filter of $L$ is a nonempty subset $F\subseteq L$ that is upward closed under $\le$ and closed under $\odot$. Let $\mathcal F(L)$ denote the set of all filters of $L$. For each filter $F$, define the equivalence class $x/F=\{y\in L:(x\to y)\odot(y\to x)\in F\}$, and set
$$\mathcal T_F=\{U\subseteq L:\text{for every }x\in U,\ x/F\subseteq U\}.$$
Then $(L,\mathcal T_F)$ is an Alexandrov topological residuated lattice (i.e., the lattice operations, $\odot$ and $\to$ are continuous, and arbitrary intersections of opens are open) which is moreover linear, meaning the topology is closed under arbitrary unions and intersections in the relevant sense for the algebraic operations. Distinct filters yield distinct topologies, so $F\mapsto\mathcal T_F$ is an injection from $\mathcal F(L)$ into $\mathrm{LTRL}(L)$, the set of all linear topological residuated lattice structures on the underlying set $L$.

Question: For every residuated lattice $L$, is $|\mathcal F(L)|=|\mathrm{LTRL}(L)|$?

The question was posed as one of two open problems in earlier work on topological residuated lattices and was addressed by He, Yang, and Wang in "Solutions to two open problems in topological residuated lattices" (Fuzzy Sets and Systems, 2021), which provides resolutions to both problems concerning the relationship between filters and linear topological residuated lattices.

Background and definitions. A skew lattice is an algebra (S; ∧, ∨) of type (2,2) in which both ∧ and ∨ are associative and idempotent and satisfy the absorption identities x ∧ (x ∨ y) = x = x ∨ (x ∧ y) and (x ∧ y) ∨ y = y = (x ∨ y) ∧ y. On any skew lattice, Green's relation D is defined by x D y iff x ∧ y ∧ x = x and y ∧ x ∧ y = y (equivalently x ∨ y ∨ x = x and y ∨ x ∨ y = y); the quotient S/D is the maximal lattice image of S. A skew lattice S is called:
• symmetric if for all a, b ∈ S, a ∧ b = b ∧ a iff a ∨ b = b ∨ a;
• normal if x ∧ y ∧ z ∧ w = x ∧ z ∧ y ∧ w holds identically;
• with 0 if there is an absorbing element 0 such that 0 ∧ x = x ∧ 0 = 0 and 0 ∨ x = x ∨ 0 = x.

A skew Boolean algebra (SBA) is a symmetric, normal, distributive skew lattice with 0 such that S/D is a Boolean lattice, equipped additionally with a relative complement operation \ making the fibers over S/D Boolean.

Problem. Consider the following two relaxations of the SBA axioms:
(A) Drop normality: study algebras S that are symmetric, possess 0, and whose maximal lattice image S/D is a Boolean lattice, but are not required to be normal.
(B) Drop symmetricity: study algebras S that are normal, possess 0, and whose maximal lattice image S/D is a Boolean lattice, but are not required to be symmetric.

For each of the two classes (A) and (B):
1. Describe the structure of its members (e.g., a decomposition or representation theorem analogous to known results for SBAs).
2. Determine whether the class forms a variety (i.e., is definable by identities in a suitable signature, possibly including a complement-like operation or 0).
3. Describe precisely how the class is related to the variety of skew Boolean algebras (inclusions, reflective/coreflective subcategories, identities that must be added to recover SBAs, etc.).

A Boolean inverse semigroup is an inverse semigroup S with zero such that the semilattice of idempotents E(S) is a (generalized) Boolean algebra and such that any pair of compatible elements (elements a, b with a*b and ab* both idempotent) admits a join in the natural partial order; morphisms are semigroup homomorphisms preserving 0 and finite compatible joins. A Boolean inverse ∧-semigroup is a Boolean inverse semigroup in which any two elements admit a meet in the natural partial order; morphisms additionally preserve meets.

A left-handed skew Boolean algebra (LSBA) is an algebra (A; ∧, ∨, \, 0) such that (A; ∧, ∨) is a left-handed strongly distributive skew lattice with zero (i.e., x ∧ (y ∨ z) = (x ∧ y) ∨ (x ∧ z), (x ∨ y) ∧ x = x, x ∧ y ∧ x = x ∧ y, etc.) and \ is a relative complement satisfying (x \ y) ∧ y = 0 = y ∧ (x \ y) and (x \ y) ∨ (x ∧ y ∧ x) = x. A left-handed skew Boolean intersection algebra (LSBIA) is an LSBA equipped with an additional binary "intersection" operation ∩ which is the meet for the natural partial order x ≤ y ⇔ x ∧ y = x = y ∧ x.

Every Boolean inverse semigroup S has an underlying LSBA obtained by retaining the operations ∧ (multiplication-based meet via idempotent structure), the compatible join ∨ restricted to the appropriate context, the relative complement, and 0; this gives a forgetful functor U: BoolInvSgp → LSBA. Similarly, a forgetful functor U^∧: BoolInv∧Sgp → LSBIA is defined on Boolean inverse ∧-semigroups.

Questions:
(1) Does U: BoolInvSgp → LSBA admit a left adjoint, and if so give an explicit construction of this left adjoint.
(2) Does U^∧: BoolInv∧Sgp → LSBIA admit a left adjoint, and if so give an explicit construction.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Web searches reveal substantial closely related work — notably the Booleanization construction giving a left adjoint to the forgetful functor from Boolean inverse semigroups to inverse semigroups with zero, and noncommutative Stone-type dualities involving left-handed skew Boolean algebras and étale groupoids (Kudryavtseva–Lawson, Bauer–Cvetko-Vah, Lawson–Lenz, Resende). However, no source explicitly settles the existence and construction of a left adjoint to the forgetful functor from Boolean inverse semigroups to LSBAs, nor the analogous statement for Boolean inverse ∧-semigroups and LSBIAs. The status is therefore unclear from the publicly available literature.

An antilattice is an algebraic structure $(N,\wedge,\vee)$ consisting of a nonempty set $N$ equipped with two binary operations $\wedge$ and $\vee$ such that each of $(N,\wedge)$ and $(N,\vee)$ is a semigroup (in fact a band: idempotent semigroup), and such that the two operations are mutually anti-absorbing, i.e. for all $x,y\in N$,
\[ x\wedge y = x\vee y \;\Longrightarrow\; x=y. \]
A congruence on $N$ is an equivalence relation $\theta$ on $N$ that is compatible with both operations; the set $\operatorname{Con}(N)$ of all congruences on $N$, ordered by inclusion, forms a complete lattice. Let $\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ denote the group of automorphisms of $N$ and $\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{Con}(N))$ the group of automorphisms of its congruence lattice. Each automorphism $\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ induces an automorphism $\hat\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{Con}(N))$ by $\hat\alpha(\theta)=\{(\alpha(x),\alpha(y)):(x,y)\in\theta\}$, and the assignment $\alpha\mapsto\hat\alpha$ defines a group homomorphism
\[ h:\operatorname{Aut}(N)\to\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{Con}(N)). \]
Classify, up to isomorphism, exactly those antilattices $N$ for which the homomorphism $h$ is an isomorphism.

Classify, up to isomorphism, exactly those antilattices $N$ for which the homomorphism $h$ is an isomorphism.

A skew lattice is an algebra $(S;\wedge,\vee)$ where $\wedge$ and $\vee$ are associative, idempotent binary operations satisfying the absorption identities $x\wedge(x\vee y)=x=(y\vee x)\wedge x$ and $x\vee(x\wedge y)=x=(y\wedge x)\vee x$. A skew lattice is distributive if it satisfies $x\wedge(y\vee z)\wedge x=(x\wedge y\wedge x)\vee(x\wedge z\wedge x)$ and $x\vee(y\wedge z)\vee x=(x\vee y\vee x)\wedge(x\vee z\vee x)$. Green's equivalence $\mathcal D$ on a skew lattice is a congruence whose classes are maximal rectangular subalgebras; for $\mathcal D$-classes $A\le B$ (with $A$ below $B$ in the induced lattice $S/\mathcal D$), the cosets of $A$ in $B$ are the subsets $A\vee b\vee A=\{a\vee b\vee a':a,a'\in A\}$ for $b\in B$, and they partition $B$. Together with the dually defined cosets of $B$ in $A$ and the coset bijections between them, this collection forms the coset structure of $S$.

A skew Heyting algebra is a skew lattice with top, equipped with a binary operation $\to$ such that for each $u$ in the algebra, the principal subalgebra $u^\wedge S\,u^\wedge:=\{u\wedge x\wedge u:x\in S\}$ (with the induced operations and with $u$ as top) is a Heyting algebra whose implication is the restriction of $\to$. A skew Boolean algebra is a skew lattice with zero in which every principal subalgebra $u^\wedge S\,u^\wedge$ is a generalized Boolean algebra.

(c) Decide whether the coset descriptions obtained in (a) and (b) yield new information about the corresponding dual spaces (in particular the étale/sheaf-theoretic dual spaces of skew Boolean algebras and the Esakia-type duals of skew Heyting algebras).

representations.normalized:
Let $M$ be a smooth compact 3-manifold without boundary. Consider the following conformal data on $M$:
- a Riemannian metric $\gamma_{ab}$,
- a symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor $A_{cd}$ that is traceless ($\gamma^{cd}A_{cd}=0$) and transverse (divergence-free, $\nabla^c A_{cd}=0$) with respect to $\gamma_{ab}$,
- a smooth scalar function $\tau$ on $M$ (the prescribed mean curvature).

The Lichnerowicz–Choquet-Bruhat–York (LCBY) system for an unknown positive conformal factor $\varphi>0$ and an unknown vector field $W^a$ on $M$ is:
$$\Delta_\gamma \varphi \;=\; \tfrac{1}{8} R(\gamma)\,\varphi \;-\; \tfrac{1}{8}\,\bigl|A + \mathbb{L}W\bigr|_\gamma^{2}\,\varphi^{-7} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{12}\,\tau^{2}\,\varphi^{5},$$
$$\nabla^{b}\!\bigl(\mathbb{L}W\bigr)_{ab} \;=\; \tfrac{2}{3}\,\varphi^{6}\,\nabla_{a}\tau,$$
where $(\mathbb{L}W)_{ab} = \nabla_a W_b + \nabla_b W_a - \tfrac{2}{3}\gamma_{ab}\nabla_c W^c$ is the conformal Killing operator and $R(\gamma)$ is the scalar curvature of $\gamma_{ab}$.

Solving the LCBY system produces an initial data set $(\bar\gamma_{ab},\bar K_{ab})=(\varphi^{4}\gamma_{ab},\, \varphi^{-2}(A+\mathbb{L}W)_{ab} + \tfrac{1}{3}\tau\varphi^{4}\gamma_{ab})$ for the vacuum Einstein constraint equations on $M$.

Problem. Determine general conditions on the conformal data $(\gamma_{ab}, A_{cd}, \tau)$, with $\tau$ not constant on $M$, which guarantee that the LCBY system admits a solution $(\varphi, W)$ with $\varphi>0$. In particular, identify a sharp class of non-CMC data extending the known constant-$\tau$ existence theory (e.g., generalizing it so as to apply whenever $|\nabla \log \tau|$ is sufficiently small, and beyond).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem of solvability of the LCBY (conformal) constraint equations for non-constant mean curvature $\tau$ on closed 3-manifolds remains only partially solved. The constant-mean-curvature case was fully classified by Isenberg (1995). For non-CMC data, existence results have been obtained in the near-CMC regime by Isenberg–Moncrief and others, and in the far-from-CMC regime by Holst–Nagy–Tsogtgerel (2009) and Maxwell (2009) under smallness assumptions on the freely specified data; Maxwell also produced non-existence and non-uniqueness counterexamples for far-from-CMC data. A fully general criterion characterizing solvability for arbitrary non-constant $\tau$ is still not known.

representations.normalized:
A skew lattice is an algebra $(S; \wedge, \vee)$ with two associative idempotent binary operations satisfying the absorption identities $x \wedge (x \vee y) = x = x \vee (x \wedge y)$ and $(x \wedge y) \vee y = y = (x \vee y) \wedge y$. On any skew lattice, Leech's natural preorder is defined by $x \preceq y$ iff $x \wedge y \wedge x = x$ and $y \vee x \vee y = y$, and the natural partial order is $x \leq y$ iff $x \wedge y = x = y \wedge x$ (equivalently $x \vee y = y = y \vee x$). Green's relation $\mathcal{D}$ is the congruence whose blocks are the maximal rectangular subalgebras; the quotient $S/\mathcal{D}$ is a (commutative) lattice. Given comparable $\mathcal{D}$-classes $A > B$, each element $b \in B$ determines cosets $A \wedge b \wedge A \subseteq A$ and $b \vee A \vee b \subseteq B$, and $A$ is partitioned into a disjoint union of $B$-cosets in $A$, all of the same cardinality; the index $[A:B]$ is defined as the number of such cosets. An "index theorem" for a variety $\mathcal{V}$ of skew lattices is a combinatorial identity (in the spirit of Lagrange-type theorems) relating the cardinalities and indices of $\mathcal{D}$-classes inside any finite member of $\mathcal{V}$, derived purely from its coset structure.

Problem: Determine whether, for every variety $\mathcal{V}$ of skew lattices, an index theorem can be obtained from the coset structure of the members of $\mathcal{V}$. If such results can be established, determine what combinatorial information about skew lattices in $\mathcal{V}$ they yield (e.g., regarding enumeration, structural decompositions, or invariants of finite skew lattices).

Consider the following single-machine scheduling problem. There are $n$ jobs $1,2,\dots,n$ to be processed without preemption on a single machine, which can process at most one job at a time and is continuously available from time $0$. Each job $j$ has an associated nonnegative real deterioration rate $b_j \ge 0$. If job $j$ starts being processed at time $t \ge 0$, then its processing time is the time-dependent (linearly deteriorating) value
$$p_j(t) = 1 + b_j t.$$
A schedule is a permutation $\pi = (\pi(1),\dots,\pi(n))$ of the jobs; processing starts at time $0$, and each job begins as soon as the preceding job finishes. Let $C_j(\pi)$ denote the completion time of job $j$ under schedule $\pi$. The objective is to minimize the total completion time
$$\sum_{j=1}^{n} C_j(\pi)$$
over all permutations $\pi$.

Determine the computational complexity of this optimization problem. In particular, decide whether it can be solved in polynomial time in $n$ (and the bit-length of the inputs $b_j$), or whether it is NP-hard, at least in the ordinary (weak) sense.

Consider the following single-machine scheduling problem with proportional time-dependent processing times. We are given a set of n jobs {1, 2, ..., n} to be scheduled (without preemption) on a single machine that can process at most one job at a time. Each job j has:
- a positive deterioration rate b_j > 0, so that if job j is started at time t > 0 its processing time equals p_j(t) = b_j · t (the machine starts at some fixed time t_0 > 0);
- a positive weight w_j > 0;
- precedence constraints described by an arbitrary acyclic directed graph G on the job set: an arc (i, j) means that job i must be completed before job j may start.

Let C_j denote the completion time of job j in a feasible schedule. The objective is to find a feasible schedule (a linear extension of G respected by the machine) that minimizes the total weighted completion time
  Σ_{j=1}^{n} w_j C_j.

Determine the computational complexity of this problem. Specifically, is the problem NP-hard (at least in the ordinary sense), or does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm solving it to optimality?

Consider a two-machine open shop scheduling problem defined as follows. There are $n$ jobs $J_1, \ldots, J_n$, each of which must be processed once on machine $M_1$ and once on machine $M_2$, in either order, with no two operations of the same job overlapping in time and no machine processing two operations simultaneously. Let constants $a \ge 0$ and $b \ge 0$ be given (not both zero), and for each job $j$ and each machine $i \in \{1,2\}$ let $b_{ij} > 0$ be a given coefficient. If operation $i$ of job $j$ starts at time $t$, then its processing time is the time-dependent (proportional-linear) function
$$p_{ij}(t) = b_{ij}(a + b t).$$
Let $C_j$ denote the completion time of job $j$ in a feasible schedule. The objective is to find a schedule minimizing the total completion time $\sum_{j=1}^n C_j$.

Determine the computational complexity of this problem: is it NP-hard (at least in the ordinary sense), or does it admit a polynomial-time algorithm?

Let X be a Lindelöf topological space (a topological space in which every open cover has a countable subcover). A continuous surjection f : X → Y onto a Tychonoff (completely regular Hausdorff) space Y is called an R-quotient mapping if the topology of Y is the finest Tychonoff topology making f continuous; equivalently, for every Tychonoff space Z and every map g : Y → Z, g is continuous whenever g ∘ f : X → Z is continuous. A space Y is separable if it has a countable dense subset.

Question: Does it hold that for every Lindelöf topological space X there exists an R-quotient mapping from X onto some infinite separable Tychonoff space?

A topological group is a group $G$ equipped with a topology making the multiplication $G\times G\to G$ and inversion $G\to G$ continuous. A topological space is called separable if it has a countable dense subset, and countably compact if every countable open cover has a finite subcover (equivalently, every infinite subset has an accumulation point). A subgroup $H\le G$ is closed if it is closed as a subset of the topological space $G$.

Working in ZFC alone (i.e., without assuming any additional set-theoretic axioms such as the Continuum Hypothesis or Martin's Axiom), does there exist a separable countably compact topological group $G$ that contains a closed subgroup $H$ which is not separable?

A Tychonoff topological space X is called pseudocompact if every continuous real-valued function on X is bounded; X is σ-compact if it is a countable union of compact subsets; X is separable if it has a countable dense subset. A locally convex space L (over the reals) is called pseudocomplete if every Cauchy net contained in some bounded set converges (equivalently, in standard usage, if every closed bounded set is complete).

Decide both of the following in ZFC alone (i.e., without any additional set-theoretic axioms beyond ZFC):

(a) Do there exist pseudocompact abelian Hausdorff topological groups G and H such that every closed subgroup of G is separable, every closed subgroup of H is separable, yet the product G × H contains a closed σ-compact subgroup that is not separable?

(b) Do there exist pseudocomplete locally convex Hausdorff topological vector spaces K and L (over the reals) such that every closed vector subspace of K is separable, every closed vector subspace of L is separable, yet the product K × L contains a closed σ-compact vector subspace that is not separable?

(Both statements are known to be consistent: under the set-theoretic assumption 2^{ω_1} = 𝔠 such groups G, H and spaces K, L can be constructed. The question asks whether the use of an extra set-theoretic hypothesis can be removed.)

$$R(h)-|K|_h^2+(\mathrm{tr}_h K)^2=0,\qquad \mathrm{div}_h K-d\,\mathrm{tr}_h K=0.$$
Evolve the data in the maximal slicing gauge: the spacetime is foliated by spacelike hypersurfaces $\Sigma_t$ of zero mean curvature ($\mathrm{tr}_h K=0$ on every leaf), with the lapse function $N$ on each leaf satisfying the elliptic equation
$$\Delta_h N = N\,|K|_h^2,\qquad N\to 1\text{ at spatial infinity}.$$
Prove a long-time (global, future-complete) existence theorem for the resulting Cauchy problem for asymptotically flat vacuum initial data that need not be a small perturbation of the trivial (Minkowski) data; that is, establish global existence of the maximal slicing foliation and the associated solution to the Einstein vacuum equations for a class of large asymptotically flat initial data strictly extending the nearly flat (small data) regime.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Global nonlinear stability of Minkowski space for small asymptotically flat data is established (Christodoulou–Klainerman, and subsequent work in wave coordinates by Lindblad–Rodnianski, and others). status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Bourgain, Rosenthal and Schechtman (1981) constructed uncountably many pairwise non-isomorphic complemented subspaces of $L_p$ for $1<p<\infty$, $p\neq 2$, indexed by countable ordinals. Let $L_1 = L_1[0,1]$ denote the Banach space of (equivalence classes of) Lebesgue integrable real-valued functions on $[0,1]$ with the norm $\|f\|_1 = \int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt$. A closed subspace $E \subseteq L_1$ is said to be complemented if there exists a bounded linear projection $P: L_1 \to L_1$ with range $E$. A Banach space $E$ is said to have the Schur property if every weakly convergent sequence in $E$ is norm convergent.

Question: Let $E$ be an infinite-dimensional complemented subspace of $L_1$ that has the Schur property. Must $E$ be isomorphic (as a Banach space) to $\ell_1$?

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ with $p \ne 2$. Consider the Banach lattice $L_p = L_p([0,1])$ with its natural order. Recall that a linear operator $T : E \to F$ between Banach lattices is called positive if $T(E_+) \subseteq F_+$, and is called regular if it can be written as the difference of two positive operators. A closed subspace $X$ of a Banach lattice $E$ is said to be regularly complemented in $E$ if there exists a bounded regular projection $P : E \to E$ with range $X$.

Question: Is every regularly complemented (closed, infinite-dimensional) subspace of $L_p$ isomorphic (as a Banach space) either to $\ell_p$ or to $L_p$?

Fix a real number $p$ with $1 \le p < \infty$ and $p \neq 2$. Let $(\Omega, \Sigma, \mu)$ be a finite atomless measure space, and consider the Banach space $L^p(\mu)$. Assume that the density character (i.e., the smallest cardinality of a dense subset) of $L^p(\mu)$ satisfies
$$\aleph_0 \;<\; \dim L^p(\mu) \;<\; \aleph_{\omega_0}.$$
A family $(x_i)_{i \in I}$ (not necessarily ordered) of nonzero vectors in a Banach space $X$ is called an unconditional basis of $X$ if every $x \in X$ admits a unique representation
$$x = \sum_{i \in I} a_i\, x_i,$$
where $\{i \in I : a_i \neq 0\}$ is at most countable and the series converges unconditionally.

Question: Does $L^p(\mu)$ admit an unconditional basis in this sense?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem, posed by Enflo and Rosenthal in 1973, asks about the existence of an unconditional basis in nonseparable $L^p(\mu)$ for density characters strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\aleph_{\omega_0}$. Enflo–Rosenthal showed that $L^p(\mu)$ fails to have an unconditional basis when the density character is at least $\aleph_{\omega_0}$, but the intermediate cardinal range remains unresolved in the literature; it is listed as a long-standing open problem.

    (12 − v)^2 + 12^2 = y^2,
    (12 − u)^2 + v^2 = z^2.

Suppose in addition that

    x^3 + z^3 = 3817,
    y^3 + x^3 = 5572.

Determine the values of x, y, z (and, if required, the auxiliary lengths u and v) that satisfy all five equations simultaneously.

Consider a spherically symmetric gravitational collapse of a matter cloud in classical general relativity, modeled by a spacetime $(M,g)$ with stress-energy tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$ satisfying an equation of state relating pressure and density (e.g., $p=\alpha\rho$ with $\alpha\in(0,1/3]$, or more general barotropic relations). Assume the collapse terminates in a curvature singularity $S$ at a finite comoving time. The singularity $S$ is called globally naked if there exist future-directed causal (null or timelike) geodesics emanating from $S$ that reach future null infinity $\mathscr{I}^+$, i.e., no event horizon censors $S$ from distant observers.

Define $S$ to be point-like (event-like) if the set of points of $S$ from which future-directed null geodesics escape to $\mathscr{I}^+$ consists of a single spacetime event, and spatially extended (object-like) if this set contains a non-degenerate spacelike or null portion (a continuous one-parameter family of escaping events).

Problem: Within a general class of spherically symmetric collapse models (e.g., generalized Vaidya, inhomogeneous dust, or perfect-fluid clouds with equation of state $p=p(\rho)$), determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the initial data — the mass profile $m(r)$, the velocity profile $v(r)$, and the equation of state — that distinguish whether the resulting globally naked singularity is point-like or spatially extended. In particular, characterize the dependence of the dimensionality and causal structure of the visible portion of $S$ on the matter fields and the equation of state.

The general characterization of when a globally naked singularity arising as the endstate of spherically symmetric gravitational collapse is point-like versus spatially extended remains an active research question. Numerous recent works (e.g., on generalized Vaidya spacetimes, dust collapse with various mass/velocity profiles, and perfect fluids with linear equation of state $p=\alpha\rho$) provide model-by-model conditions distinguishing the two cases, but no complete general criterion in terms of matter content and equation of state is established.

representations.normalized: Let $L$ be a residuated lattice (for instance a BL-algebra), and let $\mathcal{U}$ be a linear topology on $L$ (a topology admitting a neighborhood base at every point consisting of cosets of filters). Choose a base $\beta$ for $\mathcal{U}$ with the property that every member of $\beta$ that contains the top element $1$ is a filter of $L$. Let $X = \{B \in \beta : 1 \in B\}$, and let $Y$ be the family of all finite intersections of members of $X$; write $Y = \{F_i : i \in I\}$. Each $F_i$ is itself a filter of $L$. Direct $I$ by setting $i \leq j$ iff $F_j \subseteq F_i$, so that $\{F_i\}_{i \in I}$ is an upward directed system of filters. Define a topology $\mathcal{V}$ on $L$ by declaring the sets $\{x/F_i : x \in L,\ i \in I\}$ (the cosets of the filters $F_i$) to form a base. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $L$, $\mathcal{U}$, and the chosen base $\beta$ under which $\mathcal{V}$ is finer than $\mathcal{U}$, and consequently $\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{V}$.

Let Cat be one of the categories Top (topological), PL (piecewise-linear), or Diff (smooth). A compact connected Cat-manifold M is said to be irreducible if, whenever M is expressed as a connected sum M ≅ N_1 # N_2 of compact Cat-manifolds, at least one of N_1, N_2 is a homotopy sphere. The Kneser–Milnor theorem asserts that, in dimension 3, every compact Cat 3-manifold decomposes as a connected sum of finitely many irreducible Cat 3-manifolds, and that the decomposition is unique up to permutation of the summands.

Investigate to what extent the analogous statement holds in each dimension n ≥ 4 and for each Cat ∈ {Top, PL, Diff}, where the decomposition is taken up to homotopy spheres (i.e., one identifies any two decompositions that differ by inserting or removing homotopy-sphere summands and by permuting summands). Specifically, determine:

(a) (Existence) Does every compact connected Cat n-manifold admit a connected-sum decomposition into finitely many irreducible Cat-manifolds?

(b) (Uniqueness) Is any such decomposition unique up to permutation of summands and modification by homotopy-sphere summands?

Provide either proofs of existence and uniqueness in each case, or explicit counterexamples that demonstrate their failure, as functions of the dimension n and the category Cat.
representations.original:
Let Cat be one of the categories Top (topological), PL (piecewise-linear), or Diff (smooth). A compact connected Cat-manifold M is said to be irreducible if, whenever M is expressed as a connected sum M ≅ N_1 # N_2 of compact Cat-manifolds, at least one of N_1, N_2 is a homotopy sphere. The Kneser–Milnor theorem asserts that, in dimension 3, every compact Cat 3-manifold decomposes as a connected sum of finitely many irreducible Cat 3-manifolds, and that the decomposition is unique up to permutation of the summands.

Investigate to what extent the analogous statement holds in each dimension n ≥ 4 and for each Cat ∈ {Top, PL, Diff}, where the decomposition is taken up to homotopy spheres (i.e., one identifies any two decompositions that differ by inserting or removing homotopy-sphere summands and by permuting summands). Specifically, determine:

(a) (Existence) Does every compact connected Cat n-manifold admit a connected-sum decomposition into finitely many irreducible Cat-manifolds?

(b) (Uniqueness) Is any such decomposition unique up to permutation of summands and modification by homotopy-sphere summands?

Provide either proofs of existence and uniqueness in each case, or explicit counterexamples that demonstrate their failure, as functions of the dimension n and the category Cat.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question has been partially resolved. Existence of connected-sum decompositions into irreducible manifolds (up to homotopy spheres) has been established in many high-dimensional cases. Uniqueness, however, is known to fail in general: Cappell exhibited counterexamples to the Kneser conjecture in higher dimensions, and Kreck–Lück–Teichner showed failure of uniqueness in dimension 4. Subsequent work (e.g., Bokor–Crowley–Friedl–Hebestreit–Kasprowski–Land–Nicholson) gives unique factorization theorems in particular dimensions and categories (e.g., for simply connected manifolds in even dimensions ≥ 4) while non-uniqueness persists in other settings. A complete characterization across all (n, Cat) remains incomplete.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth globally hyperbolic spacetime satisfying the Einstein field equations, and let $\Sigma_0 \subset M$ be a smooth Cauchy hypersurface containing an apparent horizon $H_0$ (the outermost marginally outer trapped surface in $\Sigma_0$, i.e., a smooth closed 2-surface on which the expansion $\theta_+$ of outgoing future-directed null geodesics vanishes, bounding a region in which $\theta_+ \le 0$). Consider a smooth foliation $\{\Sigma_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ of a neighborhood of $\Sigma_0$ in the future by Cauchy hypersurfaces.

(a) Must the apparent horizon persist under Einstein evolution? That is, does each later slice $\Sigma_t$ necessarily contain an apparent horizon $H_t$, with the family $\{H_t\}$ forming a (piecewise) smooth tube in $M$? Either prove persistence under suitable hypotheses, or exhibit an explicit spacetime counterexample in which the apparent horizon disappears under evolution.

(b) Identify spacetime conditions (for instance on the matter model, energy conditions, or the geometry near $H_0$) under which a given (marginally) trapped 2-surface in $\Sigma_0$ can be extended indefinitely to the future as a spacelike 3-dimensional cylinder of trapped 2-surfaces whose areas are monotonically non-increasing.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No definitive counterexample to apparent-horizon persistence under Einstein evolution appears in the literature, and the question of generic persistence remains unresolved. Partial results exist establishing existence and smoothness of marginally outer trapped tubes / dynamical horizons under specific stability or energy assumptions (work of Andersson–Mars–Simon, Ashtekar–Krishnan, etc.), and conditional extension theorems to spacelike 3-cylinders of trapped surfaces with non-increasing area are known, but the general problem stays open.

A trisection of a closed smooth 4-manifold $M$ is a decomposition $M = X_1 \cup X_2 \cup X_3$ into three 4-dimensional submanifolds with the following properties: each $X_i$ is diffeomorphic to a 4-dimensional handlebody $\natural^{k_i} (S^1 \times B^3)$ for some integer $k_i \geq 0$; each pairwise intersection $X_i \cap X_j$ ($i \neq j$) is a 3-dimensional handlebody; and the triple intersection $\Sigma = X_1 \cap X_2 \cap X_3$ is a closed orientable surface, called the central surface of the trisection. Define the trisection genus $g(M)$ of $M$ to be the minimum of the genus of $\Sigma$ over all trisections of $M$.

Question: Is the trisection genus additive under connected sum of closed smooth 4-manifolds? That is, for any two closed smooth 4-manifolds $M_1$ and $M_2$, does the equality
$$g(M_1 \# M_2) = g(M_1) + g(M_2)$$
hold?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether the trisection genus is additive under connected sum of closed smooth 4-manifolds is reported to remain open. It is known that trisection genus is subadditive under connected sum, and additivity of relative trisection genus would imply additivity of closed trisection genus, which in turn would imply the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

A 2024 preprint "Exotic aspherical 4-manifolds" (Davis–Hayden–Huang–Ruberman–Sunukjian, arXiv:2411.19400) constructs closed aspherical smooth 4-manifolds that are homeomorphic (hence homotopy equivalent) but not diffeomorphic, refuting the smooth Borel conjecture in dimension 4. This answers the general question in the negative, but the question remains open for many specific aspherical 4-manifolds, including the 4-torus $T^4$.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold $W$ with boundary $S^3$, call a locally flat embedded disk $D \subset W$ with $\partial D \subset S^3$ nullhomologous if its relative fundamental class in $H_2(W, \partial W; \mathbb{Z})$ vanishes. A link $L \subset S^3$ (with two or more components) is called stably slice if there exists an integer $n \geq 0$ such that the components of $L$ bound a collection of pairwise disjoint, locally flat, nullhomologous disks in the 4-manifold $D^4 \# n(S^2 \times S^2)$. For such a stably slice link, define the stabilising number $\mathrm{sn}(L)$ to be the minimal such $n \geq 0$. Let $g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(L)$ denote the topological four-genus of $L$, that is, the minimal genus of a connected, oriented, locally flat surface in $D^4$ with boundary $L$.

Question: Does the inequality
$$\mathrm{sn}(L) \;\leq\; g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(L)$$
hold for every stably slice link $L \subset S^3$ with more than one component?

A complete and satisfactory proof has been given for genus g ≥ 3 (and subsequently extended) by Conway and Powell in "Embedded surfaces with infinite cyclic knot group" (arXiv:2009.13461, Geometry & Topology 27 (2023)), which provides a topological uniqueness result for locally flat closed orientable surfaces in simply connected 4-manifolds (in particular S^4) with infinite cyclic complement group. Fix an integer q ≥ 2. All manifolds below are connected compact smooth 2q-manifolds. For a nonnegative integer g, let W_g denote the g-fold connected sum of S^q × S^q with itself (with W_0 the 2q-sphere). Two such manifolds M_0 and M_1 with χ(M_0) = χ(M_1) are called stably diffeomorphic if M_0 # W_g is diffeomorphic to M_1 # W_g for some g ≥ 0. Given M, its stable class S_st(M) is the set of diffeomorphism classes of compact smooth 2q-manifolds N with χ(N) = χ(M) that are stably diffeomorphic to M. We say cancellation holds for M when |S_st(M)| = 1. The genus g(M) is the largest integer g ≥ 0 such that M is diffeomorphic to M_0 # W_g for some compact smooth 2q-manifold M_0.

For a finitely presented group π and ε ∈ {+1, −1}, define the ε-cancellation genus cg_ε(π) to be the smallest integer g_0 ≥ 0 such that cancellation holds for every compact smooth 2q-manifold M satisfying ε = (−1)^q, π_1(M) ≅ π, and g(M) ≥ g_0; if no such g_0 exists, set cg_ε(π) = ∞.

Question: Does there exist a finitely presented group π which is not polycyclic-by-finite, such that cg_ε(π) < ∞ for some ε ∈ {+1, −1}?

Let $M$ be a closed connected compact smooth $2q$-manifold. Denote by $\pi = \pi_1(M)$ its fundamental group and by $w_1 = w_1(M)\colon \pi \to \{\pm 1\}$ its orientation character. For each integer $g \ge 0$ set $W_g := \#_g (S^q \times S^q)$, the $g$-fold connected sum.

Define the stable class of $M$ to be
$$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{st}}(M) := \{[N] : N \text{ is a closed } 2q\text{-manifold with } \chi(N)=\chi(M) \text{ and } N \# W_g \cong M \# W_g \text{ for some } g \ge 0\},$$
where $[N]$ denotes the diffeomorphism class of $N$.

Let $L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi], w_1)$ denote the Wall surgery $L$-group of the group ring $\mathbb{Z}[\pi]$ with involution twisted by $w_1$. Via Wall realisation, $L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi], w_1)$ acts on $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{st}}(M)$.

Problem. Compute, in terms of the homotopy/algebraic invariants of $(M, \pi, w_1)$, the orbit set
$$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{st}}(M) \big/ L_{2q+1}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi], w_1).$$

Fix an integer $q\ge 3$ and let $M$ be a closed connected compact smooth $2q$-manifold. Let $\xi_M^{q-1}\colon B_M^{q-1}\to BO$ denote the normal $(q-1)$-type of $M$ in the sense of Kreck's modified surgery (so $B_M^{q-1}\to BO$ is a fibration through which the stable normal bundle of $M$ factors via a $(q-1)$-smoothing, i.e.\ a lift which is a $q$-equivalence). Write $\pi=\pi_1(M)$ and $w_1\colon\pi\to\{\pm1\}$ for the orientation character, and let $L_{2q+1}(\mathbb Z[\pi],w_1)$ denote Wall's odd-dimensional surgery $L$-group, which acts on the stable diffeomorphism class
$$\mathcal S^{st}(M)=\{N\colon N\text{ closed }2q\text{-manifold},\ N\#_k(S^q\times S^q)\cong M\#_k(S^q\times S^q)\text{ for some }k\ge 0\}/\!\cong.$$

For any normal $(q-1)$-smoothing $\bar\nu\colon M\to B_M^{q-1}$, Kreck's construction associates a quadratic refinement $Q_{\xi_M^{q-1}}(q)$-form on a $\mathbb Z[\pi]$-module derived from the surgery kernel in degree $q$. Forming the quotient by the action of the automorphism group $\mathrm{aut}(\xi_M^{q-1})$ of the fibration $\xi_M^{q-1}$ and by $L_{2q+1}(\mathbb Z[\pi],w_1)$ yields a well-defined map
$$\mu/\mathrm{aut}(\xi)\colon \mathcal S^{st}(M)/L_{2q+1}(\mathbb Z[\pi],w_1)\;\longrightarrow\;\bigl\{\,Q_{\xi_M^{q-1}}(q)\text{-forms}\,\bigr\}\big/\mathrm{aut}(\xi_M^{q-1}).$$

Question: Is this map injective? Equivalently, given $M_0,M_1\in\mathcal S^{st}(M)$, does there exist $\rho\in L_{2q+1}(\mathbb Z[\pi],w_1)$ with $M_0=\rho\cdot M_1$ if and only if $M_0$ and $M_1$ admit normal $(q-1)$-smoothings to $B_M^{q-1}$ whose associated $Q_{\xi_M^{q-1}}(q)$-forms are isometric?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence problem for symplectic structures on closed manifolds remains a central open question. Known necessary conditions are the existence of an almost complex structure and a degree-2 cohomology class with non-vanishing top power; whether these conditions are sufficient is completely open in dimensions $2n \geq 6$. In dimension 4, Seiberg–Witten theory provides further obstructions (e.g., $\mathbb{CP}^2 \# \mathbb{CP}^2 \# \mathbb{CP}^2$ admits no symplectic form), and the problem remains unresolved there as well.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold. A Hessian structure on $M$ compatible with $g$ is a pair $(
abla, g)$ where $
abla$ is a torsion-free, flat affine connection on $M$ (so that around every point there exist local affine coordinates $x^1,\dots,x^n$ with $
abla\,dx^i = 0$) such that, in a neighborhood of every point, there exists a smooth function $\varphi$ with
$$g_{ij} =  rac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial x^i \partial x^j}$$
in those affine coordinates; equivalently, $g = 
abla\, d\varphi$ locally. A Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is said to admit a Hessian structure if there exists a flat torsion-free affine connection $
abla$ on $M$ such that $(
abla,g)$ is a Hessian structure.

Problem: Provide necessary and sufficient conditions on a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ for it to admit a Hessian structure. In particular, give a characterization (in terms of curvature, topology, or other intrinsic invariants of $(M,g)$) that decides whether such a flat affine connection $
abla$ exists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Only partial results are known. Necessary obstructions include vanishing of Pontryagin forms, vanishing Euler characteristic, and (for compact manifolds) an infinite torsion-free fundamental group. Sufficient conditions and classification results exist in special cases (e.g., Koszul-type Hessian manifolds, compact ones with abelian fundamental group, confirmation of Chern's conjecture in the Hessian setting), but no general necessary-and-sufficient intrinsic characterization of which Riemannian manifolds admit a Hessian structure is known. The general existence question therefore appears to remain open.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional (real) Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. A left-invariant locally flat structure on $G$ is a left-invariant affine connection $\nabla$ on $G$ whose torsion and curvature tensors both vanish identically. Equivalently, such a structure corresponds to a left-symmetric (pre-Lie) algebra product $\cdot : \mathfrak{g}\times\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{g}$ satisfying
\[ x\cdot y - y\cdot x = [x,y], \qquad (x,y,z)_\cdot = (y,x,z)_\cdot \quad\text{for all } x,y,z\in\mathfrak{g}, \]
where $(x,y,z)_\cdot := (x\cdot y)\cdot z - x\cdot(y\cdot z)$.

Problem: Give a characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions on $G$, or equivalently on $\mathfrak{g}$) determining whether $G$ admits a left-invariant locally flat structure.

\[ x\cdot y - y\cdot x = [x,y], \qquad (x,y,z)_\cdot = (y,x,z)_\cdot \quad\text{for all } x,y,z\in\mathfrak{g}, \]
where $(x,y,z)_\cdot := (x\cdot y)\cdot z - x\cdot(y\cdot z)$.

Problem: Give a characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions on $G$, or equivalently on $\mathfrak{g}$) determining whether $G$ admits a left-invariant locally flat structure.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of characterizing which finite-dimensional Lie groups admit a left-invariant locally flat (equivalently, left-invariant flat torsion-free) connection — equivalently, which Lie algebras admit a left-symmetric (pre-Lie) algebra structure compatible with the bracket — is a long-standing open problem going back to Milnor. While many partial results exist (e.g. Benoist's negative counterexample to Milnor's question on complete affine structures for solvable groups, and classifications in low dimensions or special classes such as nilpotent groups), no general characterization is known. The problem is still listed as open in current literature.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth (differentiable) manifold. A foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of $M$ of codimension $q$ is a partition of $M$ into immersed connected submanifolds (the leaves) such that there exists an atlas of charts $\varphi_i : U_i \to \mathbb{R}^{n-q} \times \mathbb{R}^q$ whose transition maps have the form $(x,y) \mapsto (f_{ij}(x,y), g_{ij}(y))$. The foliation $\mathcal{F}$ is called Riemannian if there exists a Riemannian metric $g_T$ on the normal bundle $\nu\mathcal{F} = TM/T\mathcal{F}$ (a transverse metric) which is holonomy invariant, i.e., for every vector field $X$ tangent to $\mathcal{F}$ the Lie derivative $\mathcal{L}_X g_T = 0$. Equivalently, locally there exist Riemannian submersions onto $q$-dimensional manifolds whose fibers are the plaques of $\mathcal{F}$, and the local transverse metrics agree under the transition maps.

Provide an explicit construction that produces, up to foliated isomorphism, all Riemannian foliations on all finite-dimensional smooth manifolds. That is, exhibit a procedure (with prescribed building blocks and gluing data) such that:
(i) every output of the procedure is a Riemannian foliation of some finite-dimensional smooth manifold, and
(ii) every Riemannian foliation of a finite-dimensional smooth manifold is, up to isomorphism of foliated manifolds, obtained as an output of the procedure.

Consider one of the following two families of geometric objects in the Euclidean plane:
(a) a collection of n unit disks (closed disks of radius 1, with arbitrary centers), or
(b) a collection of n axis-parallel unit squares (closed squares of side length 1, with arbitrary positions).

For such a collection, define the intersection graph G whose vertex set is the n geometric objects and in which two distinct objects are joined by an edge if and only if they have a nonempty intersection. A matching in G is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges, and a maximum matching is a matching of maximum cardinality.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given the collection of n objects as input, computes a maximum matching in the intersection graph G in near-linear time, i.e., in time n · polylog(n)?

Consider the "annular-domain" variant in which the ambient region is restricted to a closed planar annulus A (the region between two concentric circles), the disks of D lie in A, and s and t lie on the two distinct boundary circles of A; admissible curves are those contained in A.

Determine the computational complexity of the annular-domain barrier-resilience problem. Specifically: is there a polynomial-time algorithm for the problem when D consists of arbitrary disks, and when D consists of unit disks, or is the problem NP-hard in either case?

Consider a multi-objective optimization problem of the form: minimize F(x) = (f_1(x), ..., f_m(x)) over x in a feasible domain X ⊂ R^n, where m ≥ 2 and each objective evaluation f_i(x) is computationally expensive (e.g., requires running a costly simulation). A point x* is Pareto-optimal if there is no x in X with f_i(x) ≤ f_i(x*) for all i and f_j(x) < f_j(x*) for some j; the Pareto front is the image of the set of Pareto-optimal points under F. A multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) is a population-based stochastic search procedure that maintains and evolves a finite set of candidate solutions through variation (crossover, mutation) and selection operators to approximate the Pareto front. A fitness approximation or surrogate model is a computationally cheap function F̂(x) (for instance a Kriging/Gaussian-process model, radial basis function network, polynomial response surface, or neural network) trained on a sample of true evaluations and used as a proxy for F during parts of the search.

Develop a principled framework for incorporating surrogate models into MOEAs for such expensive multi-objective problems. Specifically:
(a) Define how to construct, update, and manage one or several surrogate models for the m objectives (e.g., one surrogate per objective, a single aggregated surrogate, or models for scalarized sub-problems), addressing the curse of dimensionality in both n and m.
(b) Specify an infill / model-management strategy that decides which candidate solutions are evaluated by the true (expensive) F and which only by F̂, so as to balance exploration and exploitation across the Pareto front.
(c) Provide theoretical or empirical guarantees that, under a fixed budget of true evaluations, the resulting algorithm produces an approximation of the Pareto front (measured by indicators such as hypervolume, generational distance, or inverted generational distance) that is competitive with, and ideally provably converges to, the true Pareto front as the budget grows, while requiring substantially fewer true objective evaluations than a non-surrogate MOEA.

Resolve these three points jointly to give a complete, justified methodology for surrogate-assisted multi-objective evolutionary optimization of expensive objectives.

Consider a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) designed to approximate the Pareto-optimal set of a vector optimization problem $\min_{x \in X} F(x) = (f_1(x), \ldots, f_m(x))$, where $m \ge 2$. Such algorithms typically depend on strategy parameters including the mutation rate, the crossover rate, the population size, and the choice of solution encoding. A self-adaptive (or online-adaptive) MOEA is one that modifies these parameters during the run using only information observable from the algorithm's own state, such as statistics of the current population (e.g. diversity, spread, hypervolume progress) and a well-defined numerical convergence criterion for multi-objective search.

Problem: Devise a self-adaptive / online-adaptive MOEA that is effectively parameterless, in the following sense:
1. Before the run, the user supplies no values for the mutation rate, crossover rate, population size, or encoding-related parameters; the algorithm chooses and updates all of them automatically.
2. The algorithm uses a rigorously defined convergence criterion for multi-objective optimization (addressing the difficulty that, unlike the single-objective case, there is no universally accepted notion of convergence for an approximation of the Pareto front) together with signals derived from observed population behavior to drive parameter adaptation and termination.
3. On a broad class of multi-objective test problems, the resulting parameterless algorithm matches or surpasses the quality of approximations produced by carefully hand-tuned MOEAs.

Consider a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) designed to approximate the Pareto-optimal set of a vector optimization problem $\min_{x \in X} F(x) = (f_1(x), \ldots, f_m(x))$, where $m \ge 2$. Such algorithms typically depend on strategy parameters including the mutation rate, the crossover rate, the population size, and the choice of solution encoding. A self-adaptive (or online-adaptive) MOEA is one that modifies these parameters during the run using only information observable from the algorithm's own state, such as statistics of the current population (e.g. diversity, spread, hypervolume progress) and a well-defined numerical convergence criterion for multi-objective search.

Problem: Devise a self-adaptive / online-adaptive MOEA that is effectively parameterless, in the following sense:
1. Before the run, the user supplies no values for the mutation rate, crossover rate, population size, or encoding-related parameters; the algorithm chooses and updates all of them automatically.
2. The algorithm uses a rigorously defined convergence criterion for multi-objective optimization (addressing the difficulty that, unlike the single-objective case, there is no universally accepted notion of convergence for an approximation of the Pareto front) together with signals derived from observed population behavior to drive parameter adaptation and termination.
3. On a broad class of multi-objective test problems, the resulting parameterless algorithm matches or surpasses the quality of approximations produced by carefully hand-tuned MOEAs.

Either construct such an algorithm together with a proof or convincing empirical demonstration of property (3), or show that no algorithm satisfying (1)–(3) can exist under stated assumptions.

Self-adaptive MOEAs (e.g. SaMOEA/D, MOSA-EA, fuzzy-controlled memetic MOEAs) continue to be actively developed, and recent surveys still list automatic parameter control and well-defined multi-objective convergence criteria as ongoing challenges. No method has been recognized as a fully parameterless MOEA achieving competitive performance across problem classes, so the problem remains open.

Consider a multi-objective optimization problem of the form: minimize $F(x) = (f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_m(x))$ subject to $x \in \Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where $m \geq 4$ (the "many-objective" regime). A point $x \in \Omega$ is said to Pareto-dominate $y \in \Omega$ if $f_i(x) \leq f_i(y)$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ with strict inequality for at least one $i$. The Pareto-optimal set is $\{x \in \Omega : \nexists\, y \in \Omega \text{ with } y \prec x\}$, and its image under $F$ is the Pareto front.

A multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) is a population-based stochastic search procedure that, in each generation, applies variation operators and a selection operator to a finite multiset (population) $P \subset \Omega$, aiming to converge to a representative finite approximation of the Pareto front. Selection mechanisms based purely on Pareto-dominance suffer two scalability obstructions as $m$ grows:

(i) The expected fraction of mutually nondominated points in a random population tends to $1$, so dominance-based selection loses selective pressure.

(ii) The number of points required to maintain an $\varepsilon$-cover of an $(m-1)$-dimensional Pareto front grows as $\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(m-1)})$, making representative finite populations infeasibly large.

Problem. Design and rigorously analyze a class of selection and archiving mechanisms for MOEAs (e.g., based on decomposition into scalarized subproblems, indicator-based selection such as the hypervolume indicator, reference-point or reference-direction methods, or relaxed dominance relations) such that, for problems with arbitrarily many objectives $m$:

(a) the algorithm maintains positive and quantifiable selective pressure toward the Pareto front as $m \to \infty$;

(b) the population size required to achieve a prescribed approximation quality (measured by a chosen quality indicator, e.g., hypervolume difference, generational distance, or $\varepsilon$-dominance) grows at most polynomially in $m$;

(c) provable convergence and run-time guarantees can be established on a benchmark family of test problems.

Provide such an algorithmic framework together with the corresponding theoretical guarantees, or prove an impossibility result establishing lower bounds that preclude (a)–(c) simultaneously.

Let $(\mathcal{M},g_{M})$ denote the maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime of mass $M>0$, and let $(\mathcal{M},g_{M,a})$ denote the Kerr spacetime of mass $M>0$ and angular momentum parameter $a$ with $|a|<M$. Both are vacuum solutions of the Einstein equations $\operatorname{Ric}(g)=0$.

Consider an initial data set $(\Sigma,\bar g,K)$ for the vacuum Einstein equations consisting of a Riemannian 3-manifold $\Sigma$, a metric $\bar g$, and a symmetric 2-tensor $K$ satisfying the constraint equations, and assume that this data is a sufficiently small smooth perturbation (in a suitable weighted Sobolev norm) of the induced data on a Cauchy hypersurface of a fixed Schwarzschild (respectively Kerr) background with parameters $(M_0)$ (respectively $(M_0,a_0)$, $|a_0|<M_0$).

Prove the following nonlinear stability statement: the maximal globally hyperbolic vacuum development of such perturbed initial data possesses a complete future null infinity $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and an event horizon $\mathcal{H}^{+}$, and the spacetime metric asymptotically settles, in the exterior of the event horizon, to a member of the Kerr family with nearby parameters $(M_\infty,a_\infty)$, with quantitative (polynomial or exponential, in the appropriate sense) decay of the geometric quantities measuring the deviation from the limiting Kerr solution.

A multi-objective optimization problem (MOP) is a tuple (X, f) where X is a search space (e.g. a subset of {0,1}^n, R^n, or a combinatorial set) and f = (f_1, ..., f_m) : X -> R^m is a vector of m >= 2 objective functions. For x, y in X, x dominates y if f_i(x) <= f_i(y) for every i and f(x) != f(y). The Pareto set is the set of non-dominated points of X, and the Pareto front is its image under f. A multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) is a randomized iterative procedure that maintains a population P_t ⊆ X, updates it via variation operators (mutation, recombination) and selection operators (based on dominance, diversity measures such as crowding distance or hypervolume contribution), and aims to produce a population whose image approximates the Pareto front.

Provide a rigorous theory addressing the following two linked questions:

(a) Identify and formally characterize the structural features of a multi-objective optimization problem (X, f) — for instance, properties of the Pareto front geometry (connectedness, convexity, dimension), the structure of the level sets of the f_i, the ruggedness or epistasis of the objective landscape, the cardinality and distribution of the Pareto set, scaling and conflict among objectives, presence of plateaus, deceptive regions, or many-objective phenomena (m large) — that provably make (X, f) hard for any MOEA in a precise complexity-theoretic sense (e.g. super-polynomial expected runtime to reach a (1+ε)-approximation of the Pareto front, or to cover it under a given indicator).

(b) Identify and prove which algorithmic features (representation, variation operators, selection mechanisms, archive strategies, diversity maintenance, use of indicators such as hypervolume or IGD, adaptive parameter control, etc.) a MOEA must possess in order to solve, in expected polynomial time, either practically relevant real-world MOPs or well-defined nontrivial subclasses of MOPs characterized by the structural features identified in (a).

The goal is to obtain matching hardness and tractability results that together delineate, in a problem-independent way, both what makes MOPs hard for MOEAs and what algorithmic ingredients are necessary and sufficient for efficient MOEA-based solution.

Consider a constrained multi-objective optimization problem (CMOP) of the form

  minimize  F(x) = (f_1(x), f_2(x), ..., f_m(x))
  subject to  g_i(x) ≤ 0,  i = 1, ..., p,
              h_j(x) = 0,  j = 1, ..., q,
              x ∈ Ω ⊆ R^n,

where m ≥ 2. A point x is feasible if all constraints are satisfied; the constrained Pareto-optimal set consists of feasible non-dominated points under the usual Pareto-dominance order on R^m.

Most multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) treat constraints only implicitly, by modifying the Pareto dominance relation (for example via constrained-dominance rules that prefer feasible solutions or solutions with smaller constraint violation). Address the following two-part research problem:

(a) Design constraint-handling mechanisms for MOEAs that explicitly use problem-specific constraint information (rather than merely altering the dominance relation), so that the resulting algorithm provably or empirically improves convergence to, and coverage of, the constrained Pareto front on CMOPs whose feasible region is small, disconnected, or located near the unconstrained Pareto front. Specify the mechanism, prove or experimentally demonstrate that it strictly outperforms standard constrained-dominance based MOEAs, and characterize the class of CMOPs for which the improvement holds.

(b) Construct a benchmark suite of constrained multi-objective test problems whose properties (size and topology of the feasible region, location of the constrained Pareto front relative to the unconstrained one, type and number of active constraints, scalability in m and n) are precisely controllable and representative of real-world CMOPs, together with a fair evaluation protocol (performance indicators, statistical tests, and reference sets) that allows unbiased comparison of constraint-handling techniques in MOEAs.
