Background and setup.

An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set whose elements (faces) satisfy the standard axioms making it locally a "string" incidence structure: it has a minimum and a maximum face, every maximal chain (flag) has exactly $n+2$ elements, it is strongly flag-connected, and it satisfies the diamond condition (for any two faces $F<G$ differing in rank by $2$, there are exactly two faces strictly between them). Two flags are called adjacent if they differ in exactly one face.

The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ of an abstract polytope $\mathcal{P}$ acts freely on the set of flags. The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called regular if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts transitively on flags, and chiral if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly two flag orbits with the property that any two adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

For a chiral polytope $\mathcal{K}$ of rank $n$, fix a base flag and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ be the distinguished generators of $\Gamma(\mathcal{K})$ (where $\sigma_i$ corresponds to the rotation interchanging the base flag with its $i$-th adjacent flag composed with the swap to a fixed adjacent flag). The chirality group $X(\mathcal{K})$ is defined as the smallest normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq \Gamma(\mathcal{K})$ such that $\Gamma(\mathcal{K})/N$ admits an automorphism sending each $\sigma_i$ to $\sigma_i^{-1}$ (with the appropriate corrections in the other generators), i.e., the smallest normal subgroup whose quotient is the rotation group of a regular polytope. The polytope $\mathcal{K}$ is chiral if and only if $X(\mathcal{K}) \neq 1$.

The mix of two polytopes. Given two polytopes $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{P}$ of the same rank $n$ with rotation/automorphism groups presented as quotients $\Gamma(\mathcal{K}) = W/N_1$ and $\Gamma(\mathcal{P}) = W/N_2$ of a common universal group $W$ (the rotation group of the universal polytope of the appropriate Schläfli type), the mix $\mathcal{K} \diamondsuit \mathcal{P}$ is the poset associated to the group $W/(N_1 \cap N_2)$. When $\mathcal{K}$ is chiral and $\mathcal{P}$ is regular, the mix $\mathcal{K} \diamondsuit \mathcal{P}$ is itself a chiral (or regular) polytope under suitable intersection conditions, and one may consider its chirality group $X(\mathcal{K} \diamondsuit \mathcal{P})$.

Problem. Determine an explicit characterization of all pairs $(\mathcal{K},\mathcal{P})$, where $\mathcal{K}$ is a chiral abstract polytope and $\mathcal{P}$ is a regular abstract polytope of the same rank (and compatible Schläfli type so that the mix is defined), such that
$$X(\mathcal{K} \diamondsuit \mathcal{P}) \;=\; X(\mathcal{K}).$$

A k-polymatroid is a pair (E, r) where E is a finite ground set and r : 2^E → ℤ_{≥0} is a function (the rank function) satisfying: (i) r(∅) = 0; (ii) r(X) ≤ r(Y) whenever X ⊆ Y ⊆ E (monotonicity); (iii) r(X ∪ Y) + r(X ∩ Y) ≤ r(X) + r(Y) for all X, Y ⊆ E (submodularity); and (iv) r({e}) ≤ k for every e ∈ E. Given a hypergraph H = (V, E), the hypergraphic polymatroid of H is the polymatroid on the edge set E whose rank function r_H assigns to each subset F ⊆ E the value |V(F)| − c(F), where V(F) is the set of vertices incident to some edge in F and c(F) is the number of connected components of the sub-hypergraph (V(F), F). A k-polymatroid M is called hypergraphic if M is isomorphic to the hypergraphic polymatroid of some hypergraph.

Let p be a prime, q = p^a, and let V be an n-dimensional vector space over the finite field F_q. The general linear group G = GL(V) ≅ GL_n(F_q) acts on the symmetric algebra S(V*) = F_q[x_1,…,x_n] in the natural way. By a classical theorem of L. E. Dickson, the ring of invariants

  D_n := F_q[x_1,…,x_n]^{GL_n(F_q)}

is itself a polynomial algebra F_q[c_{n,0}, c_{n,1}, …, c_{n,n-1}] on explicit generators c_{n,i} (the Dickson invariants) of degree q^n − q^i.

Now consider the graded F_q-dual situation. Let Γ(V) denote the divided power algebra on V (equivalently, the graded F_q-linear dual of the polynomial algebra F_q[x_1,…,x_n], regarded as a commutative graded algebra under the dual product). The group GL_n(F_q) acts on Γ(V) by functoriality.

Determine, with explicit generators and relations, the ring of invariants

  Γ(V)^{GL_n(F_q)}

(the "dual" Dickson algebra). In particular, is it free as a graded commutative F_q-algebra, and if so, what are the degrees of a minimal set of homogeneous generators?

Generalized Hex is the following two-player game. Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with two distinguished vertices $v_1, v_2 \in V$, players alternate turns (Player 1 moves first). On each turn, the active player places a pebble of her color (Player 1 places white pebbles, Player 2 places black pebbles) on a vertex that is currently unoccupied. Player 1 wins as soon as the set of white-occupied vertices contains a path in $G$ from $v_1$ to $v_2$; otherwise Player 2 wins.

The Short Generalized Hex problem is: given $(G, v_1, v_2, k)$ where $k$ is a positive integer, decide whether Player 1 has a strategy that guarantees a win within at most $k$ of her own moves.

Determine the parameterized complexity of Short Generalized Hex when parameterized by $k$: is it fixed-parameter tractable, and if not, classify it within the W-hierarchy or AW-hierarchy.

A geodesic metric space $(X,d)$ is called CAT($-1$) if every geodesic triangle in $X$ is at least as thin as its comparison triangle in the hyperbolic plane $\mathbb{H}^2$. A cubical complex is a CW complex obtained by gluing Euclidean unit cubes $[0,1]^n$ along faces by isometries; we equip it with the induced length metric. Assume $X$ is a locally finite cubical complex whose induced piecewise-Euclidean metric is CAT($-1$). Because $X$ is then a proper CAT($-1$) (in particular Gromov-hyperbolic) space, its visual boundary $\partial_\infty X$ is a well-defined compact metrizable topological space.

Determine the topological restrictions on the visual boundary $\partial_\infty X$, and more generally on the asymptotic invariants of $X$ (such as asymptotic dimension, conformal dimension of $\partial_\infty X$, or local topological structure of $\partial_\infty X$), that arise from the existence of a CAT($-1$) cubical structure on $X$. Equivalently: characterize, or give nontrivial necessary conditions on, those compact metrizable spaces that can occur as the visual boundary of some locally finite CAT($-1$) cubical complex.

An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set (with elements called faces, ranked from -1 to n) satisfying the standard axioms of abstract polytopes: it has a unique minimum face and unique maximum face, every maximal chain (flag) has exactly n+2 elements, it is strongly flag-connected, and it satisfies the diamond condition. Such a polytope is called chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits.

For a chiral polytope P of rank n with base flag Φ = {F_{-1}, F_0, …, F_n}, let σ_1, …, σ_{n-1} be the standard generators of the rotation subgroup of Aut(P), where σ_i fixes all faces of Φ except F_{i-1} and F_i. The right Petrie path and the left Petrie path of P are the orbits of the base flag under the cyclic groups generated, respectively, by the "right" Petrie automorphism π_R = σ_1 σ_2 ⋯ σ_{n-1} and the "left" Petrie automorphism π_L = σ_1 σ_2^{-1} σ_3 σ_4^{-1} ⋯ (with alternating signs). The lengths of the right Petrie path and left Petrie path are the orders of π_R and π_L respectively.

For each integer k ≥ 2, either exhibit a chiral abstract polytope of rank 4k whose right Petrie paths and left Petrie paths have different lengths, or prove that for every chiral abstract polytope of rank 4k these two lengths must coincide.

\[ G_{n,p} = \underbrace{\mathbb{Z}/p \ast \mathbb{Z}/p \ast \cdots \ast \mathbb{Z}/p}_{n \text{ factors}}, \]
and let $\mathrm{Aut}(G_{n,p})$ be its automorphism group. Define the pure (symmetric) automorphism group
\[ \mathrm{PAut}(G_{n,p}) \subseteq \mathrm{Aut}(G_{n,p}) \]
to be the subgroup consisting of those automorphisms that send each free factor $\mathbb{Z}/p$ to a conjugate of itself (without permuting the factors). Determine the integral cohomology ring $H^*(\mathrm{PAut}(G_{n,p}); \mathbb{Z})$, and more generally describe $H^*(\mathrm{PAut}(G_{n,p}); M)$ for natural coefficient modules $M$.

Related results exist: the integral cohomology of the pure/symmetric automorphism group of a free group (the case where each $G_i = \mathbb{Z}$) has been computed, confirming the Brownstein–Lee conjecture, and these groups are known to be duality groups. An immersion of an undirected graph $H$ into an undirected graph $G$ is an injective mapping $\varphi:V(H)\to V(G)$ together with, for each edge $uv\in E(H)$, a path $P_{uv}$ in $G$ from $\varphi(u)$ to $\varphi(v)$, such that the paths $\{P_{uv}: uv\in E(H)\}$ are pairwise edge-disjoint.

Decide the following parameterized problem: given an undirected graph $G$ and an undirected graph $H$ (the parameter), does $H$ have an immersion in $G$? Specifically, determine whether this problem is fixed-parameter tractable with parameter $|H|$, i.e., whether there is an algorithm running in time $f(|H|)\cdot |V(G)|^{O(1)}$ for some computable function $f$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Grohe, Kawarabayashi, Marx, and Wollan (STOC 2011; arXiv:1011.1827) proved that for every fixed graph H, there is an O(|V(G)|^3) algorithm deciding whether G contains H as a topological subgraph; as a corollary they obtain a cubic-time algorithm for H-immersion testing, establishing that the Immersion Order Test is fixed-parameter tractable. This resolved the open question of Downey and Fellows.

An abstract 5-polytope is a partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) have ranks in {-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, with a unique minimum face (rank -1) and unique maximum face (rank 5), such that every maximal chain (flag) has length 7, the poset is strongly flag-connected, and for any two faces F < G with rank(G) - rank(F) = 2, there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G (the diamond condition).

A 5-polytope P is called chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits (equivalently, P admits all "rotational" symmetries but no reflective symmetries). P is called locally spherical if all of its proper sections of rank ≤ 4 (its facets and vertex-figures, together with their iterated facets/vertex-figures) are isomorphic to convex spherical polytopes, i.e. each facet and each vertex-figure has a Schläfli-type symbol whose associated Coxeter group is finite (spherical). P is said to be of hyperbolic type if its Schläfli symbol {p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4} is one of the symbols whose associated rank-5 Coxeter group is a compact hyperbolic Coxeter group, namely {3,3,3,5}, {5,3,3,3}, {3,3,5,3}, {3,5,3,3}, {3,4,3,3,...} of compact hyperbolic type in rank 5 (more precisely, the Schläfli symbols {3,3,3,5}, {5,3,3,3}, {3,3,5,3}, {5,3,3,5}, {5,3,3,4}, {4,3,3,5}).

Problem: Investigate locally spherical chiral 5-polytopes of hyperbolic type. In particular, determine whether finite such polytopes exist; if so, construct examples (especially with small or with infinitely many automorphism groups), and classify them up to isomorphism.

The problem appears to be still largely open. Let $G$ be a finite group, let $p$ be a prime, and let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$. An element of $G$ is called a $p'$-element if its order is not divisible by $p$. Let $k_{p'}(G)$ denote the number of conjugacy classes of $p'$-elements in $G$, and let $k(N_G(P)/P)$ denote the number of conjugacy classes of the quotient group $N_G(P)/P$, where $N_G(P)$ is the normalizer of $P$ in $G$.

Prove or disprove the following inequality:
$$k_{p'}(G) \;\le\; k(N_G(P)/P).$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The inequality $k_{p'}(G) \le k(N_G(P)/P)$ for finite groups appears as an open conjecture in finite group theory, related to local-global counting conjectures (in the spirit of the McKay and Alperin weight conjectures). Web searches did not locate a published proof or disproof, and recent work on $p$-regular conjugacy classes continues to investigate related bounds, indicating it remains open.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$. For a finite group $H$, let $\ell(kH)$ denote the number of isomorphism classes of simple $kH$-modules. A weight of $H$ (with respect to $p$) is a pair $(Q, S)$ where $Q$ is a $p$-subgroup of $H$ and $S$ is a simple projective $k[N_H(Q)/Q]$-module; two weights $(Q,S)$ and $(Q',S')$ are equivalent if they are $H$-conjugate. Write $w(kH)$ for the number of equivalence classes of weights of $H$, equivalently the number of isomorphism classes of simple projective $k[H]$-modules counted suitably; in particular for the trivial subgroup, weights of $N_H(Q)/Q$ are simple projective modules of $k[N_H(Q)/Q]$.

Let $G$ be a finite group and let $\mathcal{I}$ be a set of representatives of the $G$-conjugacy classes of $p$-subgroups of $G$. Prove or disprove:
$$\ell(kG) = \sum_{Q \in \mathcal{I}} w\bigl(k[N_G(Q)/Q]\bigr).$$

This statement is Alperin's Weight Conjecture. It remains open in general as of 2025–2026, though many partial results, blockwise refinements, and reduction theorems (e.g., reduction to simple groups, verification for many families such as symmetric/alternating groups, sporadic groups including the Monster at odd primes, and inertial blocks) have been established.

An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set P with a strictly monotone rank function onto {-1, 0, ..., n}, having a unique minimum element of rank -1 and a unique maximum element of rank n, such that every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly n+2 elements, P is strongly flag-connected, and the diamond condition holds: for any face F of rank i-1 and any face H of rank i+1 with F < H, there are exactly two faces G of rank i with F < G < H. An abstract polytope is regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on flags. The Schläfli type {p_1, ..., p_{n-1}} of a regular polytope records the orders of the Coxeter-type relations among adjacent generators of its automorphism group; the facets of a regular polytope of type {p_1, ..., p_{n-1}} have type {p_1, ..., p_{n-2}}, and the vertex-figures have type {p_2, ..., p_{n-1}}.

A regular abstract polytope is called locally toroidal if its facets and vertex-figures are all either spherical (i.e., classical convex regular polytopes) or toroidal (i.e., regular tessellations of a torus, obtained as quotients of Euclidean regular tessellations by sublattices). Locally toroidal polytopes occur only in ranks 4, 5, and 6.

Given a Schläfli symbol of locally toroidal type together with prescribed toroidal facets and/or vertex-figures, the universal regular polytope with these data is the (unique up to isomorphism) regular polytope of that type whose automorphism group is the largest possible, i.e., for which every other regular polytope of the same type with the same facets and vertex-figures is a quotient.

Problem. Determine all finite universal locally toroidal regular abstract polytopes: for every admissible Schläfli type (in ranks 4, 5, and 6) and every admissible choice of toroidal facets and vertex-figures, decide whether the corresponding universal regular polytope is finite, and when it is finite, describe it explicitly (e.g., its automorphism group and number of flags).

The classification of finite universal locally toroidal regular polytopes has been the subject of extensive work by McMullen, Schulte and others, with the rank-4 and many rank-5/6 cases settled, but some cases (notably involving certain Schläfli types in ranks 5 and 6) remain unresolved. Recent works state that "much work has been done on the toroidal case and a complete classification is now within reach," indicating substantial progress but not full completion.

Let $G$ be a finitely generated discrete group, let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero, and let $S$ be a reductive linear algebraic group over $k$. Suppose $\rho : G \to S(k)$ is a representation whose image is Zariski-dense in $S$. The relative (Malcev) completion of $G$ relative to $\rho$ is the proalgebraic $k$-group $\mathcal{G}(\rho)$ characterized by the universal property that it fits into an exact sequence
$$ 1 \longrightarrow \mathcal{U} \longrightarrow \mathcal{G}(\rho) \longrightarrow S \longrightarrow 1, $$
where $\mathcal{U}$ is prounipotent, together with a homomorphism $\widetilde{\rho}: G \to \mathcal{G}(\rho)(k)$ lifting $\rho$, and which is universal among such factorizations through proalgebraic groups that are extensions of $S$ by a prounipotent kernel.

Determine an explicit description of the completion $\mathcal{G}(\rho)$ of $G$ relative to $\rho$: that is, compute (or describe by generators, relations, structure theorems, or in terms of invariants such as the cohomology and representation theory of $G$) the prounipotent radical $\mathcal{U}$ and the extension class of the sequence above.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The question as posed in Guido's Book of Conjectures asks for an explicit determination of a relative completion of a group with respect to a representation. Such relative (Malcev) completions have been computed in special cases (e.g., Hain for mapping class groups, Knudson for SL_n over coordinate rings of curves), but a general answer for arbitrary G and ρ is not available in the literature surveyed, and the status of the specific instance in the source could not be confirmed.

Fix a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and consider $\Sigma^*$, the set of finite strings over $\Sigma$. A string $Y = y_1 y_2 \cdots y_m \in \Sigma^*$ is a subsequence of a string $Z = z_1 z_2 \cdots z_n \in \Sigma^*$ if there exist indices $1 \le i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_m \le n$ with $z_{i_j} = y_j$ for all $j$.

Define the parameterized decision problem Fixed-Alphabet Longest Common Subsequence as follows.
- Instance: An integer $k \ge 1$, sequences $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k \in \Sigma^*$, and a positive integer $m$.
- Parameter: $k$ (the number of sequences); the alphabet $\Sigma$ is fixed (independent of the input).
- Question: Does there exist $X \in \Sigma^*$ with $|X| = m$ such that $X$ is a subsequence of $X_i$ for every $i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$?

Determine the parameterized complexity of this problem with respect to the parameter $k$. In particular, decide whether it is fixed-parameter tractable, or alternatively establish hardness for some level of the W-hierarchy.

Let G be a discrete group. A model for the classifying space EG for proper actions of G is a G-CW-complex X such that the fixed point set X^H is contractible for every finite subgroup H ≤ G and is empty for every infinite subgroup. Such an X always exists; the question is whether it can be chosen to be finite-dimensional.

Following Kropholler, define the class HF of hierarchically decomposable groups as the smallest class of groups satisfying:
(i) every finite group belongs to HF;
(ii) if a group G admits a finite-dimensional contractible G-CW-complex with all isotropy groups already in HF, then G ∈ HF.
For an ordinal α, the subclasses H_αF are defined inductively, with H_0F the class of finite groups and H_1F the class of groups that act on a finite-dimensional contractible CW-complex with finite stabilizers.

Conjecture: Every group in the class H_1F admits a finite-dimensional model for its classifying space for proper actions.

Prove or disprove this conjecture. (Examples not covered by previously known sufficient conditions include the quasicyclic groups Z(p^∞) and the lamplighter group Z/2 ≀ Z.)

Let $\Gamma$ be a finitely generated discrete group. A family $\mathcal{F}$ of subgroups of $\Gamma$ is a nonempty collection of subgroups closed under conjugation and under taking subgroups. A model for the classifying space $E_{\mathcal{F}}\Gamma$ is a $\Gamma$-CW-complex $X$ such that:
(i) for every subgroup $H \le \Gamma$, the fixed-point set $X^H$ is contractible if $H \in \mathcal{F}$, and empty otherwise.
Equivalently, $X$ is a terminal object (up to $\Gamma$-homotopy) among $\Gamma$-CW-complexes with isotropy in $\mathcal{F}$. Such a model exists for every family $\mathcal{F}$ and is unique up to $\Gamma$-homotopy equivalence; one says that $\Gamma$ admits a finite-dimensional model for $E_{\mathcal{F}}\Gamma$ if some such model has finite dimension as a CW-complex.

Let $\mathcal{VC}$ denote the family of virtually cyclic subgroups of $\Gamma$ (subgroups containing a cyclic subgroup of finite index, including all finite subgroups).

Problem: Find an effective algebraic criterion, formulated purely in terms of the group-theoretic structure of $\Gamma$, which determines whether the finitely generated group $\Gamma$ admits a finite-dimensional model for the classifying space $E_{\mathcal{VC}}\Gamma$.

No general algebraic criterion is known. An abstract polytope of rank $n\ge 3$ is a partially ordered set with elements (faces) ranked from $-1$ to $n$ that satisfies the standard diamond and connectedness conditions modeling a convex polytope combinatorially. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal P)$ acts freely on the set of flags (maximal chains). A polytope $\mathcal P$ is called regular if $\Gamma(\mathcal P)$ is transitive on flags, and it is called chiral if $\Gamma(\mathcal P)$ has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits (so $\mathcal P$ admits all combinatorial rotational symmetries but no reflection).

A rank-3 abstract polytope is equivalent to a map on a surface. For an integer $g\ge 0$, let
$$n_r(g)=\#\{\text{regular polytopes whose underlying surface is orientable of genus }\le g\},$$
$$n_{\mathrm{ch}}(g)=\#\{\text{chiral polytopes whose underlying surface is orientable of genus }\le g\},$$
where polytopes are counted up to isomorphism.

Determine whether the limit
$$\lim_{g\to\infty}\frac{n_r(g)}{n_{\mathrm{ch}}(g)}$$
exists, and if so compute its value.

The problem appears in a published list of open problems on chiral polytopes and asks for the asymptotic ratio of regular to chiral polytopes counted by orientable genus. While partial enumerations (e.g., complete lists of reflexible and chiral regular maps up to genus 15, and orientable regular maps to genus 101) exist, no published result determines or even establishes existence of this limit. Related work on reflexible-to-chiral ratios addresses different parameters (such as maps with fixed number of faces or fixed type), not the cumulative count by genus.

So the request for examples is answered, though the broader determination of geometric dimensions of E_VC Γ remains an active research area.

A map is an embedding of a connected graph into a surface (without boundary) such that each connected component of the complement is homeomorphic to an open disc; the cells of the map are the vertices, edges, and faces. An automorphism of a map is a permutation of its cells that preserves incidences; the automorphism group acts semi-regularly on the set of flags (mutually incident vertex-edge-face triples). The map is called regular if the automorphism group acts transitively (hence regularly) on flags. On an orientable surface, the orientation-preserving automorphisms form a subgroup of index at most 2; a map on an orientable surface is called orientably regular if this subgroup acts regularly on the set of darts (or arcs). An orientably regular map is called chiral if it is not isomorphic to its mirror image, equivalently, if it admits no orientation-reversing automorphism.

A noncompact surface without boundary is a connected 2-manifold without boundary that is not compact (for instance, the plane, the cylinder, the Loch Ness monster surface, a surface with infinitely many ends, etc.).

Problem: Characterize, up to homeomorphism, those noncompact surfaces without boundary that admit an embedding of a chiral map.

Let Γ be a (non-abelian) infinite group. A family F of subgroups of Γ is a set of subgroups closed under conjugation and under taking subgroups. Write FIN for the family of finite subgroups of Γ. A model for the classifying space E_F Γ is a Γ-CW-complex X such that for every subgroup H ≤ Γ, the H-fixed-point set X^H is contractible if H ∈ F and empty otherwise. (Equivalently, X is a terminal object in the Γ-equivariant homotopy category of Γ-CW-complexes with isotropy in F.)

Question: Does there always exist a family F of subgroups of Γ with FIN ⊂ F such that every model for E_F Γ is infinite-dimensional (i.e., the geometric dimension gd_F(Γ) is infinite)?

A decision problem on the class of finitely presented groups is a problem that takes as input a finite presentation $\langle X \mid R\rangle$ (with $X$ a finite alphabet and $R$ a finite set of relators) of a group $G$, possibly together with some additional finite data (such as a word in the generators, a finite tuple of words, or a finite subset), and asks for a yes/no answer to a fixed property. Such a problem is called algorithmically (recursively) unsolvable if there is no Turing machine that, on every valid input, halts and outputs the correct answer.

Consider the following two decision problems on the class of finitely presented groups:

(P1) Given a finite presentation $\langle X \mid R\rangle$ of a group $G$ and a word $w$ in $X \cup X^{-1}$, decide whether $w$ represents an element of finite order in $G$.

(P2) Given a finite presentation $\langle X \mid R\rangle$ of a group $G$ and two finite tuples of words $(u_1,\dots,u_k)$ and $(v_1,\dots,v_k)$, decide whether the map $u_i \mapsto v_i$ extends to a homomorphism of $G$ into itself.

Are both (P1) and (P2) algorithmically unsolvable?

Background and definitions. An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $P$ (with a minimum and a maximum element) whose elements (called faces) are graded by rank in $\{-1,0,1,\dots,n\}$, satisfying the diamond condition and strong flag-connectedness. The maximal chains of $P$ are called flags. The automorphism group $\Gamma(P)$ acts freely on flags. The polytope $P$ is regular if $\Gamma(P)$ acts transitively on flags, and chiral if $\Gamma(P)$ has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

Given an abstract polytope $K$ of rank $n$, an extension of $K$ is an abstract polytope $P$ of rank $n+1$ all of whose facets (faces of rank $n$) are isomorphic to $K$. A covering between polytopes $P \to Q$ of the same rank is a rank- and incidence-preserving surjection that maps flags to flags. An extension $P$ of $K$ is said to cover another extension $Q$ of $K$ if there is such a covering $P \to Q$.

Problem. Let $K$ be an arbitrary regular abstract polytope. Does there exist a chiral extension $P$ of $K$ such that, for every chiral extension $Q$ of $K$, there is a covering $P \to Q$? Equivalently, does $K$ admit a universal chiral extension in the category of chiral extensions of $K$?

Say that P is a chain minor of Q if there exists a partial map ρ : W → V such that for every chain C ⊆ V of P there is a chain C' ⊆ W of Q for which ρ is defined on all of C' and the restriction ρ|_{C'} : C' → C is an isomorphism of chains (i.e., an order-preserving bijection from C' to C with respect to the chain orders).

- Input: a finite poset Q.

- Question: Is P a chain minor of Q?

Let X be a proper, cocompact CAT(0) space (i.e., a complete geodesic metric space of nonpositive curvature in the sense of Alexandrov, on which a group acts properly and cocompactly by isometries). Define the Euclidean rank r of X to be the maximal dimension of an isometrically embedded Euclidean flat in X.

Prove or disprove: for every integer k ≥ r, the space X admits a linear isoperimetric inequality for k-cycles. That is, there exists a constant C = C(X, k) such that every Lipschitz (or integral) k-cycle T in X bounds a (k+1)-chain V with mass(V) ≤ C · mass(T).

Let X be a proper, cocompact CAT(0) space (i.e., a complete geodesic metric space of nonpositive curvature in the sense of Alexandrov, on which a group acts properly and cocompactly by isometries). Define the Euclidean rank r of X to be the maximal dimension of an isometrically embedded Euclidean flat in X.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture (a form of Gromov's isoperimetric gap conjecture for Hadamard/CAT(0) spaces) appears still open in full generality. Partial results exist: Wenger and others have established Euclidean-type and sub-Euclidean inequalities below the rank, and Druţu–Lang–Papasoglu–Stadler obtained homotopical and homological inequalities with exponents arbitrarily close to 1 under additional hypotheses (finite linearly controlled asymptotic dimension). A 2025 preprint addresses the asymptotic rank two case in Hadamard spaces. No general proof for proper cocompact CAT(0) spaces is reported.

Question: Does every such $G$ admit a proper action on an acyclic CW-complex $X$ whose (CW-)dimension equals $\mathrm{vcd}\,G$?

Let P = (X, ≤) be a finite partially ordered set. A linear extension of P is a total order L = x_1 < x_2 < ⋯ < x_n on X such that x_i ≤ x_j in P implies i ≤ j. For a linear extension L, a jump is an index i ∈ {1, …, n−1} such that x_i and x_{i+1} are incomparable in P. The jump number s(P) of P is the minimum, over all linear extensions L of P, of the number of jumps in L.

The Jump Number problem is the following parameterized decision problem:
- Input: a finite poset P and a positive integer k.
- Parameter: k.
- Question: Is s(P) ≤ k?

Determine whether this parameterized problem is fixed-parameter tractable, i.e., decide whether there exists an algorithm solving it in time f(k) · |P|^{O(1)} for some computable function f.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem is fixed-parameter tractable. Kratsch and Kratsch (IPEC 2013, "The Jump Number Problem: Exact and Parameterized") gave an O*(2^w) algorithm parameterized by the width w of the poset. Since any poset with jump number at most k has width at most k+1 (a linear extension with k jumps decomposes the ground set into k+1 chains), FPT in the width parameter immediately yields FPT in the jump-number parameter k, with running time O*(2^k). Hence the original question parameterized by k is solved (positively).

Recall that $G$ is said to be of type $FP$ over $R$ if the trivial $RG$-module $R$ admits a finite resolution by finitely generated projective $RG$-modules. A CW-complex $X$ with a cellular $G$-action is called cocompact if $X/G$ has finitely many cells, and $X$ is called $R$-acyclic if $\tilde{H}_*(X;R)=0$.

Question: If $G$ is of type $FP$ over $R$, does there necessarily exist an $R$-acyclic CW-complex $X$ together with a cellular, cocompact action of $G$ on $X$ such that every cell stabilizer is a finite subgroup whose order is a unit in $R$?

Let R be a commutative ring with unit and let G be a discrete group. Consider the group ring RG and view R as the trivial RG-module. Adopt the following homological finiteness conditions on G:

• G is of type FP over R if the trivial RG-module R admits a projective resolution
   ⋯ → P_n → P_(n−1) → ⋯ → P_1 → P_0 → R → 0
  by finitely generated projective RG-modules.

• G is of type FPP over R if, in addition to being of type FP over R, the trivial RG-module R admits such a resolution by finitely generated projective RG-modules which is eventually periodic, i.e. there exist integers k ≥ 0 and q ≥ 1 such that P_(i+q) ≅ P_i as RG-modules for all i ≥ k, with the boundary maps respecting this periodicity.

Question: Does the condition "G is of type FP over R" imply that G is of type FPP over R? Equivalently, must every group whose trivial module R admits a finite-type projective resolution over RG admit one which is eventually periodic?

Let F be a prime field (i.e. F = Q or F = F_p for some prime p). A discrete group G is said to be of type FL over F if the trivial FG-module F admits a finite-length resolution by finitely generated free FG-modules; equivalently, there exists an exact sequence

  0 → F_n → F_{n-1} → ⋯ → F_0 → F → 0

of FG-modules in which each F_i is a finitely generated free FG-module.

A CW-complex X is called F-acyclic if its reduced cellular homology with coefficients in F vanishes in every degree. An action of G on a CW-complex X is called cellular if it permutes the cells, free if no nontrivial element of G fixes any point of X, and cocompact if the quotient X/G is a compact CW-complex (equivalently, X has finitely many G-orbits of cells).

Question: Does every group G of type FL over F admit a free, cellular, cocompact action on some F-acyclic CW-complex?

representations.normalized:
Let X be a separable F-space (for instance, a separable Banach space) and let T : X → X be a continuous linear operator. Recall the following notions.

(i) T is hypercyclic if there exists x ∈ X whose orbit {T^n x : n ≥ 0} is dense in X.
(ii) T is frequently hypercyclic if there exists x ∈ X such that for every nonempty open set U ⊂ X the set {n ∈ ℕ : T^n x ∈ U} has positive lower density.
(iii) T is (Devaney) chaotic if it is hypercyclic and its periodic points are dense in X.
(iv) T is topologically mixing if for every pair of nonempty open sets U, V ⊂ X there exists N such that T^n(U) ∩ V ≠ ∅ for all n ≥ N.

T is said to satisfy the Frequent Hypercyclicity Criterion if there exists a dense subset X₀ ⊂ X and a map S : X₀ → X₀ such that, for every x ∈ X₀,
 (a) the series Σ_{n≥1} T^n x converges unconditionally in X,
 (b) the series Σ_{n≥1} S^n x converges unconditionally in X,
 (c) T S x = x.

Answer the following:

(a) Identify a strong dynamical property of T that is exactly characterized (equivalent to) T satisfying the Frequent Hypercyclicity Criterion, or show that no such intrinsic dynamical characterization exists.

(b) Must every continuous linear operator T : X → X that is simultaneously chaotic, topologically mixing, and frequently hypercyclic satisfy the Frequent Hypercyclicity Criterion?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is stated as an open problem in surveys on frequent hypercyclicity. It is known that the Frequent Hypercyclicity Criterion implies chaos, mixing, and frequent hypercyclicity, and counterexamples show that frequent hypercyclicity plus chaos alone does not suffice (e.g., a chaotic frequently hypercyclic operator that is not mixing). Recent works continue to study related counterexamples (e.g., mixing chaotic composition operators failing the criterion), but no intrinsic dynamical characterization of the Frequent Hypercyclicity Criterion is known, and the converse question for chaotic + mixing + frequently hypercyclic operators remains open.

Let $G$ be a finitely generated torsion-free one-relator group, i.e. a group admitting a presentation $G = \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$ with a single relator $r$, such that $G$ has no element of finite order other than the identity. For $1 \le p < \infty$, let $\ell^p(G)$ denote the Banach space of $p$-summable complex-valued functions on $G$, regarded as a left $G$-module via the left regular representation. Let $H^2(G, \ell^p(G))$ denote the second continuous (equivalently, algebraic, viewed as a topological vector space with the quotient topology) group cohomology of $G$ with coefficients in $\ell^p(G)$, and let $\overline{H}^2(G, \ell^p(G))$ denote the reduced second cohomology, obtained by quotienting the space of 2-cocycles by the closure of the space of 2-coboundaries.

Prove or disprove: for every such $G$ and every $1 \le p < \infty$,
$$H^2(G, \ell^p(G)) = \overline{H}^2(G, \ell^p(G)) = 0.$$

An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $P$ (whose elements are called faces) satisfying the standard axioms for abstract polytopes: $P$ has a unique minimum face and unique maximum face; every maximal chain (flag) has length $n+1$; $P$ is strongly flag-connected; and $P$ satisfies the diamond condition (for any faces $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces strictly between $F$ and $G$). The automorphism group $\Gamma(P)$ consists of order-preserving bijections of $P$ to itself.

A polytope $P$ of rank $n$ is regular if $\Gamma(P)$ acts transitively on the flags of $P$. It is chiral if $\Gamma(P)$ has exactly two orbits on the flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits. A chiral polytope $P$ comes in an enantiomorphic pair: $P$ and its mirror image $P^*$ are isomorphic as polytopes only as unoriented structures, and one calls $P$ and $P^*$ the two enantiomorphic forms.

Let X be a separable infinite-dimensional Banach space and let T: X → X be a bounded linear operator. Recall that T is called frequently hypercyclic if there exists a vector x ∈ X (called a frequently hypercyclic vector) such that for every nonempty open set U ⊆ X, the set of return times N(x,U) = { n ∈ ℕ : Tⁿx ∈ U } has positive lower density, i.e. liminf_{N→∞} (1/N) · #(N(x,U) ∩ {1,…,N}) > 0.

A Borel probability measure μ on X is said to have full support if μ(U) > 0 for every nonempty open set U ⊆ X. It is T-invariant if μ(T⁻¹(A)) = μ(A) for every Borel set A, and ergodic if every T-invariant Borel set has μ-measure 0 or 1. A Gaussian measure on X is a Borel probability measure whose continuous linear images on ℝ are all (possibly degenerate) Gaussian distributions. A scalar λ ∈ ℂ is a unimodular eigenvalue of T if |λ| = 1 and there exists a nonzero vector v ∈ X (over ℂ) with Tv = λv.

Answer the following four questions:

(a) If X is an arbitrary (separable) Banach space, must every frequently hypercyclic operator T on X admit a T-invariant Borel probability measure of full support?

(b) If X is a (separable) Hilbert space, must every frequently hypercyclic operator T on X admit an ergodic Borel probability measure of full support?

(c) If X is a (separable) Hilbert space, must every frequently hypercyclic operator T on X admit an ergodic Gaussian Borel probability measure of full support?

(d) If X is a (separable) Hilbert space, must every frequently hypercyclic operator T on X have at least one unimodular eigenvalue?

Questions (b), (c), and (d) are additionally posed in the more general setting where X is an arbitrary reflexive Banach space.

Partial progress is known. Let $G$ be a finitely generated discrete group, and let $\ell^2(G)$ denote the Hilbert space of square-summable complex-valued functions on $G$, viewed as a left $\mathbb{C}G$-module via the left regular representation. The first group cohomology $H^1(G,\ell^2(G))$ may be computed as $Z^1(G,\ell^2(G))/B^1(G,\ell^2(G))$, where $Z^1$ is the space of 1-cocycles $c:G\to\ell^2(G)$ satisfying $c(gh)=c(g)+g\cdot c(h)$ and $B^1$ is the subspace of 1-coboundaries $c(g)=g\cdot v-v$ for some $v\in\ell^2(G)$. The reduced first cohomology is defined by
$$\overline{H}^1(G,\ell^2(G)) := Z^1(G,\ell^2(G))/\overline{B^1(G,\ell^2(G))},$$
where the closure of $B^1$ is taken with respect to the topology of pointwise convergence on $G$ (equivalently, in $\ell^2(G)^G$ with the product topology). There is a natural surjection
$$H^1(G,\ell^2(G))\twoheadrightarrow\overline{H}^1(G,\ell^2(G)).$$

Suppose that $G$ is a finitely generated torsion-free one-relator group, i.e., $G$ admits a presentation $\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\mid r\rangle$ with a single relator $r$ and is torsion-free, and assume that $G$ is neither $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ nor the Klein bottle group $\langle a,b\mid abab^{-1}\rangle$.

Prove or disprove: the natural epimorphism $H^1(G,\ell^2(G))\to\overline{H}^1(G,\ell^2(G))$ is an isomorphism.

Let $F$ be the free group on a finite basis $x_1, \dots, x_n$. Recall that the basic commutators on $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are defined recursively: each generator $x_i$ is a basic commutator of weight $1$, ordered $x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_n$; if all basic commutators of weight $< k$ have been defined and linearly ordered (with weight as the primary key), then a basic commutator of weight $k$ is an element of the form $[u, v]$ where $u, v$ are basic commutators with $\mathrm{wt}(u) + \mathrm{wt}(v) = k$, $u > v$, and, if $u = [u_1, u_2]$, then $v \geq u_2$. A group $G$ is called residually nilpotent if for every $g \in G$ with $g \neq 1$ there exists a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ such that $g \notin N$ and $G/N$ is nilpotent; equivalently, $\bigcap_{k \geq 1} \gamma_k(G) = \{1\}$, where $\gamma_k(G)$ denotes the $k$-th term of the lower central series.

Question: For every basic commutator $r$ on $x_1, \dots, x_n$, is the one-relator group
$$\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$$
residually nilpotent?

Significant progress has been made by Baumslag and Mikhailov, who showed that many one-relator groups defined by basic commutators (including the Hydra groups of Dison–Riley and various generalizations) are residually torsion-free nilpotent, hence residually nilpotent. No source found that resolves the original one-relator question in full generality.

An abstract d-polytope is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ with a least element $F_{-1}$ and greatest element $F_d$, whose elements (called faces) have a well-defined rank in $\{-1,0,1,\dots,d\}$, such that every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly one face of each rank, $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected, and the diamond condition holds (for every $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$). A face of rank $i$ is called an $i$-face.

For integers $0 \le k < m \le d-1$, the polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is said to be $(k,m)$-flat if every $m$-face of $\mathcal{P}$ is incident with (i.e. contains in the partial order) every $k$-face of $\mathcal{P}$.

Question: For every triple of integers $(k,m,d)$ satisfying $0 < k+1 < m \le d-1$, does there exist an abstract $(k,m)$-flat $d$-polytope?

Let $G$ be a finitely generated group and let $H \le G$ be a subgroup. A subset $A \subseteq G$ is said to be $H$-almost invariant if $A$ is a union of right $H$-cosets (i.e.\ $AH=A$) and the symmetric difference $A \triangle Ag$ is contained in finitely many right $H$-cosets for every $g \in G$. The set $A$ is called $H$-proper if both $A$ and $G \setminus A$ are not contained in finitely many right $H$-cosets. Equivalently, the existence of such an $A$ corresponds to the number of relative ends $e(G,H)$ being at least $2$.

A group $G$ is said to split nontrivially over a subgroup $K$ if $G$ can be expressed as a nontrivial amalgamated free product $G = A *_K B$ or an HNN extension $G = A *_K$ over $K$. Two subgroups $K_1, K_2 \le G$ are commensurable if $K_1 \cap K_2$ has finite index in both.

Prove or disprove the following: if $G$ is a finitely generated group and $H \le G$ admits an $H$-proper $H$-almost invariant subset $A \subseteq G$, then $G$ splits nontrivially over a subgroup commensurable with a subgroup of $H$.

The Kropholler conjecture (1988) generalizes Stallings' ends theorem. It is known in several cases: when $G$ and $H$ are Poincaré duality groups (Kropholler–Roller, Dunwoody–Swenson), for quasiconvex subgroups of hyperbolic groups (Sageev), and more recently for codimension-1 subgroups of finite splitting height (Petrosyan and collaborators, 2019–2022). A 2022 attempt at a general proof was found to have gaps (noted by Sam Shepherd), so the full conjecture remains open in general.

An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set satisfying the standard axioms (existence of a least and greatest face, the diamond condition, strong flag-connectedness, and a rank function). Its automorphism group acts on the set of flags (maximal chains). An abstract polytope is called regular if this action is transitive on flags, and chiral if it has exactly two orbits on flags with the property that any two adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

A realization of an abstract polytope $\mathcal{P}$ of rank $n$ in a Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^d$ is a mapping $\beta$ from the vertex set of $\mathcal{P}$ into $\mathbb{E}^d$ together with the induced mappings of higher-rank faces, compatible with incidence; a realization is faithful if these induced mappings are injective on each rank. For regular abstract polytopes there is a well-developed realization theory (organized via the realization cone, the structure of pure/irreducible realizations, the Wythoff-space construction, dimension and full-rank/nearly full-rank bounds, and orthogonal decomposition of realizations).

Problem: Develop an analogous, complete realization theory for chiral abstract polytopes. In particular, describe the space of realizations of a finite (and infinite) chiral abstract polytope of rank $n$ in Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{E}^d$, identify the irreducible/pure realizations and a decomposition theorem for general realizations, determine the minimum dimension required for a faithful realization (full-rank and nearly full-rank cases) and the constraints imposed by chirality (e.g., non-convexity, skewness, mirror behavior), and provide a structural organization of geometric realizations of chiral polytopes parallel to the regular case.

Searches indicate that while certain dimensional bounds for faithful realizations of chiral polytopes are known (a finite chiral polytope of rank $n$ requires a faithful Euclidean realization of dimension strictly greater than $n$, with full-rank and nearly full-rank realizations studied in low ranks), no comprehensive realization theory analogous to that for regular abstract polytopes has been developed. Let $X$ be a separable complex Banach space, and let $T:X\to X$ be a bounded linear operator. A vector $x\in X$ is called frequently hypercyclic for $T$ if for every nonempty open set $U\subseteq X$ the set $\{n\in\mathbb{N}: T^n x\in U\}$ has positive lower density, i.e. $\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\#\{1\le n\le N: T^n x\in U\}>0$. A frequently hypercyclic subspace for $T$ is an infinite-dimensional closed linear subspace $M\subseteq X$ such that every nonzero vector of $M$ is frequently hypercyclic for $T$.

For a bounded weight sequence $w=(w_n)_{n\ge 1}$ of nonzero scalars, the weighted backward shift $B_w$ on $\ell^p(\mathbb{N})$, $1\le p<\infty$, is defined by $B_w(x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots)=(w_2 x_2, w_3 x_3, w_4 x_4,\dots)$.

(a) Characterize, in terms of the weight sequence $w$, those weighted backward shifts $B_w$ on $\ell^p$ ($1\le p<\infty$) that possess a frequently hypercyclic subspace.

(b) More generally, give a characterization of those bounded linear operators on a separable complex Banach space that possess a frequently hypercyclic subspace.

Let G be a discrete group. Recall that:
- G is soluble if it admits a finite normal series with abelian factors.
- G is of type VF if it has a finite-index subgroup that admits a finite Eilenberg–MacLane space K(H,1) (equivalently, H has a finite classifying space).
- A model for EG is a G-CW-complex X such that every isotropy group is finite, and for every finite subgroup F ≤ G the fixed-point set X^F is contractible (X is a classifying space for proper G-actions). A model for EG is called cocompact if the quotient G\X is compact (equivalently, X has only finitely many G-cells).

Prove or disprove: every soluble group G of type VF admits a cocompact model for EG.

Let $G$ be a soluble group. Recall:
- $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_\infty$ if the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$ admits a projective resolution $\cdots\to P_n\to\cdots\to P_0\to\mathbb{Z}\to 0$ in which every $P_n$ is finitely generated.
- $\mathrm{cd}\,G$ is the cohomological dimension of $G$ over $\mathbb{Z}$, i.e.\ the projective dimension of the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$.
- The Hirsch length $h(G)$ of a soluble group $G$ is the (possibly infinite) sum, over a subnormal series with abelian factors, of the torsion-free ranks of those factors; this number is independent of the chosen series.
- $G$ is constructible if it can be obtained from the trivial group by a finite sequence of operations of the following two kinds: forming finite extensions, and forming HNN extensions or amalgamated free products along finitely generated subgroups, where the result remains in the class.

Prove or disprove: for every soluble group $G$, the following three conditions are equivalent.
(1) $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_\infty$.
(2) $\mathrm{cd}\,G = h(G) < \infty$.
(3) $G$ is constructible.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The conjecture (going back to Kropholler) that for soluble groups the conditions $\mathrm{FP}_\infty$, $\mathrm{cd}\,G=h(G)<\infty$, and constructibility coincide remains open in full generality. Partial results are known: for instance, Bridson–Kropholler and others have established the equality $\mathrm{hd}_k(G)=h(G)$ for elementary amenable groups under suitable hypotheses, and constructible soluble groups are known to be $\mathrm{FP}_\infty$ with $\mathrm{cd}\,G=h(G)$, but the converse implications (especially that an $\mathrm{FP}_\infty$ soluble group must be constructible) are not established.

Let $n\ge 4$ be an integer and consider the group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ of $n\times n$ integer matrices of determinant $1$, equipped with a finite generating set (for instance, the elementary matrices $E_{ij}(1)$ for $i\ne j$). Recall that for a finitely presented group $G=\langle S\mid R\rangle$, the Dehn function $\delta_G:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is defined by
$$\delta_G(k)=\max\{\mathrm{Area}(w):w\text{ a word in }S^{\pm1}\text{ of length }\le k\text{ representing }1\text{ in }G\},$$
where $\mathrm{Area}(w)$ is the minimal number $N$ such that $w$ can be written in the free group on $S$ as a product $\prod_{i=1}^{N} g_i r_i^{\pm 1} g_i^{-1}$ with $r_i\in R$. The growth type of $\delta_G$ (up to the standard equivalence $\simeq$ on functions $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$) is a quasi-isometry invariant of $G$.

Question: Is the Dehn function of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ equivalent to $k\mapsto k^2$ when $n\ge 4$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The question of whether being a CAT(0) group is preserved under finite extensions (equivalently, whether it is a commensurability invariant) is a well-known subtle problem in geometric group theory. A finite-index subgroup of a CAT(0) group is clearly CAT(0), but the converse direction (passing to finite extensions) is delicate because the natural product-action construction does not yield a cocompact action in general. Web searches did not turn up a definitive resolution, so the status appears to remain unknown/open.

A finitely generated group $G$ is called a CAT(0) group if it acts properly, cocompactly, and by isometries on a CAT(0) metric space, that is, a geodesic metric space in which every geodesic triangle is at least as "thin" as the comparison triangle of the same side lengths in the Euclidean plane (Gromov's CAT(0) inequality).

Question: Does every CAT(0) group $G$ satisfy the Tits Alternative?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The Tits Alternative for general CAT(0) groups remains open. It has been established in important special cases: groups acting properly on finite-dimensional CAT(0) cube complexes (Sageev–Wise and others) and groups acting on 2-dimensional CAT(0) complexes with bounded cell stabilizers. The general case of CAT(0) groups is still considered a major open problem in geometric group theory.

Among all lower semicontinuous functions $v : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $v \geq 0$ and $\mu + \Delta v \leq 1$ in the sense of distributions (where $\Delta$ is the Laplacian and the inequality means that $1 - \mu - \Delta v$ is a nonnegative distribution), let $u$ be the (pointwise) smallest such function. $$\Omega = \bigcup_{x \in K} B(x, \rho(x)),$$
where $B(x, r) = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^n : |y - x| < r\}$ is the open Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $x$ (with the convention $B(x, 0) = \emptyset$)?

Let $1\le k<d$ be integers and let $\Sigma=\Sigma^k\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a $k$-dimensional $\mathcal{H}^k$-measurable submanifold (sufficiently smooth where required). Consider the following geometric curvature energies:

(i) The higher-dimensional tangent-point energy of exponent $p>0$:
$$E_p(\Sigma)\;=\;\int_\Sigma\!\!\int_\Sigma \frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{tp}}(x,y)^p}\,d\mathcal{H}^k(x)\,d\mathcal{H}^k(y),$$
where $R_{\mathrm{tp}}(x,y)$ is the radius of the smallest $d$-dimensional ball tangent to $T_x\Sigma$ at $x$ and passing through $y$.

(ii) The higher-dimensional integral Menger curvature of exponent $p>0$:
$$M_p(\Sigma)\;=\;\int_\Sigma\!\cdots\!\int_\Sigma K_p(x_0,\dots,x_{k+1})\,d\mathcal{H}^k(x_0)\cdots d\mathcal{H}^k(x_{k+1}),$$
the integration being over $(k+2)$ copies of $\Sigma$, where $K_p(x_0,\dots,x_{k+1})$ equals the reciprocal $p$-th power of the circumradius (or equivalent geometric size) of the $(k+1)$-simplex spanned by the points $x_0,\dots,x_{k+1}$.

(iii) Non-smooth variants of these energies obtained by replacing one or more of the integrations in (i) or (ii) by a supremum over the corresponding variable (e.g. $\sup_{y\in\Sigma}\int_\Sigma R_{\mathrm{tp}}(x,y)^{-p}\,d\mathcal{H}^k(x)$, or $\sup_{x_0,\dots,x_j}\int\!\cdots\!\int K_p\,d\mathcal{H}^k(x_{j+1})\cdots$, and analogous mixed forms).

Solve the following:

(a) Derive the Euler–Lagrange equations for $E_p$ and for $M_p$ on smooth $k$-dimensional submanifolds for $k\ge 2$, identifying the leading-order operator and lower-order terms.

(b) Prove higher regularity of local minimizers and of critical points of $E_p$ and $M_p$ for appropriate ranges of $p$ above the scale-invariant exponent (e.g. establish $C^\infty$ or analytic regularity by a bootstrap argument).

(c) For the non-smooth variants in (iii), formulate the appropriate variational inclusions (subdifferential or measure-valued first-order conditions) that replace the Euler–Lagrange equations, and study their structure.

(d) Establish regularity results for "thick knotted surfaces" minimizing area among $k$-dimensional surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$ subject to a uniform thickness (positive reach / lower bound on $R_{\mathrm{tp}}$) constraint within a fixed isotopy class.

Available results address the Euler–Lagrange equations and $C^\infty$-regularity of critical points only in the one-dimensional (curve) case, e.g. Blatt–Reiter's regularity theory for tangent-point energies $TP^{(p,2)}$ and integral Menger curvature $\mathrm{int}M^{(p,2)}$ on curves. Let $(M,F)$ be a smooth, even-dimensional, oriented Riemannian foliation of a closed Riemannian manifold $M$, and let $E\to M$ be a leafwise flat complex Hermitian vector bundle (i.e., $E$ carries a leafwise flat connection that is compatible with its Hermitian metric, possibly of indefinite signature $U(p,q)$). On each leaf $L$ of $F$ one has the de Rham complex of leafwise differential forms with values in $E|_L$, with leafwise differential $d_F$ and adjoint $d_F^{*}$. The associated leafwise twisted signature operator
$$D_F^{E} \;=\; d_F + d_F^{*}$$
acts on the smooth leafwise $E$-valued differential forms. Its square $\Delta_F^{E} = (d_F+d_F^{*})^{2}$ preserves the natural $\mathbb Z$-grading by leafwise form degree, so the leafwise harmonic forms decompose as
$$\ker \Delta_F^{E} \;=\; \bigoplus_{k=0}^{\dim F}\ker\Delta_F^{E}\big|_{\Omega^{k}(F;E)} .$$
Passing to leafwise $L^{2}$-sections, let $\mathcal H^{*}(F;E)\subset L^{2}\Omega^{*}(F;E)$ denote the kernel of the closure of $D_F^{E}$ (equivalently, of $\Delta_F^{E}$).

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Question.} Does the leafwise $L^{2}$ kernel $\mathcal H^{*}(F;E)$ admit a direct sum decomposition by leafwise differential-form degree,
$$\mathcal H^{*}(F;E) \;=\; \bigoplus_{k=0}^{\dim F}\mathcal H^{k}(F;E),$$
where $\mathcal H^{k}(F;E)$ is the kernel restricted to forms of degree $k$? In other words, are the kernels of the twisted signature operators (in this leafwise $L^{2}$ setting) graded by the degree of differential forms?

Let $(M,g)$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) connected Riemannian manifold. For $\varepsilon>0$, call a complex Hermitian vector bundle $(E,h)\to M$ equipped with a metric connection $\nabla$ an $\varepsilon$-flat bundle if its curvature satisfies $\|R^{\nabla}\|_{g}\le\varepsilon$ pointwise on $M$ (with respect to the operator norm induced by $g$ and $h$).

For each integer $k\ge 0$, define the $k$-th almost flat Betti number of $(M,g)$ by
$$
b_{k}^{\mathrm{af}}(M,g)\;=\;\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0^{+}}\;\sup_{(E,\nabla)\;\varepsilon\text{-flat}}\;\frac{\dim_{\mathbb{C}}H^{k}(M;E)}{\operatorname{rank}(E)},
$$
where $H^{k}(M;E)$ denotes twisted de Rham cohomology with coefficients in the flat-up-to-$\varepsilon$ bundle $E$. Set
$$
b_{g}\;=\;\sum_{k=0}^{\dim M} b_{k}^{\mathrm{af}}(M,g)\;\in\;[0,\infty].
$$

Prove or disprove: if there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $b_{g}\le n$, then the metric $g$ is flat (i.e.\ has identically vanishing sectional curvature).

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}$ be an unbounded domain with rectifiable boundary $\partial\Omega$. Call $\Omega$ an arclength null-quadrature domain (ALNQD) if for every function $f$ that is analytic in $\Omega$, continuous on $\overline{\Omega}$, and integrable with respect to arclength on $\partial\Omega$, one has $\int_{\partial\Omega} f\, ds = 0$. A roof function on $\Omega$ is a positive harmonic function $u : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ that extends continuously to $\partial\Omega$ with $u = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$, and whose gradient $\nabla u$ coincides along $\partial\Omega$ with the inward-pointing unit normal vector to $\partial\Omega$ (equivalently, $u$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$ and $\partial u/\partial n = 1$ on $\partial\Omega$, where $n$ is the inward unit normal).

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}$ be an unbounded domain with rectifiable boundary $\partial\Omega$. Call $\Omega$ an arclength null-quadrature domain (ALNQD) if for every function $f$ that is analytic in $\Omega$, continuous on $\overline{\Omega}$, and integrable with respect to arclength on $\partial\Omega$, one has $\int_{\partial\Omega} f\, ds = 0$. A roof function on $\Omega$ is a positive harmonic function $u : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ that extends continuously to $\partial\Omega$ with $u = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$, and whose gradient $\nabla u$ coincides along $\partial\Omega$ with the inward-pointing unit normal vector to $\partial\Omega$ (equivalently, $u$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$ and $\partial u/\partial n = 1$ on $\partial\Omega$, where $n$ is the inward unit normal).

Question: Does every arclength null-quadrature domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}$ admit a roof function?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question has been partially resolved: Khavinson and Lundberg established that every arclength null-quadrature domain with finitely many boundary components admits a roof function (Bull. London Math. Soc., 2022; arXiv:2005.09822). The general case (without a finiteness assumption on the boundary components) does not appear to be settled.

Background and definitions. For an integer k ≥ 1 and n > k, let M be a k-dimensional smooth manifold and γ: M → ℝⁿ an immersion with image Σ = γ(M). Define the tangent-point radius r_tp(x,y) for distinct x,y ∈ Σ as the radius of the smallest ball through x and y that is tangent to the tangent plane T_xΣ at x. For exponents p > 0, the tangent-point energy is

  E_p(Σ) = ∫_Σ ∫_Σ (1/r_tp(x,y))^p dℋ^k(x) dℋ^k(y),

and the integral Menger curvature is

  M_p(Σ) = ∫_Σ ··· ∫_Σ K(x_0,…,x_{k+1})^p dℋ^k(x_0)···dℋ^k(x_{k+1}),

where K(x_0,…,x_{k+1}) is the inverse of the circumradius of the (k+2)-tuple. The scale-invariant exponents are p = 2k for E_p and p = k(k+2) for M_p. A higher-dimensional Möbius-type energy for k-submanifolds is defined analogously, with the appropriate scale-invariant exponent.

Problems. Consider the scale-invariant regime, i.e. p = 2k for the tangent-point energy E_{2k}, p = k(k+2) for the integral Menger curvature M_{k(k+2)}, and the analogous scale-invariant Möbius-type energy on k-submanifolds.

(a) Determine the optimal regularity (in the scale of Sobolev, Hölder, or Besov spaces) of an arbitrary Lipschitz curve (k = 1) or k-dimensional submanifold of ℝⁿ that has finite scale-invariant energy, for each of these energies.

(b) For the higher-dimensional generalization of the Möbius energy to k-dimensional submanifolds in ℝⁿ, determine the optimal regularity of finite-energy submanifolds.

(c) Determine the optimal (smallest) constant c_E in Fenchel-type lower bounds of the form
  E(Σ) ≥ c_E
for every closed (i.e. compact without boundary) k-submanifold Σ ⊂ ℝⁿ, where E ranges over the scale-invariant geometric curvature energies above.

(d) Let M be a k-dimensional smooth manifold and γ: M → ℝⁿ an immersion. Show, or find a counterexample to, the following statement: if γ(M) has finite scale-invariant tangent-point energy E_{2k}, or finite scale-invariant integral Menger curvature M_{k(k+2)}, then γ is automatically an embedding.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Searches indicate sharp results are known in the supercritical (above scale-invariant) regime—e.g. finite tangent-point energy E_p with p > 2k yields C^{1,μ} regularity with optimal Hölder exponent μ = 1 − 2k/p, and embeddedness follows—but the scale-invariant cases p = 2k and p = k(k+2) remain delicate. Recent work (Blatt–Reiter–Vorderobermeier, 2021, on scale-invariant tangent-point energies for knots) addresses minimizers/critical points in the scale-invariant regime for curves but does not resolve optimal regularity of arbitrary finite-energy Lipschitz objects, optimal Fenchel-type constants, or the automatic-embeddedness question in full generality for k ≥ 1. Thus the cluster of questions appears to remain open.

Let $(M,g)$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) Riemannian manifold. For points $p,q \in M$, let $\Gamma(p,q)$ denote the set of geodesic segments from $p$ to $q$ (parametrized by arclength, with no restriction on length). A subset $B \subset M \setminus \{p,q\}$ is said to block $\Gamma(p,q)$ if every $\gamma \in \Gamma(p,q)$ passes through some point of $B$.

Define two properties:

(CB, "cross blocking") For every pair of points $p,q \in M$ with $d(p,q) < \mathrm{diam}(M,g)$, the set $\Gamma(p,q)$ can be blocked by a finite set of cardinality at most $2$ (equivalently, there exist points $x,y \in M\setminus\{p,q\}$ such that every geodesic from $p$ to $q$ passes through $x$ or $y$).

(SB, "sphere blocking") For every point $p \in M$, the set $\Gamma(p,p)$ of geodesic loops at $p$ can be blocked by a single point $x \in M\setminus\{p\}$.

A compact rank one symmetric space (CROSS) is a Riemannian manifold isometric to one of: a round sphere $S^n$, a real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^n$, a complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$, a quaternionic projective space $\mathbb{HP}^n$, or the Cayley projective plane $\mathbb{OP}^2$, each equipped with its canonical metric (possibly rescaled).

Prove or disprove:

(a) A closed Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ has property (CB) if and only if $(M,g)$ is isometric to a compact rank one symmetric space.

(b) A closed Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ has both properties (CB) and (SB) if and only if $(M,g)$ is isometric to a round sphere.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture characterizing compact rank one symmetric spaces by the cross-blocking property remains open in general. Known partial results include: closed Riemannian surfaces with cross blocking are isometric to constant-curvature spheres or projective planes; Blaschke manifolds diffeomorphic to the sphere are isometric to round spheres (Berger), and Lafont-Souto and subsequent work established the SB+CB characterization of round spheres under additional hypotheses such as the Blaschke condition. The full conjecture has not been settled.

Let p be an odd prime and consider the tower of cyclotomic fields ℚ(ζ_{p^{n+1}}) for n ≥ 0, with minus parts of class numbers h_n^- = h^-(ℚ(ζ_{p^{n+1}})). Stickelberger's theorem and Iwasawa theory provide a power series construction associated with these fields: there exists a power series F(T) ∈ ℤ_p[[T]] (built from Stickelberger elements / p-adic L-functions) such that, after a suitable normalization, the special values of F at points of the form ζ − 1, where ζ runs over p^n-th roots of unity, encode (up to p-adic units) the minus parts h_n^- of the class numbers of the layers of the cyclotomic ℤ_p-extension. Concretely, assume the following statement is given:

(2) There is a power series F(T) ∈ ℤ_p[[T]], canonically attached to the cyclotomic tower, whose values at p^n-th roots of unity minus 1 produce, via a fixed explicit formula, the minus class numbers h_n^- (more precisely, the relative class numbers of the intermediate cyclotomic fields) up to p-adic units.

Question: What arithmetic information about the class numbers h_n^- can one deduce from statement (2)? In particular, what does the existence of such an interpolating power series imply about: (a) the growth of v_p(h_n^-) as n → ∞ (Iwasawa's λ- and μ-invariants), (b) divisibility properties of h_n^-, and (c) congruences between class numbers at different levels of the tower?

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk and $\mathbb{T}=\partial\mathbb{D}$ its boundary, equipped with arc-length measure $|d\zeta|$. For a real parameter $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|$ small, consider the nonlinear Loewner-type evolution equation for a family of conformal maps $f(\cdot,t):\mathbb{D}\to\Omega_t\subset\mathbb{C}$, $t\ge 0$:
$$\partial_t f(z,t) \;=\; z\,f'(z,t)\int_{\mathbb{T}} \frac{z+\zeta}{z-\zeta}\,\frac{|d\zeta|}{|f'(\zeta,t)|^{\alpha}},\qquad z\in\mathbb{D},$$
with initial condition $f(z,0)=\varphi(z)$, where $\varphi:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a univalent (conformal) map and $f'$ denotes the derivative in the spatial variable $z$. The boundary integrand $1/|f'(\zeta,t)|^{\alpha}$ is to be interpreted in a suitable boundary trace sense.

Question: Does this evolution admit a satisfactory existence and uniqueness theory for $|\alpha|$ sufficiently small, within natural classes of initial conformal maps $\varphi$ (for instance, those whose image has smooth boundary, or bounded boundary derivative away from $0$ and $\infty$)? In particular, identify a class of initial data and a notion of solution for which local-in-time existence and uniqueness hold, and determine whether the solutions extend globally in time.

Recent work on regularized Hastings–Levitov aggregation and Loewner–Kufarev type equations has established existence/uniqueness and scaling-limit results in subcritical parameter regimes (e.g., $\zeta=\alpha+\eta\le 1$), which covers the small-$|\alpha|$ regime for regularized variants. Consider rectifiable closed curves $\gamma:\mathbb{S}^1\to\mathbb{R}^3$ of fixed length. For three distinct points $x,y,z$ on the curve, let $R(x,y,z)$ denote the radius of the unique circle through these points (the circumradius), and define the (inverse) Menger curvature $c(x,y,z)=1/R(x,y,z)$. For a parameter $p\ge 2$, the integral Menger curvature is
$$\mathcal{M}_p(\gamma)=\iiint_{(\mathbb{S}^1)^3} c(\gamma(s),\gamma(t),\gamma(u))^p\,|\gamma'(s)||\gamma'(t)||\gamma'(u)|\,ds\,dt\,du.$$
Address the following questions about minimizers of geometric curvature energies on curves:

(a) Among all simple closed rectifiable curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$ of fixed length, is the round planar circle the unique minimizer of $\mathcal{M}_p$ for $p>3$ (and in particular for $p=2$ where the energy is well-defined on suitable classes)?

(b) Determine the precise geometric shape of ideal knots, i.e., minimizers within a fixed knot class of the ropelength functional $\mathcal{R}(\gamma)=\mathrm{length}(\gamma)/\Delta[\gamma]$, where $\Delta[\gamma]$ is the thickness (the largest radius $r$ such that a tube of radius $r$ around $\gamma$ is embedded).

(c) For links with three or more components in $\mathbb{R}^3$, determine the shapes of minimizers of the Möbius energy
$$E(\gamma)=\iint \Big(\frac{1}{|\gamma(s)-\gamma(t)|^2}-\frac{1}{d_\gamma(s,t)^2}\Big)|\gamma'(s)||\gamma'(t)|\,ds\,dt$$
summed over components and pairs of components, where $d_\gamma$ is the intrinsic distance.

(d) Identify global minimizing shapes for other geometric curvature energies on curves (e.g., O'Hara energies, tangent-point energies).

(e) For the elastic knot problem—minimizing the total squared curvature $\int_\gamma \kappa^2\,ds$ subject to a thickness constraint within a prescribed knot class—prove results determining the shape of minimizers for nontrivial knot classes other than the $(2,b)$-torus knots.

(f) Determine the shape of twisted elastic knots (minimizers of an elastic energy incorporating a framing/twist contribution) within nontrivial knot classes.

The question of whether the round circle minimizes integral Menger curvature among closed curves is widely regarded as open; partial progress includes that the round circle is a critical point (Hermes, 2014) and recent second-variation analyses suggesting it is an isolated local minimizer, but global uniqueness, the shapes of ideal knots, Möbius-energy minimizing multi-component links, and elastic-knot minimizers for general nontrivial knot classes remain unresolved.

Let $(T,g)$ be a closed (compact, boundaryless) Riemannian manifold. For points $x,y\in T$, let $\Gamma(x,y)$ denote the set of geodesic segments in $T$ from $x$ to $y$, and define the blocking number
\[ b_g(x,y)\;=\;\inf\bigl\{\,n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}\;:\;\text{there exist }p_1,\dots,p_n\in T\setminus\{x,y\}\text{ such that every }\gamma\in\Gamma(x,y)\text{ passes through some }p_i\,\bigr\}. \]
One says that $(T,g)$ has the finite blocking property if $b_g(x,y)<\infty$ for every pair $(x,y)\in T\times T$, and the uniform finite blocking property if in addition $\sup_{(x,y)\in T\times T} b_g(x,y)<\infty$. Suppose hypothesis $(2)$ asserts that $(T,g)$ has the finite blocking property.

Let $F(T)$ denote the invariant attached to $T$ defined as the supremum
\[ F(T)\;=\;\sup_{(x,y)\in T\times T}\;b_g(x,y)\;\in\;\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}. \]
Determine what hypothesis $(2)$ implies about the invariant $F(T)$: in particular, does the finite blocking property of $(T,g)$ force $F(T)$ to be finite (i.e. does pointwise finite blocking imply uniform finite blocking on a closed Riemannian manifold), and if so, can a bound on $F(T)$ be given in terms of geometric or topological invariants of $(T,g)$?

Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a finite group whose largest normal $p$-subgroup $O_p(G)$ is trivial. A $p$-chain of $G$ is a strictly increasing chain $C : 1 = P_0 < P_1 < \cdots < P_n$ of $p$-subgroups of $G$; set $|C| = n$ and $G_C = \bigcap_{i=0}^n N_G(P_i)$. Two chains are equivalent under the $G$-conjugation action, and $\mathcal{R}(G)/G$ denotes a set of representatives of the $G$-orbits of such chains (the radical, or all, $p$-chains depending on the standard normalization; one may take all strict $p$-chains starting at $1$).

For a $p$-block $B$ of $G$ and a chain $C$ as above, let $B_C$ denote the set of blocks $b$ of $G_C$ with Brauer correspondent $b^G = B$, and let $k(C, B, d)$ denote the number of irreducible ordinary characters of $G_C$ of $p$-defect $d$ that lie in some block in $B_C$.

Prove that for every $p$-block $B$ of $G$ which is not of defect zero, and for every nonnegative integer $d$,
$$\sum_{C \in \mathcal{R}(G)/G} (-1)^{|C|} \, k(C, B, d) \;=\; 0.$$

Let $\mathbb{D}$ denote the open unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{T}=\partial\mathbb{D}$ the unit circle, and $|d\zeta|$ the arc-length measure on $\mathbb{T}$. For a real parameter $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, consider the nonlinear, nonlocal evolution equation for a one-parameter family of conformal maps $f(\cdot,t):\mathbb{D}\to\Omega(t)\subset\mathbb{C}$,
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(z,t)\;=\;z\,f'(z,t)\,\int_{\mathbb{T}}\frac{z+\zeta}{z-\zeta}\,\frac{|d\zeta|}{|f'(\zeta,t)|^{\alpha}},\qquad z\in\mathbb{D},$$
where $f'$ denotes the derivative in $z$ and the boundary values $|f'(\zeta,t)|$ are taken in a suitable nontangential sense. Starting from a smooth univalent initial datum $f(z,0)$, analyze and contrast the qualitative behavior of the solutions for $\alpha>0$ versus $\alpha<0$. In particular:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Determine, in each sign regime, whether the boundary growth concentrates near points where $|f'(\zeta,t)|$ is small (corresponding to inward-pointing/cusp-like features of $\partial\Omega(t)$) or near points where $|f'(\zeta,t)|$ is large (corresponding to outward-pointing/protrusion features).
\item Establish whether, and in what sense, finite-time singularities (loss of univalence, cusp formation, or blow-up of curvature) can form, and characterize the asymptotic shape of $\Omega(t)$ as such a singularity is approached.
\item Identify any conserved or monotone quantities (e.g., area, capacity, or weighted moments) that distinguish the two regimes.
\end{enumerate}

representations.normalized:
Doubly-Special Relativity (DSR) is a class of relativistic theories that postulates two observer-independent scales: the speed of light c and an energy scale E_p (the Planck energy). In such theories the standard relativistic dispersion relation E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4 is replaced by a deformed relation of the form E^2 f_1(E/E_p)^2 - p^2 c^2 f_2(E/E_p)^2 = m^2 c^4, where f_1, f_2 → 1 as E/E_p → 0, and the action of boosts on energy–momentum is correspondingly nonlinear so that E_p is invariant. For a single microscopic particle with E ≪ E_p, the deformation produces only small corrections compatible with experiment.

However, an ordinary macroscopic body (e.g. a planet or a soccer ball) is a composite system whose total energy E_total greatly exceeds E_p. Naively applying the deformed dispersion relation and the deformed boost action to E_total leads to predictions that are in gross conflict with the observed Galilean/special-relativistic behaviour of macroscopic objects.

Problem: Construct, within the DSR framework, a consistent kinematical description of composite/macroscopic bodies such that:

(a) Each microscopic constituent obeys the DSR-deformed dispersion relation and deformed boost transformations with the same invariant scale E_p.

(b) The total energy–momentum of a macroscopic body composed of N microscopic constituents (with total energy possibly far above E_p) transforms under boosts and satisfies a dispersion relation that reduces, to phenomenologically required accuracy, to the ordinary undeformed special-relativistic kinematics.

(c) The prescription for combining constituent energy–momenta into a total energy–momentum is well-defined, associative (or otherwise physically consistent for arbitrary N), Lorentz-DSR covariant, and reduces appropriately in both the microscopic single-particle limit and the macroscopic many-body limit.

Provide such a construction, or prove that no such construction exists within the DSR axioms.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question—known as the "soccer-ball problem" of DSR—remains an actively discussed open problem. Multiple partial proposals exist (rescaling E_p with particle number N, nonlinear composition laws via relative locality, energy-momentum-dependent metrics over Planck cells), but no consensus resolution has been established. Recent works (e.g. Amelino-Camelia et al. on relative locality, 2022 arXiv:2203.04091, and Hossenfelder's "Soccer-Ball Problem") continue to treat it as unresolved.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $P$ be a finite $p$-group. A fusion system on $P$ is a category $\mathcal{F}$ whose objects are the subgroups of $P$ and whose morphisms are injective group homomorphisms between subgroups, satisfying: (i) for all $Q,R \le P$, every conjugation map $c_g: Q \to R$ induced by $g \in P$ with $g^{-1}Qg \le R$ is a morphism; and (ii) every morphism factors as an isomorphism in $\mathcal{F}$ followed by an inclusion. Assume in addition that $\mathcal{F}$ is saturated in the usual sense.

A subgroup $P' \le P$ is called strongly $\mathcal{F}$-closed if for every $Q \le P'$ and every morphism $\varphi : Q \to P$ in $\mathcal{F}$, one has $\varphi(Q) \le P'$.

A normal fusion subsystem $\mathcal{F}'$ of $\mathcal{F}$ on $P'$ is a saturated fusion subsystem on $P'$ which is $\mathcal{F}$-invariant and which satisfies the additional extension condition that every automorphism in $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathcal{F}'}(P')$ extends to an $\mathcal{F}$-automorphism of $P' C_P(P')$ acting trivially on the quotient $P' C_P(P')/P'$.

Prove or disprove: for every saturated fusion system $\mathcal{F}$ on $P$ and every strongly $\mathcal{F}$-closed subgroup $P' \le P$, there exists a normal fusion subsystem $\mathcal{F}'$ of $\mathcal{F}$ on $P'$.

The conjecture as stated is false in general: Aschbacher constructed examples of strongly $\mathcal{F}$-closed subgroups $T$ in a saturated constrained fusion system $\mathcal{F}$ such that no normal subsystem of $\mathcal{F}$ on $T$ exists (so-called strongly closed subgroups that are "not based"). Thus the conjecture has been refuted, although closely related positive results hold under additional hypotheses.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk. Let $u:\mathbb{D}\to[-\infty,\infty)$ be a subharmonic function and set $w=e^u$, so that $w$ is a logarithmically subharmonic weight on $\mathbb{D}$. Consider the weighted Bergman space
$$A_w^2(\mathbb{D}) = \Big\{ f \text{ holomorphic on } \mathbb{D} : \|f\|_w^2 := \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2 \, w(z)\, dA(z) < \infty \Big\},$$
where $dA$ is area measure. Assume $A_w^2(\mathbb{D})$ is a (non-trivial) reproducing kernel Hilbert space, with reproducing kernel $K_w(z,\xi)$ characterized by $f(\xi) = \langle f, K_w(\cdot,\xi)\rangle_w$ for every $f\in A_w^2(\mathbb{D})$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb{D}$.

(a) Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $C>0$ (possibly depending on $w$) such that for every nonnegative integer $N$ and every choice of complex coefficients $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N$, not all zero, the function
$$z \mapsto \sum_{j=0}^{N} \lambda_j \left.\frac{\partial^j}{\partial \bar\xi^j} K_w(z,\xi)\right|_{\xi=0}$$
has at most $C\cdot N$ zeros in $\mathbb{D}$ (counted with multiplicity), i.e. an $O(N)$ bound.

(b) Prove or disprove the analogous statement: for every $N$, every choice of points $\xi_0,\dots,\xi_N\in\mathbb{D}$, and every choice of complex coefficients $\lambda_0,\dots,\lambda_N$ (not all zero), the function
$$z \mapsto \sum_{j=0}^{N} \lambda_j K_w(z,\xi_j)$$
has at most $O(N)$ zeros in $\mathbb{D}$.

(a) Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $C>0$ (possibly depending on $w$) such that for every nonnegative integer $N$ and every choice of complex coefficients $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N$, not all zero, the function
$$z \mapsto \sum_{j=0}^{N} \lambda_j \left.\frac{\partial^j}{\partial \bar\xi^j} K_w(z,\xi)\right|_{\xi=0}$$
has at most $C\cdot N$ zeros in $\mathbb{D}$ (counted with multiplicity), i.e. an $O(N)$ bound.

(b) Prove or disprove the analogous statement: for every $N$, every choice of points $\xi_0,\dots,\xi_N\in\mathbb{D}$, and every choice of complex coefficients $\lambda_0,\dots,\lambda_N$ (not all zero), the function
$$z \mapsto \sum_{j=0}^{N} \lambda_j K_w(z,\xi_j)$$
has at most $O(N)$ zeros in $\mathbb{D}$.
