Doubly-Special Relativity (DSR) is a framework that deforms the kinematics of Special Relativity by postulating, in addition to the invariant speed of light c, a second observer-independent scale (typically the Planck energy/length). The robust formulations of DSR developed so far specify a deformed Poincaré-type action on energy-momentum space, leading to modified dispersion relations and modified composition laws for momenta, while leaving the corresponding spacetime picture undetermined.

Problem: Identify a spacetime description compatible with the DSR framework. Specifically, construct (or prove the existence/uniqueness of) a notion of "spacetime" — possibly realized through a noncommutative geometry, or only as an approximate concept valid within a limited class of observations — that satisfies all of the following:

(a) It is invariant, in an appropriate operational sense, under the DSR-deformed relativistic transformations acting in the momentum sector, with two observer-independent scales c and an energy/length scale at the Planck regime.

(b) It is consistent with the deformed dispersion relations and deformed momentum composition laws characterizing DSR kinematics.

(c) Either (i) it preserves the absolute (observer-independent) statement that two pointlike particles emitted with the same energy-momentum follow the same worldline for all inertial observers, or (ii) it provides a precise alternative replacing that statement, specifying the operational meaning of "trajectory" and "coincidence of events" in the proposed framework.

(d) If the velocity relation v = dE/dp is retained as the group velocity of a wave packet, the proposed spacetime structure must reproduce this relation in the appropriate classical/low-energy limit.

Determine whether such a spacetime picture exists and, if so, characterize it.

with $x, y \in F(X)$. Prove that every such solution must have both $x$ and $y$ constant (i.e., lying in $F$); equivalently, show that no nonconstant rational-function solutions $(x,y) \in F(X)^2$ exist.

Let $\omega=(\omega_m)_{m\ge 0}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers, and define the weighted Hardy space
$$H^2_\omega = \Big\{\,f(z)=\sum_{m\ge 0} a_m z^m \text{ analytic on the unit disk } : \|f\|_\omega^2 := \sum_{m\ge 0} |a_m|^2 \omega_m < \infty\,\Big\},$$
with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle_\omega = \sum_m a_m \overline{b_m}\,\omega_m$ for $f=\sum a_m z^m$, $g=\sum b_m z^m$. A function $h\in H^2_\omega$ is called $H^2_\omega$-inner if $\|h\|_\omega=1$ and
$$\langle z^n h,\, h\rangle_\omega = 0 \quad \text{for every integer } n\ge 1.$$
Suppose $h$ is an entire function (so its Taylor series at $0$ converges on all of $\mathbb{C}$), and let $k\ge 0$ denote the multiplicity of the zero of $h$ at the origin (with the convention $k=0$ if $h(0)\neq 0$). Assume there exists a weight sequence $\omega$ such that $h\in H^2_\omega$ and $h$ is $H^2_\omega$-inner. Must $h$ then be equal to the normalized monomial
$$h(z)=\frac{z^k}{\|z^k\|_\omega}\,?$$

Consider a class of modifications of special relativity, known as Doubly-Special Relativity (DSR), in which the Poincaré symmetries of Minkowski spacetime are deformed so as to admit two observer-independent scales: the speed of light c and an additional invariant energy/length scale (typically identified with the Planck scale). In a significant subclass of such theories (for example the DSR1 framework based on the bicrossproduct-basis κ-Poincaré Hopf algebra), the on-shell dispersion relation is modified so that the group velocity of massless quanta depends on energy, with ultra-high-energy photons propagating faster than low-energy photons (whose speed is c).

Formulate a complete and internally consistent notion of causality for such DSR theories. Concretely:

(1) Define, in a Lorentz-deformation-invariant way, a partial order on events of (possibly noncommutative or momentum-dependent) DSR spacetime that plays the role of the causal order of Minkowski spacetime, taking into account that the propagation cone of a signal depends on the energy of the carrier.

(2) Determine whether the resulting causal structure permits closed causal curves, signaling outside an observer-independent maximal cone, or other pathologies, and identify the conditions on the deformed dispersion relation and composition law of momenta under which causality (in the sense of (1)) is preserved.

(3) Derive the operational consequences for observers who can access arbitrarily high-energy probes: in particular, decide whether the notion of simultaneity/time becomes effectively absolute for such observers, and characterize the cosmological and observational signatures (e.g. for time-of-flight measurements from distant astrophysical sources) implied by the proposed causal structure.

$$S \;=\; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1}\,\frac{n}{p_n}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The unconditional convergence of the series remains an open problem of Erdős. In 2023, Tao showed that the series converges conditionally on a sufficiently strong form of the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuples conjecture, using a random sifted model of the primes. Numerical computations suggest the sum is approximately −0.052161. A 2025 preprint further studies Hölder continuity properties of a related alternating Erdős series assuming the prime k-tuples conjecture.

Let $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be an unbounded region whose boundary is regular for the Dirichlet problem (every continuous boundary datum admits a classical harmonic extension that attains the data continuously at every boundary point). Consider the following two statements about $D$:

(PI) There exists a bounded function $u : D \times [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$, not identically zero, that is continuous on $\overline{D} \times [0,1]$, vanishes on $\partial D \times [0,1]$, satisfies the heat equation $u_t = \Delta u$ in $D \times (0,1)$, and satisfies $u(x,1) = 0$ for every $x \in D$.

(PII) There exists a harmonic function $v : D \to \mathbb{R}$, not identically zero, that is continuous on $\overline{D}$, vanishes on $\partial D$, and satisfies $v(x) = O(\exp(-|x|^2))$ as $|x| \to \infty$ within $D$.

Prove or disprove: for every such region $D$, the statements (PI) and (PII) are equivalent.

Consider classical gravitation in the weak-field, non-relativistic regime, where the gravitational potential generated by a static mass distribution is conventionally taken to be the Newtonian potential V(r) = -GM/r, established empirically on solar-system distance scales. Let the observed (approximately flat) HI rotation curves of spiral galaxies at large galactocentric radii serve as test data.

(a) Determine whether the gravitational potential of a localized mass distribution must, on galactic and larger distance scales, be exactly Newtonian (i.e. proportional to 1/r for a point mass), or whether observations are equally consistent with a modified large-distance potential of the form
   V(r) = -GM/r + γ M r
(an additional linear-in-r term, with γ a universal coupling), or with another non-Newtonian asymptotic behavior.

(b) Decide whether the observed flatness of galactic rotation curves should be regarded as evidence for the existence of unseen ("dark") matter distributed in halos within standard Newton–Einstein gravity, or instead as evidence that the 1/r potential is being extrapolated beyond the range of distances on which it has been empirically validated, with the asymptotic dynamics actually governed by a non-Newtonian (e.g. linear) term.

State definitively, with theoretical and observational justification, which alternative is correct, or prove that current data cannot discriminate between them.

(a) Determine whether the gravitational potential of a localized mass distribution must, on galactic and larger distance scales, be exactly Newtonian (i.e. proportional to 1/r for a point mass), or whether observations are equally consistent with a modified large-distance potential of the form
   V(r) = -GM/r + γ M r
(an additional linear-in-r term, with γ a universal coupling), or with another non-Newtonian asymptotic behavior.

(b) Decide whether the observed flatness of galactic rotation curves should be regarded as evidence for the existence of unseen ("dark") matter distributed in halos within standard Newton–Einstein gravity, or instead as evidence that the 1/r potential is being extrapolated beyond the range of distances on which it has been empirically validated, with the asymptotic dynamics actually governed by a non-Newtonian (e.g. linear) term.

State definitively, with theoretical and observational justification, which alternative is correct, or prove that current data cannot discriminate between them.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether Newtonian gravity needs modification at galactic scales or whether flat rotation curves require dark matter remains actively debated. Recent (2022–2025) work continues to explore conformal-gravity-type linear potentials, MOND-like modifications, and f(R,T) theories as alternatives to dark matter, while also documenting tensions (e.g., strong lensing constraints on universal linear-potential parameters). No consensus resolution exists.

Consider a one-input joint-production economy with a finite set $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ of agents. There is a single input (e.g., labor) and a single output, with a production technology described by a convex production set $f$ (so the output $y$ produced from total input $x\ge 0$ satisfies a standard convexity assumption, e.g., $y\le f(x)$ with $f$ concave, nondecreasing, and $f(0)=0$). Each agent $i\in N$ has a preference relation $R_i$ over pairs (own input contribution, own output share) that is convex and monotonic (decreasing in own input, increasing in own output).

A mechanism associates to every economy $(N,f,(R_i)_{i\in N})$ an allocation specifying, for every agent, an input contribution and an output share that is feasible with respect to $f$. Define:

(i) Pareto Optimality: the chosen allocation is not Pareto-dominated by any other feasible allocation given the agents' preferences.

(ii) Egalitarian Lower Bound (ELB): for every profile $(R_1,\dots,R_n)$ and every agent $i$, the welfare of $i$ at the chosen allocation is at least the unanimity welfare of $i$, defined as the welfare $i$ would obtain by optimally exploiting the rescaled production set $\tfrac{1}{n}f$ (the $1/n$-share of the technology) under preference $R_i$ alone — equivalently, the welfare $i$ would secure if all $n$ agents had preference $R_i$ and the symmetric Pareto efficient outcome were chosen.

(iii) Population Monotonicity (PM): if a new agent joins the economy (so the set of agents grows from $N$ to $N\cup\{n+1\}$ with the technology $f$ unchanged), then no agent in the original population $N$ is strictly better off in the new allocation than in the original one.

Question: Does there exist a mechanism, defined on the domain of all such one-input joint-production problems with convex production set and arbitrary convex monotonic preferences, that simultaneously satisfies Pareto Optimality, the Egalitarian Lower Bound, and Population Monotonicity?

Consider classical gravity formulated as a metric field theory on a four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, in which the dynamical variable is a metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ and the field equations are derived from a generally covariant scalar action $S[g]=\int \mathcal{L}(g_{\mu\nu},\partial g,\partial^2 g,\ldots)\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$. Assume:

(i) General covariance (diffeomorphism invariance of the action), so that gravity is a metric-based field theory.

(ii) The equivalence principle for geodesic motion, i.e., free test particles follow geodesics of the metric connection.

These two assumptions alone do not single out a particular Lagrangian, since any generally covariant scalar functional of the metric and its derivatives is compatible with them.

Problem. Identify and rigorously formulate an additional fundamental physical or mathematical principle, independent of (i) and (ii), with the property that the combination of (i), (ii), and this new principle necessarily selects the Einstein–Hilbert Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{EH}=\tfrac{1}{2\kappa}(R-2\Lambda)$ (and hence the second-order Einstein field equations $G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}$) as the unique classical gravitational dynamics in four spacetime dimensions, making the standard theory not merely sufficient but necessary.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Lovelock's theorem (1971) shows that in four dimensions, requiring the field equations to be derived from a metric Lagrangian and to be of at most second order in derivatives, divergence-free, and symmetric uniquely selects the Einstein tensor (plus cosmological constant). This is widely regarded as a partial answer: it pinpoints "second-order equations of motion" as a uniqueness criterion, but does not by itself give a deeper physical principle making this restriction necessary. Modern variants (e.g., dimensional/stress-energy arguments, consistent Levi-Civita truncations) refine the criterion. No single universally accepted "fundamental principle" beyond such technical assumptions has emerged, so the foundational question remains open in the philosophical/physical sense while being partially addressed mathematically.

Let q be an even prime power and let n ≥ 1 be an integer. A generalized oval (or pseudo-oval) in PG(3n−1, q) is a family O of q^n + 1 mutually disjoint (n−1)-dimensional subspaces of PG(3n−1, q) with the property that any three distinct members of O span the whole space PG(3n−1, q). For each element π ∈ O there is a unique (2n−1)-dimensional subspace τ_π of PG(3n−1, q), called the tangent space of O at π, which contains π and is disjoint from every other element of O.

A generalized oval O is called regular if it arises by field reduction from an oval in the projective plane PG(2, q^n), i.e., if there exists an oval Ω in PG(2, q^n) such that O is the image of Ω under the natural map PG(2, q^n) → PG(3n−1, q) given by viewing GF(q^n) as an n-dimensional vector space over GF(q).

A generalized oval O is called a translation generalized oval with axis τ_π (for some distinguished π ∈ O) if there exists a subgroup of PGL(3n, q) consisting of involutions, each fixing τ_π pointwise (i.e., having τ_π as axis), fixing the set O setwise, and acting regularly on O \ {π}.

Question: For q even, must every translation generalized oval in PG(3n−1, q) be regular?

Consider covariant classical theories of gravity in four-dimensional spacetime whose field equations admit every Ricci-flat metric (so in particular the Schwarzschild metric) as a solution, thereby reproducing the standard Newtonian and Schwarzschild exterior phenomenology in the appropriate regimes. Two natural candidates are:

(a) The second-order Einstein theory, whose vacuum field equations are R_{μν} = 0.

(b) A higher-derivative theory of gravity, for example one derived from a Lagrangian of the form L = √(-g)(α R^2 + β R_{μν} R^{μν} + γ R_{μνρσ} R^{μνρσ}) or more generally one whose vacuum equations take the form F_{μν}(R_{αβ}, ∇R_{αβ}, ∇∇R_{αβ}, …) = 0 where F vanishes whenever R_{αβ} = 0. Such a theory admits all Ricci-flat metrics as solutions but may admit additional, non-Ricci-flat vacuum solutions.

Determine, on the basis of observational consequences, which of these covariant theories of gravity is selected by the requirement that the exterior gravitational phenomenology of an isolated spherical body match the observed Schwarzschild/Newtonian behavior. Specifically:

(i) Classify all static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum solutions of the higher-derivative theory (b) that are not Ricci-flat (in particular, the non-Schwarzschild branch).

(ii) Determine the observational signatures of these additional solutions (e.g. modifications to the exterior metric, perihelion precession, light bending, thermodynamics of black holes), and decide whether their existence can be reconciled with, or is excluded by, observations, thereby resolving whether the second-order Einstein theory is uniquely selected among such covariant theories.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial progress has been made on part (i): Lü, Perkins, Pope and Stelle (2015) demonstrated, both via a Lichnerowicz-type theorem and numerically, the existence of a non-Schwarzschild branch of static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat black-hole solutions in four-dimensional Einstein gravity supplemented by quadratic curvature terms, with vanishing Ricci scalar. Subsequent works (e.g. Kokkotas–Konoplya–Zhidenko 2017) provided accurate analytical approximations and studied their stability, quasinormal modes and thermodynamics, and further novel families have been constructed (e.g. 2023 results in JHEP). However, a complete classification of all non-Schwarzschild solutions and a definitive observational verdict deciding Eddington's uniqueness challenge in favor of one theory has not been established; the broader question remains open.

Let $q$ be an odd prime power and let $n\ge 1$ be an integer. Work in the projective space $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. A pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ is a family of $q^n+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional projective subspaces of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ such that any three of them span $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$. Equivalently, every $(n-1)$-space of $\mathcal{O}$ is contained in a unique tangent $(2n-1)$-space which meets no other element of $\mathcal{O}$. The pseudo-oval is called elementary (or arises from an oval) if there exist a field extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q$, an embedding of $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$ as a spread-induced structure in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$, and an oval (a set of $q^n+1$ points, no three collinear) $\mathcal{O}_1\subset \mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$ whose points correspond to the $(n-1)$-spaces of $\mathcal{O}$. A pseudo-oval is called classical (or a pseudo-conic) if it is elementary and $\mathcal{O}_1$ can be chosen to be a non-degenerate conic in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$.

Question: For every odd prime power $q$ and every integer $n\ge 1$, must every pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ be classical?

In standard Einstein gravity the field equation has the form G_{\mu
u} = -8\pi G\, T_{\mu
u}, where G_{\mu
u} = R_{\mu
u} - 	frac{1}{2} g_{\mu
u} R is the Einstein tensor associated to a Lorentzian metric g_{\mu
u}, G is Newton's constant (equivalently, a fixed Planck mass scale M_P = G^{-1/2} appears in the action S_{EH} = (16\pi G)^{-1}\int R\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x), and T_{\mu
u} is the energy-momentum tensor of the matter fields. The Einstein tensor satisfies g^{\mu
u} G_{\mu
u} = -R, which is generically nonzero, so G_{\mu
u} is neither conformally invariant nor traceless.

In modern microscopic descriptions of strong, electromagnetic, and weak interactions, the masses of elementary particles and of macroscopic bodies are not put in by hand as kinematical parameters but are generated dynamically, e.g. by spontaneous symmetry breaking of an underlying locally conformal-invariant action that contains no fundamental mass scales. For such a locally conformal-invariant matter theory the canonically improved energy-momentum tensor T_{\mu
u} is kinematically traceless: g^{\mu
u} T_{\mu
u} = 0 as an identity (not merely as a consequence of the matter equations of motion).

Problem. Construct a classical theory of gravity coupled to matter satisfying all of the following:

(i) The matter sector is described by a locally conformally invariant action with no fundamental mass scales, so that its energy-momentum tensor T_{\mu
u} is identically traceless and all particle and macroscopic mass scales arise from dynamical symmetry breaking in the vacuum.

(ii) The gravitational field equation consistently equates (a tensor built from the metric to) this traceless, conformally covariant T_{\mu
u}, in a manner compatible with the kinematic tracelessness of T_{\mu
u} (i.e. the geometric side of the equation must itself be traceless, or be made so by the same dynamical symmetry-breaking mechanism that generates particle masses).

(iii) The fixed, non-dynamical Planck mass M_P of Einstein gravity is replaced by a scale generated dynamically in the vacuum, so that Newton's constant emerges from the same symmetry-breaking mechanism that gives particles their masses.

(iv) In an appropriate limit or regime, the theory reproduces the empirically successful predictions of Einstein gravity (solar-system tests, Newtonian limit, etc.).

Determine whether such a theory exists, and if so identify what should replace the Einstein tensor G_{\mu
u} and the Planck mass M_P on the gravitational side of the field equation.

Mannheim and Kazanas's conformal (Weyl) gravity program proposes a concrete answer: replace the Einstein–Hilbert action with one quadratic in the Weyl tensor, so the gravitational side of the field equation is the (traceless) Bach tensor matched to a traceless dynamically-generated T_{\mu\nu}, with Newton's constant induced by spontaneous breaking of conformal symmetry. Subsequent work (e.g. Mannheim, "Making the Case for Conformal Gravity", Found. Phys. 2011) develops phenomenology (galactic rotation curves, cancellation of cosmological constant). However, conformal gravity remains controversial (issues with ghosts, solar-system limit, perturbations) and is not universally accepted as a complete resolution, so the broader question of how to reconcile Einstein gravity with dynamical mass generation and conformal matter is best classified as partially solved.

representations.normalized:
In Einstein's general theory of relativity, the active gravitational mass of a stationary, weakly self-gravitating source is identified, via the linearized field equations, with the volume integral

M = ∫ T^{00}(x) d^3x

of the time-time component of the stress-energy tensor (i.e., the energy density) over the source. This identification underlies the Newtonian limit in which the exterior potential is Φ(r) = −GM/r.

Establish whether this identification is observationally justified in either of the following two regimes, or exhibit a model-independent argument or measurement that does so:

(1) Macroscopic sources (e.g., the Sun): Show that the gravitational mass M_grav inferred from the orbital (Keplerian/post-Newtonian) motions of test bodies in the exterior field is in fact equal to ∫ ρ_E(x) d^3x, where ρ_E is the internal energy density of the source. Equivalently, rule out alternative source functionals (such as integrals of the number density of constituents, or higher moments of T^{μν}) that would reproduce the same exterior weak-field potential Φ(r) = −GM_grav/r without being equal to ∫ ρ_E.

(2) Microscopic sources: Show that for fundamental microscopic constituents the gravitational mass that enters the exterior Newtonian potential equals ∫ T^{00} over the constituent, as opposed to merely being proportional to the number of constituents or to some other moment of the internal energy-momentum distribution.

In each case, determine whether current observational information can distinguish ∫ T^{00} from alternative source moments, given that in the weak-binding limit the exterior potential is required only to scale extensively with the amount of matter in the source.

representations.normalized:
Let $q$ be an odd prime power, and let $n, m$ be positive integers. Consider the projective space $\mathrm{PG}(2n+m-1, q)$. A family $O(n,m,q)$ is defined to be a set of $q^m + 1$ subspaces of dimension $n-1$ in $\mathrm{PG}(2n+m-1, q)$ such that:
(i) any three distinct elements of the family span a $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace; and
(ii) at every element $\pi$ of the family, there is a unique $(n+m-1)$-dimensional subspace (the tangent space at $\pi$) that contains $\pi$ and is disjoint from every other element of the family.

(For $n = m$, this is called a pseudo-ovoid or egg; for $n = 1$, $m = 2$ it reduces to an ovoid of $\mathrm{PG}(3,q)$.) It is known that necessarily $m = n$ or $m = 2n$ when $q$ is even.

Question: For every $O(n,m,q)$ with $q$ odd, must $m \in \{n, 2n\}$?

Let $(X,\le)$ be a partially ordered set and let $A,B:X\to X$ be two self-maps. Assume:
1. $A$ has a unique fixed point $x^*_A\in X$, i.e.\ $F_A:=\{x\in X:A(x)=x\}=\{x^*_A\}$;
2. $B$ has a unique fixed point $x^*_B\in X$, i.e.\ $F_B=\{x^*_B\}$;
3. $A\le B$ pointwise, meaning $A(x)\le B(x)$ for every $x\in X$.

Identify additional structural and/or analytic conditions on $(X,\le)$, $A$, and $B$ (for example, monotonicity assumptions on $A$ or $B$, completeness or order-completeness of $X$, contractive or Picard-type behaviour of the operators, etc.) which guarantee the abstract Gronwall-type comparison principle
$$\forall\, x\in X,\qquad x\le A(x)\ \Longrightarrow\ x\le x^*_B.$$
Equivalently, determine general hypotheses under which every sub-fixed point of $A$ lies below the unique fixed point of the dominating operator $B$.

representations.normalized:
Setting. Let $(X,\le)$ be an ordered set and let $A:X\to X$ be an operator. A *concrete Gronwall lemma* is a statement of the following type: if $x\in X$ satisfies the operatorial inequality $x\le A(x)$, then $x\le x^*$, where $x^*$ is a specified upper bound (depending on $A$). Such a lemma is said to have an *upper bound that is a fixed point of $A$* if the bound $x^*$ used in the conclusion satisfies $A(x^*)=x^*$.

An *abstract Gronwall lemma* is a general statement of the form: if $A:X\to X$ is a Picard (respectively weakly Picard) operator on an ordered metric space $(X,d,\le)$ — that is, $A$ has a unique fixed point $x^*\in X$ and the sequence of iterates $A^n(x)$ converges to $x^*$ for every $x\in X$ — and $A$ is monotone increasing, then $x\le A(x)$ implies $x\le x^*$ (and dually for the reverse inequality). A concrete Gronwall lemma is called a *consequence of an abstract Gronwall lemma* if it can be obtained by verifying the hypotheses of such an abstract statement for a specific operator $A$ on a specific ordered (metric) space.

Problem. Determine, among all known concrete Gronwall lemmas whose upper bound in the conclusion is a fixed point of the associated operator $A$, exactly which ones can be derived as direct consequences of an abstract Gronwall lemma (in the Picard or weakly Picard operator sense above). Equivalently, classify those classical Gronwall-type inequalities of fixed-point form which fit into the abstract Picard/weakly Picard operator framework, and identify those (if any) that do not.

A dimensionless physical constant is a numerical quantity (such as the fine-structure constant, the proton-to-electron mass ratio, or the ratios of coupling constants in the Standard Model) that has no units and whose value, as currently understood, can only be determined by physical measurement rather than derived from first principles. A dimensional physical constant (such as the speed of light c, Planck's constant ℏ, Newton's gravitational constant G, or Boltzmann's constant k_B) is a constant carrying physical units.

Determine the following:

(a) What is the minimum number N of independent dimensionless physical constants from which all other dimensionless physical constants observed in nature can in principle be derived? That is, find the smallest cardinality of a set S of dimensionless constants such that every dimensionless constant appearing in a complete physical description of nature is expressible as a (possibly computable) function of the elements of S.

(b) Decide whether dimensional physical constants are necessary at all for a complete formulation of physical law, or whether, by an appropriate choice of units, every dimensional constant can be eliminated so that physics is fully specified by dimensionless constants alone.

This is listed among the canonical unsolved problems in physics. There is no derivation from first principles of constants such as the fine-structure constant, and the minimum number of independent dimensionless constants needed to describe physics remains debated (estimates such as Cabibbo–Tegmark's ~26 for the Standard Model plus cosmology have been proposed but not established as minimal). The question of whether dimensional constants are fundamental was discussed notably by Duff, Okun, and Veneziano without consensus.

Let q be a prime power and n a positive integer. Work inside the projective space PG(4n−1, q). An egg O = O(n, 2n, q) is a family of q^{2n} + 1 mutually disjoint (n−1)-dimensional subspaces of PG(4n−1, q) such that:
(E1) any three distinct elements of O span a (3n−1)-dimensional subspace; and
(E2) at every element π ∈ O there is a unique (3n−1)-dimensional subspace T_π, called the tangent space at π, that contains π and is disjoint from every other element of O.

The set of tangent spaces {T_π : π ∈ O}, viewed in the dual space PG(4n−1, q)*, again forms an egg, denoted O*(n, 2n, q) and called the translation dual of O.

An element π ∈ O is called good if, for every two distinct elements π′, π″ of O ∖ {π}, the (3n−1)-dimensional subspace ⟨π, π′, π″⟩ spanned by π, π′, π″ contains exactly q^n + 1 elements of O. The egg O is called good (at π) if some such element π exists; the same definition applies to O*.

Question: Is it true that for every egg O = O(n, 2n, q), at least one of O and its translation dual O* is good?

(E2) at every element π ∈ O there is a unique (3n−1)-dimensional subspace T_π, called the tangent space at π, that contains π and is disjoint from every other element of O.

The set of tangent spaces {T_π : π ∈ O}, viewed in the dual space PG(4n−1, q)*, again forms an egg, denoted O*(n, 2n, q) and called the translation dual of O.

An element π ∈ O is called good if, for every two distinct elements π′, π″ of O ∖ {π}, the (3n−1)-dimensional subspace ⟨π, π′, π″⟩ spanned by π, π′, π″ contains exactly q^n + 1 elements of O. The egg O is called good (at π) if some such element π exists; the same definition applies to O*.

Question: Is it true that for every egg O = O(n, 2n, q), at least one of O and its translation dual O* is good?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No published resolution of this specific question was found. It is posed as an open problem in surveys on translation generalized quadrangles, and subsequent work (e.g., characterizations of good eggs and of elementary pseudo-caps, and the classification of eggs in PG(7,2)) addresses related questions but does not appear to settle whether at least one of an egg and its translation dual must always be good. The problem appears to remain open.

Formulate a single, mathematically consistent physical theory that simultaneously reproduces (i) the predictions of quantum mechanics — i.e., a Hilbert-space description of states with unitary time evolution and the standard probabilistic interpretation — and (ii) the predictions of Einstein's general relativity, in which the gravitational interaction is encoded in a Lorentzian pseudo-Riemannian metric g on a 4-dimensional spacetime manifold M satisfying the Einstein field equations R_{μν} − (1/2) g_{μν} R + Λ g_{μν} = (8πG/c^4) T_{μν}.

Specifically, address the following questions within such a framework:

1. Can such a theory be constructed as a quantum field theory (for instance with a spin-2 mediating boson — a "graviton" — quantizing perturbations of the metric), or must it be formulated through some other structure (such as a fundamentally discrete model of spacetime, e.g. a spin-network/loop-quantization of geometric operators)?

2. Determine whether spacetime, in the resulting theory, is fundamentally continuous (modeled by a smooth manifold) or fundamentally discrete (with a minimal length scale or a combinatorial/atomic structure of geometry).

3. Identify precise, quantitative deviations (if any) of the predictions of this theory from those of classical general relativity in extreme regimes — for example at length scales near the Planck length ℓ_P = √(ħG/c^3), at cosmological scales, near black-hole singularities or horizons, and in the very early universe — and show how those deviations arise from the underlying quantum-gravitational mechanism.

A solution should provide the mathematical formulation of the theory (its state space, dynamics, observables, and gauge/diffeomorphism structure), prove its internal consistency (e.g. unitarity, renormalizability or ultraviolet completeness, anomaly freedom), and demonstrate the appropriate classical and quantum limits.

A Gronwall lemma is, in its classical form, the following statement: if $u,\alpha,\beta:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ are continuous functions with $\beta$ nonnegative and
$$u(t)\le \alpha(t)+\int_a^t \beta(s)\,u(s)\,ds\qquad\text{for all }t\in[a,b],$$
then
$$u(t)\le \alpha(t)+\int_a^t \alpha(s)\beta(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t \beta(\tau)\,d\tau\right) ds\qquad\text{for all }t\in[a,b].$$
A wide variety of generalizations exist, including discrete versions, nonlinear versions, integral inequalities with weakly singular kernels, multidimensional versions, versions on time scales, stochastic Gronwall inequalities, and abstract Gronwall lemmas formulated in ordered Banach spaces or via fixed-point principles.

Problem. Exhibit genuinely new mathematical applications of Gronwall-type lemmas, i.e., establish results in areas of mathematics (for instance in ordinary or partial differential equations, integral and integro-differential equations, stochastic equations, dynamical systems, control theory, numerical analysis, fractional calculus, or geometric analysis) whose proofs essentially rely on a Gronwall-type inequality, beyond the standard known uses (uniqueness, continuous dependence on data, stability estimates, and a priori bounds for ODEs, PDEs, and their numerical schemes).

Consider 4-dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes (M, g) satisfying the Einstein field equations of general relativity, coupled to physically reasonable matter models (e.g., vacuum, electrovacuum, or matter obeying suitable energy conditions and well-posed evolution equations).

(a) Cosmic censorship. A spacetime singularity is called "naked" if it is not contained in the black-hole region, equivalently if it lies in the causal past of future null infinity in an asymptotically flat development. Formulate and prove (or disprove) a version of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture: for generic asymptotically flat smooth initial data on a Cauchy hypersurface, the maximal globally hyperbolic development of the Einstein equations possesses a complete future null infinity, so that no naked singularities form from such generic initial data.

(b) Chronology protection. A closed timelike curve is a smooth timelike loop in (M, g); some solutions of the Einstein equations (e.g., Gödel, Kerr interior, Tipler, van Stockum) admit such curves. Establish or refute Hawking's chronology protection conjecture: any consistent theory unifying general relativity with quantum mechanics (or, in a purely classical formulation, the Einstein equations with physically reasonable quantum-corrected stress-energy) prevents the formation of closed timelike curves from initial data in which none are present, so that backward time travel is impossible.

The problem is to give a precise mathematical formulation of (a) and (b) and to prove or disprove each.

The holographic principle asserts that any consistent theory of quantum gravity defined on a (d+1)-dimensional spacetime should admit an equivalent description by a non-gravitational quantum theory living on a d-dimensional boundary (or otherwise lower-dimensional structure) of that spacetime. The best-understood realization is the AdS/CFT correspondence, which conjectures an exact duality between a quantum theory of gravity (e.g., type IIB string theory) on asymptotically anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime and a conformal field theory (CFT) living on its conformal boundary.

Address the following:

(1) Establish (or refute) the holographic principle in full generality: prove that every consistent theory of quantum gravity admits an equivalent lower-dimensional non-gravitational description.

(2) Formulate and establish a precise dS/CFT correspondence: construct a non-gravitational (possibly Euclidean) quantum theory dual to quantum gravity on asymptotically de Sitter spacetime, specify the dictionary between bulk observables and boundary correlators, and prove the equivalence at the level of an appropriately defined partition function or set of observables.

(3) Generalize AdS/CFT to a gauge–gravity duality valid for arbitrary asymptotic spacetime backgrounds (e.g., flat, cosmological, time-dependent, or with generic boundary conditions): give a precise statement of such a duality and identify the corresponding non-gravitational dual theories.

(4) Determine whether there exist consistent theories of quantum gravity, distinct from string/M-theory, that admit a holographic description; if so, construct an explicit example together with its holographic dual.

Fix a finite alphabet A. The class of extended rational (regular) expressions over A is defined inductively: every letter a ∈ A, the empty word, and the empty set are extended rational expressions; and if E and F are extended rational expressions, then so are the Boolean combinations E ∪ F, E ∩ F, and the complement Eᶜ (with respect to A*), the concatenation E·F, and the Kleene star E*. The star-height h(E) of an extended rational expression E is defined by: h(a) = h(∅) = h(ε) = 0; h(E ∪ F) = h(E ∩ F) = h(E·F) = max(h(E), h(F)); h(Eᶜ) = h(E); and h(E*) = h(E) + 1. The (generalized) star-height of a regular language L ⊆ A* is the minimum of h(E) over all extended rational expressions E that denote L.

Question: Does there exist a regular language L over some finite alphabet whose generalized star-height equals 2; equivalently, is there a regular language that cannot be denoted by any extended rational expression in which the Kleene star is nested to depth at most 1?

Problem of time. In nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, time appears as an external, classical, absolute parameter t with respect to which states evolve unitarily according to a Schrödinger equation i ℏ ∂ψ/∂t = H ψ; time is universal, identical for all observers, and is not represented by a self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space. In general relativity, time is instead one of the four coordinates of a Lorentzian spacetime (M, g), and proper time along a worldline γ is given by τ(γ) = ∫_γ √(−g_{μν} dx^μ dx^ν); the flow of time depends on the spacetime metric and the observer's worldline, and general covariance forbids any preferred global time function. In canonical quantizations of general relativity (e.g., the Wheeler–DeWitt equation Ĥ |Ψ⟩ = 0), the Hamiltonian constraint annihilates physical states, so there is no external time evolution.

Formulate a consistent theoretical framework that reconciles these two notions of time: namely, give a mathematically well-defined quantum theory of gravity (or a quantum theory compatible with general relativity) in which (i) the nonrelativistic, absolute-parameter notion of time used in quantum mechanics emerges in an appropriate limit, (ii) the dynamical, observer- and curvature-dependent notion of time of general relativity emerges in the classical limit, and (iii) the theory provides an unambiguous prescription for assigning probabilities, evolution, and observables without requiring a fixed background time parameter.

The Directed Feedback Vertex Set problem (DFVS) is defined as follows. The input is a directed graph G = (V, E) and a positive integer k. A directed feedback vertex set of G is a subset S ⊆ V such that the induced subgraph G − S (obtained by deleting the vertices of S and all incident arcs) is acyclic; equivalently, every directed cycle of G contains at least one vertex of S. The decision question is whether G admits a directed feedback vertex set of size at most k.

A polynomial kernelization for a parameterized problem (in this case, DFVS parameterized by k) is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an instance (G, k), outputs an equivalent instance (G', k') of the same problem such that |V(G')| + |E(G')| + k' ≤ p(k) for some polynomial p, and (G, k) is a yes-instance if and only if (G', k') is a yes-instance.

Question: Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set, parameterized by the solution size k, admit a polynomial kernel? That is, does there exist a polynomial-time preprocessing algorithm reducing every instance (G, k) to an equivalent instance whose total size is bounded by a polynomial in k?

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the free monoid on $A$. A language $L \subseteq A^*$ is recognizable if it is recognized by a finite monoid. A morphism $\varphi: A^* \to B^*$ between free monoids is length-preserving (lp) if $|\varphi(a)| = 1$ for every $a \in A$, i.e., $\varphi$ sends each letter to a letter.

An lp-variety of languages is an operator $\mathcal{V}$ that assigns to every finite alphabet $A$ a class $\mathcal{V}(A^*)$ of recognizable languages of $A^*$ such that:
(i) $\mathcal{V}(A^*)$ is a Boolean algebra (closed under finite union, finite intersection, and complement);
(ii) $\mathcal{V}(A^*)$ is closed under left and right quotients by words: if $L \in \mathcal{V}(A^*)$ and $u \in A^*$, then $u^{-1}L = \{v \in A^* : uv \in L\} \in \mathcal{V}(A^*)$ and $Lu^{-1} = \{v \in A^* : vu \in L\} \in \mathcal{V}(A^*)$;
(iii) for every length-preserving morphism $\varphi: A^* \to B^*$ and every $L \in \mathcal{V}(B^*)$, one has $\varphi^{-1}(L) \in \mathcal{V}(A^*)$.

An lp-variety $\mathcal{V}$ is called proper if there exist a finite alphabet $A$ and a recognizable language $L \subseteq A^*$ with $L \notin \mathcal{V}(A^*)$.

The shuffle product of two languages $K, L \subseteq A^*$ is
$$K \shuffle L = \{u_1 v_1 u_2 v_2 \cdots u_n v_n : n \geq 1,\ u_i, v_i \in A^*,\ u_1 u_2 \cdots u_n \in K,\ v_1 v_2 \cdots v_n \in L\}.$$
An lp-variety $\mathcal{V}$ is closed under shuffle if for every finite alphabet $A$ and every $K, L \in \mathcal{V}(A^*)$, also $K \shuffle L \in \mathcal{V}(A^*)$.

Question: Does there exist a largest proper lp-variety of languages that is closed under the shuffle product? That is, does there exist a proper lp-variety $\mathcal{W}$ closed under shuffle such that every proper lp-variety closed under shuffle is contained in $\mathcal{W}$?

For positive varieties, it is known (Ésik–Simon, 1998, confirming a conjecture of Perrot) that there is a largest proper positive variety closed under shuffle, namely the positive variety not containing $(ab)^*$. The analogous question for lp-varieties (where inverse morphism closure is restricted to length-preserving morphisms) appears to still be posed as an open problem, with no resolution found in the literature.

The rigorous construction of an interacting quantum field theory in 4-dimensional spacetime remains a major open problem in mathematical physics. The closely related Yang–Mills existence and mass gap problem is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and is unsolved. Rigorous constructions exist in lower dimensions (e.g., φ^4 in 2 and 3 dimensions), but no nontrivial interacting 4D theory has been constructed; in fact, φ^4_4 is widely believed (and recently strongly evidenced by Aizenman–Duminil-Copin) to be trivial.

Let $(B_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion defined on a probability space, and define the transformed process
$$B'_t \;=\; \int_0^t \operatorname{sgn}(B_{s/2})\, dB_s, \qquad t\geq 0,$$
where $\operatorname{sgn}(x)=1$ for $x\geq 0$ and $-1$ for $x<0$. Then $B'$ is again a standard Brownian motion (by Lévy's characterization), and its natural filtration $\mathcal{F}^{B'}$ is contained in $\mathcal{F}^{B}$. Since $B'$ is unchanged when $B$ is replaced by $-B$, the process $B'$ is an even functional of $B$, so $\mathcal{F}^{B'}$ is strictly smaller than $\mathcal{F}^{B}$: at least one bit of information about $B$ is lost. The question is whether exactly one bit is lost, i.e., whether $\mathcal{F}^{B}$ is generated by $\mathcal{F}^{B'}$ together with a single independent Bernoulli random variable taking two equally likely values (equivalently, whether $\mathcal{F}^{B'}$ admits an independent complement in $\mathcal{F}^{B}$ consisting of exactly one bit, for instance $\operatorname{sgn}(B_1)$ or some similar two-valued random variable).

In the standard cosmological framework, the theory of cosmic inflation postulates that, shortly after the Big Bang, the very early universe underwent a brief phase of nearly exponential accelerated expansion, typically driven by the potential energy of one or more hypothetical scalar fields (the "inflaton"). Address the following:

(a) Determine whether cosmic inflation actually occurred in the very early universe and, if it did, identify the detailed properties of this epoch (its duration, energy scale, the form of the inflaton potential V(φ), the mechanism of reheating, and the resulting spectrum of primordial scalar and tensor perturbations including the scalar spectral index n_s, its running, and the tensor-to-scalar ratio r).

(b) Identify the nature of the scalar field (or fields) responsible for inflation: specify its origin within a fundamental theory (e.g., particle physics or quantum gravity), its couplings to the Standard Model, and its potential.

(c) Decide whether, once inflation begins in some region, quantum fluctuations of the inflaton cause it to be eternally self-reproducing ("eternal inflation"), so that inflation continues forever in arbitrarily distant regions of spacetime, producing a multiverse structure.

Provide a definitive theoretical and observational resolution of (a), (b), and (c).

Consider a standard hot Big Bang cosmological model in which the universe is described by a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) spacetime with metric ds^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + a(t)^2 dΣ^2, where a(t) is the scale factor evolving according to the Friedmann equations sourced by radiation and matter. In such a model, the particle horizon at the time of last scattering (decoupling of the cosmic microwave background, CMB) subtends only a small angle (~1°) on the present-day sky, so causally disconnected regions of the CMB should not have had time to thermalize. Nevertheless, observations of the CMB show temperature anisotropies of order ΔT/T ~ 10^{-5} across the full sky, indicating an extremely homogeneous and isotropic universe.

The Horizon Problem: Explain, within a physically consistent and observationally compatible framework, why the observed distant universe is so homogeneous on scales larger than the naive causal horizon at last scattering. In particular:

(a) Determine whether the standard mechanism of an early epoch of cosmological inflation (a period of quasi-exponential expansion driven by a scalar field or equivalent dynamics) is the correct explanation, by identifying observational signatures that uniquely select it.

(b) Assess whether alternative mechanisms — such as a time-varying speed of light c(t) in the early universe, varying fundamental constants, bouncing/cyclic cosmologies, or other pre-Big Bang scenarios — can equally well or more appropriately account for the observed large-scale homogeneity and the spectrum of CMB anisotropies, and identify quantitative tests that would distinguish among these possibilities.

Let $Z=X+iY$ be a standard complex Brownian motion on a filtered probability space, with $Z_0=0$ (so that $X$ and $Y$ are independent real Brownian motions started at $0$). Set $R_t=|Z_t|$ and define the complex Brownian motion
$$Z'_t=\int_0^t \frac{Z_s}{R_s}\,dZ_s.$$
Then $M_t:=Z_t^2$ satisfies the complex stochastic differential equation
$$dM_t = 2\sqrt{|M_t|}\,dZ'_t,\qquad M_0=0, \tag{$\ast$}$$
where $\sqrt{\,\cdot\,}$ denotes a measurable choice of complex square root (e.g.\ $\sqrt{w}$ with $|\sqrt{w}|=\sqrt{|w|}$ chosen so that the equation is well posed; equivalently $2\sqrt{|M_t|}\,dZ'_t$ is interpreted as $2 R_t\, dZ'_t$ at the level of the modulus).

Consider all (continuous, $\mathbb{C}$-valued) solutions $(M_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of $(\ast)$ with $M_0=0$ that leave $0$ immediately, i.e.\ such that almost surely $\inf\{t>0 : M_t \ne 0\}=0$, where the driving noise is a complex Brownian motion $Z'$.

Question: Does there exist a strong solution to $(\ast)$ leaving $0$ immediately, i.e.\ a solution $M$ adapted to the natural (completed) filtration of the driving complex Brownian motion $Z'$?

$$p_1,\dots,p_k \quad\text{and}\quad q_1,\dots,q_k,$$
where each polynomial is given explicitly as a sparse representation: a finite list of (monomial, coefficient) pairs containing exactly the monomials with nonzero coefficients. The size of the input is the total bit-length of this representation.

Decide whether the polynomial identity
$$\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{k} q_i$$
holds in the polynomial ring.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic fixed-parameter tractable algorithm, with parameter $k$, that solves this decision problem? Equivalently, is there a deterministic algorithm running in time $f(k)\cdot N^{O(1)}$, where $N$ is the input size and $f$ is some computable function, that correctly decides the identity for all inputs?

representations.normalized:
The cosmological principle asserts that, when averaged over sufficiently large length scales, the spatial distribution of matter and energy in the observable universe is statistically homogeneous (the same at every point) and isotropic (the same in every direction). Under this assumption, the spacetime geometry on cosmological scales is modeled by the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric

ds^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + a(t)^2 [ dr^2/(1 - k r^2) + r^2 (dθ^2 + sin^2 θ dφ^2) ],

where a(t) is the scale factor and k ∈ {-1, 0, +1} characterizes spatial curvature. The standard ΛCDM cosmological model is built on this metric, with a cosmological constant Λ and cold dark matter as its dominant components. Within this framework, the observed dipole anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is usually interpreted as purely kinematic, arising from the motion of the Solar System relative to the CMB rest frame.

Settle the following interrelated questions:

(a) Is the matter–energy distribution of the universe actually statistically homogeneous and isotropic on sufficiently large scales, or is it inhomogeneous and/or anisotropic in a way that invalidates the cosmological principle?

(b) Is the observed CMB dipole purely kinematic, or does a substantial portion of it reflect an intrinsic anisotropy of the universe that would imply a breakdown of the FLRW description and of the cosmological principle?

(c) Does the Hubble tension—the persistent discrepancy between values of the Hubble constant H_0 inferred from early-universe (e.g., CMB-based) and late-universe (e.g., distance-ladder) measurements—constitute evidence that the cosmological principle is false?

(d) Assuming the cosmological principle holds, is the FLRW metric in fact the correct large-scale metric of our universe, or is a different metric (for example, one incorporating averaged backreaction from inhomogeneities) required?

(e) Are the observations conventionally interpreted as accelerated cosmic expansion (e.g., Type Ia supernova distance–redshift data) correctly interpreted as such within an FLRW + Λ framework, or are they better understood as evidence that the cosmological principle fails?

Let $Z=X+iY$ be a standard complex Brownian motion started from $0$, so that $X$ and $Y$ are independent real Brownian motions. Set $R_t=|Z_t|=\sqrt{X_t^2+Y_t^2}$, and, for $t>0$, $U_t=Z_t/R_t$ (well defined for almost every $t$ since planar Brownian motion almost surely does not return to $0$). Define a new complex Brownian motion $Z'$ by the Itô integral
$$Z'_t=\int_0^t U_s\,dZ_s,$$
and write $Z'=X'+iY'$, so that
$$X'_t=\int_0^t\frac{X_s\,dX_s+Y_s\,dY_s}{R_s},\qquad Y'_t=\int_0^t\frac{X_s\,dY_s-Y_s\,dX_s}{R_s}.$$
Then $Y'$ is a one-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the natural filtration $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ of the pair $(X,Y)$, and the natural filtration $\mathcal F^{Y'}$ of $Y'$ is strictly contained in $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$.

Say that a one-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ adapted to $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ is complementable in $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ if there exists another one-dimensional Brownian motion $C$ adapted to $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ such that $B$ and $C$ are independent and the natural filtration of the pair $(B,C)$ equals $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$.

Question: Is the Brownian motion $Y'$ complementable in $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$?

Let $Z=X+iY$ be a standard complex Brownian motion started from $0$, so that $X$ and $Y$ are independent real Brownian motions. Set $R_t=|Z_t|=\sqrt{X_t^2+Y_t^2}$, and, for $t>0$, $U_t=Z_t/R_t$ (well defined for almost every $t$ since planar Brownian motion almost surely does not return to $0$). Define a new complex Brownian motion $Z'$ by the Itô integral
$$Z'_t=\int_0^t U_s\,dZ_s,$$
and write $Z'=X'+iY'$, so that
$$X'_t=\int_0^t\frac{X_s\,dX_s+Y_s\,dY_s}{R_s},\qquad Y'_t=\int_0^t\frac{X_s\,dY_s-Y_s\,dX_s}{R_s}.$$
Then $Y'$ is a one-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the natural filtration $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ of the pair $(X,Y)$, and the natural filtration $\mathcal F^{Y'}$ of $Y'$ is strictly contained in $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$.

Say that a one-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ adapted to $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ is complementable in $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ if there exists another one-dimensional Brownian motion $C$ adapted to $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$ such that $B$ and $C$ are independent and the natural filtration of the pair $(B,C)$ equals $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$.

Question: Is the Brownian motion $Y'$ complementable in $\mathcal F^{(X,Y)}$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem appears to have been resolved positively by Brossard, Émery and Leuridan in "Skew-Product Decomposition of Planar Brownian Motion and Complementability" (Séminaire de Probabilités XLVI, LNM 2123, 2014). They show that if $W$ is a complex Brownian motion whose natural filtration is the filtration of $Z$ up to an arbitrary rotation (which is exactly the case of $Z'$ above), then for every $a,b\in\mathbb R$ with $a^2+b^2=1$, the Brownian motion $a\,\Re(W)+b\,\Im(W)$ is complementable in $\mathcal F^Z$. Taking $a=0$, $b=1$ gives complementability of $Y'$.

The identity of dark matter remains an open problem in physics and cosmology as of 2026. Direct-detection experiments (e.g., LZ, XENONnT, PandaX) have continued to set increasingly stringent limits on WIMP cross-sections without a confirmed detection, axion searches (ADMX and others) have not detected axions, and no superpartners have been observed at the LHC. Within the framework of general relativity applied to cosmology, consider a spatially homogeneous and isotropic Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker spacetime with scale factor a(t), whose dynamics are governed by the Friedmann equations sourced by an energy–momentum content including ordinary matter (with energy density evolving as ρ_m ∝ a^{-3}) and a "dark energy" component with equation-of-state parameter w (so that its energy density evolves as ρ_DE ∝ a^{-3(1+w)}). Observational data (Type Ia supernovae, CMB, baryon acoustic oscillations) indicate that ä > 0 at the present epoch, consistent with an effective dark energy component contributing roughly 70% of the present critical density and an equation of state w ≈ −1.

Address the following:

1. Identify the physical mechanism responsible for the observed late-time accelerated expansion of the universe. Specifically, determine whether this acceleration is driven by:
   (a) a pure cosmological constant Λ (w = −1 exactly, constant in time), or
   (b) a dynamical quintessence field with w(t) > −1, or
   (c) a phantom-energy component with w(t) < −1, or
   (d) a modification of general relativity at cosmological scales, or
   (e) an apparent acceleration arising from the breakdown of the cosmological principle (large-scale spatial homogeneity and isotropy), so that the inferred acceleration is an artifact of fitting an FLRW model to an inhomogeneous universe.

2. Provide a quantitative explanation of the coincidence problem: derive, from first principles or from a specified theoretical model, why the present-day energy densities ρ_DE(t_0) and ρ_m(t_0) are of the same order of magnitude despite their differing time evolutions, or rigorously demonstrate that no such explanation beyond anthropic/observer-selection reasoning is possible.

3. Determine whether the function w(t) is exactly constant equal to −1, or whether it varies with redshift, and if so characterize its functional form.

representations.normalized: Decide whether the following parameterized problem is fixed-parameter tractable. Directed Feedback Vertex Set: given a directed graph G = (V, E) and a positive integer k (the parameter), determine whether there exists a set S ⊆ V with |S| ≤ k such that every directed cycle of G contains at least one vertex of S. Equivalently, the question is whether there is an algorithm deciding this problem in time f(k) · |V|^{O(1)} for some computable function f depending only on k.

Directed Feedback Vertex Set: given a directed graph G = (V, E) and a positive integer k (the parameter), determine whether there exists a set S ⊆ V with |S| ≤ k such that every directed cycle of G contains at least one vertex of S. Equivalently, the question is whether there is an algorithm deciding this problem in time f(k) · |V|^{O(1)} for some computable function f depending only on k.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Chen, Liu, Lu, O'Sullivan, and Razgon (STOC 2008; J. ACM 2008) proved that Directed Feedback Vertex Set is fixed-parameter tractable, giving an algorithm with running time O(4^k k! · n^{O(1)}). Subsequent works have improved the running time (e.g., a linear-time parameterized algorithm and simplified variants). Thus the FPT question is resolved affirmatively; whether DFVS admits a polynomial kernel remains open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The dark flow hypothesis remains unresolved and controversial as of 2024–2025. Original claims by Kashlinsky and collaborators of a coherent bulk flow of galaxy clusters toward a sky region near Centaurus–Vela have been disputed by reanalyses (e.g., Keisler, and work using Planck data) that find no statistically significant signal once CMB primary anisotropies are properly treated, while the original group maintains the detection. Whether the effect is real, and whether it would require super-horizon gravitational influences, is still an open question.

1. Determine whether d > 4, i.e., whether the manifold M admits additional spatial dimensions beyond the three observed ones.
2. If d > 4, characterize the geometry and size of the additional dimensions. For instance, if M is locally a product M ≈ M_4 × K, where M_4 is four-dimensional spacetime and K is a compact internal manifold, determine the diameter (or characteristic length scale) of K and its topology.
3. Decide whether the dimensionality of spacetime is a fundamental input (a fixed parameter of the underlying theory) or an emergent quantity derived from more basic degrees of freedom (e.g., from a discrete, combinatorial, or quantum-information-theoretic substrate in some appropriate continuum/thermodynamic limit).
4. Identify any empirically observable signatures (e.g., deviations from the inverse-square law of gravity at short distances, Kaluza–Klein excitations, missing-energy signatures in particle collisions) that would constitute experimental evidence of d > 4, and determine whether such signatures exist in nature.

Decision problem (Planar Multiway Cut), parameterized by k:

Instance: A planar undirected graph G = (V, E) with positive edge weights w : E → ℤ_{>0}, a set of k distinguished vertices (terminals) {x_1, …, x_k} ⊆ V, and a positive integer M.

Parameter: k.

Question: Does there exist a subset F ⊆ E with total weight Σ_{e ∈ F} w(e) ≤ M such that in the graph (V, E \ F) no two distinct terminals x_i, x_j lie in the same connected component?

Determine the parameterized complexity of this problem with respect to the parameter k. In particular, decide whether it is fixed-parameter tractable (i.e., solvable in time f(k) · |V|^{O(1)} for some computable function f), or whether it is W[1]-hard.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Marx (2012) proved that Planar Multiway Cut parameterized by the number of terminals k is W[1]-hard and, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis, admits no f(k)·n^{o(√k)} algorithm, resolving the open question. Klein and Marx gave a matching 2^{O(k)}·n^{O(√k)} algorithm, showing the bound is tight.

In classical electromagnetism, Maxwell's equations as usually written impose ∇·B = 0, so that magnetic field lines have no sources and isolated magnetic charges (magnetic monopoles) do not exist. A magnetic monopole is a hypothetical point-like particle carrying a net magnetic charge g, sourcing a radial magnetic field B(r) = (g/4π) r/|r|^3. Dirac's argument shows that the consistent quantum-mechanical coexistence of an electric charge e and a magnetic charge g requires the quantization condition eg = 2π n ℏ (in suitable units), for some integer n; hence the existence of even a single magnetic monopole would imply that all electric charges are integer multiples of a fundamental unit. Various unified gauge theories (e.g., grand unified theories) predict the production of heavy magnetic monopoles in the very early, high-temperature universe.

Determine the following:
(a) Did particles carrying nonzero magnetic charge exist as physical states during some past, higher-energy cosmological epoch?
(b) If such particles did exist, do any of them remain in the present universe as relic particles that could in principle be detected?

A complete answer should either exhibit a magnetic monopole as a physically realized particle (theoretically motivated and experimentally confirmed) and characterize its present-day abundance, or else establish that no such particles exist or survive.

Dirac's argument shows that the consistent quantum-mechanical coexistence of an electric charge e and a magnetic charge g requires the quantization condition eg = 2π n ℏ (in suitable units), for some integer n; hence the existence of even a single magnetic monopole would imply that all electric charges are integer multiples of a fundamental unit. Various unified gauge theories (e.g., grand unified theories) predict the production of heavy magnetic monopoles in the very early, high-temperature universe.

Determine the following:
(a) Did particles carrying nonzero magnetic charge exist as physical states during some past, higher-energy cosmological epoch?
(b) If such particles did exist, do any of them remain in the present universe as relic particles that could in principle be detected?

A complete answer should either exhibit a magnetic monopole as a physically realized particle (theoretically motivated and experimentally confirmed) and characterize its present-day abundance, or else establish that no such particles exist or survive.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Despite decades of searches at colliders (e.g., ATLAS, MoEDAL at CERN), in cosmic rays, and in bulk matter, no magnetic monopole has been confirmed. Experiments through 2024–2025 continue to set upper bounds on monopole production cross sections and relic fluxes, and new detector proposals are being developed. The questions of whether monopoles existed in an early high-energy epoch and whether any survive today remain unresolved.

The free neutron is unstable and decays via the weak interaction (predominantly n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ) with a mean lifetime τₙ. Two experimental paradigms are used to measure τₙ:

(i) "Bottle" experiments: ultracold neutrons are stored in a material or magnetic trap, and the number of surviving neutrons is measured as a function of storage time, yielding τₙ from the exponential decay of the trapped population.

(ii) "Beam" experiments: a cold neutron beam of known flux passes through a detection volume in which the appearance rate of decay products (typically protons) is counted, yielding τₙ from the ratio of decay rate to neutron number in the beam.

These two methodologies have consistently produced values of τₙ that disagree by roughly 8–10 seconds, with bottle averages near 878 s and beam averages near 888 s — a discrepancy substantially larger than the quoted uncertainties.

Problem: Determine the true mean lifetime of the free neutron and explain the origin of the persistent discrepancy between bottle-type and beam-type measurements. This entails either (a) identifying and quantifying systematic effects in one or both classes of experiments that account for the difference, or (b) establishing a physical mechanism — for instance, a hitherto unobserved decay channel of the neutron into final states not detected by beam experiments — that reconciles the two methodologies, together with experimental confirmation.

Within the framework of relativistic quantum field theory, consider the proton as a bound state of quarks and gluons described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD), embedded in the Standard Model of particle physics (gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y). Address the following two questions:

(a) Proton stability. In the Standard Model, baryon number B is an accidental global symmetry and the proton is exactly stable. In many proposed extensions (e.g., grand unified theories with gauge groups such as SU(5), SO(10), or supersymmetric variants), B-violating operators induce proton decay through channels such as p → e^+ π^0 or p → ν̄ K^+ with a finite mean lifetime τ_p. Determine whether the proton is fundamentally stable, or whether it decays with a finite lifetime; if the latter, determine τ_p and the dominant decay channels.

(b) Proton spin decomposition ("spin crisis"). The proton has total angular momentum 1/2 (in units of ℏ). In QCD this admits a decomposition (e.g., the Jaffe–Manohar or Ji decomposition) of the form
   1/2 = (1/2) ΔΣ + ΔG + L_q + L_g,
where ΔΣ is the net contribution from quark spins (the integral of the polarized quark distributions), ΔG is the gluon spin contribution, and L_q, L_g are the orbital angular momenta of quarks and gluons, respectively. Determine quantitatively how ΔΣ, ΔG, L_q, and L_g sum to 1/2, given that polarized deep-inelastic scattering measurements indicate ΔΣ accounts for substantially less than 1/2.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple undirected graph, and let k and d be positive integers. Decide whether there exists a partition of V into pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets V_1, V_2, …, V_m (for some m ≥ 1) such that, for every i ∈ {1, …, m}:

(i) |V_i| ≤ k, and
(ii) the number of edges of G having exactly one endpoint in V_i is at most d (equivalently, each part V_i has at most d boundary edges in G).

The question is whether this decision problem is fixed-parameter tractable when jointly parameterized by k and d; that is, whether it admits an algorithm running in time f(k, d) · |V(G)|^{O(1)} for some computable function f.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem is reported as fixed-parameter tractable: the 2011 result that graph immersion testing is FPT (Grohe–Kawarabayashi–Marx–Wollan) implies that Minimum Degree Graph Partition is FPT when parameterized by (k, d), since a graph admits such a partition iff it does not contain a certain finite family of immersion-obstructions depending only on k and d.

In a quantum field theory extension of the Standard Model of particle physics that postulates a symmetry between bosons and fermions (spacetime supersymmetry), addressing the following questions:

(a) Is spacetime supersymmetry realized in nature at energies near the TeV scale, i.e., do superpartners of the known Standard Model particles exist with masses of order 10^2–10^4 GeV?

(b) If such a supersymmetry exists, by what dynamical mechanism is it broken so as to produce the observed mass splittings between Standard Model particles and their hypothetical superpartners?

(c) Does the presence of TeV-scale supersymmetry resolve the electroweak hierarchy problem by cancelling the large radiative (quantum) corrections to the Higgs boson mass, thereby stabilizing the electroweak scale against ultraviolet contributions?

(d) Does the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP), assumed stable under an unbroken R-parity, constitute a viable cold dark matter candidate accounting for the observed cosmological dark matter density?

Determine the answer to each of these four questions.

As of 2025–2026, no superpartners have been detected at the LHC. ATLAS and CMS exclusion bounds reach roughly 2.4 TeV for gluinos and first/second-generation squarks, 1.3 TeV for stops/sbottoms, and about 1 TeV for electroweakinos in simplified models, but TeV-scale SUSY is not ruled out and well-motivated scenarios remain viable. The mechanism of SUSY breaking, the resolution of the hierarchy problem, and whether the LSP constitutes dark matter all remain experimentally and theoretically unresolved.

Fix an integer n ≥ 2. For a complex projective variety X, let Aut(X) denote its group of automorphisms (as an algebraic variety), and for X smooth let Aut(X)* denote the image of Aut(X) acting on the second cohomology H^2(X;R) by pullback.

Call a group Γ abstractly realizable as a group of automorphisms (in dimension d) if there exists a projective variety X (of dimension d) such that Aut(X) is isomorphic to Γ as an abstract group.

Call a subgroup Γ ⊂ GL_m(Z) strongly realizable as a group of automorphisms if there exist a smooth complex projective variety X and a Z-defined linear algebraic representation φ: GL_m(R) → GL(H^2(X;R)) such that Aut(X)* = φ(Γ).

Determine which subgroups Γ ⊂ GL_n(Z) are abstractly realizable, and which are strongly realizable, as groups of automorphisms. In particular, decide whether every finitely generated subgroup Γ ⊂ GL_n(Z) is abstractly realizable (respectively, strongly realizable) as a group of automorphisms.

Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is the SU(3) Yang–Mills gauge theory of quarks and gluons defined by the Lagrangian density
  L = -(1/4) G^a_{μν} G^{a μν} + Σ_f \bar{ψ}_f (i γ^μ D_μ - m_f) ψ_f,
where G^a_{μν} = ∂_μ A^a_ν - ∂_ν A^a_μ + g f^{abc} A^b_μ A^c_ν is the gluon field strength, D_μ = ∂_μ - i g A^a_μ T^a is the gauge covariant derivative, T^a are the SU(3) generators with structure constants f^{abc}, and ψ_f are quark fields of flavor f with masses m_f. At energy scales below the QCD scale Λ_QCD ≈ 200 MeV the coupling g(μ) becomes large and perturbative expansions in g fail; this is the non-perturbative (low-energy) regime, characterized phenomenologically by quark confinement, a non-trivial vacuum structure (gluon condensate ⟨G^a_{μν} G^{a μν}⟩, quark condensate ⟨\bar{ψ} ψ⟩), spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry, and a mass gap.

Problem: Starting from the QCD Lagrangian above, derive in a mathematically controlled non-perturbative framework (for example, lattice gauge theory continuum limit, functional / Dyson–Schwinger methods, or a constructive quantum field theory formulation) the bound-state spectrum and structure of hadrons (in particular nucleons), the residual nucleon–nucleon interaction, and the existence and binding energies of complex atomic nuclei. Concretely, explain quantitatively how the QCD vacuum and its non-perturbative dynamics produce:
 (a) confinement of quarks and gluons into color-singlet hadrons,
 (b) the proton, neutron, and light-meson masses with their observed values,
 (c) an effective nucleon–nucleon potential reproducing nuclear binding, and
 (d) the formation, stability, and properties of nuclei such as the deuteron, helium-4, and heavier nuclei,
all as consequences of the underlying non-perturbative QCD equations.

Non-perturbative low-energy QCD remains an open problem in mathematical physics. The Yang–Mills existence and mass gap problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and is still unsolved. While lattice QCD has produced impressive numerical results (including the light hadron spectrum and recent ab initio computations of light nuclei), a mathematically rigorous derivation of nuclear structure from the QCD Lagrangian is not available.

In the Standard Model of particle physics, fermionic matter is organized into three replicated generations of quarks and leptons. Each generation consists of an up-type quark, a down-type quark, a charged lepton, and a neutrino, with identical gauge quantum numbers across generations but with widely different masses. The fermion masses arise from Yukawa couplings to the Higgs field, whose values are free parameters of the Standard Model fitted to experiment.

(a) Provide a first-principles theoretical explanation for why exactly three generations of quarks and leptons exist in nature, rather than one, two, four, or any other number.

(b) Construct a predictive theory of the Yukawa coupling matrices that determines, from first principles, the observed masses of the individual quarks (up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom) and charged leptons (electron, muon, tau) — together with the elements of the CKM (and PMNS) mixing matrices — without fitting these parameters to experimental data.

Let $d \geq 2$ be an integer. A Calabi–Yau variety of dimension $d$ is a smooth, simply connected, projective complex variety $X$ of dimension $d$ with trivial canonical bundle $K_X \cong \mathcal{O}_X$ and $H^0(X, \Omega_X^p) = 0$ for $0 < p < d$. Let $\mathrm{Aut}(X)$ denote its group of biregular automorphisms, and let
$$\mathrm{Aut}(X)^* \subset \mathrm{GL}(H^2(X;\mathbb{R}))$$
denote the image of the natural representation of $\mathrm{Aut}(X)$ on the second real cohomology of $X$. Let $\overline{\mathrm{Aut}(X)^*}^{\mathrm{Zar}}$ be the Zariski closure of $\mathrm{Aut}(X)^*$ in $\mathrm{GL}(H^2(X;\mathbb{R}))$, viewed as a real linear algebraic group, and define
$$G^0(X) := \left(\overline{\mathrm{Aut}(X)^*}^{\mathrm{Zar}}\right)^0$$
to be its neutral (connected) component.

Determine, or characterize as completely as possible, which real linear algebraic groups arise as $G^0(X)$ when $X$ ranges over all Calabi–Yau varieties of dimension $d$.

representations.normalized:
In the Standard Model extended to accommodate neutrino oscillations, three light neutrino mass eigenstates ν_1, ν_2, ν_3 with masses m_1, m_2, m_3 mix with the flavor eigenstates ν_e, ν_μ, ν_τ via the Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata (PMNS) unitary matrix, which (in the standard parametrization) contains three mixing angles, one Dirac CP-violating phase δ_CP, and (if neutrinos are Majorana) two additional Majorana phases. Determine the following physical properties of the neutrinos:

1. The absolute mass scale: give the value of the lightest neutrino mass (equivalently, determine m_1, m_2, m_3 individually rather than only the squared mass differences Δm^2_{21} and |Δm^2_{31}|).

2. The fermionic nature of the neutrinos: decide whether neutrinos are Dirac fermions (with distinct particle and antiparticle states, conserving lepton number) or Majorana fermions (their own antiparticles, allowing lepton-number-violating processes such as neutrinoless double beta decay).

3. The ordering of the mass spectrum: decide whether the hierarchy is normal (m_1 < m_2 < m_3, so that Δm^2_{31} > 0) or inverted (m_3 < m_1 < m_2, so that Δm^2_{31} < 0).

4. CP violation in the lepton sector: determine whether the Dirac CP-violating phase δ_CP equals 0 (mod π), i.e. whether CP is conserved in neutrino oscillations, or takes a nontrivial value.

Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex variety of dimension $d$, and let $f \colon X \to X$ be an automorphism. The first dynamical degree of $f$ is defined by
$$\lambda_1(f) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \bigl( (f^n)^* H \cdot H^{d-1} \bigr)^{1/n},$$
where $H$ is any ample divisor class on $X$ and $(f^n)^*$ denotes the pullback on the Néron–Severi (or cohomology) group; this limit is independent of the choice of $H$ and is an algebraic integer $\geq 1$.

For each dimension $d \geq 1$, define
$$S_1(d) = \{\lambda_1(f) : f \in \operatorname{Aut}(X) \text{ for some smooth projective complex variety } X \text{ of dimension } d\} \subset [1,\infty).$$

Consider the case $d = 3$. Determine which of the following holds:
(a) $S_1(3)$ is dense in $[1, \infty)$; or
(b) there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $S_1(3) \cap (1, 1+\varepsilon] = \emptyset$ (i.e. the set of values $> 1$ is bounded away from $1$).

representations.normalized:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the Lagrangian admits a CP-violating topological term

    L_θ = θ (g_s^2 / 32π^2) G^{a}_{μν} \tilde G^{a μν},

where G^{a}_{μν} is the gluon field strength tensor, \tilde G^{a μν} = (1/2) ε^{μνρσ} G^{a}_{ρσ} is its dual, g_s is the strong coupling, and θ ∈ [0, 2π) is the effective vacuum angle (including the contribution arg det M_q from the quark mass matrix). A nonzero θ would induce CP-violating observables, notably a neutron electric dipole moment of order |d_n| ~ 10^{-16} θ e·cm. Experimental bounds on d_n imply |θ| ≲ 10^{-10}, despite there being no symmetry principle within the Standard Model forcing θ to be small.

Address the following:

(a) Provide a dynamical or symmetry-based explanation, derivable from first principles, of why θ is so small (or vanishes); equivalently, explain why the strong interaction is, to extremely high precision, invariant under parity P and charge conjugation C (equivalently CP).

(b) Determine whether the Peccei–Quinn mechanism — i.e. introducing a global U(1)_{PQ} symmetry spontaneously broken at a scale f_a, whose pseudo–Nambu–Goldstone boson (the axion a) couples as (a/f_a)(g_s^2/32π^2) G \tilde G and dynamically relaxes the effective θ to zero — is the correct resolution of (a), and identify the underlying ultraviolet completion (e.g. KSVZ, DFSZ, or alternative) realized in nature, if any.

(c) Determine whether the axion (or axion-like particle) predicted by such a mechanism constitutes the dominant component of the cosmological cold dark matter, and if so determine its mass m_a, decay constant f_a, and the production mechanism (misalignment, topological defect decay, thermal) responsible for its present relic abundance Ω_a h^2 ≈ 0.12.

The strong CP problem remains a major open problem in theoretical particle physics. The Peccei–Quinn mechanism and the axion remain the leading proposed solution, but no axion has been experimentally detected; whether axions form the dominant dark matter component is unresolved. Ongoing experiments (ADMX, CAPP, MADMAX, ABRACADABRA, etc.) continue to search the relevant parameter space as of 2026.
