representations.normalized:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), strongly interacting matter is predicted to undergo a transition from an ordinary hadronic phase to a deconfined phase—the quark–gluon plasma (QGP)—in which quarks and gluons are no longer confined within color-singlet hadrons. The phase structure of QCD matter is parametrized by the temperature T and the chemical potentials (in particular the baryon chemical potential μ_B, and chemical potentials for strangeness and charm). In high-energy nucleus–nucleus collisions, QGP is believed to be transiently produced, and its production depends on the collision center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair √s_NN and the colliding system size A.

Provide a quantitative description, derivable from QCD and supported by experiment, of the following:

1. Determine the location of the deconfinement onset in the QCD phase diagram, both (a) as a curve/region in the (T, μ_B, μ_S, μ_C, ...) space of temperatures and chemical potentials, and (b) as a function of the collision energy √s_NN and the system size A in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

2. Identify and derive the mechanism by which energy and baryon number are stopped (i.e., deposited near mid-rapidity) in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, leading to the formation of the QGP.

3. Explain why hadron production from the QGP is described to near-perfect accuracy by sudden hadronization within the statistical-hadronization model (i.e., a model in which hadron yields are fixed by a thermal/statistical distribution at a hadronization hypersurface).

4. Determine whether quark flavor is conserved during the QGP phase (i.e., whether flavor-changing processes are negligible on the QGP lifetime scale).

5. Determine whether strangeness and charm reach chemical equilibrium in the QGP, and on what time scales.

6. Determine whether strange quarks in the QGP exhibit the same collective (hydrodynamic) flow velocities as up and down quarks.

7. Explain why the deconfined matter produced in heavy-ion collisions behaves as an almost ideal (very low specific shear viscosity η/s) fluid.

Consider a classical relativistic theory of gravity in which the gravitational field is universally coupled to matter, in the sense that all test bodies fall along the same trajectories in a given external gravitational field (the weak equivalence principle), and in which, in the weak-field, slow-motion regime, the theory reproduces Newtonian phenomenology — in particular, a static, spherically symmetric source produces an attractive 1/r potential at laboratory and solar-system scales.

In the standard Newton–Einstein formulation, this is achieved by introducing a dimensionful fundamental coupling constant G (Newton's constant), appearing in the Einstein–Hilbert action S = (1/16πG) ∫ R √(−g) d⁴x and entering the matter–gravity coupling through the combination MG.

Question: Is the introduction of a dimensionful fundamental coupling G logically necessary in any classical gravitational theory that exhibits universal coupling and reproduces Newtonian weak-field phenomenology? Equivalently, does there exist a classical gravitational theory — for example, one built from a dimensionless action with only dimensionless conformal couplings, in which the strength of the gravitational field produced by a source is set by moments (mass, size, internal structure) of the source rather than by a universal dimensionful constant — that (i) couples universally to matter, (ii) reproduces the observed 1/r Newtonian potential and its phenomenology in the appropriate regime, and (iii) contains no fundamental Newton constant G? Within Mannheim's conformal gravity program, an affirmative construction has been proposed: gravity is sourced by dimensionless conformal couplings and source moments, so that the effective Newtonian coupling emerges without a fundamental dimensionful G. Consider the nucleon described in QCD as a bound state containing, among its sea quarks, strange quarks s and antistrange quarks s̄. Define the unpolarized strange and antistrange parton distribution functions s(x,Q²) and s̄(x,Q²), as well as C-odd combinations such as the strange contribution to the magnetic form factor (strange magnetization) and the strange charge radius of the nucleon, which are sensitive to the difference between s and s̄ contributions (parity-violating elastic electron–nucleon scattering probes such C-odd quantities, while neutrino-induced charged-current dimuon production probes ∫ x[s(x)−s̄(x)]dx).

Determine whether the s and s̄ distributions in the nucleon differ significantly:
(a) Is the momentum asymmetry ∫₀¹ x[s(x,Q²) − s̄(x,Q²)] dx nonzero at a statistically significant level, and what is its sign and magnitude?
(b) Do s and s̄ have significantly different spatial distributions inside the nucleon, as reflected in nonzero strange electromagnetic form factors (strange magnetic moment μ_s and strange charge radius ⟨r²⟩_s)?

Provide a quantitative determination of these C-odd s−s̄ observables from experiment.

Experimental measurements have constrained but not definitively resolved the s−s̄ asymmetry. NuTeV dimuon analyses at NLO yielded a positive strange momentum asymmetry at only ~1.6σ significance, and global PDF fits (CT, NNPDF, MSHT) still find s(x)−s̄(x) consistent with zero within sizeable uncertainties. Parity-violating electron scattering experiments (HAPPEX, G0, Qweak) have constrained the strange magnetic moment and charge radius to be small and consistent with zero. Thus the question of a significant s–s̄ difference remains only partially answered.

Gluon saturation and the Colour Glass Condensate remain active areas of theoretical and experimental research in high-energy QCD. While there is growing phenomenological evidence (geometric scaling at HERA, forward-rapidity suppression at RHIC and the LHC), a definitive experimental confirmation of saturation and unambiguous signatures distinguishing BFKL, BK, and CCFM dynamics are still being pursued, and are among the central physics goals of the upcoming Electron-Ion Collider. The problem is widely regarded as open.

Provide a complete theoretical account of the structure and dynamics of atomic nuclei and of nuclear matter under astrophysical conditions. Specifically, address the following interrelated questions:

1. Nuclear force: Derive, from the underlying theory of strong interactions (quantum chromodynamics, with quarks and gluons), the effective interaction between nucleons (protons and neutrons) that binds them into stable nuclei as well as into rare (short-lived, neutron- or proton-rich) isotopes. Characterize its dependence on density, isospin, spin, and momentum.

2. EMC effect: Explain the experimentally observed modification of the per-nucleon deep-inelastic scattering structure function F_2^A(x)/A relative to that of a free nucleon when nucleons are bound inside a nucleus of mass number A (the European Muon Collaboration, or EMC, effect), and predict its dependence on x, A, and local nuclear density.

3. Exotic excitations near the drip lines: Describe the nature of collective and single-particle excitations (e.g., pygmy and giant resonances, halo and skin modes) in nuclei near the proton and neutron drip lines, and quantify their influence on nucleosynthesis in stellar and explosive astrophysical environments.

4. Neutron stars and dense matter: Determine the equation of state of strongly interacting matter at densities up to several times nuclear saturation density (~2.7 × 10^17 kg/m^3), including possible phase transitions to deconfined quark matter, hyperonic matter, or color-superconducting phases, and connect it to observable neutron-star properties (mass, radius, tidal deformability, cooling).

5. Origin of the elements: Identify the astrophysical sites and reaction networks (e.g., big-bang nucleosynthesis, stellar burning, s-, r-, p-, i-, rp-processes) responsible for producing the observed cosmic abundances of all chemical elements and their isotopes.

6. Stellar reaction rates: Determine quantitatively the thermonuclear reaction rates (cross sections at astrophysically relevant energies, often well below the Coulomb barrier) that govern energy generation and nucleosynthesis in stars and stellar explosions (novae, X-ray bursts, core-collapse and thermonuclear supernovae, neutron-star mergers).

7. Heaviest element: Determine the largest atomic number Z for which a bound nucleus (with measurable lifetime against spontaneous fission and other decay modes) can exist, including the location and extent of the predicted "island of stability" of superheavy nuclei.

These are widely recognized as outstanding open problems in nuclear physics and nuclear astrophysics, listed among the major unsolved questions in the field. While significant progress has been made on each (chiral effective field theory for nuclear forces, lattice QCD calculations, NICER/LIGO constraints on neutron-star equation of state, observation of r-process in GW170817, synthesis of element 118 oganesson, etc.), none of the questions has a definitive complete answer as of 2026.

representations.normalized: In Newtonian gravity, the gravitational potential φ produced by a mass density ρ is conventionally taken to satisfy the second-order Poisson equation ∇²φ = 4πG ρ. Outside an isolated, spherically symmetric source of total mass M this yields the Newtonian exterior potential φ(r) = −GM/r. However, alternative local field equations can produce the same exterior Newtonian potential. For example, the fourth-order Poisson equation ∇²(∇²φ) = g(ρ) (for a suitable source term g(ρ)) admits, outside the source, general spherically symmetric solutions of the form φ(r) = −A/r + B + C r + D r², and thus also reproduces −GM/r as the dominant short-distance exterior behavior. Both equations agree with Newton's law in the exterior region of a localized source, but differ in their predictions inside matter and on sufficiently large distance scales.\n\nProblem. Determine whether there exists an empirical observation, a symmetry, or a first principle that uniquely singles out the second-order Poisson equation ∇²φ = 4πG ρ as the gravitational field equation valid both inside sources and on all distance scales, rather than admitting an alternative such as the fourth-order Poisson equation that yields the same Newtonian exterior potential as a dominant short-distance solution. Equivalently: produce either (i) a test, observation, or principle that excludes all higher-order linear local alternatives whose exterior solutions contain the −GM/r term, or (ii) a concrete consistent alternative theory (with field equation different from the second-order Poisson equation) that agrees with all current gravitational observations.

The question is conceptual: no observation has tested the second-order Poisson equation strictly inside matter, and higher-derivative Poisson-type equations (which arise e.g. in conformal gravity and other fourth-order gravity theories) remain viable in producing the Newtonian exterior potential. The proponent of conformal/fourth-order Newtonian gravity (Mannheim and collaborators) continued to pursue this alternative, and no decisive observation or principle uniquely selecting the standard second-order Poisson equation has been established. The question therefore remains open.

Off-forward (a.k.a. skewed or generalized) parton distributions (GPDs) extend the ordinary parton distribution functions of a hadron to nonzero momentum transfer between the incoming and outgoing hadron states. For a nucleon they are defined as off-diagonal matrix elements of bilocal light-cone quark and gluon operators,

  F^q(x, ξ, t) = ∫ (dz⁻/4π) e^{i x P⁺ z⁻} ⟨P'| q̄(−z/2) γ⁺ q(z/2) |P⟩ |_{z⁺=z_⊥=0},

(and analogous structures for helicity-flip, gluon, and tensor operators), where P, P' are the initial/final hadron momenta, ξ is the skewness measuring the longitudinal momentum transfer, and t = (P' − P)² is the invariant momentum transfer. Such distributions enter the amplitude for hard exclusive processes, most notably deeply virtual Compton scattering γ*(q) N(P) → γ(q') N(P').

Problem. Provide a heuristic physical interpretation of the off-forward parton distributions F^q(x, ξ, t) (and their gluon and helicity-dependent analogues) as intrinsic properties of a hadron, and identify precisely which hadron-structure observables—e.g., transverse spatial parton densities, orbital angular momentum contributions to the nucleon spin, energy-momentum tensor form factors, or other dynamical quantities—are determined by these distributions. In particular, characterize:

(a) the position-space content of GPDs (for example, via Fourier transform in transverse momentum transfer at ξ = 0);
(b) the relation of their Mellin moments to local matrix elements of the QCD energy-momentum tensor and the resulting decomposition of nucleon spin into quark/gluon angular momentum;
(c) what new, model-independent information about the internal structure of the nucleon is obtained from measurements of deeply virtual Compton scattering and related hard exclusive reactions that is not contained in ordinary parton distribution functions or elastic form factors.

Consider an incompressible Newtonian fluid in three spatial dimensions whose velocity field $u(x,t):\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p(x,t):\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}$ satisfy the Navier–Stokes equations
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla) u = -\nabla p + \nu\,\Delta u + f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\]
where $\nu>0$ is the kinematic viscosity and $f$ is a (possibly stochastic) external forcing. In the high–Reynolds-number regime, solutions exhibit turbulent behavior characterized by apparently random, multi-scale fluctuations with coherent internal structures (vortex filaments, sheets, intermittent bursts).

Develop a closed, first-principles theoretical framework that, starting from the Navier–Stokes equations above, derives the statistical properties of fully developed three-dimensional turbulence. In particular, the framework should:

1. Predict, with controlled error, the single-time multi-point velocity correlation functions 
\[
 C_n(x_1,\dots,x_n;t) = \langle u_{i_1}(x_1,t)\cdots u_{i_n}(x_n,t)\rangle
\]
for all $n\ge 2$, where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes ensemble (or long-time) averaging.

2. Determine the inertial-range scaling exponents $\zeta_n$ defined by
\[
 S_n(r) := \langle |[u(x+r,t)-u(x,t)]\cdot \hat r|^n\rangle \sim r^{\zeta_n},\qquad \eta\ll r\ll L,
\]
where $L$ is the integral scale and $\eta=(\nu^3/\varepsilon)^{1/4}$ is the Kolmogorov dissipation scale with $\varepsilon$ the mean energy dissipation rate, and explain the observed deviations from the Kolmogorov 1941 prediction $\zeta_n=n/3$ (the intermittency/anomalous scaling problem).

3. Characterize quantitatively the geometry, statistics, and dynamics of the coherent internal structures of the flow (e.g., the fractal/multifractal dimension of the dissipation set, distributions of vorticity, and the statistics of vortex filaments).

The problem is to construct such a model (or to prove that no closed-form statistical theory of this kind can exist).

The problem of constructing a first-principles statistical theory of three-dimensional turbulence, including a rigorous explanation of intermittency and anomalous scaling exponents, is widely regarded as one of the outstanding open problems in classical physics and applied mathematics. It is listed among unsolved problems in physics and is closely tied to the open Navier–Stokes regularity Clay Millennium Problem. No accepted closed theoretical framework exists as of 2026.

Consider the classical theory of gravity in four spacetime dimensions formulated through a diffeomorphism-invariant action principle on a pseudo-Riemannian manifold (M, g). The Einstein–Hilbert action S_EH = (1/16πG) ∫_M (R − 2Λ) √(−g) d^4x depends on a free parameter Λ, the cosmological constant, because diffeomorphism invariance alone permits the addition of an arbitrary multiple of ∫_M √(−g) d^4x to the gravitational Lagrangian. The cosmological constant problem refers to the fact that no symmetry of the standard theory forbids a Λ term in the input Lagrangian, while observation requires its effective value to be extremely small (or zero).

Question: Within classical Einstein gravity (i.e. without invoking quantum effects or matter cancellation mechanisms), is it possible to solve or avoid the cosmological constant problem if the starting gravitational action is not selected by a principle that intrinsically excludes a cosmological constant term? Equivalently, formulate and justify an additional geometric invariance principle on (M, g) — beyond diffeomorphism invariance — that uniquely determines the gravitational action and rules out any ∫_M Λ √(−g) d^4x term at the level of the input Lagrangian, or prove that no such purely classical invariance principle can do so while remaining consistent with the standard Newtonian and post-Newtonian limits.

representations.normalized:
Let $a_\mu = (g_\mu - 2)/2$ denote the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon, defined via the Dirac form factor decomposition of the muon's electromagnetic vertex at zero momentum transfer. Within the Standard Model, $a_\mu$ admits a decomposition
$$a_\mu^{\mathrm{SM}} = a_\mu^{\mathrm{QED}} + a_\mu^{\mathrm{EW}} + a_\mu^{\mathrm{HVP}} + a_\mu^{\mathrm{HLbL}},$$
where $a_\mu^{\mathrm{HVP}}$ is the hadronic vacuum polarization contribution (starting at order $\alpha^2$) and $a_\mu^{\mathrm{HLbL}}$ is the hadronic light-by-light contribution (starting at order $\alpha^3$). These hadronic pieces dominate the total theoretical uncertainty on $a_\mu^{\mathrm{SM}}$.

Problem: Develop a theoretical determination of the higher-order QCD (hadronic) contributions $a_\mu^{\mathrm{HVP}}$ and $a_\mu^{\mathrm{HLbL}}$ — for example via dispersive analyses based on $e^+e^- \to \mathrm{hadrons}$ data, lattice QCD, or effective field theory techniques — that reduces the total Standard Model theoretical uncertainty on $a_\mu$ to a level commensurate with sub-ppm experimental precision, so that a meaningful comparison between $a_\mu^{\mathrm{SM}}$ and the measured value $a_\mu^{\mathrm{exp}}$ can be used to test the Standard Model and constrain possible extensions. Quantify and control all sources of uncertainty in the hadronic contributions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

As of 2025/2026, substantial progress has been made on the hadronic contributions via lattice QCD and dispersive methods. The Muon g-2 Theory Initiative released an updated White Paper in 2025 with prediction $a_\mu = (116592033 \pm 62) \times 10^{-11}$ (530 ppb), now consistent with the Fermilab experimental result at 127 ppb. However, tensions remain between different evaluations of the HVP contribution (e.g., between lattice QCD and earlier $e^+e^-$ data-driven results, and among $e^+e^-$ datasets), and the hadronic pieces still dominate the theory error. The problem is therefore actively progressing but not fully resolved.

Consider a container partially filled with a granular medium consisting of solid, macroscopic particles of various sizes (for example, spheres of differing radii and possibly differing densities) subjected to a periodic vertical vibration described by a prescribed acceleration profile (e.g., sinusoidal motion of amplitude A and frequency ω). Under suitable ranges of vibration parameters, one observes two phenomena:

(a) Convection-like circulation: the bulk grains move in steady circulation patterns reminiscent of fluid convection rolls, typically rising in the interior and descending in thin layers near the container walls.

(b) Size segregation (the "Brazil-nut" phenomenon): when the medium consists of particles of differing sizes, the largest particles migrate upward and accumulate at the free surface, despite often being denser or having larger mass than the surrounding small particles.

Provide a first-principles theoretical derivation, starting from the mechanics of individual grain–grain and grain–wall interactions (including inelastic collisions, friction, and gravity), that:

1. Predicts the onset, geometry, and velocity field of the convective circulation as a function of the vibration parameters (A, ω), particle properties (size distribution, density, friction and restitution coefficients), and container geometry; and

2. Explains, quantitatively, why the largest particles rise to the top under shaking, identifying the dominant mechanism (e.g., void-filling/percolation of small grains, wall-driven convective transport, inertial effects, or condensation), determining the regimes in which each mechanism dominates, and predicting when the "reverse Brazil-nut effect" (large particles sinking) instead occurs.

The goal is a unified, predictive mathematical model whose qualitative and quantitative predictions match laboratory observations of vibrated polydisperse granular materials.

The mechanism is generally described as still not fully established, and the problem is regarded as open.

A material is said to be superconducting when, below a critical temperature T_c, its electrical resistance drops to zero and magnetic flux is expelled from its interior (the Meissner effect). Conventional superconductivity in metals with T_c below roughly 25 K is described by Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) theory, in which electrons form Cooper pairs through an attractive interaction mediated by lattice vibrations (phonons). However, several classes of materials—most notably the copper-oxide (cuprate) perovskites, the iron-based pnictides and chalcogenides, and certain organic and heavy-fermion compounds—exhibit superconductivity at temperatures substantially exceeding 25 K, in some cases above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen (77 K), and hydrogen-rich hydrides under extreme pressure exhibit superconductivity near room temperature. Standard phonon-mediated BCS theory does not quantitatively account for the high transition temperatures observed in these materials.

(a) Identify and rigorously characterize the microscopic pairing mechanism (or mechanisms) responsible for superconductivity in high-T_c materials—particularly in the cuprates and iron-based superconductors—including the nature of the effective attractive interaction between charge carriers, the symmetry of the superconducting order parameter, and the role of competing or coexisting orders such as antiferromagnetism, charge/spin density waves, and the pseudogap phase.

(b) Determine whether it is possible, in principle, to design or synthesize a material that exhibits superconductivity at room temperature (≈ 293 K) and at ambient atmospheric pressure (≈ 1 atm). If such a material exists, specify constraints (e.g., on composition, electronic structure, lattice dynamics) under which it may be realized; if no such material can exist, provide a proof of an upper bound on T_c at ambient pressure derived from fundamental principles.

The microscopic mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity (especially in cuprates) remains one of the foremost unsolved problems in condensed matter physics, with multiple 2025 reviews and research articles characterizing it as still unsolved after more than 35 years. Although hydrogen-rich hydrides show near-room-temperature superconductivity under extreme pressure and 2025 SLAC work stabilized a new class at room pressure, no material exhibiting superconductivity at room temperature and atmospheric pressure has been confirmed. Recent advances (e.g., MIT, Penn State, SLAC) offer partial insights but do not resolve the mechanism or achieve ambient room-temperature superconductivity.

u}$ (so $g^{\mu
u}T_{\mu
u}=0$), and in which particle masses are generated dynamically through a scale-breaking Higgs mechanism that preserves the tracelessness of $T_{\mu
u}$. Because $T_{\mu
u}$ remains traceless after symmetry breaking, any cosmological-constant term $\Lambda g_{\mu
u}$ that is induced as a consequence of this scale breaking must be of the same order of magnitude as the other contributions to $T_{\mu
u}$; in a cosmological setting this means $\Lambda$ is naturally of order the energy density $ho$ of the particles in the Universe.

Within the Robertson–Walker cosmology derived from such a conformal theory, with Hubble parameter $H_0$ and matter density of order $ho$, determine whether the inclusion of an induced cosmological-constant term of order $ho$ produces a present-day age of the Universe large enough to exceed the inferred ages of the oldest astrophysical constituents (e.g. globular clusters). That is, show whether a cosmological term of magnitude $|\Lambda|\sim ho$, arising from the scale-breaking mechanism in the traceless conformal $T_{\mu
u}$, resolves the cosmological age problem in conformal cosmology.

Subsequent work in conformal cosmology (notably astro-ph/9601071 and later papers) developed this idea in detail and argued that an induced cosmological term of order the matter density does yield an age of the Universe of order 1/H_0, alleviating the age problem. The proposal is therefore partially developed/affirmed within that framework, though it has not been definitively resolved as a generally accepted resolution of the age problem outside conformal gravity.

Consider electron–positron annihilation into hadrons at center-of-mass energy √s. Two-particle Bose–Einstein correlations of identically charged pions are parametrized, assuming a Gaussian spherical emitter, by
  C₂(Q) = 1 + λ₂ exp(−r²Q²),
where Q² = −(p₁ − p₂)² is built from the four-momenta p₁, p₂ of the two pions, λ₂ is an incoherence parameter, and r = r_{ππ} is the Gaussian source-size parameter.

Empirically, across √s ranging from roughly 10 GeV to 91 GeV, the extracted r_{ππ} is essentially independent of √s, even though the mean charged-hadron multiplicity ⟨n⟩ grows substantially with √s.

(a) Provide a theoretical explanation, within the framework of multiparticle production in e⁺e⁻ annihilation, of why r_{ππ} should be (nearly) independent of √s despite the growth of ⟨n⟩.
(b) Construct an explicit source model — for example, treating hadronic jets as independent pion-emitting sources and relating r_{ππ} to the normalized factorial cumulant moments of the multiplicity distribution — that quantitatively reproduces the observed flat behavior of r_{ππ}(√s) over 10 GeV ≲ √s ≲ 91 GeV.

A follow-up work proposes that treating hadron jets as independent pion sources, combined with the dependence of normalized factorial cumulant moments on the number of sources, quantitatively reproduces the nearly energy-independent r_{ππ} measured in e⁺e⁻ annihilation between 10 and 91 GeV (rising only ~3.5%). This provides a quantitative model that fits the data, so the phenomenological challenge is partially resolved, though a fully first-principles derivation is not established.

Consider an amorphous (non-crystalline) condensed-matter system, such as a supercooled liquid that, upon cooling below a characteristic temperature T_g, fails to crystallize and instead forms a glass: a disordered, out-of-equilibrium solid whose static structure factor remains liquid-like while its mechanical response (e.g., shear modulus, viscosity exceeding ~10^12 Pa·s) is solid-like. The glass transition is operationally identified by a continuous but dramatic, super-Arrhenius slowdown of structural relaxation times as T → T_g, accompanied by non-exponential (stretched-exponential) relaxation functions, growing dynamic heterogeneity, and a drop in configurational entropy that, if extrapolated, would vanish at a finite Kauzmann temperature T_K < T_g.

Provide a first-principles theoretical framework that resolves the following:

1. Characterize the nature of the glass transition between a homogeneous fluid (or ordinary crystalline solid) and a glassy phase. In particular, determine whether the apparent transition at T_g is purely a kinetic crossover, a genuine thermodynamic phase transition to an "ideal glass" at some lower temperature (e.g., T_K), a dynamical (mode-coupling-type) transition, or something else; and identify any associated diverging static or dynamic correlation length.

2. Identify the microscopic physical processes (structural, energetic, and dynamic) that produce the universal phenomenology of glasses and the glass transition, including super-Arrhenius growth of the relaxation time, non-exponential relaxation, dynamic heterogeneity, two-level-system low-energy excitations, the boson peak, aging, and the apparent universality of these features across molecular, polymeric, colloidal, and metallic glass formers.

Recent reviews (e.g., Nature Reviews Physics 2022 and 2026) emphasize that, while significant progress has been made via swap Monte Carlo, replica/RFOT theory, and dynamic heterogeneity studies, no consensus first-principles theory exists, and central questions about a possible underlying thermodynamic transition and the microscopic origin of universal glassy phenomena remain open.

In a disordered (amorphous) solid at low temperatures (below roughly 3 K), acoustic phonons of wavelength $\lambda$ propagate with a finite mean free path $\ell$. Experimentally, across a very wide variety of structurally and chemically distinct disordered solids (glasses, polymers, disordered crystals, etc.), the dimensionless ratio $\lambda/\ell$ is observed to be both very small (of order $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$, often quoted near $1/150$) and approximately the same numerical value, and this near-constancy holds over a broad range of phonon frequencies.

Provide a first-principles explanation of this universality. Specifically, derive from a microscopic model of disordered solids: (i) why $\lambda/\ell$ is nearly independent of the chemical composition and microscopic structure of the amorphous solid, (ii) why its numerical value is so small, and (iii) why this near-universal behavior persists over a wide range of phonon frequencies and below an energy scale corresponding to roughly 3 K.

The universality of the small ratio λ/ℓ in low-temperature amorphous solids has been studied within the tunneling two-level-system (TLS) framework for over five decades, but the origin of the universality and smallness of the ratio remains unresolved. Recent proposals (e.g., elastically coupled generic blocks, and two-type TLS models with inversion-symmetric vs. non-symmetric states) offer promising partial explanations, but no first-principles derivation is generally accepted.

representations.normalized:
In high-energy electron–positron annihilation into hadrons, identical-boson Bose–Einstein correlations (BEC) and identical-fermion Fermi–Dirac correlations (FDC) between pairs of final-state hadrons can be used to infer an effective spatial size r of the emitting source for each hadron species. From the measured emitter radius r and the typical energy E carried by the emitted hadron, one defines an approximate minimum emitter energy density by

  ρ ≈ E / ((4/3) π r³).

Empirically, when this estimate is applied to pairs of identical pions and identical kaons produced in e⁺e⁻ → hadrons, the resulting energy densities are compatible with values predicted by current models of hadron production. However, when the same procedure is applied to identical-proton and identical-Λ pairs, the inferred emitter energy density is of order 100 GeV/fm³, far exceeding the densities anticipated in any standard model of hadronization in e⁺e⁻ annihilation.

Problem: Construct a model of hadron production in e⁺e⁻ annihilation (or identify a mechanism within an existing framework such as string fragmentation, cluster hadronization, or statistical/thermal hadronization) that reproduces, simultaneously:

(a) the moderate, model-consistent emitter energy densities inferred from BEC measurements of identical-pion and identical-kaon pairs, and

(b) the extremely large (~100 GeV/fm³) emitter energy densities inferred from BEC/FDC measurements of identical-proton and identical-Λ pairs,

and explain physically why baryon emitters appear so much more compact (and thus apparently so much denser) than meson emitters in this analysis.

A targeted web search did not surface any publication that resolves the apparent ~100 GeV/fm³ emitter energy density inferred for proton and Λ emitters in e⁺e⁻ → hadrons relative to pion/kaon emitters. A photomultiplier tube is a vacuum device in which a photo-cathode emits electrons that are subsequently amplified through a chain of dynodes. In the complete absence of incident light, such a device still produces a "dark" electron emission rate. Empirically, as the temperature of the photomultiplier is lowered from room temperature, the dark electron emission rate initially decreases (as expected from thermionic emission), but below roughly 220 K it levels off and then begins to rise again, continuing to increase down to liquid-helium temperatures (≈ 4 K). The electrons are observed to appear in correlated bursts whose rate and multiplicity both grow as the temperature is lowered. Known mechanisms for electron emission in the absence of light — thermionic emission, field emission, and ionizing radiation — cannot account for this behavior.

Provide a physical mechanism, with a quantitative model, that explains why the dark electron emission rate from the photo-cathode of a photomultiplier increases as the temperature is decreased toward cryogenic temperatures, and that reproduces the observed burst statistics (clustered emissions whose rate and per-burst multiplicity grow with decreasing temperature).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The phenomenon remains without a confirmed physical explanation. A 2008 measurement (Meyer) documented the anomalous rise in dark rate below ~220 K down to 4 K, and a 2010 popular-science write-up explicitly stated that no known physics mechanism accounts for it. Trapping/lattice-energy hypotheses have been proposed but not established. No subsequent work appears to provide a generally accepted explanation.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The mechanism behind sonoluminescence remains unresolved as of 2025. The thermal hot-spot/bremsstrahlung picture is the leading candidate and accounts for much spectroscopic and timing data, but no single mechanism quantitatively explains all observations, and competing proposals (collision-induced emission, quantum/vacuum-based mechanisms, plasma models) remain active. Recent reviews and encyclopedic sources continue to list the precise mechanism as unknown.

Let $(X,\le)$ be an ordered function space (for instance a space of real-valued continuous functions on an interval $[a,b]$ endowed with the pointwise order) and let $A : X \to X$ be an order-preserving operator. A concrete Gronwall-type lemma typically has the following form: every $x \in X$ satisfying the inequality $x \le A(x)$ admits an explicit upper bound $u(x) \in X$ with $x \le u(x)$, where $u(x)$ is obtained from the data appearing in $A$ (for example, in the classical Gronwall lemma, the inequality $x(t) \le \varphi(t) + \int_a^t \psi(s)\, x(s)\, ds$ yields the upper bound $u(x)(t) = \varphi(t)\exp\!\int_a^t \psi(s)\, ds$, which in general is not a fixed point of the associated operator $A(x)(t) = \varphi(t) + \int_a^t \psi(s)\, x(s)\, ds$).

Problem: Characterize, among the known concrete Gronwall-type lemmas (i.e., concrete realizations of $x \le A(x) \Rightarrow x \le u(x)$ on ordered function spaces), exactly those for which the explicit upper bound $u(x)$ is itself a fixed point of the corresponding operator $A$, that is, $A(u(x)) = u(x)$.

Bose–Einstein correlations (BEC) describe the enhancement, at small four-momentum difference Q, of the joint production probability of pairs of identical bosons (e.g. π±π±) in high-energy multiparticle final states, arising from the symmetrization of the two-boson wave function. By analogy with the generalised Pauli principle, which extends antisymmetrization from two identical nucleons to the proton–neutron isospin doublet, one may attempt to incorporate isospin invariance into BEC to obtain a Generalised Bose–Einstein Correlation (GBEC) framework. In this framework, when a pair of pseudoscalar mesons belonging to the same isospin multiplet (such as the pion triplet) is produced, together with its accompanying hadrons, from an overall isosinglet (I=0) source, symmetrization in the combined space–isospin variables would predict definite relations between the low-Q correlation functions of non-identical charge combinations (such as π±π⁰) and those of identical pairs (such as π±π±, π⁰π⁰).

Problem. Formulate a consistent GBEC framework for high-energy hadron production (in particular e⁺e⁻ → hadrons) by imposing isospin invariance, deriving from it quantitative relations between the two-particle BEC functions C₂(Q) of the π±π± and π±π⁰ systems (and, more generally, of mesons in a common isospin multiplet produced from an I=0 source). Then determine whether such GBEC predictions can be experimentally established at high energies, by identifying observables and event selections (ensuring an I=0 initial subsystem) for which the predicted relations between π±π⁰ and π±π± (or analogous K±K⁰ and K±K±) correlation functions can be tested, and assess whether existing or feasible measurements confirm the framework.

The theoretical GBEC framework relating π±π± and π±π⁰ (and K±K± with K±K⁰) via isospin invariance has been proposed (Alexander–Lipkin, 1999) and some related measurements of π⁰π⁰ BEC at LEP exist, but no direct experimental verification of the GBEC relations between non-identical isospin partners (e.g. π±π⁰) at high energies is reported. A recent BESIII prospects paper (2024) still discusses such tests as future possibilities, indicating the question remains experimentally open.

representations.normalized: Among the naturally occurring stable isotopes of elements heavier than iron, there exists a small group of approximately 35 proton-rich nuclides—commonly called the p-nuclei—that cannot be synthesized by either the slow neutron-capture process (s-process) or the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process), because they lie on the proton-rich side of the valley of beta stability and are shielded from neutron-capture pathways by stable isobars. These nuclides are observed in the Solar System with characteristic, very low isotopic abundances (typically 0.01%–1% of the element's total abundance). Identify and characterize the astrophysical process (or combination of processes) and the stellar or explosive sites responsible for the nucleosynthesis of the full set of p-nuclei, in such a way that the predicted abundance pattern quantitatively reproduces the observed Solar System abundances across the entire mass range, including the light p-nuclei with mass number A < 100 and the isotopes in the range 150 ≤ A ≤ 165 where current γ-process (photodisintegration) models in core-collapse supernovae fail to match observations.

These nuclides are observed in the Solar System with characteristic, very low isotopic abundances (typically 0.01%–1% of the element's total abundance). Identify and characterize the astrophysical process (or combination of processes) and the stellar or explosive sites responsible for the nucleosynthesis of the full set of p-nuclei, in such a way that the predicted abundance pattern quantitatively reproduces the observed Solar System abundances across the entire mass range, including the light p-nuclei with mass number A < 100 and the isotopes in the range 150 ≤ A ≤ 165 where current γ-process (photodisintegration) models in core-collapse supernovae fail to match observations.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The astrophysical origin of the p-nuclei remains an open problem. While the γ-process (photodisintegration during explosive O/Ne burning in core-collapse supernovae) accounts for many p-nuclei, current models systematically underproduce the light p-nuclei (A < 100) and isotopes in the 150 ≤ A ≤ 165 range. Alternative or complementary sites (e.g., νp-process, rp-process, Type Ia supernovae) continue to be investigated, with no fully consistent solution as of recent reviews.

A gapped quantum many-body system on a lattice in d spatial dimensions is said to exhibit topological order if its ground space is degenerate, the degeneracy depends on the topology of the underlying manifold, and the different ground states are locally indistinguishable (no local operator can distinguish them). A self-correcting quantum memory is a local, geometrically realized quantum spin Hamiltonian H on a lattice in d spatial dimensions such that, when coupled to a thermal bath at any sufficiently small but nonzero temperature T > 0, the encoded logical information (i.e., the ground-space degeneracy) is preserved for a time that grows at least exponentially in the linear system size L, without any active error correction. Equivalently, one requires that the topologically ordered phase remains stable against arbitrary local thermal fluctuations: the lifetime of stored logical qubits diverges in the thermodynamic limit at fixed T > 0.

Question: Does there exist a three-dimensional local commuting (or, more generally, local gapped) lattice Hamiltonian whose ground space realizes topological order that remains stable at some nonzero temperature, in the sense above? Equivalently, can a three-dimensional self-correcting quantum memory exist?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence of a three-dimensional self-correcting quantum memory, equivalent to thermal stability of topological order in 3D, remains an open problem. All rigorously established self-correcting quantum memories require four or more spatial dimensions. Partial progress includes Haah's cubic code (polynomial lifetime), partial self-correction in layer codes, and recent proposals such as a 2026 preprint claiming exponential-lifetime 3D constructions, but these remain unverified and the general problem is regarded as open.

representations.normalized:
Consider a two-dimensional electron system subjected to a strong perpendicular magnetic field at low temperature, so that the single-particle spectrum is organized into highly degenerate Landau levels. At certain rational filling factors ν = p/q (with q odd, and also at certain even-denominator values such as ν = 5/2), the interacting electron system exhibits the fractional quantum Hall effect: the longitudinal resistivity vanishes and the Hall conductivity is quantized at σ_{xy} = ν e²/h, with charged elementary excitations ("quasiparticles") carrying a fractional electric charge e* = e/q and obeying fractional (anyonic) exchange statistics.

(a) Identify and rigorously justify a microscopic mechanism — in terms of an interacting many-body wavefunction or an effective low-energy field theory — that explains the formation of an incompressible quantum liquid at general fractional fillings, including the even-denominator filling ν = 5/2, accounting for the observed quantization of σ_{xy}, the fractional quasiparticle charge, and the gap to bulk excitations.

(b) Determine whether the quasiparticle excitations above the ν = 5/2 ground state (and, more generally, above ground states of even-denominator fillings such as ν = 12/5) obey non-Abelian braiding statistics: i.e., decide whether the unitary representation of the braid group acting on the degenerate manifold of states with a fixed configuration of quasiparticle positions is non-Abelian, and characterize that representation.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The mechanism for odd-denominator fractional quantum Hall states is well understood via Laughlin's wavefunction and composite-fermion theory, but the precise nature of the ν = 5/2 state (Moore–Read Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, PH-Pfaffian, or alternatives) and definitive experimental confirmation that its quasiparticles obey non-Abelian braiding statistics remain unresolved as of 2025–2026. Recent Aharonov–Bohm interferometry in bilayer graphene and observation of large activation gaps at ν = 5/2 in proximitized trilayer graphene are promising but have not yet conclusively demonstrated non-Abelian braiding.

Let X be a nonempty set and A: X → X a self-map. Denote by F_A := {x ∈ X : A(x) = x} the fixed-point set of A, and by A^n the n-th iterate of A. The map A is called a Bessaga operator if there exists x* ∈ X such that F_A = F_{A^n} = {x*} for every integer n ≥ 1 (equivalently, A and each of its iterates share the same unique fixed point).

Given a convergence structure "→" on X (an abstract notion of sequential convergence) and a partial order "≤" on X, a self-map A: (X, →, ≤) → (X, →, ≤) is called an increasing Picard operator if:
 (i) A is monotone increasing with respect to ≤;
 (ii) A has a unique fixed point x* ∈ X;
 (iii) for every starting point x ∈ X, the sequence of iterates (A^n(x))_{n≥1} converges to x* in the sense of →.

Consider the broad class of concrete Gronwall-type lemmas. Such a lemma typically asserts that, for a suitable operator A acting on an ordered set (X, ≤) of admissible functions, the inequality x ≤ A(x) (or A(x) ≤ x) implies an a-priori bound on x in terms of a fixed point of A. Among the concrete Gronwall lemmas that cannot be deduced from any abstract Gronwall lemma of fixed-point type, address the following questions:

(a) For which of these lemmas is the associated operator A a Bessaga operator?

(b) Whenever (a) holds, can one equip X with a convergence structure → and a compatible order ≤ such that A: (X, →, ≤) → (X, →, ≤) becomes an increasing Picard operator?

Consider Bose-Einstein correlations (BEC) among identical hadrons produced in e+e− → hadrons. From a Goldhaber-type or Gaussian fit to the two-particle BEC enhancement near zero relative four-momentum, one extracts a length scale r, conventionally interpreted as the spatial size of the hadron emitter. Empirically, when r is measured separately for pairs of identical hadrons of different species and is plotted as a function of the hadron mass m, the resulting function r(m) decreases with m in a way compatible with r(m) ∝ 1/√m. In addition, naive estimates of the energy density inside the emitter volume of radius r(m) come out anomalously large. By analogy, in a non-relativistic Bose-Einstein condensate of atoms of mass m_atom held at a fixed very low temperature, the mean inter-atomic separation scales as 1/√m_atom and represents an inter-particle distance rather than the size of the trap or cloud.

Problem: Determine the correct physical interpretation of the BEC-derived length scale r in e+e− → hadrons. Specifically, decide whether r(m) should be interpreted as
(a) the spatial extent (radius) of the hadron-emitting source, or
(b) a typical inter-particle separation between identical hadrons in the produced multi-hadron system (analogous to the inter-atomic separation in a Bose condensate),
or some other well-defined geometric/dynamical quantity, in a way that is simultaneously consistent with (i) the observed 1/√m scaling of r(m), (ii) the inferred high energy densities, and (iii) the analogy with Bose-Einstein condensates. Provide a theoretical framework justifying the chosen interpretation.

Recent literature (e.g., MDPI Physics 2019, LHCb/CMS BEC studies, and reviews) still discusses the mass dependence r(m) ∝ 1/√m and offers competing interpretations — including emitter size, inter-particle separation between overlapping hadrons, and uncertainty-principle-based explanations — without a consensus settled interpretation. In the theory of liquid crystals, a nematic phase is a state of matter in which rod-like molecules exhibit long-range orientational order (described by a director field) but no positional order, while a smectic-A phase has, in addition to orientational order along the director, one-dimensional translational (layered) order with the layer normal parallel to the director. The transition between the nematic and smectic-A phases is conventionally modeled by a complex scalar order parameter ψ (whose magnitude measures the amplitude of the smectic density wave and whose phase encodes layer displacement) coupled to fluctuations of the nematic director, giving rise to a Landau–Ginzburg–de Gennes free energy that bears a formal analogy with the Ginzburg–Landau theory of superconductors (with the director playing the role of the gauge field).

Determine whether the continuous nematic to smectic-A phase transition can be characterized by a single universality class. Concretely:

(a) Does there exist a well-defined set of critical exponents (e.g. ν_∥, ν_⊥, α, η) that govern the asymptotic critical behavior of the nematic–smectic-A transition independently of the microscopic details of the liquid-crystal material, in the sense of the renormalization-group notion of universality?

(b) If so, identify this universality class (for instance, the three-dimensional XY class, an anisotropic gauge-coupled class analogous to the inverted superconductor transition, or another class) and produce a theoretical derivation that reproduces the experimentally observed anisotropic exponents and the variation of effective exponents with the McMillan ratio T_NA/T_NI.

(c) If no single universality class suffices, give a rigorous explanation of the apparent non-universality, including the role of the coupling between the smectic order parameter and nematic director fluctuations, of the splay elastic constant, and of proximity to the tricritical (Landau) point where the transition becomes first order.

The universality of the nematic to smectic-A transition remains an outstanding open problem in soft-matter physics. Consider a semiconductor nanocrystal modeled as a spherical quantum dot of radius R, in which charge carriers (electrons and holes) experience three-dimensional quantum confinement. Within the effective-mass approximation with simple parabolic bands, the energy E₁(R) of the lowest optical (excitonic) absorption transition is predicted to scale as E_g + C/R² (plus a Coulomb correction of order 1/R), giving a "parabolic" dependence on inverse size. Experimental measurements on a variety of semiconductor quantum dot systems show that the actual size dependence of the lowest optical absorption transition energy deviates significantly from this 1/R² law (i.e., it is nonparabolic in 1/R).

Problem: Identify and rigorously justify the physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) responsible for the observed nonparabolicity of the energy-versus-size dependence of the lowest optical absorption transition in semiconductor quantum dots. In particular, determine the relative contributions of effects such as conduction-band nonparabolicity (k·p / Kane-model corrections beyond the parabolic effective mass), valence-band mixing and degeneracy, finite confinement potential and surface/interface effects, size-dependent dielectric screening, and electron–hole Coulomb and exchange interactions, and provide a predictive quantitative model that reproduces the measured E₁(R) curves across the strong-confinement regime.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The literature attributes much of the nonparabolic E(R) dependence to conduction-band nonparabolicity (Kane-type k·p corrections), valence-band mixing/degeneracy, finite-barrier confinement, and size-dependent dielectric screening, with pseudopotential and multiband k·p calculations reproducing measured trends for systems like CdSe and InP. However, a single universally accepted quantitative theory across all materials and sizes does not yet exist, so the problem is considered partially solved.

Recall the classical Gronwall lemma: if $u, \beta : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ are continuous, $\alpha \ge 0$ is constant, and
$$u(t) \le \alpha + \int_a^t \beta(s)\, u(s)\, ds \qquad \text{for all } t \in [a,b],$$
then $u(t) \le \alpha \exp\!\left(\int_a^t \beta(s)\, ds\right)$ for all $t \in [a,b]$. Many extensions exist (Bihari, Bellman, Pachpatte, Wendroff, integral and discrete versions, versions on time scales, versions in ordered Banach spaces, fixed-point-theoretic abstract versions, etc.).

Problem. Formulate and prove genuinely new Gronwall-type lemmas, in both:
(a) Concrete form: explicit integral, sum, or functional inequalities yielding pointwise majorization of an unknown nonnegative function $u$ in terms of given data, with sharp or explicit bounds, going beyond the existing classical, Bihari, Pachpatte, Wendroff, time-scale, fractional, and stochastic variants.
(b) Abstract form: lemmas stated in ordered topological vector spaces, ordered Banach spaces, lattices, or via fixed-point principles (e.g. Perov-, Maia-, or Picard-operator type results), which yield as particular cases the classical and known generalized Gronwall inequalities.

Specifically: produce at least one new concrete inequality and one new abstract inequality, prove the corresponding bound, and demonstrate that the abstract version recovers the classical Gronwall lemma as a special case and is not equivalent to any previously published Gronwall-type result.

representations.normalized:
Consider liquid helium-4 near its superfluid (lambda) transition at temperature $T_\lambda$. As $T \to T_\lambda$, the specific heat at constant pressure exhibits a singular behavior characterized by the critical exponent $\alpha$ defined through
$$C(T) \sim A_\pm |t|^{-\alpha} + B, \qquad t = (T - T_\lambda)/T_\lambda,$$
with separate amplitudes $A_\pm$ above and below the transition. The transition is expected to belong to the three-dimensional XY universality class (O(2) symmetry, $d=3$), so $\alpha$ is universal and may be computed by renormalization-group methods (perturbative field theory, high-temperature expansions, Monte Carlo lattice simulations, or the conformal bootstrap). On the experimental side, a microgravity measurement of the specific heat of helium-4 within nanokelvins of $T_\lambda$ has yielded a value of $\alpha$ near $-0.0127 \pm 0.0003$, while different theoretical determinations cluster near values such as $-0.0151$ (Monte Carlo / conformal bootstrap) and $\approx -0.008$ to $-0.011$ (various field-theoretic resummations), exceeding stated uncertainties.

Problem: Identify and quantitatively account for the discrepancy between the experimentally measured value of the heat-capacity critical exponent $\alpha$ at the superfluid lambda transition of helium-4 and the value(s) predicted by theoretical analyses of the three-dimensional XY universality class. In particular, determine whether the discrepancy arises from (a) systematic effects in the experiment (e.g., residual gravitational rounding, finite-size effects, corrections to scaling), (b) underestimated theoretical uncertainties or neglected correction-to-scaling terms, or (c) a genuine failure of the three-dimensional XY model to describe the lambda transition; and provide a reconciled value of $\alpha$ with rigorous error bounds.

Let A be a finite alphabet and let A* denote the free monoid of all finite words over A. A language over A is a subset of A*. Fix:

(i) a family B of languages over A, called the basis;
(ii) a collection O of operations on languages over A (each operation taking a tuple of languages and producing a language, e.g. union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, inverse homomorphism, quotient by a word, etc.);
(iii) a set R of formal rules governing how the operations in O may be combined and iterated (for instance, restrictions on alternation depth, on the use of complement, or on the form of allowed compositions).

Say that a language L ⊆ A* is expressible from (B, O, R) if L can be obtained by starting from members of B and applying operations from O in a manner that conforms to the rules R.

General expressibility problem: Give an explicit, decidable characterization of the class of all languages L ⊆ A* that are expressible from (B, O, R), for any specified choice of (B, O, R).

Concrete instance to address: provide a procedure that, given finite descriptions (e.g. by finite automata) of a language L and of the basis B, together with the specification of O and R, decides whether L is expressible from (B, O, R), or prove that no such procedure exists.

This is a general framework problem encompassing many classical questions about regular languages (Schützenberger's theorem on star-free languages, dot-depth hierarchy, concatenation hierarchies, etc.). Consider charged-current neutrino reactions on a lead target,
  ν_e + ^{208}Pb → e^- + ^{208}Bi^*,
the excited bismuth nucleus subsequently de-exciting by emission of one or more neutrons. Assume an incoming electron-neutrino flux whose energy spectrum is parameterized by a Fermi–Dirac (or pinched thermal) distribution
  f(E_ν; T, η) ∝ E_ν^2 / (1 + exp(E_ν/T − η)),
characterized by a temperature T (and, optionally, a pinching parameter η) appropriate to the neutrinosphere of a core-collapse supernova.

(a) Derive, from a microscopic nuclear-structure model of ^{208}Pb (e.g. QRPA or shell-model treatment of the allowed Fermi and Gamow–Teller strengths together with forbidden multipoles), the doubly differential cross section
  d^2σ / (dE_e dcosθ_e)
for the outgoing electron, as a function of the incident neutrino energy E_ν, the electron kinetic energy E_e, and the electron emission angle θ_e, including Coulomb corrections (Fermi function or effective momentum approximation) for the outgoing electron in the field of the daughter nucleus.

(b) Determine the corresponding singly differential spectrum dσ/dE_e after folding with the supernova neutrino flux f(E_ν; T, η), and quantify its sensitivity to the temperature parameter T. In particular, identify observables built from the electron spectrum (for example moments ⟨E_e⟩, ⟨E_e^2⟩, or ratios of partial cross sections leading to one-neutron and two-neutron emission channels) that allow a reliable reconstruction of T from the measured electron differential cross sections in the event of a galactic core-collapse supernova, and estimate the precision with which T can be inferred given realistic detector energy resolution and statistics.

Theoretical estimates of charged-current neutrino-^{208}Pb cross sections have been computed in QRPA and shell-model frameworks (e.g., Engel–Fuller–Vogel; Volpe et al.; Paar et al.; Almosly et al., 2016), and the HALO detector at SNOLAB exploits 1n/2n branching ratios as a temperature diagnostic. The problem is therefore partially solved.

Consider quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the vacuum between two parallel, perfectly conducting plates separated by a distance $a$, where the boundary conditions modify the zero-point fluctuations of the electromagnetic field (the Casimir configuration). For low-frequency photons propagating perpendicular to the plates, one-loop QED predicts a modification of the phase velocity given (to leading order) by
$$\frac{v_\perp}{c} = 1 + \frac{11\pi^2}{8100}\,\frac{\alpha^2}{(m_e a)^4},$$
where $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant and $m_e$ is the electron mass (in natural units $\hbar = c = 1$).

Question: Determine rigorously whether light signals can in fact propagate between two closely spaced conducting plates with a phase and/or signal velocity strictly exceeding the standard vacuum speed of light $c$, as predicted by the above formula, and provide an experimental or theoretical confirmation (or refutation) of this superluminal propagation. In particular, establish whether the predicted effect represents a genuine signal velocity greater than $c$ consistent with causality, and verify the prediction experimentally.

The Scharnhorst effect remains a theoretical QED prediction without confirmed experimental verification. The predicted velocity shift is extraordinarily small (relative deviation on the order of 10^{-36} for plate separations of order 1 μm), and direct experimental tests have been infeasible. A November 2025 preprint proposes and claims a multipass Casimir–Lloyd interferometric observation, but this has not been independently confirmed, so the problem is best classified as open.

A quantum computer is called noisy intermediate-scale (NISQ) if it consists of on the order of 50–1000 physical qubits whose gate operations and measurements are subject to noise rates too high to support arbitrarily long quantum computations without error correction. A fault-tolerant quantum computer is one in which logical qubits, encoded into many physical qubits via a quantum error-correcting code, can sustain arbitrarily long computations with logical error rate below any prescribed threshold, provided physical error rates lie below a code- and architecture-dependent threshold value (the threshold theorem). Address the following:

(a) Determine whether physical quantum computing systems can be scaled and improved beyond the NISQ regime to achieve genuine fault tolerance, i.e., the experimental realization of a logical qubit whose logical error rate is suppressed exponentially with code distance.

(b) Determine whether the number of physical qubits, together with their gate fidelities, coherence times, connectivity, and classical-control overhead, can be scaled sufficiently to implement large-scale quantum error correction supporting logically reliable quantum algorithms.

(c) Identify which physical platforms for realizing qubits (e.g., superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonic systems, semiconductor spin qubits, topological qubits, or others) are the most promising candidates for achieving scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation, and characterize quantitatively the relative advantages and obstacles of each.

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the free monoid of words over $A$. A language $L \subseteq A^*$ is called star-free if it can be obtained from the finite languages by finitely many applications of Boolean operations (union, intersection, complement) and concatenation, but without the use of the Kleene star.

A marked product of languages $L_0, L_1, \dots, L_k \subseteq A^*$ is a language of the form $L_0 a_1 L_1 a_2 L_2 \cdots a_k L_k$ where $a_1, \dots, a_k \in A$.

The Straubing-Thérien concatenation hierarchy is the family of classes of languages $\{\mathcal{V}_n\}$, indexed by half-integers $n \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{N}$, defined inductively by:
- Level $0$: $\mathcal{V}_0 = \{\emptyset, A^*\}$.
- Level $n + \tfrac{1}{2}$: the class of all finite unions of marked products of languages in $\mathcal{V}_n$.
- Level $n + 1$: the class of all Boolean combinations of languages that are marked products of languages in $\mathcal{V}_n$.

The union $\bigcup_{n} \mathcal{V}_n$ is exactly the class of star-free languages.

Problem. Find an algorithm that, given as input a half-integer $n \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{N}$ and a star-free language $L \subseteq A^*$ (presented, for instance, by a finite automaton or a finite syntactic monoid recognizing it), decides whether $L \in \mathcal{V}_n$. Equivalently, prove or disprove that membership in $\mathcal{V}_n$ is uniformly decidable across all levels $n$ of the hierarchy.
representations.original:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the free monoid of words over $A$. A language $L \subseteq A^*$ is called star-free if it can be obtained from the finite languages by finitely many applications of Boolean operations (union, intersection, complement) and concatenation, but without the use of the Kleene star.

A marked product of languages $L_0, L_1, \dots, L_k \subseteq A^*$ is a language of the form $L_0 a_1 L_1 a_2 L_2 \cdots a_k L_k$ where $a_1, \dots, a_k \in A$.

The Straubing-Thérien concatenation hierarchy is the family of classes of languages $\{\mathcal{V}_n\}$, indexed by half-integers $n \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{N}$, defined inductively by:
- Level $0$: $\mathcal{V}_0 = \{\emptyset, A^*\}$.
- Level $n + \tfrac{1}{2}$: the class of all finite unions of marked products of languages in $\mathcal{V}_n$.
- Level $n + 1$: the class of all Boolean combinations of languages that are marked products of languages in $\mathcal{V}_n$.

The union $\bigcup_{n} \mathcal{V}_n$ is exactly the class of star-free languages.

Problem. Find an algorithm that, given as input a half-integer $n \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{N}$ and a star-free language $L \subseteq A^*$ (presented, for instance, by a finite automaton or a finite syntactic monoid recognizing it), decides whether $L \in \mathcal{V}_n$. Equivalently, prove or disprove that membership in $\mathcal{V}_n$ is uniformly decidable across all levels $n$ of the hierarchy.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The membership problem for the Straubing-Thérien hierarchy is known to be decidable for levels 0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, and, following work of Place and Zeitoun on separation and covering, for level 2 as well (and the corresponding half-integer level 5/2 is decidable in restricted settings such as two-letter alphabets, by Glaßer–Schmitz). However, decidability of membership at every level of the hierarchy remains open in general; the problem is solved only for finitely many low levels.

[{"title": "The Complexity of Separation for Levels in Concatenation Hierarchies", "url": "https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.FSTTCS.2018.47", "snippet": "Separation is decidable for the levels 1/2, 1, 3/2 and 2 for both the dot-depth and Straubing-Thérien hierarchies.", "claim": "Membership and separation are known to be decidable up to level 2 of the Straubing-Thérien hierarchy."}, {"title": "New decidable upper bound of the second level in the Straubing-Thérien concatenation hierarchy", "url": "https://hal.science/hal-00990443v1", "snippet": "Decidable upper bound for level 2 in the Straubing-Thérien hierarchy.", "claim": "Decidability results have been obtained for the second level of the hierarchy."}, {"title": "Level 5/2 of the Straubing-Thérien Hierarchy for Two-Letter Alphabets", "url": "https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-46011-X_21", "snippet": "Effective characterization of level 5/2 for two-letter alphabets.", "claim": "Level 5/2 is decidable only in restricted alphabet settings; general decidability beyond level 2 is not established."}]

Consider the theoretical modeling of neutrino-nucleus scattering across a wide range of incident neutrino energies. In the low-energy regime (roughly below a few tens of MeV), the cross sections are typically computed using approaches such as Elementary Particle Theory (treating the nucleus as a single object whose form factors are constrained by symmetries), Effective Field Theories of the strong and weak interactions, the nuclear shell model, and the Random-Phase Approximation (RPA), which builds correlated particle-hole excitations on top of a mean-field ground state. In the high-energy regime (roughly above a few hundred MeV), the standard description is the Relativistic Fermi Gas model, in which the target nucleus is treated as a degenerate gas of non-interacting nucleons with momenta filling a Fermi sphere.

Formulate and answer the following question. Given a (hypothetical) enlarged set of measured neutrino-nucleus cross sections σ(Eν, A, Z) on a variety of nuclei (A, Z) over a broad range of neutrino energies Eν spanning the transition region between the two regimes:

(a) Construct a quantitative interpolation scheme that smoothly matches the low-energy nuclear-structure-based predictions (EPT/EFT/shell model/RPA) to the high-energy Fermi-Gas predictions, in a way that is consistent with all the measured data and respects exact symmetry constraints (CVC, PCAC, current conservation, sum rules).

(b) Using this scheme, give controlled extrapolations of σ(Eν, A, Z) to neutron-rich nuclei of astrophysical relevance (e.g. those participating in r-process nucleosynthesis or core-collapse supernova environments) that are not currently accessible experimentally, together with rigorous theoretical uncertainty estimates.

Does there exist such an interpolation/extrapolation framework that is simultaneously consistent with all available data, respects the relevant nuclear and electroweak symmetries, and provides quantitatively reliable predictions for neutron-rich nuclei?

Neutrino-nucleus cross section modeling across the transition between low- and high-energy regimes remains an active and unresolved area, as documented in recent reviews (NuSTEC white papers, Snowmass reports). Tensions between data and models persist for medium-energy quasi-elastic and resonance regions, and extrapolations to neutron-rich nuclei for astrophysics still carry large theoretical uncertainties. No unified, fully validated framework currently exists.

Consider a topological superconductor that, in suitable regimes, is predicted to host Majorana zero modes (MZMs): non-Abelian anyonic quasiparticle excitations that are their own antiparticles, localized at boundaries or defects, with zero excitation energy and obeying non-Abelian braiding statistics. A topological qubit is a qubit whose logical states are encoded nonlocally in the joint fermionic parity of pairs of well-separated MZMs, with quantum gates implemented by braiding such modes, conferring protection against local decoherence.

Resolve the following two questions:

(a) Can a scalable topological quantum computer—based on encoding qubits in the nonlocal degrees of freedom of non-Abelian anyons (e.g. Majorana zero modes) and performing logical operations by braiding them—be physically realized?

(b) Provide a conclusive experimental demonstration of Majorana zero modes, in the sense of unambiguously distinguishing them from trivial alternatives (such as Andreev bound states, partially separated Andreev bound states, or disorder-induced subgap states) by exhibiting their defining signatures, including non-Abelian braiding statistics and topologically protected fermion parity.

As of early 2026, the question remains open. Microsoft's February 2025 announcement of the "Majorana 1" topological qubit processor and its accompanying Nature paper explicitly did not establish a conclusive demonstration of Majorana zero modes; the referees declined to endorse that claim, and the authors note their measurements do not by themselves determine whether the observed low-energy states are topological. The community continues to debate whether reported signatures arise from MZMs or from Andreev bound states, and no convincing demonstration of non-Abelian anyon braiding has yet been reported.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem remains open as of 2025–2026. Several groups (IonQ, UCLA/UC Riverside, NTT/OptQC, Quantum Brilliance, Stanford) have demonstrated proof-of-concept room-temperature quantum devices and components (notably photonic and nitrogen-vacancy-based systems), and roadmaps target large-scale optical quantum computers without cryogenic cooling by ~2030. Consider the proposal of a low-energy beta-beam facility, in which radioactive ions that undergo beta decay are produced, accelerated to (relatively low) Lorentz boost factors, and stored in a circulating ring so that the resulting pure (anti-)electron-neutrino beam emerging from beta decay can be directed toward a low-energy neutrino-nucleus experiment. Two architectural scenarios are envisaged:

(a) the facility is embedded in a dedicated exotic-ion laboratory (such as a high-intensity radioactive ion beam facility of GSI/GANIL/EURISOL/RIA type), or

(b) the facility is appended to a high-energy beta-beam complex at a large hadron laboratory (CERN-type), with an additional low-energy storage ring downstream.

For either scenario, the two essential technical requirements are:
(i) the attainable production intensity of suitable beta-unstable ions (e.g., 6He, 18Ne) must be sufficient to yield a useful neutrino flux at the detector; and
(ii) a storage ring capable of accumulating and circulating these ions at the desired (low) gamma factor must be available.

Problem: Determine whether either of the scenarios (a) or (b) can simultaneously meet requirements (i) and (ii) at a level sufficient to make a low-energy beta-beam facility feasible for neutrino-nucleus interaction studies.

Define the following complexity classes of decision problems on inputs of length n:

- BPP (bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time): the class of languages L for which there exists a probabilistic Turing machine running in time poly(n) that, on every input x, outputs the correct answer (whether x ∈ L) with probability at least 2/3.
- BQP (bounded-error quantum polynomial time): the class of languages L for which there exists a uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits over a fixed finite universal gate set that, on every input x, outputs the correct answer with probability at least 2/3.
- NP (nondeterministic polynomial time): the class of languages L for which there exists a polynomial-time deterministic verifier V and a polynomial p such that x ∈ L iff there exists a witness w with |w| ≤ p(|x|) and V(x,w) accepts.

Resolve the following questions:

(a) Determine the precise inclusion relationship between BPP and BQP. In particular, is BPP = BQP, or is the inclusion BPP ⊆ BQP strict? Exhibit either an unconditional separation (a language in BQP \ BPP) or a proof of equality.

(b) Determine the relationship between BQP and NP. In particular, decide whether BQP ⊆ NP, whether NP ⊆ BQP, and whether BQP and NP are incomparable; provide an unconditional proof.

(c) Consider the class of decision problems that can be solved with bounded error in polynomial time within any "plausible" physical theory (i.e., a model of computation realizable by the laws of physics, taken to extend beyond standard quantum mechanics if applicable). Determine whether this class can strictly contain BQP, and if so, exhibit a physically motivated model of computation and a problem in that model's efficient class that is provably outside BQP.

All three questions are widely recognized as longstanding open problems. No unconditional separation between BPP and BQP is known (such a separation would imply P ≠ PSPACE). The relation between BQP and NP is also unresolved; oracle separations exist in both directions but no unconditional results. Whether physically realizable computation can exceed BQP remains speculative and unresolved.

Concretely: exhibit a scheme Π together with a security definition (e.g., IND-CCA2 security for encryption or EUF-CMA security for signatures) in which the adversary is modeled as a quantum polynomial-time algorithm (possibly with quantum oracle access), and prove unconditionally that no such adversary can win the corresponding security game with non-negligible advantage. Equivalently, prove the existence of cryptographic primitives (one-way functions, trapdoor permutations, or public-key encryption) whose security holds against quantum polynomial-time adversaries, without relying on unproven computational hardness assumptions such as the hardness of Learning With Errors, lattice shortest-vector problems, code-decoding problems, or multivariate quadratic systems.

The problem is open. Current post-quantum candidates (lattice-based, code-based, hash-based, multivariate, isogeny-based) are conjectured but not proven to resist quantum attacks; their security reduces to computational hardness assumptions (e.g., LWE/SVP) that themselves are unproven. An unconditional proof would imply, in particular, that P ≠ NP and resolve major open questions in complexity theory, so no such proof is known. NIST standardized several PQC algorithms in 2024 based on conjectured hardness, not on unconditional proofs of security.

Consider a hypothetical neutrino source consisting of radioactive ions decaying at rest, which produces a pure flavor neutrino flux (a "beta-beam at rest") whose energy spectrum is determined by the known beta-decay kinematics of the parent isotope and can therefore be computed with high precision. Suppose this source is coupled to a detector with a very low recoil-energy threshold (well below 1 keV scale), so that elastic neutrino–electron (and/or neutrino–nucleus) scattering events at small energy transfer can be recorded. The differential cross section for such scattering receives a Standard Model weak contribution plus an additional contribution proportional to the square of the neutrino magnetic moment μ_ν (in units of the Bohr magneton μ_B), the latter being strongly enhanced as the recoil energy tends to zero.

Question: Determine whether such a configuration can improve the current direct experimental upper limits on the neutrino magnetic moment μ_ν by close to an order of magnitude, and compute the precise sensitivity on μ_ν (in units of μ_B) that remains achievable after a detailed simulation of the detector response, including realistic energy resolution, threshold effects, and background subtraction.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Feasibility studies indicate that a low-energy beta-beam source combined with low-threshold detectors could in principle probe neutrino magnetic moments at the level of a few × 10⁻¹¹ μ_B, comparable to or slightly better than current direct limits, but this requires very high ion production rates (≳ 10¹⁵ s⁻¹) and no such facility has been realized. Current best direct laboratory limits on μ_ν come from reactor and dark-matter direct-detection experiments (e.g., CONUS, XENONnT), with the precise achievable beta-beam sensitivity depending on detector-response simulations that have not been definitively settled. The status of the specific claim of nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement therefore remains unresolved.

[{"title": "Prospects for Detecting a Neutrino Magnetic Moment with a Tritium Source and Beta-beams", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0312156", "snippet": "Low-energy beta-beams with sufficiently rapid production of ions could improve the limits on the neutrino magnetic moment to the level of a few × 10⁻¹¹ μ_B, requiring ion production ≥ 10¹⁵ s⁻¹.", "claim": "Beta-beam sensitivities of order 10⁻¹¹ μ_B are projected but contingent on demanding source intensities."}, {"title": "First upper limits on neutrino electromagnetic properties from CONUS", "url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjc/s10052-022-10722-1", "snippet": "CONUS sets upper limits on neutrino electromagnetic properties from coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering at a reactor.", "claim": "Current direct limits on μ_ν continue to be set by reactor and direct-detection experiments, not beta-beams."}, {"title": "PDG 2025: Neutrino properties listings", "url": "https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/listings/rpp2025-list-neutrino-prop.pdf", "snippet": "Particle Data Group compilation of current direct limits on neutrino magnetic moments.", "claim": "No beta-beam-based limit on μ_ν has superseded existing direct limits as of 2025."}]
