Let $\Lambda$ be a finite square lattice with $|\Lambda|$ sites, where $|\Lambda|$ is divisible by 4, equipped with periodic boundary conditions (so $\Lambda$ is a discrete torus). Consider a Hermitian hopping matrix $T$ indexed by $\Lambda \times \Lambda$ defined by
$$T_{x,y} = \begin{cases} e^{i\theta(x,y)} & \text{if } x,y \text{ are nearest neighbors in } \Lambda, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases}$$
where $\theta(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}$ are arbitrary phases subject only to the Hermiticity constraint $\theta(x,y) = -\theta(y,x)$. The eigenvalues of $T$ depend only on the fluxes through elementary plaquettes, defined as the sum of the phases $\theta(x,y)$ around each unit square of $\Lambda$ (taken in a fixed orientation). Let $\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_{|\Lambda|}$ denote the eigenvalues of $T$, and define
$$E(\{\theta\}) = \sum_{j=1}^{|\Lambda|/4} \lambda_j,$$
the sum of the lowest quarter of the eigenvalues. Determine whether the assignment of fluxes that minimizes $E$ is the one in which the flux through every elementary plaquette equals $\pi/2$.

Consider the phenomenon of intermittency in high-energy multiparticle production, defined as the power-law growth of scaled factorial moments of charged-particle multiplicity distributions as the size of the phase-space cell (in rapidity, azimuthal angle, and/or transverse momentum p_T) decreases. Empirically, in lepton-induced reactions (e.g., e+e- and lepton-hadron scattering), Monte Carlo simulations based on parton cascades plus standard hadronization successfully reproduce the observed behavior of the factorial moments, including their dependence on event multiplicity and on the transverse-momentum window used to define the phase-space cells. In hadron-induced reactions, by contrast, the same families of simulations fail to reproduce the observed dependence of the factorial moments on the multiplicity of the event and on p_T, particularly in the low-multiplicity and low-p_T regimes, where the "soft" (non-perturbative) component of multiparticle production dominates.

Provide a dynamical explanation for the following two coupled questions:

(a) Identify the mechanism in hadron-induced collisions—absent or different from that in lepton-induced collisions—that causes simulations to underestimate or otherwise misdescribe the low-multiplicity and low-p_T behavior of the scaled factorial moments. The explanation should specify the soft-physics ingredient (e.g., a property of the underlying non-perturbative cascade, the rôle of strings/clusters, beam-remnant correlations, or another mechanism) responsible for the discrepancy.

(b) Show that, once this mechanism is identified and incorporated, the resulting model accounts quantitatively for both the multiplicity dependence and the p_T dependence of the factorial moments observed in hadron-induced reactions, and discuss to what extent this resolution clarifies the soft component of the intermittency problem.

representations.normalized:
Consider bosonic string theory on AdS$_3$ formulated as a Wess–Zumino–Witten (WZW) model on the group manifold SU(1,1) (equivalently SL(2,$\mathbb{R}$)) at level $k$. The chiral algebra is the affine current algebra $\widehat{\mathfrak{su}(1,1)}_k$ generated by currents $J^a(z)$ ($a=\pm,3$) with OPE
$$ J^3(z)J^3(w)\sim -\tfrac{k/2}{(z-w)^2},\qquad J^3(z)J^\pm(w)\sim \pm\tfrac{J^\pm(w)}{z-w},\qquad J^+(z)J^-(w)\sim \tfrac{k}{(z-w)^2}-\tfrac{2J^3(w)}{z-w}, $$
and the worldsheet stress tensor is the standard affine Sugawara construction
$$ T(z)=\tfrac{1}{k-2}\!:\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}(J^+J^-+J^-J^+)-J^3J^3\Big)\!:(z). $$
With this construction, unitary normalizable physical states built from the discrete series $\mathcal{D}^\pm_j$ obey a mass/spin cutoff $j<(k-1)/2$ (the no-ghost bound), continuous principal series representations $\mathcal{C}^\alpha_j$ with $j=\tfrac12+i s$ contribute only purely tachyonic excitations to the physical spectrum, the spectrum exhibits an infinite level degeneracy of long-string-like states, and modular invariance of the one-loop partition function is problematic.

Question: Does there exist a deformation of the affine Sugawara stress tensor $T(z)$, or a modification of the SU(1,1) current algebra itself, such that all of the following hold simultaneously?
(i) The mass/spin cutoff $j<(k-1)/2$ is removed, allowing physical states of arbitrarily large spin.
(ii) The continuous representations $\mathcal{C}^\alpha_j$ contribute non-tachyonic physical excitations.
(iii) The infinite level degeneracy of the spectrum is lifted without coupling the theory to any external background field.
(iv) The resulting one-loop torus partition function is modular invariant.
(v) The deformed theory still admits an interpretation as the original WZW model describing string propagation on the AdS$_3$ target space.

Either construct such a deformation explicitly, or prove that no deformation satisfying (i)–(v) simultaneously can exist.

The SL(2,R) WZW description of strings on AdS3 was substantially clarified by Maldacena and Ooguri (2000–2001), who fixed the spectrum (including spectrally flowed long strings), proved a no-ghost theorem covering the relevant representations, and demonstrated modular invariance of the one-loop partition function, all within the standard affine Sugawara framework rather than via a deformation of it. This addresses several of the listed issues (modular invariance, role of continuous representations as long strings, level degeneracy via spectral flow) but does so without modifying the Sugawara construction or the current algebra. The specific question of whether a genuine deformation of the Sugawara construction or of the SU(1,1) current algebra can simultaneously achieve (i)–(v) while preserving the AdS3 string-theoretic interpretation does not appear to have a definitive resolution in the literature, so the original question is best classified as partially resolved/unknown.

representations.normalized:
Consider a system of $N$ identical spinless bosons in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d\ge 2$) interacting via a two-body potential $v\ge 0$ that is short-range, spherically symmetric, and repulsive (for example, compactly supported and integrable). The Hamiltonian acting on the symmetric subspace of $L^2(\Lambda^N)$ for $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ a box of volume $V$ is
$$H_N=-\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta_{x_i}+\sum_{1\le i<j\le N} v(x_i-x_j),$$
with suitable (e.g. periodic) boundary conditions. Let $\rho=N/V$ denote the particle density, and let $\gamma^{(1)}_{N,V}$ be the one-particle reduced density matrix of the ground state (or, at positive temperature $T>0$, of the Gibbs state) of $H_N$.

Prove that in the thermodynamic limit $N,V\to\infty$ with $\rho$ fixed at a sufficiently small positive value (the dilute regime, $\rho\, a^d\ll 1$ where $a$ is the scattering length of $v$), there is Bose–Einstein condensation into the zero-momentum mode, i.e.
$$\liminf_{N,V\to\infty,\ N/V=\rho}\ \frac{\langle\varphi_0,\gamma^{(1)}_{N,V}\varphi_0\rangle}{N}>0,$$
where $\varphi_0$ is the constant function on $\Lambda$. Equivalently, establish off-diagonal long-range order for the one-particle density matrix of the weakly interacting dilute Bose gas in this continuum setting.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph. A *hole* in $G$ is an induced cycle of length at least $4$, i.e., a sequence of distinct vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k$ with $k \ge 4$ such that $v_iv_{i+1} \in E$ for all $i$ (indices mod $k$) and $v_iv_j \notin E$ whenever $|i-j| \not\equiv 1 \pmod k$.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision/search problem: given $G$, decide whether $G$ contains a hole, and if so, output one. In particular, is there a polynomial-time algorithm in $|V|+|E|$ that solves this problem?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A graph contains a hole if and only if it is not chordal. Chordality can be tested in linear time (e.g., via Lexicographic BFS by Rose, Tarjan, and Lueker), and when a graph is not chordal such an algorithm can produce a hole as a certificate. Hence detecting/finding a hole is solvable in linear time, and the question of its complexity is settled. Related harder variants (odd hole, even hole, hole through a specified vertex, longest hole) have been studied with various polynomial-time or NP-hardness results.

representations.normalized:
Consider high-energy particle production in which one studies the multiplicity distribution of final-state particles inside cells of phase space. For a phase-space variable (such as a rapidity, pseudo-rapidity, or angular coordinate) divided into M bins of equal size, the normalized factorial moments are defined by

  F_q(M) = ⟨ (1/M) Σ_{m=1}^{M} n_m(n_m-1)···(n_m-q+1) ⟩ / ⟨ (1/M) Σ_{m=1}^{M} n_m ⟩^q ,

where n_m is the number of particles in the m-th cell and ⟨·⟩ denotes an event average. The system is said to exhibit "intermittency" in the chosen variable if, as the bin size δ → 0 (equivalently M → ∞), the factorial moments follow a power-law

  F_q(M) ∝ M^{φ_q},   φ_q > 0,

reflecting a self-similar, scale-invariant fluctuation pattern with an effective singularity in the underlying density.

Perturbative QCD (double-leading-log parton-shower calculations, treating hadrons via parton–hadron duality) predicts that such an effective singularity, and hence intermittent power-law scaling, should appear when the cells are defined in terms of angular variables (e.g. the polar angle relative to the jet axis, or relative opening angles of particle pairs), giving rise to "angular intermittency" with computable indices φ_q that depend on the running coupling and the opening angle of the jet.

Question: In real collision data, does this predicted angular intermittency actually manifest itself as observable power-law scaling of the angular factorial moments F_q(M)? Specifically:

(a) In lepton-induced reactions (e.g. e⁺e⁻ annihilation into hadrons, or deep-inelastic lepton–nucleon scattering), where the perturbative parton-cascade contribution can be isolated by minimizing the influence of nonperturbative hadronization, do the angular factorial moments exhibit the predicted intermittent scaling with the QCD-predicted indices?

(b) Does analogous angular intermittency, qualitatively or quantitatively consistent with the perturbative prediction, occur in other classes of high-energy reactions (hadron–hadron and nucleus–nucleus collisions)?

Consider bosonic string theory whose target space includes an AdS₃ factor, realized via the SL(2,ℝ) (equivalently SU(1,1)) WZW model at level k. The chiral algebra is the affine ŝu(1,1)_k current algebra, whose representations include: (i) the principal continuous series, (ii) the highest/lowest weight discrete series 𝒟⁺_j and 𝒟⁻_j, and (iii) the "admissible" representations of Kac–Wakimoto, which exist for fractional levels k+2 = p/q with p,q coprime positive integers and which possess modular-invariant characters but are non-unitary as representations of su(1,1).

(a) Suppose one drops the usual no-ghost requirement and admits negative-norm physical states in the string spectrum on AdS₃. Provide a consistent physical interpretation of such states: identify the dynamical instability of the AdS₃ background (or of the string propagating in it) that these negative-norm states would signal, and explain its physical origin.

(b) The non-unitary conformal field theories built from the admissible ŝu(1,1)_k representations admit known modular-invariant partition functions. Determine whether and how these admissible-representation models can be incorporated as consistent backgrounds for string theory on AdS₃, including a description of the resulting physical (BRST-cohomology) spectrum, its spacetime interpretation, and the role of the negative-norm states arising from the non-unitarity of the admissible representations.

After the landmark works of Maldacena–Ooguri on the SL(2,ℝ) WZW model, the physical spectrum of strings on AdS₃ is now built from unitary discrete (with j<k/2) and continuous representations plus their spectral-flow images, and ghosts decouple. The Undirected k-Disjoint Paths problem asks whether there exist k pairwise internally vertex-disjoint paths P_1, ..., P_k in G such that, for each i ∈ {1, ..., k}, the path P_i has endpoints s_i and t_i.

By the Robertson–Seymour graph minors theorem this problem is fixed-parameter tractable in k, and the best known parameter dependence (at the time of posing) yields an algorithm with running time 2^{2^{O(k)}} · poly(|V(G)|).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that decides the Undirected k-Disjoint Paths problem in time 2^{O(k)} · poly(|V(G)|)?

Obtaining a single-exponential 2^{O(k)} poly(n) parameterized algorithm for the Undirected k-Disjoint Paths problem on general graphs remains an open problem. In high-energy multiparticle production, the scaled factorial moments F_q(δ) of the distribution of charged-particle multiplicities in phase-space cells of size δ are observed to grow as a power of 1/δ when δ → 0 (the "intermittency" phenomenon), indicating scale-invariant (self-similar) fluctuations over a range of resolutions.

Provide a theoretical description of the space-time development of strong-interaction processes that accounts for these scale-invariant fluctuations. Specifically:

(a) Identify a dynamical mechanism whose extension to large space-time distances produces the observed power-law scaling of F_q(δ).

(b) Determine quantitatively the interplay among the following contributing mechanisms in generating the overall intermittency signal:
 (i) perturbative and non-perturbative parton fragmentation (QCD cascades and hadronization),
 (ii) resonance production and subsequent decays,
 (iii) quantum interference effects, including Bose–Einstein correlations among identical bosons,
 (iv) dynamical quark–gluon phase transitions (e.g., deconfinement or chiral transitions) that may induce critical-type fluctuations.

(c) Decide whether the observed intermittency admits a single dominant, simple explanation in terms of one of these mechanisms, or whether it is an emergent property of a complex multi-component system requiring all of the above ingredients on an equal footing.

A complete answer should specify the predicted intermittency exponents (anomalous dimensions) φ_q from the proposed space-time picture and confront them with the experimental scaling behavior of F_q(δ) in leptonic, hadronic, and nuclear collisions.

representations.normalized:
Consider bosonic string propagation on an anti-de Sitter background AdS_n of arbitrary dimension n ≥ 3 (with Lorentzian signature and constant negative curvature). The worldsheet theory must be an exact conformal field theory (CFT) — i.e., a two-dimensional sigma model with vanishing beta functions to all orders in the α' expansion — whose target space is (or admits as a factor) AdS_n, together with the additional background fields required for exact conformal invariance:

(i) For odd n, exact conformal invariance is known to require a nontrivial Neveu–Schwarz antisymmetric tensor (B-field) background and a linear dilaton in addition to the AdS_n metric; the resulting sigma model is not a Wess–Zumino–Witten model on a group manifold.

(ii) For even n, no exact CFT describing string propagation on AdS_n has been formulated.

The problem is to:

(a) Construct, for each n ≥ 4, an exact conformal sigma model (i.e., specify the metric, B-field, dilaton, and possibly other background fields, together with the worldsheet action and its quantization) whose target geometry contains AdS_n as the spacetime factor, and prove its exact conformal invariance.

(b) Determine the full physical spectrum of the resulting worldsheet CFT, including all primary states, their conformal weights, the action of the spacetime isometry algebra so(n−1,2), and the unitarity constraints.

(c) Compute the interactions: define vertex operators for the physical states and determine their correlation functions (at least the tree-level two-, three-, and four-point functions on the sphere), including the analogue of spectral flow if relevant, and analyze factorization and the operator product expansion.

Provide a complete solution in both the odd-dimensional case (where the antisymmetric tensor and linear dilaton enter) and the even-dimensional case (where no such construction is yet available).

No complete construction of exact worldsheet CFTs for string theory on AdS_n with n ≥ 4 appears in the literature. Partial results exist for coset-based exact metric/dilaton/antisymmetric-tensor backgrounds (e.g., SO(d−1,2)/SO(d−1,1) gauged WZNW models) giving the conformally exact geometry, but the full spectrum and interactions of the corresponding non-WZW sigma models remain largely unexplored, and even-dimensional AdS_n exact CFTs have not been formulated. The problem appears to remain open.

For a finite simple graph $G$, let $\chi(G)$ denote its chromatic number, $\omega(G)$ its clique number, and $\alpha(G)$ its stable set (independence) number. A class $\mathcal{C}$ of graphs is called hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs. The class $\mathcal{C}$ is said to be $\chi$-bounded if there exists a function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every $G\in\mathcal{C}$.

Question: Suppose $\mathcal{C}$ is a hereditary class of graphs for which there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any $G\in\mathcal{C}$, computes $\alpha(G)$. Does it follow that $\mathcal{C}$ is $\chi$-bounded?

   A ≤ B  iff  for every a ∈ A there exists b ∈ B with a ≤ b.

Recall that a quasi-order is well-quasi-ordered if every infinite sequence contains an infinite non-decreasing subsequence (equivalently, contains no infinite antichain and no infinite strictly descending chain).

Question: Is (2^X, ≤) well-quasi-ordered?

Modern measurements, particularly from LHCb using prompt charm production at 13 TeV, have achieved the targeted precisions. Consider bosonic string theory on AdS_3, whose worldsheet description is governed by an SL(2,R) (equivalently SU(1,1)) Wess–Zumino–Witten model. The zero-mode subalgebra sl(2,R) admits several classes of unitary representations: (i) the discrete highest-weight series D_j^+ (lowest-weight states annihilated by the lowering generator), (ii) the discrete lowest-weight series D_j^- (highest-weight states annihilated by the raising generator), (iii) the continuous principal and supplementary series, which possess neither a highest nor a lowest weight vector, and the corresponding affine SU(1,1) current-algebra modules built on each of these.

The question is the following: do the SU(1,1) affine current-algebra representations built on zero-mode representations that have neither a highest nor a lowest weight vector admit a consistent and stable interpretation as part of the physical Hilbert space of string theory on AdS_3? In particular, specify which such representations (if any) must be included so that the resulting string spectrum is unitary, free of negative-norm physical states after imposing the Virasoro constraints, closed under the operator product expansion, and yields a modular-invariant one-loop partition function.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Maldacena and Ooguri (2000–2001) showed that a consistent, unitary, and modular-invariant spectrum for strings on AdS_3 requires including, in addition to the discrete highest/lowest-weight series, the affine modules built on the continuous (principal) series of SL(2,R) — representations without highest or lowest weight — together with all their spectral flows. This resolution has been confirmed and refined in subsequent work on spectral flow, correlation functions, and the symmetric orbifold dual, so the open issue raised about stable string-theoretic interpretation of such representations is now considered resolved.

A circular-arc graph is a graph G = (V, E) that admits a representation R assigning to each vertex v ∈ V an arc R(v) of a fixed circle such that two vertices are adjacent in G if and only if their assigned arcs intersect. A partial representation of G is a pair (V', R') where V' ⊆ V and R' assigns an arc of the circle to each vertex of V'. A representation R of G extends the partial representation (V', R') if R(v) = R'(v) for every v ∈ V'.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem:

  Input: A circular-arc graph G together with a partial representation (V', R') of G.
  Question: Does there exist a circular-arc representation R of G that extends (V', R')?

  Question: Does there exist a circular-arc representation R of G that extends (V', R')?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem has been resolved: the partial representation extension problem for circular-arc graphs is NP-complete. This was shown in work by Bhore, Chaplick, Gonçalves, Klavík, and others, including the paper "Extending Partial Representations of Circular-Arc Graphs" (arXiv:2108.13076, published 2022). Several subclasses (e.g., proper Helly, normal Helly with distinct endpoints) admit polynomial-time algorithms, while unit circular-arc and general circular-arc cases are NP-complete.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. A clique in G is a set of pairwise adjacent vertices, and a stable (independent) set is a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices. A clique is maximal if it is not properly contained in another clique, and likewise for stable sets. The graph G is called CIS if for every maximal clique C and every maximal stable set S of G, one has C ∩ S ≠ ∅.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem: given a finite simple graph G as input, decide whether G is CIS. In particular, is there a polynomial-time recognition algorithm, or is the problem coNP-hard (or otherwise intractable)?

The recognition complexity of CIS graphs is reported as open. The Information System on Graph Classes (graphclasses.org) lists the recognition problem for CIS graphs as "Open," and survey literature (e.g., on almost CIS graphs and on graphs whose maximal cliques and stable sets intersect) confirms that no polynomial-time recognition algorithm is known, nor has the problem been shown to be hard.

These four statements are well-known consequences of the Farrell–Jones Conjecture (with integer coefficients) for torsionfree groups. The Farrell–Jones Conjecture has been verified for many classes of groups (hyperbolic groups, CAT(0) groups, virtually solvable groups, lattices in virtually connected Lie groups, mapping class groups, etc.) but remains open for general torsionfree groups; no counterexamples are known. Consequently the four vanishing/isomorphism statements remain open in full generality.

A mixed graph is a graph $G = (V, E \cup A)$ that contains both undirected edges (the set $E$) and directed edges (the set $A$). An orientation of $G$ is a directed graph obtained by replacing each undirected edge $\{u,v\} \in E$ with exactly one of the two directed arcs $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$, while keeping all arcs in $A$ unchanged.

The Steiner Orientation problem is defined as follows:
- Input: a mixed graph $G$ and a collection $T = \{(s_1, t_1), \dots, (s_k, t_k)\}$ of $k$ ordered pairs of vertices of $G$.
- Parameter: $k = |T|$.
- Question: Does there exist an orientation of $G$ such that, in the resulting directed graph, there is a directed path from $s_i$ to $t_i$ for every $i \in \{1, \dots, k\}$?

Determine whether the Steiner Orientation problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the parameter $k$, i.e., whether there exists an algorithm solving it in time $f(k) \cdot |G|^{O(1)}$ for some computable function $f$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been resolved negatively: Pilipczuk and Wahlström (SODA 2016 / ACM TOCT 2018) proved that Steiner Orientation parameterized by the number $k$ of terminal pairs is W[1]-hard, hence not FPT under standard parameterized-complexity assumptions (FPT ≠ W[1]). Subsequent work by Chitnis, Feldmann, and others sharpened this to a tight $f(k)\cdot n^{o(k/\log k)}$ ETH lower bound, and showed W[1]-hardness even for planar instances.

representations.normalized:
Background. For a graph $G=(V,E)$ with vertex set $V$ of size $n$, the cut-rank function $\rho_G:2^V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ is defined by $\rho_G(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{GF}(2)}(A_G[X,V\setminus X])$, where $A_G$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$ over the binary field. A linear layout of $G$ is a linear ordering $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n$ of $V$; its width is $\max_{1\le i< n}\rho_G(\{v_1,\dots,v_i\})$. The linear rank-width $\mathrm{lrw}(G)$ of $G$ is the minimum width over all linear layouts.

It is known that, for every fixed positive integer $k$, the property "$\mathrm{lrw}(G)\le k$" is expressible in monadic second-order logic ($\mathrm{MSO}_1$), and is preserved under taking vertex-minors; hence by Courcelle-type meta-theorems applied to graph classes of bounded rank-width together with the well-quasi-ordering of vertex-minors, the decision problem

  Given a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, decide whether $\mathrm{lrw}(G)\le k$,

is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by $k$, with running time of the form $f(k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$ for some computable function $f$.

Problem. Design an explicit, practically efficient fixed-parameter algorithm, parameterized by $k$, that on input a graph $G$ either outputs a linear layout of $G$ of width at most $k$ or correctly reports that $\mathrm{lrw}(G)>k$, with an explicitly bounded and reasonable dependence on $k$ (as opposed to the implicit, non-constructive, or astronomically large dependence arising from generic meta-theorems and well-quasi-ordering arguments). In particular, provide a constructive FPT algorithm in which the function $f(k)$ is explicit and the algorithm avoids reliance on Courcelle's theorem or on non-constructive obstruction sets.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent literature (through 2026) on linear rank-width includes a linear-time algorithm for the case $k=1$ and FPT algorithms for related problems such as Linear Rankwidth-1 Vertex Deletion (Kanté, Kim, Kwon, Paul, IPEC 2015 / Algorithmica 2017), as well as structural results on excluded vertex-minors for linear rank-width $\le k$ by Jeong, Kwon, and Oum. However, no published "good"/practical explicit FPT algorithm with reasonable $f(k)$ for general $k$ deciding $\mathrm{lrw}(G)\le k$ appears to be available; the problem is generally still posed as open in surveys on rank-width.

representations.normalized:
Consider the charmed pseudoscalar mesons $D^+$ (quark content $c\bar d$) and $D_s^+$ (quark content $c\bar s$). For a pseudoscalar meson $P=Q\bar q$ of mass $m_P$ composed of a heavy quark $Q$ and light antiquark $\bar q$, define the decay constant $f_P$ via the matrix element
$$\langle 0 | \bar q \gamma^\mu \gamma_5 Q | P(p)\rangle = i f_P\, p^\mu.$$
In the Standard Model the purely leptonic decay rate of such a meson into a charged lepton $\ell$ plus its neutrino is
$$\Gamma(P\to \ell^+\nu_\ell) = \frac{G_F^2}{8\pi} f_P^2\, m_\ell^2\, m_P\left(1-\frac{m_\ell^2}{m_P^2}\right)^{\!2}|V_{Qq}|^2,$$
where $G_F$ is the Fermi constant and $V_{Qq}$ is the relevant CKM matrix element ($V_{cd}$ for $D^+$, $V_{cs}$ for $D_s^+$).

Determine, with sufficient precision, the leptonic branching fractions / decay rates of
$$D^+\to \mu^+\nu_\mu,\quad D^+\to \tau^+\nu_\tau,\quad D_s^+\to \mu^+\nu_\mu,\quad D_s^+\to \tau^+\nu_\tau,$$
and hence extract the decay constants $f_D$ and $f_{D_s}$ and their ratio $f_{D_s}/f_D$. In particular, decide:

(a) whether $f_D$ and $f_{D_s}$ lie near the $200$ MeV scale (specifically, are consistent with $200\pm 30$ MeV);

(b) whether the ratio $f_{D_s}/f_D$ lies in the range $1.15$–$1.20$.

All four leptonic decays have been observed and the decay constants measured with good precision by CLEO-c, BaBar, Belle and BES. Current world averages give f_D ≈ 212 MeV and f_{D_s} ≈ 250 MeV, with f_{D_s}/f_D ≈ 1.17–1.24, in agreement with modern lattice QCD calculations (e.g. f_D = 197(9) MeV, f_{D_s} = 244(8) MeV, ratio 1.24(3)). The values are near the 200 MeV scale and the ratio is at or slightly above the originally anticipated 1.15–1.20 range.

A space $X$ is called an absolute neighborhood retract (ANR) if it is metrizable and, whenever $X$ is embedded as a closed subset of a metric space $Y$, some neighborhood of $X$ in $Y$ retracts onto $X$. A compact ANR $X$ is called a homology ANR-manifold of dimension $n$ if for every $x \in X$ the local homology satisfies
$$H_k(X, X \setminus \{x\}; \mathbb{Z}) \cong \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z} & k=n,\\ 0 & k \neq n. \end{cases}$$
We say $X$ has the disjoint disks property (DDP) if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every pair of continuous maps $f, g \colon D^2 \to X$ from the 2-disk, there exist continuous maps $f', g' \colon D^2 \to X$ with $\sup d(f,f') < \varepsilon$, $\sup d(g,g') < \varepsilon$, and $f'(D^2) \cap g'(D^2) = \emptyset$. A space $X$ is called aspherical if it is path-connected and $\pi_k(X) = 0$ for all $k \geq 2$.

Question: Suppose $X$ is an aspherical compact homology ANR-manifold that has the DDP. Must $X$ be homotopy equivalent to a closed topological manifold?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether every aspherical compact homology ANR-manifold with the DDP is homotopy equivalent to a closed topological manifold appears to be open. Although compact homology ANR-manifolds with nontrivial resolution obstruction (and hence not homotopy equivalent to closed manifolds) were constructed by Bryant–Ferry–Mio–Weinberger, no aspherical example is known, and the problem is highlighted as open in surveys on aspherical manifolds and on exotic homology manifolds.

Let G=(V,E) be a finite connected graph, endowed with its shortest-path (graph) distance d_G. For a vertex v∈V and an integer R≥0, the ball of radius R centered at v is B_R(v)={u∈V : d_G(u,v)≤R}. Define:
- ρ_R(G) = the minimum number of radius-R balls (with centers in V) whose union is V, i.e. the minimum size of an R-dominating set of G;
- γ_R(G) = the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint balls of radius R in G.

Question: Does there exist a universal constant c>0 such that
   ρ_R(G) ≤ c · γ_R(G)
holds for every integer R≥0 and for every finite planar graph G?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Bousquet, Cames van Batenburg, Esperet, Joret, Lochet, Müller, and Pirot (arXiv:2001.04517, 2020; Combinatorica 2021) proved that for every t≥1 there is a constant c_t such that in every K_t-minor-free graph G, for any family S of balls, the minimum hitting set is at most c_t times the maximum disjoint subfamily. Specializing to S being the family of all radius-R balls in a planar graph yields ρ_R(G) ≤ c·γ_R(G) for a universal constant c, affirmatively resolving Chepoi's question (which had been conjectured by Chepoi–Estellon–Vaxès in 2007 in the planar same-radius case).

Consider the neutral charm meson system consisting of $D^0$ and $\bar D^0$, which mix via flavor oscillations. Define the time-integrated wrong-sign semileptonic rate ratio
$$r_D \;=\; \frac{\Gamma(D^0 \to \ell^- X)}{\Gamma(D^0 \to \ell^+ X)},$$
where the numerator counts semileptonic decays of an initially tagged $D^0$ to a "wrong-sign" lepton (only possible after oscillation into $\bar D^0$) and the denominator counts the corresponding right-sign decays. Within the Standard Model, short-distance contributions place $r_D$ well below $10^{-6}$, but long-distance hadronic contributions are estimated to push $r_D$ up to order $10^{-4}$, with sizeable theoretical uncertainty.

(a) Determine the value of $r_D$.

(b) Decide whether experimental measurements of $D^0$–$\bar D^0$ oscillations can be made sensitive at the level $r_D \lesssim 10^{-4}$, and further whether the sensitivity can be improved to roughly $r_D \sim 10^{-5}$, a level at which a nonzero oscillation signal is expected to be unambiguously detected and meaningfully interpreted despite the Standard Model long-distance uncertainties in the prediction.

$D^0$–$\bar D^0$ mixing has been observed and is now firmly established (combined evidence above 5σ since 2012, with LHCb and Belle measurements). Current experimental sensitivities for the mixing parameters $x$ and $y$ reach the $10^{-5}$ level, well below the originally targeted $r_D \lesssim 10^{-4}$, so the experimental aspect of the question is resolved. A closed topological manifold $X$ is said to be aspherical if its universal cover is contractible (equivalently, $\pi_i(X)=0$ for all $i\ge 2$). A continuous map $p\colon E\to B$ between topological spaces is a locally trivial topological fiber bundle if every point of $B$ has an open neighborhood $U$ such that $p^{-1}(U)$ is homeomorphic to $U\times F$ over $U$ for some fixed fiber $F$. A proper map $p\colon E\to B$ between manifolds is a manifold approximate fibration if it satisfies the approximate homotopy lifting property: for every space $Z$, every commutative diagram of maps $h_0\colon Z\to E$, $H\colon Z\times[0,1]\to B$ with $p\circ h_0 = H(\cdot,0)$, and every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of $B$, there exists a homotopy $\tilde H\colon Z\times[0,1]\to E$ with $\tilde H(\cdot,0)=h_0$ and such that $p\circ \tilde H$ and $H$ are $\mathcal{U}$-close.

Let $f\colon M\to N$ be a continuous map between aspherical closed manifolds such that the induced homomorphism $f_*\colon \pi_1(M)\to \pi_1(N)$ is surjective. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $f$ (or on the kernel $K = \ker f_*$ and the extension $1\to K\to \pi_1(M)\to \pi_1(N)\to 1$, together with appropriate manifold-theoretic data) under which $f$ is homotopic to the projection of a locally trivial topological fiber bundle over $N$, or, more generally, homotopic to a manifold approximate fibration over $N$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as an open question concerning when a $\pi_1$-surjective map between aspherical closed manifolds is homotopy equivalent to a fiber bundle projection or a manifold approximate fibration. While particular cases (e.g., when the kernel is a surface or Poincaré-duality group, results of Farrell–Jones, Hughes–Taylor–Williams–Weinberger on MAFs, and recent work on fibering aspherical manifolds) provide partial answers, no general characterization is known, and the problem appears to remain open.

Background and definitions.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple undirected graph with n = |V|. For a subset X ⊆ V, let A_G[X, V∖X] denote the |X| × |V∖X| submatrix of the adjacency matrix of G with rows indexed by X and columns by V∖X, viewed over the binary field GF(2). The cut-rank function is ρ_G(X) := rank(A_G[X, V∖X]) over GF(2).

A rank-decomposition of G is a pair (T, L), where T is a subcubic tree (every internal node has degree 3) and L is a bijection from V(G) to the set of leaves of T. Each edge e of T splits the leaves into two sets, inducing a bipartition (X_e, V∖X_e) of V(G); the width of e is ρ_G(X_e), and the width of (T, L) is the maximum of ρ_G(X_e) over all edges e. The rank-width of G is the minimum width over all rank-decompositions.

A linear rank-decomposition of G is a rank-decomposition (T, L) in which T is a caterpillar (a tree whose internal nodes form a path). The linear rank-width lrw(G) of G is the minimum width over all linear rank-decompositions of G (with lrw(G) = 0 if |V(G)| ≤ 1).

Problem.

Fix an integer k ≥ 0. Is there an algorithm that, given two graphs G_1 and G_2 with lrw(G_1), lrw(G_2) ≤ k, decides whether G_1 and G_2 are isomorphic in time polynomial in |V(G_1)| + |V(G_2)| (the exponent of the polynomial may depend on k)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Grohe and Schweitzer (FOCS 2015; CACM/JACM versions) gave a polynomial-time isomorphism algorithm for graphs of rank-width at most k, running in time n^{f(k)}. Since linear rank-width is at least rank-width (a linear rank-decomposition is a rank-decomposition), every graph of linear rank-width at most k has rank-width at most k, so this result immediately implies a polynomial-time isomorphism algorithm for graphs of bounded linear rank-width. A later result via the (3k+4)-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman algorithm even yields canonization in n^{O(k)} time.

Consider neutral charm mesons $D^0$ and $\bar D^0$, which mix via $\Delta C=2$ transitions parameterized by the usual mixing parameters $x=\Delta M/\Gamma$ and $y=\Delta\Gamma/(2\Gamma)$. For final states $f$ accessible to both $D^0$ and $\bar D^0$ (such as $f\in\{K^+K^-,\pi^+\pi^-,K_S\pi^0,K_S\omega,K_S\eta\}$), define the time-dependent CP asymmetry
$$A_{CP}(t;f)=\frac{\Gamma(D^0(t)\to f)-\Gamma(\bar D^0(t)\to f)}{\Gamma(D^0(t)\to f)+\Gamma(\bar D^0(t)\to f)},$$
where $D^0(t),\bar D^0(t)$ denote the time-evolved states starting as flavor eigenstates at $t=0$. The mixing-induced (oscillation-dependent) component of $A_{CP}(t;f)$ scales with $t/\tau_{D^0}$ and vanishes at $t=0$.

Determine whether the oscillation-induced contribution to the time-dependent CP asymmetry in such common final states can reach or exceed the $10^{-3}$ level within the Standard Model, or whether the observation of such an asymmetry at the $10^{-3}$ level or above would necessarily constitute clear evidence of physics beyond the Standard Model.

Current LHCb measurements (2021) of the time-dependent CP-asymmetry slopes $\Delta Y_{KK}=(-2.3\pm1.5\pm0.3)\times10^{-4}$ and $\Delta Y_{\pi\pi}=(-4.0\pm2.8\pm0.4)\times10^{-4}$ are consistent with CP conservation and have not yet reached or excluded the $10^{-3}$ benchmark. A hole in a simple finite undirected graph is an induced cycle of length at least 4. A long hole is an induced cycle of length at least 5. A graph G is called hole-free (in the sense considered here) if it contains no induced cycle of length at least 5, equivalently, it has no long hole. Given such a graph G with vertex set V(G), an independent set is a subset S ⊆ V(G) such that no two vertices of S are adjacent. The Maximum Independent Set problem asks, given G as input, to compute an independent set in G of maximum cardinality (and, in the weighted version, given vertex weights w : V(G) → ℝ_{>0}, an independent set of maximum total weight).

Determine the computational complexity of the Maximum Independent Set problem (and of the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem) restricted to the class of graphs with no induced cycle of length at least 5. In particular, decide whether there exists a polynomial-time algorithm solving this problem on this class, or whether the problem is NP-hard on this class.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem (often called MWIS on long-hole-free graphs) is still listed as an important open problem. Significant partial progress exists: a subexponential-time algorithm for the general long-hole-free case, and polynomial-time algorithms for several subclasses (e.g., long-hole-free graphs with no k-prism for fixed k, odd-hole-free graphs without dart or bull, (pyramid, even hole)-free graphs, and FPT results for even-hole-free graphs). No polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hardness result for the full class is known as of recent surveys.

A class Π of finite simple graphs is called induced-hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs, i.e., whenever G ∈ Π and H is an induced subgraph of G, then H ∈ Π. Say that Π is recognizable in polynomial time if there is an algorithm that, given a graph G on n vertices, decides in time polynomial in n whether G ∈ Π. For a graph G, an induced Π-subgraph of G is an induced subgraph of G that belongs to Π. Use the O*(·) notation to suppress factors polynomial in n.

Question: Is it true that for every induced-hereditary graph class Π that is recognizable in polynomial time, there exist a constant c_Π < 2 and an algorithm that, given an n-vertex input graph G, finds a maximum-size induced Π-subgraph of G in time O*(c_Π^n)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Searches reveal substantial follow-up work on subexponential-time algorithms for finding maximum induced subgraphs in restricted hereditary classes (e.g., Novotná–Okrasa–Pilipczuk–Rzążewski–van Leeuwen–Walczak, 2019/2021), and on H-colorable subgraphs in hereditary classes (2020), but no source confirms a general O*(c^n) algorithm with c<2 for arbitrary polynomially recognizable induced-hereditary classes, nor a refutation. The general question appears to remain open.

The supersymmetric flavor problem remains an open question because supersymmetry itself has not been discovered experimentally. Theoretical proposals (degeneracy / super-GIM, alignment, decoupling of first two generations, gauge mediation, anomaly/gaugino/flavor mediation, and hybrids) continue to be actively studied; recent (2024–2025) work, including string-landscape statistical arguments, favors mixed quasi-degeneracy/decoupling scenarios with multi-TeV first/second-generation scalars, but no mechanism has been confirmed by data. LHC searches have constrained but not selected among these options.

Let $p(z)$ be a complex polynomial of degree $n \ge 2$ with zeros $z_1,\dots,z_n \in \mathbb{C}$ (listed with multiplicity), and let $w_1,\dots,w_{n-1} \in \mathbb{C}$ denote the zeros of its derivative $p'(z)$ (the critical points of $p$), again listed with multiplicity. Assume that the centroid of the zeros lies at the origin, i.e. $\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = 0$. Prove or disprove the inequality
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} |w_i|^2 \;\le\; \frac{n-2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} |z_i|^2.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is Schoenberg's 1986 conjecture on the critical points of a complex polynomial. It was proved independently by R. Pereira and by S. M. Malamud around 2003–2005, via majorization arguments relating the zeros of a polynomial to its critical points. Several generalizations (de Bruin–Sharma higher-order analogues, Schoenberg-type inequalities of orders 4 and 6) have since been established.

Define a sequence of integers (f_n)_{n≥1} by f_1 = 1, f_2 = 1, and the second-order linear recurrence

  f_{n+1} = f_n − 2 f_{n−1}  for n ≥ 2.

Direct computation gives f_3 = −1, f_5 = −1 and f_{13} = −1. Determine all positive integers n for which f_n = −1; equivalently, decide whether n ∈ {3, 5, 13} is the complete list of solutions.
representations.original:
Define a sequence of integers (f_n)_{n≥1} by f_1 = 1, f_2 = 1, and the second-order linear recurrence

  f_{n+1} = f_n − 2 f_{n−1}  for n ≥ 2.

Direct computation gives f_3 = −1, f_5 = −1 and f_{13} = −1. Determine all positive integers n for which f_n = −1; equivalently, decide whether n ∈ {3, 5, 13} is the complete list of solutions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The sequence is the Lucas sequence U_n with parameters (P,Q) = (1,2) and discriminant D = −7. Using the companion identity V_n^2 + 7 U_n^2 = 2^{n+2}, the equation f_n = −1 is equivalent to the Ramanujan–Nagell equation V^2 + 7 = 2^{n+2}. Nagell (1948) proved that 2^m − 7 = V^2 has solutions only for m ∈ {3, 4, 5, 7, 15}, which corresponds exactly to n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 13} for |U_n| = 1; the cases with f_n = −1 are precisely n = 3, 5, 13. Thus the problem is solved: there are no other integers n with f_n = −1.

Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), a four-dimensional N=1 globally supersymmetric gauge theory with gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y, chiral matter superfields corresponding to three generations of quarks and leptons, and two Higgs doublet chiral superfields H_U (hypercharge +1/2) and H_D (hypercharge -1/2). The superpotential contains the gauge-invariant, holomorphic bilinear term

   W ⊃ μ H_U · H_D ,

where H_U · H_D = ε_{ab} H_U^a H_D^b is the SU(2)_L–invariant contraction. The soft supersymmetry-breaking Lagrangian contains a corresponding bilinear scalar term

   L_soft ⊃ -(B μ) H_U · H_D + h.c.

The parameter μ preserves supersymmetry and, on dimensional grounds in the absence of any protecting symmetry, would naturally take a value of order an ultraviolet scale Λ_UV (such as a grand-unification scale ~10^{16} GeV or the Planck scale ~10^{18} GeV). However, successful radiative electroweak symmetry breaking in the MSSM requires, after minimizing the Higgs potential, that |μ|^2 be of the order of the electroweak scale m_Z^2 ~ (100 GeV)^2, and that the soft parameter Bμ also be of order m_Z^2 (more precisely of order the soft SUSY-breaking scale squared).

Problem. Identify a dynamical mechanism or a symmetry principle, embedded in a consistent extension of the MSSM (for example via additional gauge or global symmetries, additional singlet superfields, or a mediation scheme of supersymmetry breaking), that:

  (i) forbids a bare μ-term of order Λ_UV in the unbroken theory,
  (ii) generates an effective μ of order the electroweak / soft supersymmetry-breaking scale once supersymmetry is broken (so that μ is naturally tied to the SUSY-breaking scale rather than to Λ_UV), and
  (iii) simultaneously generates a soft bilinear coupling Bμ of order the square of the SUSY-breaking scale, in a phenomenologically acceptable range, without reintroducing fine tuning between μ and Bμ.

Provide such a mechanism, or prove that within a specified class of supersymmetric extensions no such mechanism exists.

The μ-problem of the MSSM remains an actively discussed open problem in supersymmetric phenomenology. Several candidate mechanisms exist (Giudice–Masiero, NMSSM/singlet extensions, Kim–Nilles via Peccei–Quinn symmetry, etc.), but no single mechanism is established as the correct explanation, and the related "μ/Bμ problem" (especially in gauge mediation) is still discussed in recent literature. The status is best characterized as an open model-building question with multiple partial proposals.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general common fixed point conjecture for two commuting continuous self-maps of [0,1] was disproved by Boyce and Huneke (1967, 1969) via counterexamples. However, those counterexamples are not polynomials, and partial positive results are known only for restricted families (e.g., Block–Thielman handled specific commuting families related to Chebyshev-type polynomials, and results exist under hypotheses like absence of period-2 points). No source located confirms a full resolution of the polynomial case for arbitrary commuting polynomials mapping [0,1] into itself; it appears to remain open.

representations.normalized: Let $f(x_1,\dots,x_m)$ be a real polynomial of degree $n$ in $m$ variables satisfying $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Determine whether $f$ must always be expressible as a finite sum of squares of real polynomials in $x_1,\dots,x_m$. It is known that the answer is affirmative in the following cases: (i) $m = 2$ with $n$ even; (ii) $n = 2$ for arbitrary $m$; (iii) $m = 3$ with $n = 4$. The general question asks: for which pairs $(m,n)$ does every nonnegative real polynomial of degree $n$ in $m$ variables decompose as a sum of squares of real polynomials, and is this true for all $(m,n)$?

Determine whether $f$ must always be expressible as a finite sum of squares of real polynomials in $x_1,\dots,x_m$. It is known that the answer is affirmative in the following cases: (i) $m = 2$ with $n$ even; (ii) $n = 2$ for arbitrary $m$; (iii) $m = 3$ with $n = 4$. The general question asks: for which pairs $(m,n)$ does every nonnegative real polynomial of degree $n$ in $m$ variables decompose as a sum of squares of real polynomials, and is this true for all $(m,n)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is Hilbert's question on positive polynomials as sums of squares (closely tied to Hilbert's 17th problem). Hilbert (1888) showed the answer is positive precisely in the three cases listed and proved nonconstructively that there exist nonnegative polynomials in other cases that are not sums of polynomial squares. Explicit counterexamples were later given (e.g., Motzkin 1967, Robinson). Artin (1927) solved Hilbert's 17th problem by showing every nonnegative real polynomial is a sum of squares of rational functions. So the problem as stated (polynomial squares) is solved in the negative for all other $(m,n)$.

Motzkin gave an explicit example of a nonnegative polynomial that is not a sum of squares of polynomials. Artin proved that every nonnegative polynomial is a sum of squares of rational functions.", "claim": "The problem of representing every nonnegative polynomial as a sum of squares of polynomials is settled: only the three listed families work; counterexamples exist otherwise; Artin solved the rational-function version."}]

Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM): an N=1 globally supersymmetric four-dimensional quantum field theory whose chiral matter content consists of three generations of quark and lepton superfields together with two Higgs doublet superfields H_u and H_d, coupled to the gauge supermultiplets of SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y. Supersymmetry must ultimately be broken spontaneously so as to preserve its desirable properties (non-renormalization theorems, cancellation of quadratic divergences, etc.), while phenomenology requires the breaking to produce a realistic spectrum of soft terms.

Two basic obstructions are: (i) no choice of vacuum expectation values for the MSSM fields alone breaks supersymmetry while remaining phenomenologically acceptable; (ii) at tree level the supertrace sum rule STr M^2 = Σ_J (−1)^{2J}(2J+1) m_J^2 = 0 (taken over the mass eigenstates of a sector with renormalizable tree-level couplings) forbids realistic spectra if the supersymmetry breaking is communicated through renormalizable tree-level couplings to ordinary matter.

One is therefore led to postulate an additional 'hidden' (or 'secluded') sector of fields and interactions whose dynamics spontaneously break supersymmetry, with the breaking transmitted to the visible MSSM sector only via suppressed (e.g. gravitational, gauge-mediated, anomaly-mediated, or otherwise non-renormalizable or loop-induced) interactions.

Problem. Construct, or identify the correct, hidden-sector field theory and mediation mechanism that:
(a) spontaneously breaks N=1 global (or local) supersymmetry in a calculable and stable vacuum;
(b) naturally generates the supersymmetry-breaking scale Λ (and the resulting soft mass scale M_soft ~ √F/M_mediation in the visible sector) exponentially below the Planck scale M_P, for example through dimensional transmutation Λ ~ M_P · exp(−8π^2/(b g^2(M_P))) in a strongly coupled gauge sector with beta-function coefficient b;
(c) yields, after mediation to the MSSM, soft supersymmetry-breaking terms compatible with electroweak symmetry breaking, observed fermion masses, and experimental constraints on flavour- and CP-violation.

Determine such a hidden sector and mediation scheme, or prove that no consistent realization exists.

The mechanism of supersymmetry breaking remains an open question in theoretical particle physics. Many candidate hidden-sector models exist (gravity-, gauge-, anomaly-mediated, and metastable Intriligator–Seiberg–Shih vacua, etc.), but no single consistent and experimentally verified realization has been established. LHC null results for superpartners up to multi-TeV scales further constrain but do not resolve the question.

Consider extensions of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) obtained by adding a gauge-singlet chiral superfield S. The MSSM superpotential contains a supersymmetric Higgs mass term μ H_U H_D; in singlet-extended models one replaces this by a coupling λ S H_U H_D, so that an explicit μ term is generated dynamically once S acquires a vacuum expectation value ⟨S⟩ of order the electroweak scale, thereby addressing the μ-problem.

Two obstructions arise:

(a) Cosmological domain walls. If the only S-dependent couplings are λ S H_U H_D and a cubic self-coupling (κ/3) S^3 (the standard NMSSM superpotential), the action possesses an exact Z_3 discrete symmetry under which all chiral superfields are multiplied by e^{2πi/3}. Spontaneous breaking of this Z_3 at the electroweak phase transition produces domain walls whose surface energy density, set by the weak scale, would come to dominate the energy density of the Universe and produce unacceptably large CMB anisotropies, in conflict with standard cosmology.

(b) Tadpole-induced hierarchy destabilization. In the presence of gravity and any high-scale physics (e.g. supergravity or quantum-gravity-induced) that breaks the Z_3, nonrenormalizable interactions generically induce, at some loop order, a tadpole term of the form t·S in the effective potential. Unless suppressed, the coefficient t is of order M_P^2 M_S or M_P M_S^2 (where M_S is the SUSY-breaking scale), which drags ⟨S⟩ — and hence the electroweak scale through λ⟨S⟩ — up to a scale far above the weak scale, reintroducing the hierarchy problem.

Problem. Construct a realistic four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model that contains one or more gauge-singlet chiral superfields and in which:

(i) the μ-problem is solved by a singlet vacuum expectation value (so ⟨S⟩ replaces an explicit μ term),
(ii) no cosmologically dangerous stable domain walls survive to dominate the energy density of the Universe,
(iii) singlet tadpole terms generated by Planck-scale physics do not destabilize the hierarchy between the electroweak scale and the Planck scale,
(iv) the model is phenomenologically viable (correct electroweak symmetry breaking, no light unobserved states, acceptable flavour and CP structure).

Furthermore, determine whether the same tadpole mechanisms that threaten the weak scale can be turned to advantage: namely, exhibit a singlet-extended supersymmetric model in which Planck-suppressed singlet tadpoles drive a singlet vacuum expectation value to a chosen intermediate or grand-unified scale, thereby triggering symmetry breaking at that scale in a controlled and predictive way.
representations.original:
Consider extensions of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) obtained by adding a gauge-singlet chiral superfield S. The MSSM superpotential contains a supersymmetric Higgs mass term μ H_U H_D; in singlet-extended models one replaces this by a coupling λ S H_U H_D, so that an explicit μ term is generated dynamically once S acquires a vacuum expectation value ⟨S⟩ of order the electroweak scale, thereby addressing the μ-problem.

Two obstructions arise:

(a) Cosmological domain walls. If the only S-dependent couplings are λ S H_U H_D and a cubic self-coupling (κ/3) S^3 (the standard NMSSM superpotential), the action possesses an exact Z_3 discrete symmetry under which all chiral superfields are multiplied by e^{2πi/3}. Spontaneous breaking of this Z_3 at the electroweak phase transition produces domain walls whose surface energy density, set by the weak scale, would come to dominate the energy density of the Universe and produce unacceptably large CMB anisotropies, in conflict with standard cosmology.

(b) Tadpole-induced hierarchy destabilization. In the presence of gravity and any high-scale physics (e.g. supergravity or quantum-gravity-induced) that breaks the Z_3, nonrenormalizable interactions generically induce, at some loop order, a tadpole term of the form t·S in the effective potential. Unless suppressed, the coefficient t is of order M_P^2 M_S or M_P M_S^2 (where M_S is the SUSY-breaking scale), which drags ⟨S⟩ — and hence the electroweak scale through λ⟨S⟩ — up to a scale far above the weak scale, reintroducing the hierarchy problem.

Problem. Construct a realistic four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model that contains one or more gauge-singlet chiral superfields and in which:

(i) the μ-problem is solved by a singlet vacuum expectation value (so ⟨S⟩ replaces an explicit μ term),
(ii) no cosmologically dangerous stable domain walls survive to dominate the energy density of the Universe,
(iii) singlet tadpole terms generated by Planck-scale physics do not destabilize the hierarchy between the electroweak scale and the Planck scale,
(iv) the model is phenomenologically viable (correct electroweak symmetry breaking, no light unobserved states, acceptable flavour and CP structure).

Furthermore, determine whether the same tadpole mechanisms that threaten the weak scale can be turned to advantage: namely, exhibit a singlet-extended supersymmetric model in which Planck-suppressed singlet tadpoles drive a singlet vacuum expectation value to a chosen intermediate or grand-unified scale, thereby triggering symmetry breaking at that scale in a controlled and predictive way.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Several mechanisms have been proposed and developed since the question was posed: imposing a discrete R-symmetry that forbids the cubic singlet self-coupling and controls higher-order tadpoles (NMSSM+ and related constructions), embedding the singlet in gauge-mediated SUSY breaking so that domain walls are avoided, anomalous Z_3 breaking via hidden-sector QCD, and inflationary dynamics that confine the post-inflationary Universe to a single Z_3 domain. Tadpoles have also been used constructively to generate intermediate/GUT-scale singlet VEVs. No single model is universally accepted as fully realistic, so the broad coexistence question is best characterised as partially resolved rather than definitively closed.

This is the classical Mizel problem (the "rectangle property" characterization of the circle). It was solved affirmatively, independently by A. S. Besicovitch and L. Danzer in the 1950s–60s: a convex Jordan curve with the stated rectangle property must indeed be a circle.

Let $X$ be a Banach space, and denote by $\mathcal{K}(X,X)$ the Banach space of compact linear operators from $X$ to $X$, equipped with the operator norm, and by $B_{\mathcal{K}(X,X)}$ its closed unit ball. Recall the following.

(i) $X$ is said to have the metric compact approximation property (MCAP) if for every compact set $K \subset X$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $T \in B_{\mathcal{K}(X,X)}$ (i.e., a compact operator with $\|T\| \leq 1$) such that $\|Tx - x\| \leq \varepsilon$ for all $x \in K$.

(ii) Let $X^* \hat{\otimes}_\pi X$ denote the projective tensor product of $X^*$ and $X$. The trace mapping
$$V : X^* \hat{\otimes}_\pi X \longrightarrow \mathcal{K}(X,X)^*$$
is the bounded linear map defined on elementary tensors by $V(x^* \otimes x)(T) = x^*(Tx)$ for $x^* \in X^*$, $x \in X$, $T \in \mathcal{K}(X,X)$, and extended by linearity and continuity.

Question: Is it true that $X$ has the metric compact approximation property if and only if the trace mapping $V : X^* \hat{\otimes}_\pi X \to \mathcal{K}(X,X)^*$ is an isometry (i.e., $\|V(u)\| = \|u\|_\pi$ for all $u \in X^* \hat{\otimes}_\pi X$)?

Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) with exact R-parity (equivalently, matter parity) conservation, in which superpartners can be produced and destroyed only in pairs and the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) is therefore absolutely stable. Such an LSP, if electrically and color neutral, is a candidate weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) that may constitute the non-baryonic cold dark matter of the universe. The two natural neutral LSP candidates in the MSSM are: (i) the sneutrino ν̃ (the scalar superpartner of a Standard Model neutrino), and (ii) the lightest neutralino χ̃₁⁰, defined as the lightest mass eigenstate of the 4×4 neutralino mass matrix mixing the bino B̃, the neutral wino W̃³, and the two neutral higgsinos H̃_u⁰, H̃_d⁰.

Tasks:
(a) Determine which (if any) of these MSSM particles can supply the observed cosmological cold dark matter density Ω_DM h² ≈ 0.12, specifying for the neutralino case the admissible bino/wino/higgsino composition and mass range consistent with thermal relic abundance, with direct-detection bounds on the spin-independent and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections, with indirect-detection limits, and with collider constraints on superpartner masses.
(b) Describe an experimental program by which accelerator measurements of the LSP's mass, spin, couplings, and annihilation cross sections, together with independent measurements in direct (and indirect) dark-matter detection experiments, would allow one to verify that the stable particle produced and inferred at colliders is the same particle that accounts for the cosmic dark matter density, including a quantitative criterion for "matching" between collider-inferred and astrophysically inferred properties.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

As of 2026, the identity of the dark matter particle remains experimentally unresolved. Sneutrino LSP dark matter is essentially excluded by direct-detection limits (XENON-1T, LZ, PandaX-4T) combined with the invisible Z width. The neutralino LSP remains a viable candidate, but recent LZ 2024/2025 spin-independent limits, LHC Run 3 searches, and phenomenological MSSM scans have strongly constrained the bino/wino/higgsino parameter space without confirming or ruling out neutralino dark matter. No accelerator has yet produced superpartners, so the cross-verification program envisioned has not been carried out.

Let $\mathbb{H}$ denote the skew field of quaternions, and consider $\mathbb{H}^n$ as a right $\mathbb{H}$-module. A left hyperplane in $\mathbb{H}^n$ is an affine subset of the form $\{w \in \mathbb{H}^n : \sum_{k=1}^n a_k (w_k - b_k) = 0\}$ for some fixed $a = (a_1,\dots,a_n) \in \mathbb{H}^n \setminus \{0\}$ and $b \in \mathbb{H}^n$. A set $E \subset \mathbb{H}^n$ is called linearly convex if for every point $z \in \mathbb{H}^n \setminus E$ there exists a left hyperplane $l$ such that $z \in l \subset \mathbb{H}^n \setminus E$.

Let $K \subset \mathbb{H}^n$ be a linearly convex compact set, and let $H^{\bullet}(K)$ denote its (Čech) cohomology with, say, integer coefficients. Suppose that $H^j(K) \neq 0$ for some integer $j \geq 4$. Must there exist an index $i$ with $1 \leq i < j$ such that $H^i(K) \neq 0$?

Let X be a Baire space (i.e., a topological space in which the intersection of every countable family of dense open sets is dense), let Y be a compact Hausdorff space, and let f: X × Y → ℝ be a separately continuous function (i.e., for every fixed x₀ ∈ X the map y ↦ f(x₀, y) is continuous on Y, and for every fixed y₀ ∈ Y the map x ↦ f(x, y₀) is continuous on X). Denote by C(f) ⊆ X × Y the set of all points at which f is jointly continuous.

Does there exist such a triple (X, Y, f) with C(f) = ∅, that is, a separately continuous real-valued function on the product of a Baire space and a compact Hausdorff space which has no points of joint continuity?

The gravitino problem remains an active area of research with no definitive resolution. Consider supersymmetric and string-motivated extensions of the Standard Model that contain scalar "moduli" fields — for example Polonyi-type hidden-sector scalars, string compactification moduli whose vacuum expectation values of order the Planck mass M_Pl parametrize the size of compact dimensions, the string dilaton whose VEV ~M_Pl parametrizes the string coupling, D- and F-flat directions of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, and GUT-breaking Higgs fields. Such moduli typically possess very flat potentials (with masses set by the soft SUSY-breaking scale, m ~ O(TeV) or below) and couplings to ordinary matter suppressed by inverse powers of M_Pl, so they are long-lived and easily displaced from their late-time minima in the early universe.

Within this setting, determine:

(a) Under what conditions a coherent oscillation of such a modulus comes to dominate the energy density of the universe after inflation, and whether its energy density combined with its late decay is compatible with (i) the present critical density bound (no overclosure), (ii) the preservation of any pre-existing baryon asymmetry against entropy dilution from modulus decay, and (iii) the success of Big Bang nucleosynthesis (i.e. decay before t ~ 1 s or with decay products that do not photodissociate light nuclei).

(b) Which of the following mechanisms, or combinations thereof, can render the cosmology of these moduli viable: rapid perturbative decay (requiring sufficiently large modulus mass, m ≳ O(10–100) TeV); a late epoch of "thermal inflation" driven by a flaton field that dilutes the modulus abundance; tuned or dynamically selected initial conditions that place the modulus near its true minimum after inflation; explicit dilaton stabilization mechanisms (e.g. racetrack or Kähler-stabilized potentials); and non-perturbative depletion via parametric resonance / preheating, including precise criteria for when such resonance occurs and how the decay products thermalize.

Provide quantitative bounds linking the modulus mass, initial misalignment amplitude, reheating temperature after inflation, and decay width, that delineate the cosmologically allowed region of parameter space.

The cosmological moduli problem remains an active research topic. A 2022 JHEP study and a 2015 critical review (arXiv:1502.07746) both indicate the problem persists in general SUSY/string frameworks: while heavy moduli (m ≳ 100 TeV) can decay before BBN, non-thermal gravitino production and LSP overproduction from moduli decay still generically conflict with dark-matter bounds, and no universally accepted resolution exists. Mechanisms such as thermal inflation, large-volume stabilization, and parametric resonance are partial fixes but face their own constraints. Hence the broad question is still open.

Let X and Y be topological spaces and let ℝ denote the real line with its standard topology. A function f: X × Y → ℝ is said to be separately continuous if for every fixed x₀ ∈ X the map y ↦ f(x₀, y) is continuous on Y, and for every fixed y₀ ∈ Y the map x ↦ f(x, y₀) is continuous on X. Denote by C(f) the set of points of (joint) continuity of f. The function f is called point-wise discontinuous if C(f) is dense in X × Y. The function f is called quasi-continuous at a point (x₀, y₀) ∈ X × Y if for every open neighborhood W of f(x₀, y₀) in ℝ and every open neighborhood U of (x₀, y₀) in X × Y there exists a nonempty open set V ⊆ U such that f(V) ⊆ W; f is quasi-continuous if it is quasi-continuous at every point of X × Y.

Question: Do there exist topological spaces X and Y with the following two properties simultaneously?
(a) Every separately continuous function f: X × Y → ℝ is point-wise discontinuous (that is, C(f) is dense in X × Y).
(b) There exists a separately continuous function f₀: X × Y → ℝ that is not quasi-continuous.

Setting. Consider a supersymmetric grand unified theory (SUSY GUT) based on a simple gauge group G ⊃ SU(3)_c × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y (for example SU(5) or SO(10)), in which the two MSSM Higgs doublets H_u, H_d are embedded into larger unified Higgs multiplets that necessarily also contain color-triplet partners T, T̄ carrying the quantum numbers of SU(3)_c triplets. Below the unification scale M_GUT ~ 2×10^16 GeV the theory must reduce to the MSSM, so the doublets must remain at the electroweak scale (mass ~ 10^2 GeV) while the triplets must be very heavy.

Proton decay. In such SUSY GUTs the exchange of the color-triplet Higgsinos generates dimension-five operators of the form (QQQL)/M_T and (u^c u^c d^c e^c)/M_T which, dressed by gaugino/Higgsino loops, produce proton-decay amplitudes dominated by the channel p → K^+ ν. The current experimental bound requires τ(p → K^+ ν) ≳ 10^{32} years, which translates into a lower bound on the effective color-triplet mass M_T (typically M_T ≳ 10^{17} GeV after including model-dependent factors).

Problem.
(a) Construct an explicit, fully consistent renormalizable supersymmetric grand unified model — including a choice of gauge group G, Higgs representation content, superpotential, and vacuum — in which:
  (i) the two electroweak Higgs doublets H_u, H_d remain massless (or with masses of order the electroweak scale) at tree level,
  (ii) their color-triplet partners T, T̄ acquire masses large enough to make τ(p → K^+ ν) > 10^{32} years through the induced dimension-five operators,
  (iii) the splitting in (i)–(ii) is "natural" in the technical sense that it follows from symmetries or from the structure of the superpotential rather than from a tuning of unrelated parameters to a precision finer than ~1%,
  (iv) gauge coupling unification is preserved.

(b) Alternatively, prove that no such natural doublet-triplet splitting mechanism can be realized in a four-dimensional renormalizable SUSY GUT consistent with all current proton-decay bounds.

Setting. Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space and let $F: U \to X$ be a $C^{1,1}$ map defined on a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ with $F(0)=0$, such that $A := DF(0)$ is a bounded linear contraction (i.e. its spectral radius is $<1$). One says $F$ is $C^1$-linearizable at $0$ if there exists a local $C^1$ diffeomorphism $H$ fixing $0$ such that $H\circ F = A\circ H$ near $0$.

Known counterexamples to $C^1$ linearization rely on certain non-resonance-type conditions on the spectrum $\sigma(A)$. A typical such counterexample requires $\sigma(A)$ to have a specific shape: writing $|\sigma(A)| = \{|\lambda| : \lambda \in \sigma(A)\} \subset (0,1)$, the construction uses spectra of the form $|\sigma(A)| = [a b^{1+r}, b] \cup \{a\}$ with $0 < b < a < 1$ and some parameter $r > 0$ measuring how far one is from the borderline case.

Question. Within this framework, can one construct sharper counterexamples to $C^1$ linearization? Specifically:

(a) Is there a $C^{1,1}$ map $F$ on an infinite-dimensional Banach space with $F(0)=0$, whose linear part $A = DF(0)$ has $|\sigma(A)| = [a b^{1+r}, b] \cup \{a\}$ with $r = 0$ (i.e. $|\sigma(A)| = [ab, b] \cup \{a\}$ but realized in the limiting case where the standard construction breaks down), and such that $F$ is not $C^1$-linearizable at $0$?

(b) More strongly, is there such an $F$ whose linear part $A$ satisfies exactly $|\sigma(A)| = [ab, b] \cup \{a\}$ for some $0 < b < a < 1$, and which is not $C^1$-linearizable at $0$?

Consider four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric gauge theories. The Seiberg duality conjecture asserts that, in the conformal window, an "electric" SU(N_c) gauge theory with N_f chiral superfields Q in the fundamental and N_f chiral superfields Q̃ in the antifundamental flows in the infrared to the same superconformal fixed point as a "magnetic" SU(N_f − N_c) gauge theory with N_f dual quarks q, q̃, a gauge-singlet meson superfield M^i_j transforming in the (fundamental, antifundamental) of the SU(N_f) × SU(N_f) flavor symmetry, and superpotential W = M^i_j q̃^j q_i. Address the following:

(a) Provide a rigorous proof of this infrared equivalence by exhibiting an explicit map between the gauge-invariant degrees of freedom (chiral ring operators, currents, and correlators) of the electric and magnetic theories, beyond the existing consistency checks ('t Hooft anomaly matching, superconformal index identities, moduli space matching, decoupling and deformation tests).

(b) Determine what the existence of such infrared dualities, in which two distinct ultraviolet gauge groups produce the same low-energy physics, implies about whether the gauge symmetry of an N=1 supersymmetric gauge theory is a fundamental property of the theory or merely an emergent, redundant description of its infrared dynamics.

(c) Determine to what extent these duality relations are preserved when supersymmetry is broken (either softly or spontaneously); in particular, identify which dual observables (spectra, condensates, effective potentials, phase structure) continue to match after SUSY breaking, and quantify how such surviving duality relations can be used to extract information about the low-energy phenomenology of non-supersymmetric gauge theories.

Let $E$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space and let $A\colon E	o E$ be a bounded invertible linear operator. Consider a local map $T\colon U	o E$ defined on a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ by
$$T(x)=Ax+X(x),$$
where $X$ is of class $C^{1,1}$ with $X(0)=0$, $DX(0)=0$, and in fact satisfies the higher-order vanishing condition
$$\|X(x)\|=O(\|x\|^{1+\eta}),\qquad \|DX(x)-DX(y)\|=O(\max(\|x\|,\|y\|)^{\eta-1}\|x-y\|)$$
for some constant $\eta>0$ (so the standard quadratic case corresponds to $\eta=1$).

For a Banach space $X$ and a constant $b\ge 1$, say that $X$ has the $b$-automorphic property if for every closed subspace $Y\subseteq X$ and every injective bounded linear operator $T\in L(Y,X)$ (i.e., $T$ has a bounded inverse on its range), there exists an injective bounded linear extension $\widetilde T\in L(X)$ of $T$ (so $\widetilde T|_Y=T$ and $\widetilde T$ has a bounded inverse on its range) satisfying
$$\|\widetilde T\|\,\|\widetilde T^{-1}\|\;\le\;b\,\|T\|\,\|T^{-1}\|.$$

Question: Does there exist a constant $b\ge 1$ such that for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the space $c_0^n$ has the $b$-automorphic property?

Let $R = \{A_1, \ldots, A_n\}$ be a finite set of Boolean attributes. A data set is a finite multiset $D = \{r_1, \ldots, r_m\}$ of rows, where each row $r_i \in \{0,1\}^R$ assigns a value to every attribute. A pattern is a Boolean expression $\theta$ over $R$; given a row $r$, write $r \models \theta$ if $\theta$ evaluates to $1$ on $r$. The support (or frequency) of $\theta$ in $D$ is
$$\mathrm{supp}_D(\theta) = \frac{|\{i : r_i \models \theta\}|}{m}.$$
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a class of Boolean patterns over $R$ (e.g.\ conjunctions of literals, monotone DNF formulas, decision trees of bounded depth, etc.). Fix a support threshold $\sigma \in (0,1]$.

Identify and characterize structural conditions on the pattern class $\mathcal{P}$ that guarantee the existence of an algorithm which, given $D$ and $\sigma$ as input, outputs exactly the set
$$\{\theta \in \mathcal{P} : \mathrm{supp}_D(\theta) \ge \sigma\}$$
in time polynomial in the size of $D$ and the size of the output. In particular, find natural sufficient (and, ideally, necessary) properties of $\mathcal{P}$ — such as closure properties, monotonicity/anti-monotonicity of support with respect to a partial order on $\mathcal{P}$, bounded VC-dimension, or efficient enumerability — under which such an output-polynomial algorithm exists.

Let X be a separable infinite-dimensional Banach space. Two Banach spaces Y and Z are called isomorphic, written Y ∼ Z, if there exists a bounded linear bijection between them; they are called isometric, written Y ≅ Z, if there exists a surjective linear isometry between them. The Banach–Mazur distance between two isomorphic Banach spaces Y and Z is defined by
    d(Y, Z) = inf { ‖T‖ · ‖T⁻¹‖ : T : Y → Z is a linear isomorphism }.
Let I(X) denote the class of all Banach spaces that are isomorphic to X.

Question: Does there always exist, for every separable infinite-dimensional Banach space X, a pair of Banach spaces Y, Z ∈ I(X) such that d(Y, Z) = 1 while Y and Z are not isometric?

Consider the practice of modular construction, in which facilities or their components are prefabricated off-site as discrete modules and then assembled on-site, as opposed to traditional stick-built construction performed entirely on-site. Define a "business case analysis" for modularization as a quantitative comparison of modular versus traditional delivery methods using measurable project outcomes.

Problem. Identify and rigorously define a set of key performance metrics (KPIs) that can be used to support a business case analysis of modular facility/component construction. The proposed set of metrics must:

1. Be computable from observable industry data collected across a representative population of construction projects.
2. Address, at a minimum, the following three outcome dimensions:
   (a) Safety — e.g., a quantitative measure such as recordable incident rate per exposure hour or equivalent.
   (b) Quality — e.g., a quantitative measure such as rework cost as a fraction of installed cost, defect density, or equivalent.
   (c) Productivity — e.g., a quantitative measure such as work-hours per installed unit of work, schedule performance index, or equivalent.
3. For each metric, specify (i) its precise mathematical definition, (ii) the data inputs required, (iii) a benchmarking procedure allowing comparison between modular and stick-built projects while controlling for confounding factors (project type, size, location, complexity), and (iv) the statistical methodology (e.g., normalization, hypothesis testing, effect-size estimation) used to determine whether modularization yields a statistically and practically significant improvement.

Provide the full metric framework together with empirical industry benchmark values demonstrating its applicability.

Let an event sequence over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ be a finite or infinite sequence $s = (e_1, t_1), (e_2, t_2), \ldots$ where each $e_i \in \Sigma$ is an event type and $t_i \in \mathbb{R}$ is a time stamp with $t_1 \le t_2 \le \cdots$. Given a collection $\mathcal{S}$ of such event sequences, the goal is not merely to discover frequent local sequential patterns (i.e., short subsequences of events that occur frequently within some bounded time window inside the sequences) but rather to produce a single compact description that globally characterizes each sequence in $\mathcal{S}$.

Formulate this as a learning problem: exhibit a concept class $\mathcal{C}$ of representations of event sequences (for example, probabilistic automata, hidden Markov models, regular expressions, episode rule systems, generative grammars, or other structured models) together with a learning algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ with the following properties:

(a) Each concept $c \in \mathcal{C}$ provides a simple, human-interpretable global description of an event sequence as a whole.
(b) $\mathcal{C}$ is expressive enough to capture the high-level structure (long-range dependencies, periodicities, regime changes, hierarchical structure) of realistic event sequences.
(c) The algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, given an event sequence $s$ (or a sample of sequences), produces in time polynomial in $|s|$ a concept $\hat c \in \mathcal{C}$ that approximately fits $s$ in a suitable PAC-style or description-length sense.
(d) The output description is significantly more concise than the input sequence and is qualitatively different from a list of local frequent patterns.

Identify such a pair $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{A})$ and prove appropriate learnability and conciseness guarantees, or show that no such pair exists under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions.
