Setup. Let $(e_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ be a normalized monotone subsymmetric basis of a Banach space $X$ (i.e., $(e_i)$ is a Schauder basis with basis constant $1$ that is equivalent, with the same constants, to all of its subsequences). Two basic sequences $(u_i)_{i=1}^n$ and $(v_i)_{i=1}^n$ are called $C$-equivalent if for every choice of scalars $(a_i)_{i=1}^n$,
$$ C^{-1} \Bigl\| \sum_{i=1}^n a_i u_i \Bigr\| \le \Bigl\| \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i \Bigr\| \le C \Bigl\| \sum_{i=1}^n a_i u_i \Bigr\|. $$

Assume that $(e_i)$ has the following property: for each constant $C \ge 1$ there exists a constant $D \ge 1$ such that every normalized weakly null sequence $(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ in any Banach space $Y$ admits a subsequence $(y_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ with the following stabilization property — whenever $i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_n$ are indices such that $(y_{i_j})_{j=1}^n$ is $C$-equivalent to $(e_i)_{i=1}^n$, one has
$$ \Bigl\| \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i_j} y_{i_j} \Bigr\| \le D \,\Bigl\| \sum_{j=1}^\infty a_j y_j \Bigr\| $$
for every scalar sequence $(a_j)_{j=1}^\infty$ (whenever the right-hand side is finite).

Question. Must $(e_i)$ be equivalent to the unit vector basis of $c_0$ or of $\ell_1$? If not, give a characterization of all normalized monotone subsymmetric bases $(e_i)$ satisfying the above property.

representations.normalized:
Consider an industrial construction project that requires temporary access structures (scaffolding) to support multidisciplinary work crews over a planning horizon. Let the project consist of a finite set of work tasks T, each task t ∈ T characterized by a location, a required access elevation, a time window [s_t, e_t], and a discipline d_t ∈ D. Access to each task may be provided by one of several mutually exclusive options chosen from a set A, which includes:

(i) bulk (stick-built) scaffolding erected on site, with erection cost c^E and teardown cost c^T per unit volume;
(ii) modular scaffolding pre-assembled in a fabrication yard and shipped with project modules, with fabrication cost c^F, transport cost c^S, and reduced field assembly cost c^M;
(iii) permanent engineered platforms installed during initial construction, with capital cost c^P amortized over the asset life;
(iv) mobile elevated work platforms (e.g., JLG/scissor lifts), with rental cost c^R per unit time and operational constraints (footprint, reach, terrain).

A scaffold, once erected, may serve multiple tasks during its standing period; "teardown and rebuild" refers to dismantling a scaffold and later re-erecting an equivalent structure at the same location to serve a later task. Let x_{t,a} ∈ {0,1} indicate that task t is served by access option a ∈ A, and let y_{j,τ} ∈ {0,1} indicate that scaffold instance j is standing during period τ. Subject to:
(a) every task is served by exactly one feasible access option during its time window,
(b) capacity, reach, and safety constraints for each option,
(c) yard fabrication and shipment lead-time constraints linking option (ii) to module delivery schedules,
(d) constructability constraints determining when option (iii) can replace bulk scaffolding,

formulate and solve the mixed-integer optimization problem of minimizing total expected access cost

   min  Σ_j Σ_τ (c^E + c^T) y_{j,τ}·1{erect or teardown at τ} + Σ_t Σ_a c_{t,a} x_{t,a}

over all admissible assignments, with the additional structural requirements that the resulting plan (1) eliminates avoidable teardown–rebuild cycles, (2) coordinates multidiscipline task scheduling so that shared scaffolds serve overlapping disciplines, (3) maximizes the share of modular yard-built scaffolds shipped with project modules, (4) selects permanent platforms wherever life-cycle cost is lower than repeated bulk scaffolding, and (5) selects mobile elevated work platforms whenever their rental and operational cost dominates fixed scaffolding for the relevant task set.

Develop a tractable algorithmic framework (e.g., decomposition, heuristic, or approximation scheme) that produces provably near-optimal access plans for industrial-scale instances, and characterize the trade-off frontier between the five access strategies above.

representations.normalized:
Consider heavy-ion collisions at fixed-target energies on the order of about 10 GeV per nucleon (energies characteristic of dense, baryon-rich fireballs), in which strongly interacting matter is compressed to high baryon density. In such collisions, two competing scenarios for strange-hadron production are considered:

(a) A deconfined quark-gluon plasma (QGP) phase is transiently formed, and strange and antistrange quarks produced in the deconfined phase hadronize into the observed final-state strange (anti)baryons; or

(b) No deconfined phase is formed, and the observed strange-hadron abundances arise from chemical equilibration in a purely hadronic (confined) final state.

Assume that the specific entropy per baryon in the confined and deconfined scenarios is approximately equal at these energies, so that bulk thermodynamic observables alone cannot easily discriminate between (a) and (b).

The problem is twofold:

1. Determine whether a quark-gluon plasma is in fact formed in dense, baryon-rich fireballs produced in heavy-ion collisions at these energies.

2. Determine whether measurements of strange antibaryon production (for example, yields, ratios, and excitation functions of antihyperons such as $\bar{\Lambda}$, $\bar{\Xi}$, and $\bar{\Omega}$) provide observables that can rigorously discriminate scenario (a) from scenario (b), and exhibit explicit signatures (e.g. characteristic hierarchies of yield ratios or features of the energy-dependence) whose presence or absence in experimental data settles the question in (1).

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Subsequent literature notes that the experimental detector capability needed to measure strange antibaryons at the AGS only became available near the end of the AGS heavy-ion program, and the available results did not permit a convincing evaluation of QGP formation in baryon-rich fireballs at AGS energies. While strangeness and strange-antibaryon enhancement have since contributed to the QGP discovery narrative at higher (SPS/RHIC) energies, the specific AGS-energy question of QGP formation in dense baryon-rich matter remains without a definitive experimental resolution.

Let $R = \{A_1, \dots, A_n\}$ be a finite set of Boolean attributes, and let $\mathcal{D}$ be a database of transactions, where each transaction is a subset of $R$ (equivalently, a binary vector in $\{0,1\}^n$). For a subset $X \subseteq R$, the frequency $\mathrm{fr}(X, \mathcal{D})$ is the fraction of transactions in $\mathcal{D}$ that contain $X$. Fix a threshold $\sigma \in (0,1]$ and let $\mathcal{F}_\sigma(\mathcal{D}) = \{(X, \mathrm{fr}(X,\mathcal{D})) : X \subseteq R,\ \mathrm{fr}(X,\mathcal{D}) \geq \sigma\}$ be the collection of frequent sets together with their observed frequencies.

A standard way to use $\mathcal{F}_\sigma(\mathcal{D})$ to induce a probability distribution $P$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ is the maximum-entropy principle: choose $P$ to maximize the Shannon entropy $H(P) = -\sum_{t \in \{0,1\}^n} P(t)\log P(t)$ subject to the marginal constraints
$$\sum_{t : X \subseteq t} P(t) = \mathrm{fr}(X, \mathcal{D}) \qquad \text{for every } (X, \mathrm{fr}(X,\mathcal{D})) \in \mathcal{F}_\sigma(\mathcal{D}).$$

Problem: Identify and justify alternative principled methods—other than the maximum-entropy principle—for inducing a probability distribution on $\{0,1\}^n$ from the collection $\mathcal{F}_\sigma(\mathcal{D})$ of frequent sets and their frequencies. In particular, provide algorithms or variational principles (for example, based on minimum description length, Bayesian model averaging, distance minimization with respect to suitable divergences, or graphical-model fitting) that produce a distribution consistent (exactly or approximately) with the given frequent-set frequencies, and analyze their existence, uniqueness, computational tractability, and behaviour relative to the maximum-entropy solution.

The question is an open-ended research problem posed as an alternative-methods challenge. Subsequent work has explored related directions (e.g., MDL-based pattern set selection by Vreeken et al., Markov random field fitting to itemset constraints, and Bayesian approaches), but the problem as a general open-ended call for principled alternatives to maximum entropy for inducing distributions from frequent sets has no definitive closure, and is best regarded as open.

Let X be a Banach space. Denote by L(X) the Banach space of bounded linear operators on X (with the operator norm) and by K(X) its closed subspace of compact operators. For a closed subspace Y of a Banach space Z, write Y^⊥ = { g ∈ Z* : g|_Y = 0 } for its annihilator in the dual Z*.

Say that Y is a semi M-ideal in Z if for every g ∈ Z* with ‖g|_Y‖ = ‖g‖ and every h ∈ Y^⊥ one has
   ‖g + h‖ = ‖g‖ + ‖h‖.

Say that Y is an M-ideal in Z if Z* admits an ℓ_1-direct sum decomposition Z* = Y^⊥ ⊕_1 V for some closed subspace V ⊂ Z* (equivalently, every g ∈ Z* decomposes uniquely as g = v + h with v ∈ V, h ∈ Y^⊥, and ‖g‖ = ‖v‖ + ‖h‖). Every M-ideal is a semi M-ideal.

Question: Does there exist a Banach space X such that K(X) is a semi M-ideal in L(X) but K(X) is not an M-ideal in L(X)?

Consider a capital project execution setting in which a project can be designed and built either by (a) adopting a portfolio of industry-proven standardized designs and components, or (b) producing a fully customized design. Let the project outcome be described by a random vector R = (R_cost, R_time, R_quality, R_safety) of execution-risk metrics, with joint distribution F_S under the standardized strategy S and F_C under the customized strategy C. Assume that for each component random variable, lower values are preferred, and that decision-makers' preferences over outcomes can be encoded by a (possibly multi-attribute) utility functional U acting on the distribution of R.

Develop a rigorous quantitative framework that:

1. Defines a measurable "value of standardization" functional V(F_S, F_C) capturing the expected reduction in cost, schedule, quality, and safety risk attained by choosing S over C, under a stated multi-attribute utility model U and stated stochastic dominance or risk-measure criteria (e.g., expected utility, conditional value-at-risk, second-order stochastic dominance).

2. Specifies the statistical estimation procedure by which F_S and F_C, and hence V, are to be estimated from historical project execution data, including assumptions on data generation, identifiability, and confidence quantification.

3. Provides a formal communication scheme that maps the estimated functional V and its uncertainty into a decision-relevant summary (e.g., a set of certified inequalities, dominance statements, or risk-adjusted value scores) such that a decision-maker adopting the framework will, under stated rationality axioms, prefer S whenever V exceeds an explicit threshold.

Establish conditions under which the framework yields a provable, defensible demonstration that standardized designs reduce execution risk relative to customization, and characterize the limits of such a demonstration.

In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions (such as Pb–Pb collisions at the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron), one observes an enhanced production of strange antibaryons (anti-Λ, anti-Ξ, anti-Ω) relative to a baseline of proton–proton or proton–nucleus collisions scaled by the number of participating nucleons. A long-standing theoretical prediction asserts that such an enhancement, increasing with the strangeness content of the (anti)baryon, is a signature of a transient deconfined phase of matter (the quark–gluon plasma, QGP) in which colored quark and gluon degrees of freedom are locally liberated and chemically equilibrate strangeness on short timescales via gluon fusion.

Problem. Determine whether the observed pattern of strangeness production in high-energy nucleus–nucleus collisions, and in particular the hierarchical enhancement of multi-strange antibaryons, requires the formation of a locally color-deconfined phase (quark–gluon plasma) for its explanation, or whether it can be accounted for quantitatively by purely hadronic mechanisms (e.g., hadronic rescattering, canonical strangeness suppression in small systems, string-fusion or color-rope models, and baryon–antibaryon annihilation effects) without invoking deconfinement. Provide either (i) a hadronic-phase dynamical model that reproduces, within experimental uncertainties, the magnitudes, strangeness-hierarchy, system-size, energy, and centrality dependence of the measured strange and multi-strange (anti)baryon yields; or (ii) an argument showing that no such hadronic explanation is possible and that QGP formation is necessary.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent experimental and theoretical work, culminating in the CERN 2000 announcement and RHIC/LHC results, established a broad consensus that strange-antibaryon enhancement together with other observables is consistent with QGP formation in heavy-ion collisions; multi-strange hyperon enhancement is now widely considered an established QGP signature. representations.normalized:
Consider the delivery of large industrial capital projects (e.g., petrochemical plants, manufacturing facilities, power generation, and similar industrial infrastructure). The traditional, experience-based execution paradigm is the design-bid-build method, in which the owner first contracts a designer to complete the design, then solicits competitive bids from contractors based on the completed design, and finally awards the construction contract to a chosen contractor. This sequential approach is widely associated with adversarial relationships, fragmented information flow between stakeholders, frequent change orders, cost overruns, and schedule slippage.

A project delivery method is a system that defines the contractual relationships, risk allocation, and workflow integration among the project participants — owner, designers, general contractors, subcontractors, and specialty trade partners — and the timing of their engagement during a project's life cycle (planning, design, procurement, construction, commissioning, and operations).

Problem: Identify and characterize a best-practice project delivery method (or a precise combination of contractual, organizational, and procedural practices) for industrial projects that achieves all of the following objectives simultaneously:

1. Provides a step-change improvement over the design-bid-build paradigm rather than an incremental one.
2. Substantially improves collaboration among all project team members, including owner, designers, contractors, and trade partners, via early involvement, shared risk/reward, and aligned incentives.
3. Enables high predictability of final project cost and schedule relative to baseline estimates.
4. Systematically eliminates non-value-added activities, in alignment with lean construction principles.
5. Enables and integrates the use of modern technologies, including but not limited to building information modeling (BIM) in design, robotic layout and automation in construction, and augmented reality in operations and maintenance.

Specify the contractual structure, governance mechanisms, performance metrics, and implementation steps of the proposed delivery method, and provide a justification that the method meets criteria (1)–(5) for industrial-scale projects.

Let R = {A_1, ..., A_n} be a finite set of Boolean attributes, and let d be a binary data set consisting of N rows, where each row r ∈ d is a function r : R → {0,1}. For a subset X ⊆ R, define its support in d by

  s(X, d) = |{r ∈ d : r(A) = 1 for all A ∈ X}| / N,

i.e., the fraction of rows in which all attributes of X take value 1.

For a Boolean formula α over the attributes in R, let g(α, d) denote the fraction of rows of d that satisfy α. By a standard inclusion–exclusion expansion, g(α, d) can be written as a signed linear combination

  g(α, d) = Σ_{X ⊆ R} c_X(α) · s(X, d),

where the coefficients c_X(α) ∈ ℤ depend only on the formula α (and vanish for sets X not appearing in the expansion).

Given a family D of subsets of R (thought of as the "available" or frequent sets), define the truncated approximation

  g_D(α, d) = Σ_{X ∈ D} c_X(α) · s(X, d),

and the approximation error

  e(α, D, d) = | g(α, d) − g_D(α, d) |.

Problem. Provide tight upper bounds, as a function of structural properties of the collection D (such as its downward closure, maximum element size, antichain structure, or which subsets of supp(α) are missing) and of structural properties of the Boolean formula α (such as its size, number of terms, or DNF/CNF complexity), on the worst-case error

  sup_d  e(α, D, d),

where the supremum is taken over all binary data sets d on the attribute set R. In particular, identify conditions on D relative to α that guarantee e(α, D, d) = 0, and quantify how the error grows when those conditions fail.

Recall the following definitions:
(i) An injective operator T ∈ L(X,Y) is called a semi-embedding if T(B_X) is closed in Y.
(ii) An injective operator T ∈ L(X,Y) is called a Gδ-embedding if T(K) is a Gδ-subset of Y for every closed bounded set K ⊂ X.

Let L_1 = L_1[0,1] be the usual Lebesgue space. Suppose that there exists a Gδ-embedding from L_1 into a Banach space X.

Question: Must there then exist a semi-embedding from L_1 into X, i.e., an injective operator T ∈ L(L_1, X) such that T(B_{L_1}) is closed in X?

In ultra-relativistic nucleus–nucleus collisions, define the specific strangeness yield as the number of produced strange quark–antiquark pairs per unit of produced entropy (or, operationally, per produced pion). Empirically, in fixed-target heavy-ion collisions at CERN SPS energies (per-nucleon beam energies in the range of roughly 20–200 GeV), the specific strangeness yield is observed to rise rapidly with increasing center-of-mass collision energy and to vary strongly with the size of the colliding system (reaction volume).

Determine which of the following mechanisms is responsible for this rapid variation:

(a) The explored SPS energy range lies near the threshold of the deconfinement phase transition, so that the rapid change reflects the transition between hadronic matter and a deconfined quark–gluon phase as a function of energy and system size; or

(b) The deconfined phase is already produced throughout the relevant SPS regime, and the rapid variation of the specific strangeness yield is instead controlled by changes in the dynamics and lifetime of the hot, highly compressed deconfined quark matter as the collision energy and system size are varied.

Provide a quantitative, theoretically and experimentally supported identification of the dominant mechanism (or the relative contribution of each), specifying the role of the onset of deconfinement versus the role of fireball lifetime and dynamics in determining the specific strangeness yield at SPS energies.

Let $U$ be a finite set, and let $\mathcal{D} \subseteq 2^U$ be a downward-closed family of subsets of $U$ (that is, if $Y \in \mathcal{D}$ and $Z \subseteq Y$, then $Z \in \mathcal{D}$). Define the positive border of $\mathcal{D}$ as
$$\mathrm{Bd}^{+}(\mathcal{D}) = \{Y \in \mathcal{D} : \text{for every } Z \subseteq U \text{ with } Y \subsetneq Z,\ Z \notin \mathcal{D}\},$$
i.e. the maximal elements of $\mathcal{D}$, and the negative border as
$$\mathrm{Bd}^{-}(\mathcal{D}) = \{Y \subseteq U : Y \notin \mathcal{D}\text{ and every proper subset of } Y \text{ is in } \mathcal{D}\},$$
i.e. the minimal subsets of $U$ that do not lie in $\mathcal{D}$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite downward-closed collection $\mathcal{D}$,
$$\sum_{\emptyset \neq Y \in \mathcal{D}} (-1)^{|Y|+1} \;\le\; |\mathrm{Bd}^{+}(\mathcal{D})| + |\mathrm{Bd}^{-}(\mathcal{D})|.$$

Let $X$ be a real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|$ and let $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a normalized Schauder basis of $X$. For $x = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n(x)\, x_n \in X$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}$, a greedy $m$-term approximation of $x$ is any partial sum
$$G_m(x) = \sum_{n \in \Lambda} a_n(x)\, x_n,$$
where $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{N}$ is a set of cardinality $m$ such that $|a_n(x)| \ge |a_k(x)|$ for every $n \in \Lambda$ and every $k \notin \Lambda$ (with ties broken arbitrarily). The basis $(x_n)$ is called $1$-greedy if for every $x \in X$ and every $m \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$\|x - G_m(x)\| \le \inf\Big\{\Big\|x - \sum_{j \in \Lambda} \alpha_j x_j\Big\| : \Lambda \subset \mathbb{N},\ |\Lambda| = m,\ \alpha_j \in \mathbb{R}\Big\}.$$
The basis $(x_n)$ is called symmetric if there exists a constant $C \ge 1$ such that for every permutation $\pi$ of $\mathbb{N}$, every choice of signs $\varepsilon_n \in \{-1,+1\}$, and every finitely supported sequence of scalars $(a_n)$,
$$\Big\|\sum_n a_n x_n\Big\| \le C\,\Big\|\sum_n \varepsilon_n a_n x_{\pi(n)}\Big\|.$$
Construct an example of a Banach space $X$ with a normalized Schauder basis $(x_n)$ that is $1$-greedy but not symmetric.

The problem appears to be solved. The 2024 survey "Twenty-five years of greedy bases" reports that Dilworth and collaborators constructed an isometrically greedy (i.e., 1-greedy) subsymmetric basis that fails to be symmetric, providing a direct example. Furthermore, isometrically greedy bases that are not even subsymmetric are known: the Haar system in $L_p$ for $p\in(1,2)\cup(2,\infty)$ admits an equivalent norm under which it becomes 1-greedy, while it is not subsymmetric (hence not symmetric).

Consider the Critical Path Method (CPM) for project scheduling, in which a project is modeled as a directed acyclic graph G=(V,E) whose vertices represent activities with prescribed durations d:V→R_{≥0} and whose edges encode precedence constraints; the earliest start times are computed by a longest-path forward pass, the latest start times by a backward pass, and the critical path is the longest path determining the minimum total project duration. Contrast this with alternative, more collaborative scheduling paradigms used outside the traditional construction industry, such as the Last Planner System, pull-based/takt planning, and location-based scheduling, in which commitments are negotiated among trade participants, tasks are released by downstream readiness signals, and reliability of weekly work plans (measured for example by Percent Plan Complete) is tracked.

Formulate and answer the following:

(a) Define a precise comparison framework for evaluating the collaborative capabilities of CPM versus these alternative methods. In particular, propose quantitative metrics (for instance, number of independent participant decision variables, sensitivity of the schedule to local re-planning, propagation distance of a local change, and a formal notion of plan reliability) that can be evaluated on a common project graph model.

(b) Determine whether CPM, equipped with its standard forward/backward pass and float computations, admits an extension or modification that incorporates the collaborative features of these alternative methods while preserving its longest-path optimality guarantees; or prove that no such extension can simultaneously achieve both.

(c) Describe explicitly how the alternative collaborative methods can be combined with CPM in a hybrid scheduling algorithm, or used as a complete replacement, and analyze the resulting schedule with respect to the metrics defined in (a).

Concretely:

1. Let $D$ be a collection of $n$ documents over a vocabulary of $m$ terms, encoded as a sparse nonnegative term–document matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m \times n}$ (for example, by raw counts or by tf–idf weights). For an integer $k \ll \min(m,n)$, let $A_k$ denote the best rank-$k$ approximation of $A$ in the Frobenius (equivalently spectral) norm, obtained by truncating the singular value decomposition $A = U \Sigma V^{\top}$ to its $k$ largest singular values; this defines the latent semantic indexing (LSI) representation of terms and documents in $\mathbb{R}^k$, in which document and query similarities are measured by inner products of their projected vectors.

Provide a rigorous theoretical explanation for the empirical effectiveness of LSI on high-dimensional sparse discrete data. Specifically: identify a generative or structural model of term–document data (for example, a probabilistic topic-mixture model with a small number of latent topics, possibly with polysemy and synonymy) under which one can prove that truncated SVD of the discrete observation matrix recovers, with high probability and quantitative error bounds, the underlying low-dimensional semantic structure, and consequently preserves or enhances the relevant similarity relationships between documents and queries despite the data being discrete, sparse, and noisy.

Partial theoretical explanations exist. Papadimitriou, Raghavan, Tamaki and Vempala gave a probabilistic analysis of LSI under a corpus-generation model showing that SVD recovers latent topics with high probability under suitable separability assumptions. Hofmann's probabilistic LSI and subsequent topic-model analyses (LDA, nonnegative matrix factorization recovery results by Arora et al., and Ding–Rohe–Zhu type spectral analyses) provide further model-based justifications. A fully general theoretical account of LSI's effectiveness on arbitrary discrete data, however, is not established; results are model-dependent.

representations.normalized:
Consider a capital construction project with a finite planning horizon partitioned into discrete time periods t = 1, ..., T, and a finite set I of material and equipment item types required to execute the project. The project is decomposed into a set W of advanced work packages, each work package w ∈ W having a scheduled execution window [s_w, e_w] ⊆ {1, ..., T} and a demand vector d_{w,i} ≥ 0 specifying the quantity of item i ∈ I required to complete w. For each item i, suppliers offer two delivery strategies:

(JIT) Just-in-time: an order of size q places the items on site at the period of consumption, at unit acquisition cost c_i^{JIT}, with stochastic lead time L_i^{JIT} of known distribution, and a probability ρ_i(q) of a delivery disruption causing a delay of random length D_i.

(JIC) Just-in-case: an order of size q places items on site well ahead of consumption, at unit acquisition cost c_i^{JIC} ≤ c_i^{JIT}, but incurs holding cost h_i per unit per period of on-site storage, and capital tie-up cost α·c_i^{JIC} per unit per period.

Let x_{w,i} ∈ [0,1] denote the fraction of demand d_{w,i} fulfilled via the JIT strategy and 1 − x_{w,i} the fraction via JIC. Let S(x) denote the (random) project completion time induced by the strategy vector x = (x_{w,i}), determined by the critical-path scheduling of work packages subject to material-availability constraints derived from realized lead times and disruptions. Let C(x) denote the expected total cost

C(x) = E[ Σ_{w,i} ( x_{w,i} c_i^{JIT} + (1 − x_{w,i}) (c_i^{JIC} + (h_i + α c_i^{JIC}) τ_{w,i}) ) d_{w,i} + π · max(0, S(x) − T*) ],

where τ_{w,i} is the on-site holding duration under JIC for item i in package w, T* is the contractual completion deadline, and π is the per-period schedule-overrun penalty.

Problem. Devise an analytical (algorithmic) procedure that, given the data (T, I, W, {d_{w,i}}, {s_w, e_w}, lead-time and disruption distributions, costs c_i^{JIT}, c_i^{JIC}, h_i, α, π, T*), produces a strategy vector x* ∈ [0,1]^{|W|·|I|} minimizing C(x) subject to the chance constraint

P( S(x) ≤ T* ) ≥ 1 − ε,

for a prescribed reliability level 1 − ε ∈ (0,1). Establish structural properties of optimal solutions (e.g., conditions under which a pure JIT or pure JIC policy is optimal for a given item class), and provide a tractable solution method together with provable performance guarantees relative to the true stochastic optimum.

Consider a capital project executed under the engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) delivery model, in which a project owner contracts a single entity to (i) perform detailed engineering design, (ii) procure all required materials and equipment, and (iii) construct the facility in the field. Let the work process be modeled as a directed workflow graph W = (V, E), where each vertex v ∈ V represents a discrete work activity (e.g., produce a design deliverable, issue a purchase order, fabricate, install) carried out by some role r(v) belonging to engineering, procurement, or construction, and each edge (u, v) ∈ E represents a transfer of information, materials, or authorization from activity u to activity v. Associate to each activity v a duration d(v) ≥ 0, a cost c(v) ≥ 0, and a defect/rework probability ρ(v) ∈ [0,1]; associate to each edge (u, v) an information-transfer latency ℓ(u,v) ≥ 0 and a fidelity loss φ(u,v) ∈ [0,1] capturing degradation between the engineering representation produced upstream and the representation usable in the field downstream.

Assume the availability of a fixed set T of contemporary design and communication technologies (for example, model-based design with structured 3D/4D/5D data, cloud-based collaboration platforms, mobile field access, automated clash detection, and direct model-to-fabrication or model-to-installation data exchange). Each technology t ∈ T, when applied to a subset of activities and edges, induces transformations of d, c, ρ, ℓ, and φ subject to specified adoption constraints and interface requirements.

Problem: Construct a redesigned EPC workflow graph W* = (V*, E*) together with an assignment of technologies from T to its activities and edges that minimizes a chosen objective combining total project duration, total project cost, expected rework, and end-to-end information fidelity loss from engineering design to field execution, subject to (a) all functional requirements of design, procurement, and construction being satisfied, (b) feasibility and interoperability constraints among the chosen technologies, and (c) preservation of regulatory, safety, and quality obligations. Characterize the structural features (activity decomposition, sequencing, hand-offs, information artifacts, and technology choices) that any optimal or Pareto-optimal redesigned process must possess in order to achieve more efficient and effective transfer of engineering design information to the field than the conventional EPC process.

Within the framework of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3) non-abelian gauge theory of quarks and gluons, determine:

(a) the non-perturbative structure of the QCD vacuum (including condensates such as the quark condensate ⟨q̄q⟩ and the gluon condensate ⟨G_{μν}^a G^{μν,a}⟩, as well as topological structure) as a function of baryon chemical potential μ_B at zero or low temperature; and

(b) the order, location, and thermodynamic properties (e.g., critical exponents, latent heat, surface tension, and order parameters distinguishing color confinement from deconfinement) of the confinement–deconfinement phase transition of QCD matter at finite baryon density, as a function of (T, μ_B).

Provide a quantitative description of how the vacuum structure rearranges across this transition and characterize the boundary in the (T, μ_B) plane separating the confined (hadronic) phase from the deconfined (quark–gluon) phase.

The structure of the QCD vacuum and the nature of the confinement–deconfinement transition at finite baryon density remain open problems. Let R be a relation schema, and let D(R) denote the class of all finite data sets (instances) over R. A Boolean query on D(R) is a function β : D(R) → {0,1}. Fix a class Q of Boolean queries on D(R) and a positive integer k.

Determine k Boolean queries α₁, …, α_k on D(R) (not required to belong to Q) with the following property: there exists a function F : {0,1}^k × Q → {0,1} such that, for every data set d ∈ D(R) and every query β ∈ Q,
   β(d) = F(α₁(d), …, α_k(d), β).
That is, the k bits (α₁(d), …, α_k(d)) constitute a sufficient summary of d for answering every query in Q.

Equivalently, find α₁, …, α_k such that whenever two data sets d, d′ ∈ D(R) satisfy α_i(d) = α_i(d′) for all i = 1, …, k, then β(d) = β(d′) for all β ∈ Q.

Characterize, for a given schema R, query class Q, and integer k, when such α₁, …, α_k exist, and provide a method for constructing them when they do.

Definition. For an integer m with 1 ≤ m < n, a compact set K ⊂ R^n is called m-convex if for every point x ∈ R^n \ K there exists an affine m-dimensional plane T(x) ⊂ R^n with x ∈ T(x) and T(x) ∩ K = ∅.

Problem. Let K ⊂ R^n be a compact set such that for every affine hyperplane T ⊂ R^n the intersection T ∩ K is (m−1)-convex (as a compact subset of T ≅ R^{n−1}, in the sense above). Find an additional geometric or topological condition on K which, combined with this hyperplane-section hypothesis, is sufficient to ensure that K itself is m-convex.

Consider an industrial facility (e.g., a refinery, petrochemical plant, or power generation unit) that periodically undergoes a planned Shutdown/Turnaround/Outage (STO): a major, scheduled event during which operations are halted so that inspection, maintenance, repair, and capital project work can be performed simultaneously across many interconnected systems. An STO is characterized by a large, temporary workforce, tight schedule constraints, significant safety risk, and substantial financial impact due to lost production.

Formulate, justify, and validate:

(a) An organizational and management methodology for the execution phase of an STO. The methodology should specify (i) the governance and decision-making structure (roles, responsibilities, escalation paths), (ii) the work-breakdown and scheduling framework used to coordinate concurrent maintenance, inspection, and capital activities, (iii) the resource-allocation and contractor-management procedures, (iv) the change-control and risk-management processes employed when scope, schedule, or safety conditions deviate from plan, and (v) the communication and reporting cadence linking field execution to project leadership.

(b) A set of performance metrics (key performance indicators) for monitoring and assessing STO execution. For each metric, give a precise quantitative definition (formula, units, data sources, measurement frequency), explain which aspect of execution it captures (e.g., schedule adherence, cost performance, safety, quality/rework, productivity, scope stability, startup reliability), and describe target values or benchmarks against which it should be compared.

Provide a method that allows quantitative comparison of alternative execution methodologies on the basis of these metrics, and demonstrate, with reasoning grounded in operational data or accepted benchmarking practice, that the proposed methodology and metric set are superior to plausible alternatives.

Consider a brane-world compactification of the form $M_4 \times K$, where $M_4$ is four-dimensional spacetime and $K$ is a compact internal manifold with one or more codimension-$\geq 2$ branes (defects) of arbitrary tension $T$ supported on submanifolds of $K$. Write the higher-dimensional metric in warped form
$$ds^2 = e^{2A(y)}\,\eta_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu dx^\nu + \tilde g_{mn}(y)\,dy^m dy^n,$$
with the warp factor $A$ and internal metric $\tilde g$ depending only on the transverse coordinates $y\in K$. The Einstein equations are sourced by a bulk cosmological constant (possibly arising from fluxes or a bulk supergravity sector) together with delta-function brane stress-energies of tension $T$. A "Rubakov–Shaposhnikov absorption" of the brane tension is a smooth one-parameter family of regular solutions $(\tilde g(y;T), A(y;T))$ on the closed manifold $K$ for which $M_4$ remains exactly Ricci-flat for a continuous range of $T$.

(a) For $K$ closed and one-dimensional (codimension 1), determine whether any global solution of the bulk Einstein equations with prescribed boundary/junction conditions at the brane loci can absorb a continuous range of brane tensions $T$ into the transverse curvature while keeping $M_4$ flat, or whether sum rules (integrated Einstein equations / Gauss–Bonnet-type identities on $K$) obstruct such solutions and force a fine-tuning between $T$ and the bulk parameters.

(b) For a codimension-2 brane embedded in a closed two-dimensional internal space $K$, with a conical deficit angle $\delta(T)$ generated by the brane tension, determine whether the global Gauss–Bonnet constraint
$$\int_K \tilde R\,\sqrt{\tilde g}\,d^2y + \sum_i \delta_i(T_i) = 4\pi\chi(K),$$
together with regularity of $\tilde g$ and $A$ at all brane positions and away from them, allows a continuous family of solutions absorbing arbitrary tension $T$, or whether only a discrete set of tensions is compatible with closure of $K$ (so that no continuous modulus exists to absorb a generic supersymmetry-breaking tension shift).

(c) Determine the minimal codimension (in particular whether codimension $\geq 3$ is required) of the transverse space for which a continuous absorption modulus exists, allowing arbitrary brane tension to be absorbed into the internal geometry without reintroducing fine-tuning of the four-dimensional cosmological constant.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether transverse curvature can absorb brane tension in a self-tuning way—without fine-tuning of the four-dimensional cosmological constant—remains an active and unresolved problem. Codimension-1 self-tuning proposals are known to suffer from global obstructions / hidden fine-tunings, and while codimension-2 (6D supergravity) constructions have been studied extensively (e.g., "accidental SUSY" and related works), it is still open whether bulk supersymmetry guarantees stability and whether a continuous absorption modulus exists; the issue of deficit-angle sum rules forcing a discrete spectrum of admissible tensions is widely acknowledged.

Consider a capital project that progresses through a sequence of front-end loading (FEL) phases FEL-1, FEL-2, FEL-3, each terminating in a stage-gate decision at which approvers must decide whether to advance the project, rework it, or cancel it. Let the state of engineering at the end of FEL phase k be described by a deliverables vector D_k = (d_k^{(1)}, ..., d_k^{(n)}) whose components represent the completion levels and quality of engineering deliverables (process flow diagrams, P&IDs, equipment lists, plot plans, specifications, etc.), and let C be the (random) final installed cost and S the (random) final schedule duration of the project.

Define:
(i) the maturity M_k ∈ [0,1] of front-end engineering design (FEED) at gate k as a scalar functional M_k = M(D_k) that captures the degree of definition of the engineering scope;
(ii) the accuracy A_k of the estimate at gate k as a probabilistic description of the conditional distribution of (C, S) given D_k, summarized for example by the conditional standard deviations σ_C(D_k), σ_S(D_k), or by predictive intervals at prescribed confidence levels.

The problem is to:
1. Construct a rigorous, reproducible quantitative definition of the maturity functional M(D_k) and of the accuracy measure A_k, based on observable engineering deliverable attributes, that is consistent across projects and project types.
2. Establish the relationship between M_k and A_k, including conditions under which higher maturity implies a provably tighter predictive distribution of (C, S).
3. Design a communication scheme (a small set of summary statistics or visual encodings) that conveys both M_k and A_k to stage-gate decision-makers in a way that supports an optimal go/no-go/rework decision rule minimizing the expected loss
   E[ L(decision; C, S) | D_k ],
   for a specified loss function L, and prove that the proposed scheme is sufficient for this decision problem (i.e., no information relevant to the optimal decision is lost by reporting only the proposed summaries).

Provide explicit constructions of M and A, the proof of sufficiency, and a validation methodology using historical project data.

The question is a broad industry research problem about quantifying engineering maturity and estimate accuracy in front-end loading phases of capital projects. Frameworks such as the Construction Industry Institute's PDRI (Project Definition Rating Index) and AACE International's cost estimate classification system (e.g., Recommended Practice 18R-97) provide partial, widely used heuristics, but there is no agreed-upon rigorous quantitative theory linking FEED maturity to predictive accuracy and stage-gate decision optimality. The problem appears to remain open as a research question.

Consider a compact brane-world model in which our four-dimensional universe is realized as a 3-brane embedded in a higher-dimensional bulk with at least two transverse spatial dimensions. Assume the bulk theory is supersymmetric, while supersymmetry is broken on the brane, generating a brane vacuum energy of order the supersymmetry-breaking scale. Suppose the higher-dimensional Einstein equations admit a one-parameter family of static classical solutions, labeled by the four-dimensional cosmological constant k, in which the brane tension is balanced by curvature of the transverse compact dimensions; in particular, there exists a "flat" branch with k = 0 in which the brane vacuum energy is absorbed entirely into the transverse curvature, together with nearby solutions having k ≠ 0 in which the four-dimensional slices are curved (de Sitter or anti-de Sitter).

(a) Determine whether bulk supersymmetry alone is sufficient to guarantee that, once brane supersymmetry breaking backreacts on the bulk geometry, the k = 0 solution is dynamically stable within this family.

(b) Compute, or characterize qualitatively, the effective potential V(k) for the modulus k that is induced by quantum loop corrections (including those suppressed by Newton's constant), and decide whether V(k) is necessarily minimized at k = 0, or whether its minimum can lie at some k ≠ 0.

Provide a dynamical selection mechanism that singles out the phenomenologically required k = 0 branch, or else show that no such mechanism exists within the stated assumptions.

Searches indicate the problem of dynamically selecting the k=0 branch among the family of nearby curved brane-world solutions, and of showing that loop-induced potentials for the modulus k are minimized at k=0, remains an open question in the literature on brane supersymmetry breaking. Concretely: propose a mathematical formalism that (i) defines the basic objects of data mining (datasets, patterns, models, queries, and the notion of "interestingness" of a discovered pattern), (ii) unifies the principal tasks of data mining (association rule discovery, clustering, classification, frequent pattern mining, and anomaly detection) within a single language, (iii) provides a notion of algorithmic correctness and complexity for mining procedures, including how local patterns relate to global models, (iv) admits meaningful statistical guarantees (e.g., generalization, significance, or false-discovery control) for patterns extracted from finite samples, and (v) supports compositional reasoning so that mining operators can be combined, optimized, and reasoned about as in a query algebra. A bounded linear operator $T: X \to Y$ between Banach spaces is called nuclear if it admits a representation
$$T(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} x_n^*(x)\, y_n, \qquad x \in X,$$
with $x_n^* \in X^*$, $y_n \in Y$, and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \|x_n^*\|\,\|y_n\| < \infty$. The operator $T$ is called compact if the image of the closed unit ball of $X$ has compact closure in $Y$. Every nuclear operator is compact, but in general the converse fails.

Question: Do there exist infinite-dimensional Banach spaces $X$ and $Y$ such that every compact linear operator $T: X \to Y$ is nuclear?
representations.original:
A bounded linear operator $T: X \to Y$ between Banach spaces is called nuclear if it admits a representation
$$T(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} x_n^*(x)\, y_n, \qquad x \in X,$$
with $x_n^* \in X^*$, $y_n \in Y$, and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \|x_n^*\|\,\|y_n\| < \infty$. The operator $T$ is called compact if the image of the closed unit ball of $X$ has compact closure in $Y$. Every nuclear operator is compact, but in general the converse fails.

Question: Do there exist infinite-dimensional Banach spaces $X$ and $Y$ such that every compact linear operator $T: X \to Y$ is nuclear?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is settled affirmatively. Grothendieck (1955) conjectured that for any infinite-dimensional Banach spaces $X,Y$ there must exist a bounded operator $X\to Y$ that is not nuclear (and in particular asked the compact-vs-nuclear version). In 1983 G. Pisier constructed an infinite-dimensional Banach space $P$ for which the projective and injective tensor norms coincide on $P\otimes P$, which yields infinite-dimensional Banach spaces such that every compact (indeed every bounded) operator between them is nuclear, disproving Grothendieck's conjecture and answering the question in the affirmative.

  Str M^2_bulk = Σ_J (-1)^{2J} (2J+1) Tr M^2_J,

summed over all bulk fields of spin J. Phenomenological viability (in particular, an induced four-dimensional curvature that is not parametrically of solar-system scale) requires the consistency condition

  Str M^2_bulk = 0,

which is not automatically enforced by local bulk supersymmetry once the brane sector breaks all supersymmetries.

Problem: For each candidate non-BPS soliton background realizing such a brane-world scenario, compute the complete bulk Kaluza–Klein spectrum and determine whether the condition Str M^2_bulk = 0 holds without fine-tuning. Classify which backgrounds (if any) satisfy this vanishing supertrace identity.

representations.normalized:
Consider the extreme Reissner–Nordström (ERN) black hole solution of four-dimensional Einstein–Maxwell theory embedded as the bosonic sector of N=2, d=4 supergravity. The metric depends on the ADM mass M and electric/magnetic charges (Q,P); the extreme limit is reached when the BPS bound M = |Z| = |Q+iP| is saturated and the two horizons of Reissner–Nordström coincide at r_H = M, giving horizon area A = 4πM².

Three different prescriptions assign an entropy to this black hole:
(i) The Euclidean semiclassical action computed by taking the extremal limit ab initio (with arbitrary period for Euclidean time, and topology distinct from the non-extreme case) yields S = 0, consistent with a strong form of the third law of thermodynamics.
(ii) Microscopic state counting of BPS states in string theory yields S = A/4 = πM².
(iii) The Bekenstein–Hawking area law applied directly to the extreme horizon also gives S = πM².

Problem. Determine which of these prescriptions assigns the physically correct thermodynamic entropy to the extreme Reissner–Nordström black hole, and characterize precisely the conditions (in terms of the near-horizon geometry, Euclidean topology, choice of ensemble, and the limit T→0 of the temperature) under which the semiclassical Euclidean derivation that yields S = 0 is valid, and the conditions under which it breaks down so that the area-law / microscopic value S = πM² is recovered. In particular, decide whether the discrepancy reflects a genuine breakdown of the semiclassical near-horizon description at zero temperature or merely an inequivalent choice of boundary conditions in the path integral.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The discrepancy has been clarified but is not universally regarded as fully settled. String-theoretic BPS state counting (Strominger–Vafa and successors) supports S = A/4 = πM² for extremal charged black holes, and this is now the widely accepted physical value. The S = 0 result of the Euclidean semiclassical computation has been attributed to subtleties of the extremal topology (arbitrary Euclidean time periodicity, distinct topology from the non-extreme case) and to taking the extremal limit before quantization; recent works (e.g., 2505.16309) re-examine the nonextremal-to-extremal limit and recover the area law. Conceptual analyses (e.g., 1904.03232) continue to debate whether the semiclassical near-horizon description genuinely breaks down at T = 0.

A Banach space $X$ is said to have the approximation property (AP) if for every compact subset $K \subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a bounded finite-rank linear operator $T : X \to X$ such that $\|Tx - x\| < \varepsilon$ for all $x \in K$. Equivalently, the identity operator on $X$ can be approximated uniformly on compact sets by finite-rank operators. A Banach space $X$ is said to have the hereditary approximation property if every closed (infinite-dimensional) subspace of $X$ has the approximation property.

Question: Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space that is not isomorphic to a Hilbert space. Must $X$ contain a closed infinite-dimensional subspace that fails to have the approximation property?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is answered in the negative. Johnson and Szankowski (Annals of Mathematics, 2012, "Hereditary approximation property") constructed an infinite-dimensional Banach space, not isomorphic to a Hilbert space (in fact with a symmetric basis and not even asymptotically Hilbertian), all of whose closed infinite-dimensional subspaces have the approximation property. Thus there exist non-Hilbertian Banach spaces without any subspace failing AP.

Consider four-dimensional N=2 supergravity coupled to vector multiplets, and the family of stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat black-hole-type solutions characterized by mass M, electric charge Q, magnetic charge P, and angular momentum J. The Bogomol'nyi (BPS) bound takes the form M ≥ |Q + iP| and does not involve J, while the extremality (no-naked-singularity) bound is more restrictive once J ≠ 0: an extreme Reissner–Nordström-like configuration saturating M = |Q + iP| but carrying nonzero angular momentum lies beyond its extremality limit and exhibits naked singularities, yet is still permitted by the supersymmetry algebra.

(a) Identify a general principle, intrinsic to classical (super)gravity, that would enforce cosmic censorship for such stationary rotating BPS-saturating configurations, ruling out those with naked singularities even though they saturate the Bogomol'nyi bound.

(b) Determine whether the microscopic counting/state-building rules of string theory (for instance, the requirement that angular momentum be added only by exciting fermionic degrees of freedom, which simultaneously increase the mass) can be shown, in full generality, to (i) forbid configurations with J ≠ 0 that saturate M = |Q + iP|, and (ii) instead force exact saturation of the appropriate extremality bound that includes J, so that the extremality bound is never exceeded.

Provide either a proof of such a principle and a matching microscopic derivation, or a counterexample.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of why angular momentum must respect the extremality (rather than just the BPS) bound, and a general gravitational principle enforcing cosmic censorship for rotating supersymmetric configurations, remains an open conceptual problem. representations.normalized:
Augmented Reality (AR) refers to interactive technologies that overlay computer-generated sensory content (visual, auditory, or haptic) onto a user's perception of the real physical environment in real time. Serious Gaming (SG) refers to the use of game-based mechanics, simulations, and interactive virtual environments designed for purposes beyond entertainment, such as training, decision support, planning, safety education, and collaboration. Together, these are referred to as ARSG approaches.

The construction industry encompasses activities such as design, planning, scheduling, cost estimation, on-site execution, safety management, workforce training, quality control, inspection, and stakeholder coordination across the life cycle of built assets.

Problem: Systematically identify and characterize the opportunities for implementing ARSG approaches in the construction industry. Specifically:

1. Enumerate concrete classes of construction tasks, processes, or decision problems (across design, training, safety, planning/scheduling, on-site execution, inspection, and stakeholder communication) where ARSG approaches can plausibly improve project outcomes.

2. For each identified opportunity, specify (a) which ARSG modality is most suitable (e.g., marker-based AR, markerless AR, mixed-reality headsets, mobile AR, immersive serious games, multiplayer simulation-based training), (b) the data and model inputs required (e.g., BIM models, point clouds, schedules, cost data, sensor feeds), and (c) the project outcome metrics expected to be improved (e.g., schedule adherence, cost overrun reduction, safety incident rates, defect rates, training effectiveness, decision quality).

3. Identify the technical, organizational, and human-factors barriers to adoption, and propose research directions or experimental protocols that could validate whether the proposed ARSG implementations actually yield measurable improvements in the chosen outcome metrics.

Model-based engineering replaces traditional document-centric deliverables with integrated digital models that evolve continuously throughout a project. In this paradigm, the form of engineering output, its scheduling, and the way value is delivered differ fundamentally from those in document-based workflows, so conventional productivity ratios (e.g., direct engineering work hours per issued-for-construction quantity) do not straightforwardly apply.

Formulate a rigorous, generally applicable framework for quantifying engineering productivity in a model-based engineering setting. Specifically, propose:

(a) A precise definition of "engineering output" suitable for model-based deliverables, taking into account model maturity levels, completeness, fidelity, reuse, and interoperability.

(b) A productivity measure P, expressed as a function of measurable inputs (e.g., labor hours, computational resources, tool usage) and outputs defined in (a), that is:
    - well-defined and reproducible across projects and organizations,
    - sensitive to changes in model maturity and information content over time,
    - comparable in a meaningful way to legacy document-based productivity measures during the industry's transition period.

(c) A validation methodology that demonstrates the proposed measure correctly reflects productivity gains or losses on representative engineering projects.

Provide the framework, prove (or argue rigorously) that it satisfies the stated properties, and identify the conditions under which the measure is consistent across organizations adopting model-based engineering at differing levels of maturity.

representations.normalized:
Consider a four-dimensional supergravity theory containing gravity, gauge fields, and scalar fields, with known fermionic supersymmetry transformation laws δψ for the gravitino and δχ for the spin-1/2 fields. The standard Witten–Nester construction associates to a spinor field ε satisfying suitable asymptotic conditions a 2-form whose integral over a sphere at spatial infinity gives the ADM mass minus a sum of central-charge contributions (electric, magnetic, etc.), and whose exterior derivative is a manifestly non-negative bulk quadratic form in the supersymmetry variations δψ and δχ. This yields generalized Bogomol'nyi (BPS) bounds of the schematic form

   M ≥ F(Q_e, Q_m, …),

with saturation when ε is a Killing spinor.

A scalar field φ that is not protected by a gauge symmetry can carry a non-conserved "primary scalar charge" Σ defined by the asymptotic expansion φ = φ_∞ + Σ/r + O(1/r²). In known examples (e.g. the massless dilaton coupled to Einstein–Maxwell with action ∫(R − 2(∂φ)² − e^{−2aφ}F²) √(−g) d⁴x), configurations carrying non-trivial Σ independent of the electric/magnetic charges generically possess naked singularities and violate the standard no-hair theorems.

Problem. Formulate and rigorously prove a generalized Bogomol'nyi bound of the form

   M ≥ G(Q_e, Q_m, Σ, …)

in such a supergravity theory, derived via a Nester-type 2-form constructed from the fermionic SUSY transformation laws, in which the primary scalar charge Σ appears explicitly on the right-hand side. The derivation must allow boundary conditions on the spinor ε and on the spacetime fields that are sufficiently general to admit the naked singularities implied by non-trivial primary scalar hair, while still yielding a positive-semidefinite bulk integrand and a well-defined boundary integral at infinity. Determine the precise function G and characterize the configurations saturating the bound.

Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional (real or complex) Banach space. A sequence $(x_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ in a Banach space is called a Schauder basic sequence if every vector in its closed linear span has a unique expansion as a norm-convergent series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n x_n$. Such a basic sequence is called unconditional if there exists a constant $C \geq 1$ such that for every finitely supported scalar sequence $(a_n)$ and every choice of signs $(\varepsilon_n) \in \{-1,+1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$,
$$\Big\| \sum_n \varepsilon_n a_n x_n \Big\| \leq C \Big\| \sum_n a_n x_n \Big\|.$$
Equivalently, an infinite-dimensional closed subspace $Y \subseteq X$ is said to have an unconditional basis if it admits a Schauder basis that is unconditional.

Question: Must every infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ contain an infinite-dimensional closed subspace with an unconditional basis?

Consider a project that consists of two overlapping phases: an engineering (design) phase E and a construction phase C. The engineering phase produces a sequence of deliverables (drawings, specifications, procurement packages) over time, while the construction phase consumes those deliverables as inputs in order to execute work on site. Let E(t) denote the cumulative fraction (in [0,1]) of total engineering work completed by time t, and let C(t) denote the cumulative fraction of construction work completed by time t. Construction can begin at a start time t_s ≥ 0 only after some prerequisite fraction α = E(t_s) of engineering has been completed. After t_s, both phases proceed in parallel until E(T_E) = 1 and C(T_C) = 1.

Assume:
(i) Construction progress at any time t ≥ t_s is constrained by the engineering buffer, i.e. C(t) ≤ E(t − τ) for some processing lag τ ≥ 0 (so construction cannot consume engineering deliverables that have not yet been produced).
(ii) If at any time after t_s the construction work front catches up to the engineering deliverable front, the construction crew is forced to stop or slow down (a flow disruption).
(iii) Engineering and construction proceed at maximum sustainable rates r_E and r_C respectively (possibly time-varying within known bounds).

Determine the minimum value of α ∈ [0,1] — the fraction of engineering that must be completed before construction is allowed to start — such that, under the modeling assumptions (i)–(iii), construction can proceed from t_s to project completion without any forced stoppage caused by waiting on engineering deliverables. Provide α as a function of the rate parameters (r_E, r_C), the lag τ, and the total durations, together with conditions under which such an α exists.

Consider the low-energy effective field theory limit of string theory, which (in a given background) takes the form of a supergravity action coupled to a finite collection of moduli/dilaton-like scalar fields, gauge fields and fermions, together with a spectrum of fundamental microscopic objects (strings, D-branes, NS5-branes, Kaluza-Klein modes, momentum modes, bound states thereof). A static, asymptotically flat, four-dimensional supergravity solution is said to carry "primary scalar hair" if it possesses one or more scalar charges Σ_i (defined via the asymptotic expansion φ_i(r) = φ_i^∞ + Σ_i/r + O(1/r^2) of the canonically normalized scalars at spatial infinity) that are independent free parameters of the solution, not fixed as functions of the mass, angular momentum, and conserved gauge charges (in contrast to "secondary hair," in which Σ_i is determined by these other charges). Many such low-energy solutions exhibit naked singularities.

Problem. Determine whether full (non-perturbative) string theory contains microscopic sources—i.e., admissible configurations of its elementary degrees of freedom (fundamental strings, D-branes, solitonic branes, and their bound states), possibly together with consistent boundary conditions on the moduli at infinity—that can act as sources for primary scalar hair in the above sense. Equivalently: either (a) exhibit an explicit microscopic string-theoretic construction whose long-distance fields realize a supergravity solution with a non-trivial independent scalar charge Σ_i not fixed by the mass and gauge charges; or (b) prove that no such microscopic source exists, thereby establishing that the corresponding low-energy supergravity solutions with primary scalar hair (and their associated naked singularities) are excluded from the string-theory landscape.

The question of whether string theory admits microscopic sources for primary scalar hair remains unresolved. Recent work continues to construct gravitational solutions with primary scalar hair in modified gravity (e.g. Beyond Horndeski, Einstein-Weyl-Maxwell-conformal scalar theories) but does not produce an explicit microscopic string-theoretic source. Likewise, ongoing programs on black-hole "hair modes" and microscopic counting in string theory have not settled whether primary scalar hair can arise from fundamental string degrees of freedom, nor have they ruled it out. No definitive answer was found in the search.

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ (for instance the periodic torus $\mathbb{T}^3$),
$$\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u = -\nabla p + \nu \Delta u + f, \qquad \nabla \cdot u = 0,$$
where $u : \Omega \times [0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field, $p$ is the pressure, $\nu > 0$ is the kinematic viscosity, and $f$ is a (possibly stochastic or deterministic) forcing. For sufficiently high Reynolds number the resulting dynamics is widely observed to be turbulent and chaotic, and the long-time behaviour is governed by a complicated attracting set in an infinite-dimensional phase space.

Several mathematical frameworks have been proposed as effective descriptions of such chaotic/turbulent dynamics, including: (i) Reynolds averaging, in which one decomposes $u = \bar u + u'$ and derives evolution equations for the mean, leading to the (unclosed) Reynolds-stress closure problem; (ii) fractal/Hausdorff/box-counting dimension of the global attractor; (iii) Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen (SRB) measures, i.e. invariant measures whose conditional distributions on unstable manifolds are absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, used to describe statistical asymptotics of chaotic flows; (iv) Smale horseshoes embedded in the dynamics, providing symbolic-dynamics descriptions of chaos; and (v) shadowing, where true orbits remain close to numerically computed pseudo-orbits.

Problem. Produce a mathematically rigorous and quantitatively effective description of the chaotic/turbulent long-time dynamics of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations that
(a) is well-defined for the full turbulent regime (high Reynolds number),
(b) yields closed, computable predictions for statistical observables (mean flow, correlations, energy spectra, transport coefficients, etc.) suitable for engineering use, and
(c) avoids the limitations of the existing candidates above: in particular, it should resolve or bypass the closure problem of Reynolds averaging, it should produce engineering-relevant quantities (unlike bare fractal dimension), it should not depend on the existence of an SRB measure that is not known to exist for generic Navier–Stokes flows, and it should not require shadowing the entire turbulent attractor at currently infeasible computational cost.

Equivalently: identify and rigorously justify a notion of "averaging" (or alternative effective description) of chaotic/turbulent Navier–Stokes dynamics whose outputs are both mathematically meaningful and practically useful.

Let X be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. A Schauder basis (e_n) of X is called symmetric if for every permutation π of the positive integers, the sequence (e_{π(n)}) is also a Schauder basis of X equivalent to (e_n); equivalently, there is a constant C ≥ 1 such that for every permutation π, every choice of signs (ε_n) ∈ {−1, +1}^N, every finitely supported scalar sequence (a_n), and with the convention that only finitely many a_n are nonzero,

    C^{−1} ‖∑ a_n e_n‖ ≤ ‖∑ ε_n a_n e_{π(n)}‖ ≤ C ‖∑ a_n e_n‖.

Two Schauder bases (e_n) and (f_n) of X are called equivalent if there exist constants 0 < c ≤ C < ∞ such that for every finitely supported scalar sequence (a_n),

    c ‖∑ a_n e_n‖ ≤ ‖∑ a_n f_n‖ ≤ C ‖∑ a_n e_n‖.

Suppose X admits at least two symmetric Schauder bases that are not equivalent to each other. Must X then admit infinitely many symmetric Schauder bases that are pairwise non-equivalent?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is answered in the negative. C. J. Read constructed a Banach space possessing, up to equivalence, exactly two symmetric bases ("A Banach space with, up to equivalence, precisely two symmetric bases", Israel Journal of Mathematics, 1981). Therefore having at least two non-equivalent symmetric bases does not force the existence of infinitely many pairwise non-equivalent symmetric bases.

Consider capital projects (e.g., industrial facility construction) that can be delivered either through (a) conventional stick-built methods, in which fabrication and assembly occur primarily on-site, or (b) modularization, in which significant portions of the facility are pre-fabricated and pre-assembled off-site as transportable modules and then installed on-site. For a fixed project scope of work S, let Q_C(S) and Q_M(S) denote quantitative measures of delivered quality (e.g., rework rate, defect density, conformance to specification) and let R_C(S) and R_M(S) denote quantitative measures of safety performance (e.g., recordable incident rate, lost-time injury rate, total exposure-hours weighted incident frequency) under conventional and modular delivery, respectively.

Develop a rigorous, data-driven framework that:

1. Defines comparable, normalized metrics Q and R applicable to both conventional and modular delivery for an equivalent scope S.
2. Quantifies the differences Δ_Q(S) = Q_M(S) − Q_C(S) and Δ_R(S) = R_M(S) − R_C(S), including statistical confidence intervals, across a representative population of projects.
3. Identifies which specific modularization processes and technologies (e.g., off-site controlled-environment fabrication, automated welding, digital twin–based design verification, advanced logistics planning) contribute to observed improvements, and estimates the marginal contribution of each.
4. Determines the conditions on project type, size, location, and complexity under which modularization yields statistically significant improvements in safety and/or quality compared to conventional execution.

Provide both the methodology and the empirical estimates of the magnitude and direction of the effects.

Consider the low-energy effective action of heterotic string theory in four dimensions, restricted to the gravity–dilaton sector (with the antisymmetric tensor field set to zero), with action
S = ∫ d^4x √(-g) e^{-2φ} ( R + 4 (∂φ)^2 ),
in the "string frame", where g_{μν} is the spacetime metric and φ is the dilaton.

The Schwarzschild solution, written in string-frame coordinates as
ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} dr^2 + r^2 dΩ^2,    φ = 0,
is an exact solution of this action. Applying the Buscher T-duality transformation along the time-like Killing vector ∂_t — i.e., the formal Buscher rules
g_{tt} → 1/g_{tt},   e^{-2φ} → e^{-2φ}/|g_{tt}|,
with the remaining metric components unchanged — produces a new asymptotically flat, static, spherically symmetric solution of the same low-energy effective action which is everywhere massless (ADM mass zero) and carries only "primary" dilaton (scalar) charge Q_d, with the original mass parameter M of the Schwarzschild solution reappearing entirely as the dilaton charge Q_d of the dual configuration. In the low-energy supergravity analysis this transformation preserves the (absence of) unbroken supersymmetries and the asymptotic behavior.

Questions:
(a) Is this time-like Buscher T-duality transformation a legitimate symmetry of the full (non-perturbative) string theory, in the same sense that ordinary space-like Buscher T-duality is?
(b) If it is not a genuine string symmetry, how should the resulting purely scalar, massless solution of the low-energy effective action — which saturates no Bogomol'nyi bound involving the mass while still being an exact solution — be physically interpreted within string theory?

representations.normalized: Consider the universe modeled as a large collection of interacting particles (objects/molecules) whose dynamics are governed by time-reversible microscopic laws, and which on macroscopic scales is observed to be expanding (a cosmological arrow of time). Suppose that at some instant the velocity of every particle in the universe is simultaneously reversed (i.e., the state (x_i, v_i) is replaced by (x_i, -v_i) for every particle i), while all positions are kept fixed. Determine whether, under the resulting dynamics, the universe would continue to expand, or whether instead the macroscopic expansion would reverse into a contraction. Equivalently: does the cosmological arrow of time (expansion versus contraction of the universe) persist under simultaneous reversal of all microscopic velocities, in the way that chaotic/mixing dynamics is believed to make the thermodynamic arrow of time persist under such reversal?

Let $\ell_2$ denote the separable real Hilbert space of square-summable sequences $x=(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ with norm $\|x\|_2=\big(\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n^2\big)^{1/2}$ and the induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2$. A map $f:(M,d_M)\to(N,d_N)$ between metric spaces is a uniform homeomorphism if it is a bijection and both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are uniformly continuous. A subset $B\subseteq\ell_2$ is bounded if $\sup_{x\in B}\|x\|_2<\infty$.

Question: Does there exist a bounded subset $B\subseteq\ell_2$ such that $\ell_2$ is uniformly homeomorphic to $B$ (with the metric inherited from $\ell_2$)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

A theorem of Aharoni–Maurey–Mityagin shows that $\ell_p$ for $2<p<\infty$ is not uniformly homeomorphic to any bounded subset of itself, answering negatively the analogous question for those spaces. However, the case of $\ell_2$ specifically (which embeds linearly into $L_0$ and so is not excluded by that criterion) does not appear to be settled by the sources found, and the question is commonly listed as open in the Banach-space-theory problem literature.

Consider the construction industry as an organizational sector that adopts information technologies (IT) to support distributed, collaborative work carried out by virtual teams (groups whose members coordinate primarily through digital communication and collaboration platforms rather than co-located meetings). Define a measurable index of IT adoption (for example, penetration of cloud-based project management tools, building information modeling platforms, real-time data sharing systems, and remote collaboration software) for a given industry, and a measurable index of virtual team performance (for example, on-time delivery, defect rates, communication latency, and member satisfaction). Address the following:

(a) Determine whether, by these measures, the construction industry exhibits a statistically significant lag in IT adoption relative to a chosen benchmark set of comparison industries (e.g., manufacturing, finance, software, healthcare).

(b) If such a lag exists, quantify the causal or correlational effect of this lag on virtual team performance within construction firms, controlling for confounders such as project size, geographic distribution, and workforce demographics.

(c) Identify and characterize the IT-use patterns and collaboration behaviors of the next generation of construction-industry workers (those entering the workforce as digital natives), and propose a framework specifying which of these patterns, if systematically adopted, would maximize the performance of virtual teams in the construction industry.

Consider N = 1, four-dimensional supergravity, whose bosonic sector coincides with pure Einstein gravity. The only static, asymptotically flat, spherically symmetric black-hole solution of the bosonic equations of motion is the Schwarzschild solution, parametrized by a single real mass parameter M ∈ ℝ; for M > 0 it describes a black hole, for M = 0 it reduces to Minkowski space, and for M < 0 it contains a naked singularity. The Bogomol'nyi/positivity bound in this theory asserts M ≥ 0. One way to derive this bound is by a Nester-type spinorial construction, which requires imposing suitable asymptotic boundary conditions and dominant-energy-type conditions. An alternative route is to associate the classical Schwarzschild solution with a genuine quantum state |ψ_M⟩ in the Hilbert space of quantum N = 1, d = 4 supergravity, such that ⟨ψ_M|Ĥ|ψ_M⟩ = M, and to derive M ≥ 0 directly from the positivity of the supercharge algebra {Q, Q†} ≥ 0 acting on this state.

Problem: Establish whether, within N = 1, d = 4 supergravity, the classical Schwarzschild black-hole solution can be consistently identified with such a quantum state of the quantum supergravity theory in a way that yields the positivity bound M ≥ 0 as a consequence of the quantum theory itself (in particular, of the supersymmetry algebra), without invoking classical energy or boundary conditions. Equivalently, prove or disprove the existence of a quantum supergravity state corresponding to the Schwarzschild geometry from which M ≥ 0 follows by quantum-mechanical positivity arguments.

No definitive construction or no-go result for such a quantum-state identification was located.

Resolve the paradox of the plankton by constructing a mathematically rigorous and physically realistic dynamical model that exhibits the following features:

(a) The model describes a population of N ≫ 1 phytoplankton species with densities u_i(x,t), i = 1,...,N, evolving in a bounded fluid domain Ω ⊂ R^d (d = 2 or 3) carrying an incompressible turbulent (or chaotic) velocity field v(x,t) with ∇·v = 0.

(b) The species compete for a small number k ≪ N of limiting nutrient resources c_j(x,t), j = 1,...,k, whose dynamics include diffusion, advection by v, consumption by the species, and an external supply.

(c) The coupled equations take the general advection–reaction–diffusion form
    ∂_t u_i + v·∇u_i = D_i Δu_i + u_i F_i(c_1,...,c_k) − m_i u_i,
    ∂_t c_j + v·∇c_j = D_j' Δc_j + S_j(x,t) − Σ_i α_{ij} u_i F_i(c_1,...,c_k),
with biologically meaningful growth functions F_i (e.g., Monod kinetics) and constants D_i, D_j', m_i, α_{ij} > 0.

(d) In the well-mixed (spatially homogeneous) limit, the model reduces to a competition system for which the classical competitive exclusion principle holds: at most k species persist at equilibrium.

(e) For the full spatially extended model with a generic chaotic/turbulent advection field v, prove that there exist parameter regimes in which a number of species ≫ k coexist for all time in the sense of persistence (e.g., liminf_{t→∞} ∫_Ω u_i dx > 0 for every i), and characterize the mechanism (e.g., chaotic mixing, filamental nonequilibrium structures, oscillatory or chaotic attractors) responsible for this coexistence.

The problem is to exhibit such a model, give a rigorous proof of long-term coexistence of arbitrarily many species under only k ≪ N limiting nutrients, and show that the explanation is both mathematically consistent and physically adequate for plankton communities in turbulent oceanic environments.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The paradox of the plankton remains an active and unresolved problem. Numerous partial mechanisms have been proposed since Hutchinson (1961), including chaotic competition dynamics (Huisman–Weissing), spatial heterogeneity, mesoscale turbulence, "kill-the-winner" viral dynamics, and stochastic effects. No single mathematically and physically complete model has been accepted as the definitive resolution, and ecologists continue to propose new solutions, indicating the problem is still open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The question is a longstanding problem in nonseparable Banach space theory. Surveys and works by Argyros–Mercourakis, Kalenda, and Fabian–Godefroy–Montesinos–Zizler discuss closely related classes (WLD, σ-Asplund generated, Lindelöf Σ in weak topology), and counterexamples are known showing that subspaces of WCG need not be WCG and that some WCD spaces are not subspaces of any WCG space. However, the search did not locate a definitive resolution (positive or negative) of the precise question as stated for Banach spaces that are Lindelöf in their weak topology, so its current status is reported as unknown.

Consider a large capital project involving multiple stakeholders: Suppliers (who provide equipment, components, and associated technical data and documentation), a design Contractor, a construction Contractor, a commissioning Contractor, and an Owner team. Each Supplier produces a stream of structured and unstructured artifacts (e.g., specifications, datasheets, drawings, certificates, test reports, operation and maintenance manuals, change notices) that must be delivered to the appropriate recipients at the right time and in a usable form to support downstream design, procurement, construction, commissioning, and operations.

Formulate and analyze a methodology — comprising data models, exchange protocols, governance rules, and verification procedures — that ensures the accurate and timely transfer of all Supplier-originated data and documentation to the design, construction, and commissioning Contractors and to the Owner team. The methodology should address at least the following:

1. A precise specification of the data and documentation items that must be transferred, including required attributes, formats, and acceptance criteria.
2. A timing/scheduling model that links each item to milestones in the design, construction, and commissioning workflows, and that quantifies "timeliness" via measurable service-level criteria.
3. A correctness/accuracy model, including validation, version control, and traceability of revisions across organizational boundaries.
4. An efficiency criterion (e.g., minimizing rework, manual re-keying, latency, or total cost of information handover) under which candidate approaches can be compared.
5. A demonstration that the proposed approach is superior, with respect to the chosen criteria, to current standard practice for Supplier data handover in large engineering projects.

Identify the most efficient and innovative such approaches, and characterize the conditions under which they are optimal.
