representations.normalized: Design a translatable standard code of accounts for the construction industry that enables consistent measurement and reporting of productivity across projects, organizations, and regions. Specifically: (i) define a hierarchical taxonomy of cost and work-activity account categories whose definitions are unambiguous and translatable between different accounting systems and languages; (ii) specify mapping rules (bijective where possible, otherwise many-to-one with documented aggregation) between this taxonomy and existing common industry coding systems; (iii) define quantitative productivity metrics (e.g., installed quantity per work-hour) attached to each leaf-level account so that data collected under different native systems can be normalized and aggregated; and (iv) prove or demonstrate that, under the proposed mapping, productivity values computed from heterogeneous source codings are invariant (within a stated tolerance) when re-expressed in the standard code. Provide criteria under which the standard is complete (covers all construction work types), consistent (no overlapping definitions), and minimal (no redundant categories).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as an industry-level research and standardization goal rather than a settled mathematical theorem. No widely adopted, fully translatable standard code of accounts achieving uniform construction productivity measurement appears to exist; efforts such as the Construction Industry Institute (CII) benchmarking program and ISO/AACE-related coding standards address parts of the issue but do not provide a universally accepted, translatable solution. The problem is therefore treated as open.

Significant progress has been made, especially at the minimal-tension point k=1 with pure NS-NS flux, where the worldsheet theory on AdS_3 × S^3 × T^4 has been shown to be exactly dual to the symmetric orbifold Sym^N(T^4), with tree-level n-point correlators matched via a localization onto holomorphic covering maps (Eberhardt–Gaberdiel–Gopakumar and follow-ups, including the 2024 "Solving AdS_3 string theory at minimal tension: tree-level correlators"). However, an exact formulation and correlator-level match for general level k and for mixed/pure R-R flux backgrounds remains open.

representations.original: Let $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ denote the Riemann zeta function for $\mathrm{Re}(s) > 1$. Determine whether $\zeta(5) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^5}$ is irrational, i.e., prove or disprove that $\zeta(5) \notin \mathbb{Q}$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The irrationality of ζ(5) remains an open problem. Apéry (1978) proved ζ(3) is irrational, and Ball–Rivoal (2001) showed infinitely many odd zeta values are irrational. Zudilin (2001) proved at least one of ζ(5), ζ(7), ζ(9), ζ(11) is irrational, but no individual odd zeta value beyond ζ(3) has been proven irrational.

A norm $\|\cdot\|$ on a real Banach space $X$ is called strictly convex (or rotund) if for all $x,y \in X$ with $\|x\|=\|y\|=1$ and $x\neq y$, one has $\left\|\tfrac{x+y}{2}\right\| < 1$; equivalently, the unit sphere of $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ contains no nontrivial line segment. Two norms $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ on $X$ are equivalent if there exist constants $0 < c \le C < \infty$ such that $c\|x\|_1 \le \|x\|_2 \le C\|x\|_1$ for every $x \in X$. A Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ is said to admit an equivalent strictly convex norm if there exists a strictly convex norm on $X$ equivalent to $\|\cdot\|$.

Provide an intrinsic characterization (for example, of topological, structural, or set-theoretic nature) of the class of Banach spaces $X$ that admit an equivalent strictly convex norm.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of finding a general intrinsic characterization of Banach spaces admitting an equivalent strictly convex norm remains open. Partial results are known: every separable Banach space admits such a renorming (Clarkson/Day), while Haydon constructed scattered compacta $K$ such that $C(K)$ fails to be strictly convex renormable. Topological characterizations in special settings (e.g., for $C(K)^*$ over scattered $K$) have been obtained by Smith, Orihuela, Troyanski and others, but no general checkable criterion is known, and recent work (e.g., 2022–2024 arXiv papers on strictly convex renormings and the diameter-2 property) continues to investigate the question.

Consider a population of construction firms that execute large capital projects (e.g., industrial facilities, infrastructure, and commercial buildings). Suppose that emerging and future robotics technologies (autonomous earthmoving equipment, bricklaying and rebar-tying robots, exoskeletons, drones for surveying and inspection, robotic welders, 3D-printing systems, mobile manipulation platforms, etc.) can in principle be deployed at construction sites. Develop a framework, supported by quantitative or systematic qualitative analysis, that answers the following two questions:

(a) Preparation and implementation. Determine concrete strategies, organizational processes, workforce training programs, safety protocols, procurement practices, and project-delivery models by which construction firms can prepare for and successfully implement current and future robotics technologies on their projects. The framework should specify (i) criteria for selecting which tasks and projects are suitable candidates for robotic execution, (ii) metrics (e.g., productivity, cost, schedule, safety, quality) for evaluating implementation outcomes, and (iii) a staged adoption roadmap with measurable milestones.

(b) Influence on technology development. Determine effective mechanisms by which construction firms (acting individually or as a consortium) can shape the development trajectory of robotics technologies so that the resulting products match their particular operational needs. The framework should specify (i) channels for communicating end-user requirements to robotics developers, (ii) collaborative R&D or pilot-testing structures, (iii) standards and interoperability requirements that should be advocated, and (iv) procurement and investment levers that incentivize developers to address industry-specific constraints.

The problem is to construct, justify, and validate such a framework, including any underlying mathematical models (e.g., technology adoption diffusion models, cost-benefit and real-options analyses, multi-criteria decision analysis, or game-theoretic models of buyer–developer interaction) that support the recommendations.

Consider the Wess–Zumino–Witten model based on the non-compact group SU(1,1) (equivalently SL(2,R)), whose chiral algebra is the affine current algebra sl(2,R)_k at level k. The unitary representations of the global sl(2,R) algebra include: (i) the highest- and lowest-weight discrete series D_j^± (with j a real Casimir parameter), and (ii) the principal and supplementary continuous series C_j^α (parameterized by j = 1/2 + is, s ∈ R, and a real number α ∈ [0,1)). All these global representations are infinite-dimensional, and the corresponding affine modules have infinite degeneracy at every excitation level, so the naive trace

χ(τ, ν) = Tr( q^{L_0 − c/24} z^{J_0^3} ),  q = e^{2πiτ}, z = e^{2πiν},

is divergent. Moreover, no closed character formula is available for the affine modules built on the continuous-series representations.

Problem. Give a precise definition of characters (or suitable partition-function building blocks) for the affine SU(1,1) modules — including in particular those based on the continuous series — such that:

(a) the resulting objects are well-defined (after a specified regularization or distributional interpretation),
(b) they admit explicit formulas reproducing the known character formulas for the discrete series in an appropriate limit,
(c) they transform in a controlled way under the modular group SL(2,Z), and
(d) they combine into a modular-invariant one-loop torus partition function of the SU(1,1) WZW model consistent with unitarity of the underlying conformal field theory.

Determine such characters explicitly, prove their modular transformation properties, and exhibit a modular-invariant partition function built from them.

For positive integers $s_1,\dots,s_d$ and signs $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_d\in\{+1,-1\}$, define the alternating multiple zeta value
$$\zeta(\bar s_1^{\,\varepsilon_1},\dots,\bar s_d^{\,\varepsilon_d}) \;=\; \sum_{k_1>k_2>\cdots>k_d\ge 1}\;\prod_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\varepsilon_j^{\,k_j}}{k_j^{s_j}},$$
where an overline on an argument $s_j$ indicates $\varepsilon_j=-1$ and absence of an overline indicates $\varepsilon_j=+1$. For a finite string $w$ of (possibly barred) positive integers, let $w^n$ denote the concatenation of $n$ copies of $w$, with $w^0$ the empty string and $\zeta(\emptyset):=1$.

Define
$$A(z) \;=\; \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^{n}\,\zeta(\{\bar 1\}^{n}),$$
where $\{\bar 1\}^{n}$ denotes the string of $n$ copies of $\bar 1$.

Prove or disprove: for every complex number $t$ (in the domain of convergence, with the identity holding as an identity of formal/analytic power series),
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\Bigl[\,t^{2n}\,\zeta(\{\bar 1,1\}^{n}) \;+\; t^{2n+1}\,\zeta(\bar 1,\{\bar 1,1\}^{n})\Bigr] \;=\; A\!\left(\frac{t}{1-i}\right)\,A\!\left(\frac{t}{1+i}\right),$$
where $i=\sqrt{-1}$.

Consider a workplace safety or industrial operations setting in which low-frequency, high-impact adverse events (such as fatalities and near-fatalities) occur as a rare point process in time. Let $\{E_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ denote the sequence of such severe events, and let $\{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ be a high-dimensional stream of observable operational, behavioral, and environmental measurements (e.g., near-miss reports, equipment readings, audit findings, behavioral observations, maintenance logs).

(a) Determine whether there exist precursors or leading indicators: that is, measurable functionals $f(X_{t-\tau:t})$ of the recent history of $X$ on some lead time $\tau > 0$ such that the conditional probability $\Pr(E_{t+h} = 1 \mid f(X_{t-\tau:t}))$ is significantly elevated compared to the baseline rate $\Pr(E_{t+h}=1)$, for a useful prediction horizon $h>0$.

(b) If such precursors exist, characterize them explicitly — i.e., identify the families of statistics, signal patterns, or event types in $X$ that carry predictive information about $E$.

(c) Provide a methodology to (i) identify candidate precursors from historical data despite the severe class imbalance caused by the rarity of $E$, (ii) statistically validate their predictive power (e.g., via appropriate hypothesis tests, calibration, and out-of-sample performance metrics suitable for highly imbalanced rare-event prediction), and (iii) operationally utilize them to design interventions that demonstrably reduce $\Pr(E_{t+h}=1)$.

Formally, address the existence, identification, statistical analysis, and decision-theoretic use of leading indicators for predicting and preventing such rare high-severity events.

Consider a project modeled as a finite collection of tasks T = {t_1, ..., t_n}, each task t_i endowed with a planned start time s_i, planned duration d_i, planned cost c_i, and a set of measurable quality attributes q_i ∈ R^k. Over time, actual realized values (s_i*, d_i*, c_i*, q_i*) are observed, possibly with noise and with partial completion fractions p_i(τ) ∈ [0,1] at observation time τ. Develop a rigorous quantitative framework for assessing project progress and performance that:

(a) Defines a set of scalar or vector-valued indicators I_1, ..., I_m (functions of the observed data up to time τ and of the planned data) that summarize cost performance, schedule performance, scope/quality performance, and risk exposure, generalizing classical earned-value metrics such as CPI = EV/AC and SPI = EV/PV.

(b) Establishes formal statistical or decision-theoretic properties of these indicators (e.g., unbiasedness, consistency, predictive validity for project outcomes, robustness to reporting noise, and identifiability of the underlying performance state).

(c) Specifies how the historical record {(planned, actual)} across many completed projects can be aggregated to produce calibrated forecasts and improvement recommendations for future projects, with explicit error bounds.

Determine which choice of indicators is provably most informative — in a precisely formulated sense (for example, maximizing mutual information with final project outcome, minimizing expected forecast error, or being a sufficient statistic for the underlying performance parameters) — among the class of indicators computable from the available task-level data.

Consider bosonic string theory on the group manifold SU(1,1) ≅ SL(2,ℝ) (covering AdS₃) described by the SL(2,ℝ) WZW model at level k with k < −2. The affine SL(2,ℝ) current algebra admits, among its unitary representations, the discrete lowest-weight representations D⁻(j) labeled by a real spin parameter j, on which the Casimir takes the value −j(j−1) and which contain a primary annihilated by the lowering modes with J₀³ eigenvalue j. Physical string states are obtained by imposing the Virasoro constraints (L_n − δ_{n,0})|phys⟩ = 0 (n ≥ 0) on the tensor product of this current-algebra module with an internal unitary CFT of appropriate central charge so that the total Virasoro central charge equals 26.

Question: For the discrete representations D⁻(j), is the spin restriction
    k/2 ≤ j < 0
both necessary and sufficient to ensure that the space of Virasoro-physical states contains no negative-norm (ghost) states? Equivalently, can one establish a no-ghost theorem, valid at every level k < −2, asserting that under the above spin bound (and its analogue for D⁺(j)) the physical Hilbert space of the SL(2,ℝ) WZW string is positive-definite?

Consider bosonic string theory on the group manifold SU(1,1) ≅ SL(2,ℝ) (covering AdS₃) described by the SL(2,ℝ) WZW model at level k with k < −2. The affine SL(2,ℝ) current algebra admits, among its unitary representations, the discrete lowest-weight representations D⁻(j) labeled by a real spin parameter j, on which the Casimir takes the value −j(j−1) and which contain a primary annihilated by the lowering modes with J₀³ eigenvalue j. Physical string states are obtained by imposing the Virasoro constraints (L_n − δ_{n,0})|phys⟩ = 0 (n ≥ 0) on the tensor product of this current-algebra module with an internal unitary CFT of appropriate central charge so that the total Virasoro central charge equals 26.

Question: For the discrete representations D⁻(j), is the spin restriction
    k/2 ≤ j < 0
both necessary and sufficient to ensure that the space of Virasoro-physical states contains no negative-norm (ghost) states? Equivalently, can one establish a no-ghost theorem, valid at every level k < −2, asserting that under the above spin bound (and its analogue for D⁺(j)) the physical Hilbert space of the SL(2,ℝ) WZW string is positive-definite?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Maldacena and Ooguri (hep-th/0001053, 2000; J. Math. Phys. 42 (2001) 2929) proved a no-ghost theorem for bosonic string theory on AdS₃/SL(2,ℝ) at all levels k > 2 (in their conventions, equivalently k < −2 in the conventions used here), showing that the spin bound k/2 < j < 0 (together with the analogous bound for D⁺(j) and the inclusion of spectrally flowed sectors) is precisely the condition that yields a ghost-free physical spectrum. Earlier partial results (Evans–Gaberdiel–Perry, Hwang) proved the theorem under the same bound for the unflowed sectors. The problem is therefore considered solved.

Let X be a topological space. An open cover U of X is called an ω-cover if X is not a member of U and for every finite subset F ⊆ X there exists U ∈ U with F ⊆ U. An infinite open cover {U_n : n ∈ ℕ} of X is called a γ-cover if every point x ∈ X belongs to all but finitely many of the sets U_n.

For a family U of subsets of X, define L(U) to be the smallest family containing U that is closed under the operation of taking lim inf of sequences, where for a sequence (A_n) of subsets of X one sets liminf_n A_n = ⋃_{n} ⋂_{k ≥ n} A_k.

Call X a δ-set if for every open ω-cover U of X one has X ∈ L(U). Call X a γ-set if every open ω-cover of X contains a countably infinite subfamily that is a γ-cover of X (equivalently, every open ω-cover has an infinite subcover such that each point of X lies in all but finitely many members).

Since any γ-cover {U_n} satisfies X = liminf_n U_n, the γ-property implies the δ-property.

Question: Is the δ-property equivalent to the γ-property? That is, must every δ-set be a γ-set?

Let f: A → A be a smooth area-preserving twist diffeomorphism of the closed annulus A = S^1 × [0,1] (or, equivalently, consider the standard family of area-preserving twist maps depending on a parameter α). For an irrational number α satisfying a Diophantine condition, KAM theory guarantees the existence of an f-invariant essential closed curve on which the dynamics is smoothly conjugate to the rigid rotation by α. Define
   U_α = the union of all f-invariant essential closed curves on which f is smoothly conjugate to rotation by α-Diophantine rotation numbers (the "KAM set"),
viewed as a subset of A, and let ∂U_α be its topological boundary in A.

Question: Is every boundary point x ∈ ∂U_α accessible both from inside U_α and from the complement A \ U_α? That is, for each x ∈ ∂U_α, do there exist continuous arcs γ_1: [0,1] → A and γ_2: [0,1] → A with γ_1(1) = γ_2(1) = x, γ_1([0,1)) ⊂ U_α, and γ_2([0,1)) ⊂ A \ U_α?

Consider the use of digital project models on construction projects, including three-dimensional computer-aided design (3D CAD), building information modeling (BIM), and Virtual Design and Construction (VDC). 3D CAD refers to digital three-dimensional geometric representations of project components; BIM refers to a coordinated, object-based digital representation of a built asset together with semantic data about its components, relationships, and lifecycle attributes; VDC refers to the integrated use of multidisciplinary performance models of design–construction projects, including the product, the work processes, and the organization, to support explicit, public business objectives.

(a) Identify and justify the near-term needs (within a three- to five-year horizon) for improved and expanded use of such project models on construction projects, characterizing each need by its scope (technical, process, organizational, contractual, or data/interoperability), the stakeholder roles affected, and measurable outcomes that would indicate the need has been met.

(b) Propose a prioritization framework for the construction industry to rank gaps in development focus across these needs. The framework should specify (i) a set of evaluation criteria (for example, expected impact on cost, schedule, quality, safety, and sustainability; feasibility; cost of implementation; breadth of applicability; and dependencies among gaps), (ii) a method for scoring and weighting these criteria, and (iii) a procedure for producing a defensible ranked list of gaps together with recommended actions.

Consider a construction project that requires the procurement, delivery, and on-site storage of a set of materials and equipment items over a planned schedule horizon. For each item i in a finite set I, let d_i(t) denote the demand (consumption) profile required to keep construction tasks on schedule, let q_i(t) denote the on-site inventory level at time t, let h_i denote the per-unit, per-time-unit inventory carrying cost (covering storage, handling, insurance, deterioration, and capital), let s_i denote a per-delivery setup/transport cost, and let L_i denote the supplier lead time. Let x_i(t) denote the delivery (replenishment) policy, subject to: (i) on-site space, safety, and access constraints; (ii) schedule-driven availability requirements q_i(t) ≥ d_i(t) over the windows when item i must be available; (iii) supplier and logistics constraints; and (iv) uncertainty in demand timing and lead times.

Part A. Formulate a rigorous framework that identifies the optimal structural elements and best practices of a Material Planning process (as a component of Materials Management) for such a project, and provide a precise specification of measurable, documentable benefits B(π) attributable to following a Material Planning policy π (e.g., reductions in expected total cost, schedule delay risk, and waste).

Part B. Formulate the Jobsite Delivery Timing problem as an optimization

   min_{x_i(·)}  E[ Σ_i ∫_0^T ( h_i q_i(t) + s_i · 1{delivery at t} ) dt + penalty terms for shortage and excess ]

subject to the constraints above, and determine whether there exists a delivery timing policy x* (e.g., just-in-time, periodic, or state-dependent) that simultaneously minimizes expected total inventory carrying cost and the probability of stock-out-induced schedule delay. Characterize such policies, prove optimality or near-optimality bounds, and identify conditions under which the optimum is attainable in practice.
